FDA Consumer February 1981 / 1

Consumer Forum Saccharin View Contested 

We at the American Council on Science and 

Health (ACSH) strongly disagree with Commissioner Goyan's characterization of the saccharin safety issue (FDA CONSUMER, June 1980) in which he warns a "young saccharin user" that "prolonged use of saccharin should be avoided, particularly by young people like you" and that "two cans of diet sodas daily is possibly flirting with trouble." 

Dr. Goyan's "worst case" scenario for the young saccharin user presented only one side of the scientific evidence. Take for example, the results of the Canadian rat feeding study publicized in 1977. 

While this study did indeed report a statistically significant excess of bladder tumors in some second generation male rats, it is difficult to relate these findings to human experience. Little or no discussion has appeared in the scientific literature about how well this two-generation study predicts human cancer risk. Further, there have been few comparisons of this type of study with other more traditional animal studies. In fact, other regulatory agencies with responsibility to test chemical cancer hazards do not routinely use two-generation tests in their evaluations. While the Canadian test results may further our understanding of how cancer develops under extreme conditions, ACSH believes it is inappropriate to completely ignore the larger body of evidence showing saccharin's lack of hazard.

The Commissioner's description of the National 

Academy of Sciences evaluation of saccharin and the more recent human studies of artificial sweeteners and bladder cancer also failed to give the whole story. The National Academy of Sciences study group concluded that saccharin is a weak carcinogen in rats and should therefore be regarded as a predicted, but unquantifiable risk to humans. However, the majority of this group did not believe that an immediate ban on saccharin would be a sound regulatory step. Neither did they believe that saccharin should be freely available with no special labeling.

The National Cancer Institute/Food and Drug 

Administration study of bladder cancer and artificial sweeteners found no overall risk to the general population from artificial sweetener use. It did note that some persons who use excessive amounts of artificial sweeteners and those who use artificial sweeteners and also smoke heavily may increase their chances of contracting bladder cancer. However, the study authors noted, "Because of inconsistencies in the patterns observed, the elevations in risk (among subgroups) require cautious interpretation and further analysis" (Lancet, April 19, 1980, P. 840). Your readers might have derived greater benefit if the Commissioner had simply repeated this study's conclusion, which stated: "We conclude that past AS (artificial sweetener) use has had a minimal effect, if any, on bladder cancer rates. We also conclude that the positive associations in this study do not by themselves establish a causal link between AS use and bladder cancer. However, we think it noteworthy that the pattern of positive associations is consistent with experimental data that suggest that artificial sweeteners are weakly carcinogenic when given alone and potentiating when given with other carcinogens." 

The Harvard study of artificial sweeteners, like the National Cancer Institute study, found no overall association between bladder cancer and artificial sweetener use. In explanation of these negative findings the study authors suggested three, not as Dr. Goyan suggested, one, possibilities: 1) artificial sweeteners are not human bladder carcinogens; 2) artificial sweeteners are weak carcinogens whose effects are difficult to measure; and 3) if they are carcinogens, a sufficient amount of time may not have passed to allow scientists to observe their effects. Here again, the evidence for saccharin's health risk is far less conclusive than the 

Commissioner would have us believe. 

The heart of the saccharin safety issue is what significance can, or should, be attached to the term "weak carcinogen." Simply labeling a substance as a weak carcinogen on the basis of a twogeneration rat feeding study tells us little about its cancer risk to people under normal conditions of use. There are quite a few substances that we might reasonably label as weak carcinogens. Sun- 

2/ February 1981 FDA Consumer

light, for instance, is a weak carcinogen because it is partly composed of ultra-violet radiation. Some essential vitamins and nutrients, such as vitamin D and selenium, are also weak carcinogens based on high dose laboratory test results. We might even go so far as to say that mother's milk is weakly carcinogenic because it contains trace amounts of estrogen, a proven animal carcinogen. Thus, it is obvious that we must consider something more than laboratory test evidence in weighing a chemical's health risks. These safety judgments must also include some perspective in relation to other similar hazards around us.

As the Commissioner rightly states in his letter, the decision to use or not use saccharin-sweetened products rests with each consumer. However,

ACSH believes that consumer education is not well served when only part of the story is told. 

Unfortunately, controversies like that raised by saccharin cannot be easily or simply resolved. Matters of food safety, particularly when they involve disputed evidence and widely used substances, are by their nature complex. But unlike the position adopted by Commissioner Goyan and the FDA, ACSH believes that American consumers would prefer to make these decisions for themselves. 

Given a fair and impartial presentation of the facts known about saccharin's safety, we think consumers are fully capable of making their own choice in the market. We hope that in the future, the agency will rely more on science and education than political advocacy. 

We invite consumers who want to read a complete summary of the benefits and risks of saccharin to request ACSH's free report by sending a self-addressed stamped business sized envelope to, American Council on Science and Health, 1995 

Broadway, New York, New York 10023. 

Elizabeth M. Whelan

Executive Director 

American Council on Science and Health 

New York, N.Y.

Caffeine Calculations Questioned 

We wish to correct what we believe is a significant error in Caution Light on Caffeine (FDA 

CONSUMER, October 1980). It was reported that irreversible birth defects were observed in FDA's recent teratology study on laboratory rats at the two highest dose levels of caffeine (80 mg/kg and 

125 mg/kg), the amount of caffeine . . a human might get from drinking 12 to 24 cups of strong coffee a day." In point of fact, the two highest dose levels in the FDA study are equivalent to more than 25 cups and more than 40 cups of coffee per day, respectively. 66 To reach the equivalent of 80 mg/kg dose level, a relatively light person weighing 50 kg would have to consume 4000 mg of caffeine (50 × 80 

4000), representing 47 cups of average strength coffee. Using FDA's highest estimate of the caffeine content in a strong cup of coffee-155 mg- (FDA TALK PAPER, October 9, 1980), 4000 mg is the equivalent of 25.8 cups. And, for the dosing to be equivalent to that experienced by the experimental animals, a person would have to drink those 25 cups all at once.

FDA Consumer / February 1981 / 3

In fact, a woman weighing 60 kg-the average weight in the first trimester of pregnancy-drinking an average cup of coffee (85 mg) would have to drink more than 55 cups of coffee all at once in order to receive a dose of 80 mg/kg. It was only at or above this dose level that irreversible defects (complete or partial absence of toes) were observed. 

We believe that use of the correct calculation casts a different light on the implications of the FDA study. It also serves to emphasize the difficulty inherent in attempting to interpret these types of studies in human terms. 

We recognize, of course, that caffeine may affect people differently. Common sense suggests that a pregnant woman who has questions about her caffeine consumption should consult her physician about that and all aspects of her diet, as part of her normal prenatal care. 

George E. Boecklin President

National Coffee Association of U.S.A., Inc. 

New York, New York

As pointed out in the October issue of this maga zine, Anatomy of a Scientific Study: Rodents, 

Pregnancy, and Distilled Water, the “no effect" level in the caffeine study was 40 milligrams a day for each kilogram of body weight. That means there was no effect on the pregnant rodents that were fed 40 milligrams or less a day. The effect level would be somewhere between 40 and 80 mg/kg. 

There will always be some disagreement on how much caffeine is in a cup of coffee as well as what size the average cup is, as the accompanying article (About Your Caffeine Intake . . .) pointed out in the October issue. As that piece noted, the National 

Coffee Association uses a 5-ounce cup as standard, but average size cups vary by user. Likewise, the amount of caffeine in a cup varies by the strength of the brew, possibly the length of brewing, and other factors. Other studies show that cup sizes range up to nearly 9 ounces, while caffeine content was recorded at almost 200 milligrams in some cases. Taking all these things into consideration, the amount of caffeine fed to the rodents in the experiment that had an effect on offspring may be equal to the average person drinking 12 to 25 cups a day.

However, as has been pointed out by FDA, there is no proof at this time that humans metabolize caffeine in the body in the same way the rodents did in the study. We quite agree with Mr. Boecklin's closing remark that pregnant women should consult their physicians with any questions about caffeine intake and other dietary habits. 

Natural vs. Synthetic Vitamins 

In your September, 1980 issue, page 31, you state: "MYTH: That a natural vitamin in a food is superior to an added or synthetic vitamin . . "FACT: . . . to the body the natural molecules look the same as the synthetic molecules . . ."

While the natural and synthetic forms of many vitamins are identical, this is not true for vitamin E. Natural vitamin E is d-alpha tocopherol. Synthetic vitamin E consists of the following 8 different forms: 

STANDARD NOMENCLATURE COMMON NAME 

2R,4'R,8'R d-Alpha tocopherol 2R,4'S,8'R 2R,4'R.8'S 2R,4'S,8'S 2S,4'R,8'R 2S,4'S,8'R 2S,4'R,8'S 2S,4'S,8'S 

1-Alpha tocopherol

Some of the above 8 forms have never been isolated and tested separately for biological activity, so it is not known if some of them are biologically active. 

What is known is that natural vitamin E, d-alpha tocopherol, has a potency of 1.49 international units of vitamin E per milligram, while synthetic 

4 February 1981 FDA Consumer

vitamin E, the mixture of 8 different forms, has a potency of only 1.10 international units per milligram.

We hope you will be able to correct this "MYTH: FACT:" about natural vitamin E in a fu ture issue of the CONSUMER. 

Gerald G. Wilson

Vice President, Fine Chemicals 

Henkel Corp. 

Minneapolis, Minnesota

The following response was prepared by Glen Shue of the regulatory affairs staff in the Bureau of 

Foods: 

When vitamin E is used as the name for the whole family of tocol and tocotrienol derivatives exhibiting the biological activity of d-alpha-tocopherol, it is not correct to say that the "natural" and "synthetic" forms are identical. However, when vitamin E is considered to be d-alpha-tocopherol, the natural and synthetic forms are identical and, as the September 1980 issue of FDA CONSUMER 

states, they "look the same" to the body. Also, since the vitamin E content on food labels is declared in biological activity expressed in International Units, and one IU of any form of vitamin E is equal, the varying potencies of different forms of vitamin E are of no nutritional consequence in the labeling of vitamin E supplements.

Tampons, TSS, And Medical

Device Law 

How could a common personal hygiene product-sold by the billions and used by millions of women for almost half a century-suddenly be implicated in a serious, mysterious, and sometimes fatal disease? That's what happened with menstrual tampons, which were presumed "safe" until last year when they were found to be associated with toxic shock syndrome. The subsequent scrutiny of toxic shock and tampons piqued the public's interest in how these products-and other medical devices-are sanctioned before being allowed on the market. 

Li ast June, the U.S. Centers for

Disease Control (CDC) reported that a mysterious, newly recognized disease, toxic shock syndrome-afflicting mainly young women during their menstrual periods-was associated with use of tampons. Then, in 

September, CDC and FDA announced that one brand of tampons,

Rely, was associated with a higher risk of the disease than other brands. 

Rely was soon off the market (and

FDA moved to require warning labels for other brands) but the question was raised: Why had Rely been allowed on store shelves in the first place? Many people were surprised that the Government had never required tampons to be tested before they could be sold. 

It is improbable that safety testing would have uncovered an occurrence as rare as toxic shock, which seems to affect only between 3 and 15 out of every 100,000 women of menstruating age per year. But the issue did focus attention on how FDA regulates not only tampons but other medical devices as well.

The law differentiates between drugs which affect the body chemically-and medical devices-which work by other means. The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act generally requires that new drugs be thoroughly tested, to show that they are safe and effective, before they can be sold. 

But, in 1976 when Congress passed the Medical Device Amendments to that law, a more flexible approach was provided for regulating medical devices. 

Prior to the 1976 amendments, FDA had to prove that a hazard existed before it could stop the sale of unsafe medical devices. Nonetheless,

FDA made the most of its weak device muscle, forcing numerous "quack" products off the market. 

But the law was not adequate to deal with the growing number of legitimate medical devices-such as kidney dialysis machines and cardiac pacemakers that were finding wider and wider use as medical technology skyrocketed during the 1950's, '60's, and into the '70's. 

Congress responded to this need with the 1976 Medical Device

Amendments. The amendments were a complex addition to FDA's authority, so complex that they boggled the minds of laymen and lawyers alike.

Former FDA Chief Counsel Richard 

Cooper once said that it would be hard to imagine a more complex set of statutory requirements than those involving food and drugs, but that

FDA Consumer/ February 1981 | 7

with the Medical Device Amendments Congress not only succeeded in imagining them, it actually enacted them. 

Congress felt that the amendments --though complex-provided the flexibility that was needed for regulating an industry as diverse as medical devices. Some 6,300 device firms, with annual sales estimated at $8.3 billion, make and sell products ranging from adhesive strips to blood gas analyzers, from tongue depressors to cancer detection kits.

The law enables FDA to match the degree of regulatory control with a particular product's potential risk. 

This flexibility provides FDA with the balance it needs to walk the fine line of protecting the public health while not unnecessarily impeding innovation in medical technology.

One of the main features of flexibility in the law is the provision that requires FDA to classify each of the 

1,800 types of medical devices into one of three regulatory categories.

The degree of control necessary to assure the safety and effectiveness of a particular type of device determines its category. The three categories are: 

Class I-Devices with the least po tential for harm. These are subject to general controls, with the manufacturer required to register with FDA and comply with Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP's) regulations set by the Agency. Class I devices in clude tongue depressors, adhesive bandages, hospital beds, and hot water bottles.

Class II-These devices must measure up to specified performance standards before they can be marketed. The standards set specifications for the construction, components, ingredients, and other properties of the device that have a bearing on how safely and effectively it will perform. The electrocardiograph (EKG) machine is an example of a device that is in Class II.

When a performance standard is set for EKG machines, it will include, among other things, the degree of accuracy that a unit must attain in measuring the beat of a patient's heart. Other Class II devices include hearing aids, incubators for newborn babies, ultrasound equipment, and a variety of laboratory testing kits.

Class III-These present the great est potential for intensifying or causing illness or injury. These are usually life-supporting, or are implanted in the body for more than 30 days.

Included in the category are pacemakers (which are both life-supporting and implanted), intrauterine devices for contraception (IUD's), and intraocular lenses (plastic devices surgically implanted in the eye to replace a damaged natural lens). Class

III devices must be tested in laboratory, animal, and human experiments, and shown to be safe and effective before they can be placed on the market. 

FDA expects that when it has finished classifying the 1,800 types of devices that were on the market when the device law went into effect, about 100 will be in Class III, about 

1,200 in Class II, and the remainder in Class I. To assist it with this massive "sorting" process, FDA relies heavily on the recommendations of advisory committees of non-Government experts. Thus far, FDA has issued final rules classifying about onethird of the 1,800 types of devices.

The job should be completed by the middle of next year. 

Congress provided a "grandfather clause" for devices that were on the market at the time the amendments went into effect in May 1976. Manu facturers of pre-amendment Class III 

devices are given at least 30 months after the products have been classified to complete any necessary studies. The products may remain on the market during that 30-month period.

Pre-amendment Class II devices may remain on the market until performance standards are set for them. 

It is this "grandfather clause" that came into play with tampons. All brands of tampons currently being sold as well as Rely-have been on the market since before May 1976.

FDA placed tampons in Class II in 

February 1980. 

To improve the monitoring of problems associated with the use of medical devices, FDA, in November, proposed a regulation that would require manufacturers to promptly notify FDA of any problems with the products. It is another facet of the flexible approach to device regulation: To walk the fine line of protecting the public from unsafe or ineffective products while not unnecessarily impeding development of new technology that can benefit the public. 

Bill Rados is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

FDA Consumer February 1981 / 9

Balding Is Forever, Experts Say 

Seven medical scientists, including two dermatologists—all members of an advisory panel to FDA-have concluded that hair-growth products that are sold over the counter don't work. In its report, the panel said that hair growth is cyclical, not continuous. The growth pattern also reverses, leaving a full head of hair nothing but a memory. 

by Richard C. Thompson 

It w will come as no surprise to the League of Bald- Headed Men or candidates for this fraternity that products claiming to grow hair or prevent hair loss are not effective. 

None of the products work, says the panel of medical scientists and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) should take action to remove them from the market as being misbranded.

The Bald-Headed League-a club based in Dunn, N.C.-has probably known this all along. Its 4,000 members (among them, former President Ford, Senator Henry 

Jackson, and actors Telly Savalas and Phil Silvers) have, as the League says, "learned to cultivate a sense of pride in their condition.' 

FDA published in the FEDERAL Register last No vember the panel's proposal to remove such hair products from the market. The Agency is now looking over the comment it has received before making a final decision. 

Products for hair growth and prevention of hair lossoften sold through the mail or through barber and beauty shops are considered legally to be over-the-counter (OTC) drug products that FDA must regulate. They are drug products because their manufacturers claim they have a biological effect—they can cause hair to grow. 

They are OTC because they are available without a doctor's prescription. 

FDA, for the past 9 years, has been studying the safety and effectiveness of ingredients in some 300,000 OTC products, using expert advisory panels of medical scientists from throughout the United States for each group of products under study. Many ingredients have been found to be unsafe or not effective, and products with such ingredients have been changed by their makers or taken off the market.

The hair-growth and hair-loss-prevention products were scrutinized by the OTC Advisory Review Panel on Miscellaneous External Drug Products. The seven voting panel members-all medical scientists, including two dermatologists-reviewed the medical literature on the hair product ingredients. They also looked at product labels and instructions, and at data submitted by manufacturers and other interested people.

The panel's action placed the ingredients in OTC Category II, which covers unsafe, not effective, and misbranded drugs.

The panel did find the ingredients safe for external use when used as specified. But again, they could not do what was claimed for them; they could not grow hair or prevent hair loss.

Only three manufacturers submitted information to the panel when FDA announced in the FEDERAL REGISTER 

that hair products would be reviewed. 

One manufacturer-located in Matawan, N.J.—offered a hair and scalp treatment for preventing hair loss, claiming that its several ingredients “activated cellular respiration of the scalp, stimulated blood circulation, and strengthened hair roots." This came to the panel as a formula, with no data and no actual product. A search of the scientific literature found nothing to support the manufacturer's claims. 

A second manufacturer-in Brooklyn, N.Y.-offered a laboratory report on a "hair stimulant and grower" that featured lanolin, coconut oil, and similar ingredients, but with no data on the effectiveness of these ingredients, singly or in combination. Again, the scientific literature showed no evidence of their usefulness. 

The third manufacturer-in Houston, Tex.-supplied data on a treatment series of scalp conditioner, scalp cleanser, shampoo, hair-growth stimulator, and antiseptic dressing. This was intended to treat "sebum hair loss,' supposedly caused by sebum (a naturally occurring chemical compound in human skin) destruction of the hair follicle. The data, however, was from the early 1950's on studies done with rats, and the sebum theory of hair loss had been long ago abandoned by most medical scientists. 

This treatment included a hormone ingredient (estradiol or estrogen) that the panel found might involve some risk. In a form strong enough to reduce sebum production-if that is the goal-the easily absorbed estrogen can cause male breast enlargement and other feminizing traits. In a weaker, but safer dose, it does not reduce the sebum production. Therefore, the panel concluded, it serves no purpose in a hair-treatment product. 

In all, there were 18 labeled ingredients in the marketed hair products. Six of these were classified by the panel as "active." They were: ascorbic acid, benzoic (misspelled on one label as "benzoaic") acid, estradiol (the hormone), lanolin, tetracaine hydrochloride, and 

10 February 1981 / FDA Consumer

wheat germ oil (for vitamin E and thiamine). But their action, the panel decided after studying the data, did not lead to hair growth or prevent hair loss.

In addition to looking at labeled ingredients, the panel members found in the medical literature that amino acids, essential oils, proteins, tar oil, and vitamins have historically been used in hair-growth and hair-loss prevention products. But clinical studies of these agents, as well as their known chemical and biochemical actions, convinced the panel that they could have no effect on hair growth or hair loss, and they do not belong in OTC hair drug products. 

Did the panel report address every ingredient used in

OTC products to prevent hair loss or stimulate hair growth? Likely not. Because of the size and complexity of the marketplace, this would be an impossible task for any category of products. But if the panel's proposed regulation is published as a final order, there is little chance that products and ingredients not considered by the panel might slip through the regulatory cracks. The proposed regulation is drafted to apply to any OTC drug product that is labeled, represented, or promoted for use as a hair grower or hair-loss prevention agent.

In its report, the panel gives a thoughtful summation of the hair growth and hair-loss cycle on the human head and scalp, which is what these products claim to treat. 

Hair growth, the report says, is cyclical, not continuous. A hair follicle (the growing site) grows a hair for a specific period of time. The hair then enters a brief transition stage, and finally a longer resting stage. The resting hair sits in the follicle several months before being shed. 

The cycle then repeats, with a new hair growing in the follicle site.

Several factors affect hair growth, including the rate and duration of growth and the numbers of hairs that at a given time are in the growing stage. For human scalp hairs, this is about 85 percent. Scalp hairs grow for 3 to 5 years, going in and out of their growing and resting stages before they are finally shed. Therefore, if they are not cut they would have a much longer final length than, say, an eyebrow hair, which grows for only 6 months before it is shed.

Hormones produced by the body, but not those applied externally, affect the diameter and pigmentation of hair and the entire hair cycle. This is most apparent at puberty in the male, when fine, short (vellus) beard hairs, pale and with no pigment, become coarse, long, pigmented terminal hairs.

This process is reversed in the adult male who has inherited the gene for male-pattern baldness (alopecia).

Here, the scalp hair that started out coarse becomes fine, short, vellus hair as the hairline gradually recedes. 

In the adult male the hairline is likely to be “M”shaped. In women and children it is usually straight across. If the male has inherited the gene for baldness, the point of the "M" will gradually recede, and the crown hair will begin to thin out. Eventually the thinning crown and the receding point connect, and all that remains is a horseshoe pattern and a memory. 

This slow loss of hair is caused by the growth cycles becoming shorter and shorter, producing finer (now vellus) hair. Finally for a particular hair the growth cycle ends completely.

Thinning of hair can occur in women who have inherited the gene for pattern loss, but thinning is never as great as it is in men.

Some physical conditions can cause diffuse loss of hair in both men and women. These include drug therapy, iron deficiency, fever, radiation, hormonal thyroid imbalance, several illnesses, and crash dieting and starvation. 

There is also sometimes a hair loss in women following childbirth as the hormonal balance suddenly shifts, causing scalp hairs to go quickly from a growing to a resting stage and then being shed.

Hair loss from these conditions is usually temporary. 

From male-pattern baldness it is not, and products offered for such baldness claim to treat a condition that is untreatable by OTC drugs.

There are products, the panel noted, that have a cosmetic effect on hair that cling to the hair shaft and make it seem thicker. But this is a not a drug action, and hair growth is not involved.

The panel report points out that nothing that's done to the hair shaft, once it emerges from the scalp, will influence hair growth. Whatever might affect growth must work on the hair root. Permanent waving, shaving, bleaching, and other trauma to the hair shaft does not affect the hair itself as long as the root is not involved. 

Tight ponytails and braids or excessive teasing, however, can tug at the root and follicle and affect hair growth. 

In summary, the panel concluded that "all claimed hair-grower and hair-loss-prevention ingredients reviewed are not effective for OTC external use. 99 Now, like the hair they have claimed to treat, these products too are receding.

Richard C. Thompson is a member of FDA's public affairs staff. 

12 February 1981 FDA Consumer

Relief For Warts; None For Nail Biters 

There's

There's good news for those afflicted with Verruca vulgaris, but not very happy tidings for victims of onychophagia and onychocryptosis, according to the Advisory Panel on 

Miscellaneous External Drug Prod ucts.

For those who are not in the bi ological sciences Verruca vulgaris is the common wart, and the panel found one ingredient in over-thecounter (OTC) drugs that is safe and effective for removing it. 

On the other hand, those who suffer from onychophagia (the morbid habit of biting the nails) and onychocryptosis (ingrown toenails) are out of luck. The panel found nothing that will break the biting habit or relieve the discomfort of ingrowing toenails.

The panel's reports were published by FDA in the October 3 and Octo ber 17, 1980, issues of the FEDERAL

REGISTER. Additionally, the panel had this to say:

There are a number of warts caused by viruses. Besides the common wart, there are juvenile warts, plantar warts, and genital warts. A patient may have one or hundreds. Cures for warts abound in folk remedies, but as far as medical drugs are concerned, the expert panel found that only one out of the 10 ingredients studied is safe and effective as a wart remover. This ingredient is salicylic acid.

In addition, the panel classed five ingredients as not safe and effective: benzocaine, camphor, castor oil, iodine, and menthol. Four others need further testing: acetic acid (glacial), ascorbic acid, calcium pantothenate, and lactic acid. 

Labels on wart remedies may claim that they are for removal of common 

warts or plantar warts, the panel said.

But the labels must contain warnings, such as "Do not use if you are a diabetic or have poor blood circulation,' "Do not use on moles, birthmarks, unusual warts with hair growing from them, genital warts, or warts on the face or mucous membranes." The labels also should advise users of wart medicine to see a doctor if the wart doesn't improve in 12 weeks. 

One thing the labels can't say, according to the expert panel, is that the medicine provides "quick," "painless," or "effective" removal of the wart. Wart removal may not be quick and can be painful depending on the individual wart. The panel objected to the use of the word “effective" in labeling because it felt this would imply 

100 percent effectiveness, which cannot be guaranteed for any OTC wartremover product. 

Nailbiting and thumbsucking are not so pleasant habits indulged in by considerable numbers of people. According to the expert panel's statistics, 43 percent of preadolescent children, 25 percent of college-age people, and 

10 percent of adults are nailbiters, while 16 to 46 percent of the child population are thumbsuckers.

One way of discouraging these habits has been to paint bitter substances such as denatonium benzoate and sucrose octaacetate on the nails, thumbs, and other fingers. These substances are safe enough, the panel said, but there is not enough evidence to show they are effective. More testing would be required before they could be included in over-the-counter drug products. 

Acceptable labeling for these products may indicate that they are to be used as nailbiting or thumbsucking deterrents in people aged 4 years and older, the panel said. Warnings should include: "Avoid contact with eyes" and "For topical use only."

At the other extremity are ingrown toenails, a misnamed condition, the panel said, since the nail doesn't actually grow into the flesh, but instead becomes imbedded in it. Incorrect nail cutting, injury to the nail, and tightfitting shoes or hosiery can all contribute to this condition. Unfortunately, for those whose toes are so afflicted, there are no safe and effective ingredients to relieve the discomfort of ingrown toenails.

The panel could not substantiate the safety or effectiveness of two ingredients offered for relief of ingrown toenail symptoms-chloroxylenol (parachloro-metaxylenol) and urea. The group also recommended that sodium sulfide and tannic acid be tested further to determine their effectiveness for this use.

As for labeling, the panel recommended that labels on ingrown-toenail products say they are for temporary relief of discomfort from ingrown toenails and recommended that they include such warnings as: "Do not use this product for more than 7 days" and "If you have diabetes or circulatory impairment, see a doctor for treatment of ingrown toenail." Labels cannot claim the product will give fast pain relief.

The recommendations of the Advisory Review Panel on OTC Miscella neous External Drug Products are not binding on FDA. The Agency published the panel's reports so those who are interested may comment on them before final standards are established for these products.

A funny creature is the flea. 

You cannot tell a he from she. 

But he can tell, and so can she. 

And so can your pet when he has them. Here's what to do about them. 000 ми

The Unscratching Of Fido by Linda Isner 'It's hard to make fleas flee. 

But not impossible.' 

Anyone who has ever been plagued by itchy insect bites can sympathize with a pet that seems to be fighting a losing battle against. fleas. Fleas are a major parasitic skin problem of dogs and cats and are particularly troublesome during the warm seasons-April through September/October-in the northern

States. In warm areas of the country, such as California and Florida, they are a year round concern.

It certainly is not easy to get rid of fleas. Under ideal conditions (i.e., having a host, high humidity, and warm temperatures), fleas can survive up to 26 months. They can live out the winter in your house if they have warm, moist conditions, possibly producing a new generation of adult fleas every 3 weeks.

Between meals the female flea will lay some 20 of the 400-500 eggs she will produce in her lifetime. The eggs may be deposited on or off your pet. 

Since the eggs are not sticky, some deposited on the animal may fall off into the surrounding environment.

Thus, the most effective flea treatment is ridding both the animal and its environment of fleas and their eggs. 

On dogs, fleas are usually found in the vicinity of the hindquarters, especially on the back, tail base, or inside the hind legs. The circular, raised area appearing on the skin following a bite (which is a reaction to insect saliva) often is hidden by the dog's hair. Cats, in general, appear to be less irritated by the bites. However, as with dogs, some cats can be hypersensitive and find even one flea bite intolerable. Fleas usually go for the lower back, neck, and throat of the cat. The bite may appear as a raised area covered with a small, reddish brown crust. Most of the serious consequences of your pet's flea infestation, such as hair loss and secondary bacterial infection, come from the animal scratching itself. 

For years, various insecticides applied in a number of ways have been used on pets to kill fleas and provide relief to the animal. These insecticides are powerful and sometimes quite toxic, especially to cats. They should be used with care. The following are a few of the chemical groups more commonly used as flea insecticides:

Organophosphates-Generally considered to contain some of the most potent insecticidal compounds. 

Most toxic of the insecticides listed. 

Should be used only with extreme caution in cats. Should not be used on kittens. It has been noted recently that the flea population has built up a resistance to some of the organophosphates. This resistance is thought to coincide with heavy use of compounds in certain areas of the country. (Organophosphates, along with the carbamates, may be listed as "cholinesterase inhibitors" on the labeling.) 

Carbamates-Less toxic than the organophosphates. May be used on cats, but not kittens. Effects are short-lived. Re-treatment is usually necessary in 3 to 5 days. • Pyrethrins-Least toxic of the insecticides listed. In addition to killing fleas, it repels them. Frequently a 

FDA Consumer / February 1981 / 21

Sprays, powders, and dips are some of the tr ments that can be used to keep a pet free of fleas. However, care must be taken to keep areas that pets inhabit clean so that flea eggs can't accumulate and eventually set the anim scratching again.

The insecticides may be applied in a variety of ways, including: • Flea collars, medallions-May be irritating to the skin. Usually contain organophosphates and/or carbamates. 

Sprays-Effective, but the noise may frighten the animal and it may object to the cold sensation of the spray. Usually contain organophosphates, carbamates, and/or pyrethrins. • Powders-Effect may be sporadic because they are easily removed. Simple to apply, but messy.

Usually contain organophosphates, carbamates, and/or pyrethrins. • Dips-Effective but hard to use.

Best done by a trained professional. 

Usually contain organophosphates or carbamates. 

Dab ons-New product on the market. Insecticide applied like a roll-on deodorant. Hair may accumulate on the cloth tip applicator. May contain carbamates.

Pet owners should try to identify the active ingredient group or groups to which a product belongs. (If that is not possible, ask your veterinarian, local humane society, or a knowledgeable salesperson.) It is normally advisable to use one of these treatments at a time and to re-treat only as recommended because, when used in excess, these products may lead to toxicity. You should avoid overdosing your pets through exposure to different sources of organophosphates and carbamates, which are popular pesticides frequently found in other household and garden products. The signs of overdosage may include vomiting, diarrhea, shaking, weakness, depression, hyperactivity, or small (constricted) pupils. If these signs appear, you should seek veterinary medical treatment for your pet. 

It is no wonder, with the drawbacks of the insecticide preparations, that dog and cat owners eagerly embraced a new type of product that came onto the market a couple of years ago promising relief for flearidden pets in a natural, safe, and effective way. These new products, promoted as oral flea repellants, come in tablet form containing as principal ingredients: vitamin B, (thiamine), Brewer's yeast (which consists mostly of various members of the Vitamin B family), or garlic.

The tablet is to be fed to the dog or cat and purportedly produces an odor on the animal's skin that cannot be detected by humans but is repulsive to fleas. Other claims are that the tablets make the animal taste bad to the flea or that tablets high in vitamin B, prevent the inflammation normally associated with such bites. 

FDA has received no well-controlled studies substantiating any of these claims. The Agency has received complaints about the tablets and has taken a number of regulatory actions against them based on the fact that they are advertised to be effective against flea infestation when there is insufficient evidence to confirm this. To date, there are no overthe-counter oral products approved for repelling or controlling fleas. Furthermore, the consumer is paying a high price-considering the cost of the ingredients-for a product with effectiveness that's unconfirmed by adequate scientific investigations. 

Pet owners should consider if a repellant, as opposed to an insecticide, is what is wanted. Even if the repellant succeeds in keeping fleas off the animal, the fleas still may be alive, in the area, and able to infest not only other animals but humans as well. 

The fleas can be carriers of disease and other conditions (e.g., dogs or cats may get tapeworms after grooming themselves and ingesting fleas which may harbor immature stages of the tapeworm). 

If you are facing a flea problem, as a pet owner you should seriously consider taking the following steps: 

Shampoo your pet. If the shampoo is insecticidal it will kill or remove fleas. Otherwise, it at least will bring some relief to the animal and allow you to monitor the effects of other treatments. Shampoos, however, have little or no residual (i.e., lasting after the shampoo) flea-killing effect. • Use one of the insecticide preparations for pets. Be sure to follow directions carefully and observe all precautions listed. Speak to your veterinarian about the proper use of the product, even if it is an over-thecounter preparation. As an alternative, take your pet to the veterinarian. for therapy and/or recommendations since the veterinarian has access to more potent treatments which also may be more effective. • Treat the pet's environment. 

Vacuum the house and possibly even your pet frequently to get rid of adult fleas, fleas in their immature stages, and flea excrement, which provides nourishment for some forms of the immature fleas. (Not all stages of the insect's life cycle are equally susceptible to insecticides. The egg and cocoon are particularly resistant.) Be sure to remove and discard the vacuum bag immediately. 

Use insecticide spray after vacuuming, removing animals and possibly plants out of the area first. Be sure to include carpets, floors, stuffed furniture, and your pet's sleeping place in this treatment. Repeat applications are generally necessary, beginning 22-3 weeks after the initial treatment. 

You may protect yourself from flea bites by using topical insect repellants. (Do not use these on your pets, though.) If you notice you already have a small, itchy bump or bumps-frequently there will be more than one bite in the same area you may wish to treat yourself with a topical steroid cream (cortisone) for relief of the irritation. 

The only sure cure against flea bites in man or beast, however, is eradication of the flea. 

Linda Isner is an industry information specialist with FDA's Bureau of Veterinary Medicine. 

FDA Consumer / February 1981 / 23

There's Something To Be Said 

For Never Saying, 'Please Pass The Meat'

Inflation and the trend toward more "natural" lifestyles have heightened the interest in vegetarianism. The experts say that extreme vegetarian diets can be dangerous, but there are also indications that other meatless diets may be quite beneficial. by Roger W. Miller

et's hear it now for vegetarians!

No, they're not a band of religious fanatics who wear their hair shirts by denying themselves some of the finer moments of dining, and in the process jeopardize their health with deficiencies of vitamins and nutrients. 

The fact is that vegetarians as a group may be a whole lot healthier than the rest of us. They can also be credited with adopting a very efficient means of getting their body essentials-a consideration of no small merit on this planet of finite resources. 

True, vegetarians have to go through life tortured by the smelland only the smell of barbecued ribs, frying bacon, Big Macs, and other such animal delicacies. And it also may be true that because they don't eat hot dogs they don't get much out of baseball. But that doesn't make them un-American.

Economists, ecologists, philosophers, and nutritionists who look at vegetarians often have to come up with plus marks for these flesh teetotalers. With hamburger about to break the $2 a pound barrier, it's not hard to understand why economists can applaud vegetarians. And with cattle having to eat 16 pounds of grain to produce 1 pound of meat, it's easy to see why vegetarians get approving nods from ecologists. 

Philosophers can admire the discipline that vegetarians impose to maintain their proper diets. And nutritionists have to agree that vegetarians, because they eat less fat and are more careful about their diets, are less likely to suffer from obesity. 

The idea that vegetarians can't get what their bodies need without meat was pretty well put into the myth category in 1974 when the Food Nutrition Board of the National Academy of Sciences issued a statement on vegetarian diets. Concluded the board: "A vegetarian can be well nourished if he eats a variety of plant foods and gives attention to the critical nutrients (needed by all people)." 

The underscoring of the "if" in that statement was provided by the 

Food and Nutrition Board. The un derscoring is necessary because the more restricted the diet, the more difficult it is to get all of the nutrients needed.

The people who-in the words of one of civilization's better known vegetarians, George Bernard Shaw- "refuse to dine off the carcasses of dead animals" generally fall into categories based on the animal foods left in their diets. The categories are: ⚫ Vegans, or pure vegetariansconsume only plant food, and the purists among them only raw plant food. • Lacto vegetarians-eat dairy products as well as plant foods. Many 

Seventh-Day Adventists practice this type of vegetarianism.

Lacto-ovo vegetarians-tolerate eggs as well as dairy products along with their plant foods. 

Other vegetarians may consume poultry and fish, leaving only red meat to the gastronomic heathens.

The more restrictive the vegetarian's diet the more likely nutrition will be limited. Of concern in recent years have been the extremist diets of groups such as the very restrictive 

24 February 1981 / FDA Consumer

levels of the Zen macrobiotics regimen. Indeed, the Food and Nutrition 

Board warned in its 1974 statement that such extremely restrictive diets endanger health. 

Families who practice stricter forms of vegetarianism should be sure that their growing children are getting enough calories and some other nutrients, such as vitamins D and B₁2. Studies to date indicate that children may not be able to thrive as well as adults on the more limited diets. 

In addition to George Bernard 

Shaw and the Seventh-Day Adventists, other well-known vegetarians include the Trappist Monks and Hindus. The Monk group shuns meat because it considers it a luxury and thus in conflict with its quest for the simple life. Hindus avoid meat because they believe in transmigration of souls; thus, butchering an animal would be tantamount to butchering a person.

Studies on the health of vegetarians aren't too definitive. It is known that Seventh-Day Adventists generally have fewer deaths due to heart disease, but this may also be traced to the fact that they usually don't smoke or drink. The saturated fats in animal products contribute to high blood cholesterol levels, which is one of the risk factors for heart disease. 

Some 40 to 45 percent of the calories in the average American's diet comes from fat. Much of that fat, of course, comes from animal sources. 

The high fat content in our diets may be related to several diseases including colon and some other forms of cancer. 

Needless to say, the high content of fat in the U.S. diet also contributes to obesity. Overweight people are more prone to heart disease, high blood pressure, and diabetes. 

Still another advantage to never saying "please pass the meat" is that vegetarians, because of the high fiber content in their diets, usually don't contribute to America's several hundred million dollar a year laxative habit. 

The high fiber intake may also discourage overeating, and therein deny those extra pounds a chance to attach themselves. One fills up fast on grains and such. Consequently, fat vegetarians are a rare species. The high fiber content, however, may make it more difficult for some people, such as growing children and pregnant women, to obtain enough calories. Also, high fiber may interfere with the absorption of zinc, iron, and other minerals.

A leading proponent for the vegetarian way of life in recent years has been Frances Moore Lappe, author of DIET FOR A SMALL PLANET. 

Lappe pointed out that eating meat to get protein is about as efficient as paddling a canoe with a tennis racket. It takes 16 pounds of grain to add 1 pound to beef in the feedlot, Lappe notes. With a ratio like that or even with the average livestock ratio, including chickens, of 7 or 8 pounds of grain or soybeans for 1 pound of flesh, it's easy to see how the world's food shortages might be greatly lessened if vegetarianism swept the world. 

However, if meat is hard to produce, it does a good job of providing protein as well as iron and B vitamins once it is inside a person's stomach. Meat provides high quality protein, and protein is required throughout life. Indeed, protein provides building blocks for muscle and tissue. Protein is made from amino acids. Meat contains more of the indispensable or essential amino acids that the body cannot make by itself in the quantities and proportions needed.

Plant foods do not contain the amount or balance of essential amino acids needed by humans. However, if certain combinations of plant foods are eaten or if plant foods are taken with some animal protein, the missing amino acids are filled in. A number of these combinations have been around a long time, indicating that some of those old wives who told tales possibly knew what they were talking about. For example, baked beans and brown bread complement each other, with one providing the amino acid the other is low in. The same is true for macaroni and cheese and the beans and cheese combination that is served as tamale pie. 

Lentil-rice soup makes a good protein combination, as does breakfast cereal and milk. 

Dairy products, including eggs, provide high-quality protein, and are thus good meat substitutes. Legumes (soybeans, chickpeas), nuts including peanuts, and meat substitutes made from plant protein (usually with a soybean base) are also protein sources for vegetarian diets. In addition to providing protein, these meat alternatives supply varying amounts of other essential nutrients. 

In its statement on vegetarianism, the Food and Nutrition Board cited a 

1954 study of vegetarians, which found that nutrient intake for all vegetarian groups equaled or exceeded necessary amounts, with the exception of vitamin B12. That vitamin was low in the total vegetarian diet. B₁₂ is found in all animal products including eggs and milk products. Additional sources are fortified foods including soy milk, cereals, and meat substitutes. B₁2 substitutes are also available. 12 12 

The Food and Nutrition Board said that vegetarians will get along nutritionally well by using a good variety in the diet. "The greatest risk comes from undue reliance on a single plant food source, usually a cereal grain or starchy root crop," the board said.

Here are the board's recommendations for filling the tummy with the right stuff while sparing the lives of animals:

Legumes (particularly soybeans)-rich in protein, B-vitamins, and iron. (It's difficult for women to get enough iron in their usual diets, and even more difficult when red meats are left out.) • Grains for carbohydrates, proteins, thiamin, iron, and trace minerals. • Nuts and other seeds-provide fat (which supplies energy), and B-vitamins in addition to protein and iron. • Dark green, leafy vegetablessources of calcium, riboflavin, and carotene (used to make vitamin A).

These vegetables should be used liberally by vegetarians. 

Vegetarians are advised to provide themselves with two servings daily of the high-protein meat alternatives of legumes, nuts, peanuts, eggs, meat analogs, and dairy products.

So, let's hear it again for vegetarians. Many of them have earned and deserve their wholesomer-than-thou attitude. 

Roger W. Miller, who is editor of 

FDA CONSUMER, enjoys steaks, pork chops, and hamburgers and admires vegetarians.

Update 

Stirred Up Over Saccharin In Letter to a Young Saccharin User (June 

1980), FDA Commissioner Jere Goyan summed up the current status of saccharin from FDA's view by responding to a letter from a 12-year-old concerned about drinking diet soda. The 12-year-old's letter, which was an adaptation of a letter received by FDA from a 20-year-old, and Goyan's reply caused quite a stir. Here's a report. "Sham" and "propaganda" were the words quoted in a WALL STREET JOURNAL article that was headed "FDA Fabricates Letter To Push Sac charin View." The quoted words were from Edward Frantel, president of the Seven-Up Co. Frantel and the Calorie Control Council, a group representing the manufacturers of diet sodas, had protested the June 1980 article in FDA CONSUMER titled Letter To a Young Saccharin User. 

Frantel's complaint, expressed in a letter to 

FDA Commissioner Jere Goyan, was that the incoming letter printed in the magazine was "not genuine" and that Goyan's response prejudged the saccharin issue. In statements to the press, Frantel also charged that the article interjected "emotionalism" into the controversy. That was the same charge made by Robert Kellen, head of the Calorie Control Council.

The letter from the 12-year-old was similar to one the Agency had received from a 20-year-old named Dana Jaeger of Santa Barbara, Calif. The incoming letter was changed by Roger W. Miller, editor of FDA CONSUMER, because Miss Jaeger could not be reached to give her permission for use of her letter and because the response was drafted in such a manner that it might have been interpreted as "talking down" to a 20-year-old person. 

In addition to making the letterwriter 12 years old, the name of Terry Jacobs was used instead of 

Dana Jaeger and Miss Jaeger's reference to using saccharin daily in her coffee was dropped. However, the concern about the effects of drinking two cans of diet soda a day was retained. 

In his reply to Frantel, Commissioner Goyan said that changing the name and age of the letterwriter was a mistake. He also said that his characterization of the soft drink industry was "perhaps harsher than necessary." The article had informed the 12-year-old that "there was much confusion about the saccharin issue, in part because some people prefer it that way in order to sell a few more bottles of soda."

Goyan noted in his response that the original letterwriter did offer "a genuine expression of concern about the possible harmful effects of saccharin." He also said that FDA's position had been and continues to be that saccharin is a weak carcinogen (cancer-causing agent). He cited studies that led to the position and added, "I believe this information was fairly presented in my response in

FDA CONSUMER." 

The Commissioner's letter was an attempt to explain to young people the possible hazards identified with saccharin use. The explanation stated that in a Canadian study pregnant rodents were found more likely to develop bladder cancer. 

However, it was the second generation male rats in that study that were the principal ones to develop bladder cancer. 

It was also reported in the letter that FDA had proposed to "let saccharin be used as a tabletop sweetener" while evidence was being developed that might show it provides a benefit to people on weight-control diets or who are diabetic. That may have been misinterpreted, as FDA's proposal involved the manufacturer submitting a New Drug

Application for marketing the product as a tabletop sweetener.

Color Decisions Delayed 

How FDA keeps track of the color additives used in foods, drugs, and cosmetics was the subject of a 

March 1980 FDA CONSUMER article, The Color 

Additive Scoreboard. A new timetable for the testing of some of these colors is the subject of this update.

Industry has been given additional time to test 23 color additives used in foods, drugs, or cosmetics before FDA decides whether to approve the colors for permanent use or order them withdrawn from the market.

All the colors have been used since before 1960. 

Most are used only in drugs and cosmetics. Based on the available evidence, FDA believes that all 23 can continue to be used safely during the testing period.

In February 1977, FDA set a cut-off date of January 31, 1981, for submission of the tests. But the

Agency said in a proposal published in the FED- 

ERAL REGISTER November 14, 1980, that there have been unforeseen and unavoidable delays in conducting the studies and these justify granting permission for more time.

The Agency's proposal is in response to a peti- 

FDA Consumer/ February 1981 / 29

tion from three industry groups-the Cosmetic, Toiletry and Fragrance Association, the Pharma ceutical Manufacturers Association, and the Certi fied Color Manufacturers Association. 

The 23 colors are on what is known as a "provisional list." This list was established by the 1960

Color Additive Amendments to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. They required that colors used in foods, drugs, and cosmetics be proved safe for their intended uses.

The law said colors already in use in 1960 could continue to be used on a provisional, or interim, basis while tests were going on to determine whether they should be permanently approved or withdrawn from the market.

The testing program envisioned by the 1960 law was delayed for several years during litigation over these requirements in the Federal courts. By 1977, final decisions had been made on about 75 colors. 

In February 1977, FDA set a timetable to resolve the status of the remaining colors on the provisional list and it is this timetable, involving 23 colors, on which FDA is now acting. The final decisions for the other colors for which the timetable was set in 1977 have already been made or will be made by January 31, 1981. 

Following is a list of the 23 colors and the date by which the final testing report is proposed to be due at FDA. The proposed date by which a final 

FDA decision will be made is one year from each due date.

A pilot program to test, over the next 3 years, patient package inserts for ten prescription drugs was announced in September 1980 by the Secretary of

Health and Human Services. What the program is all about was detailed in Rx With a Dose of Info, in the December 1980-January 1981 issue of FDA 

CONSUMER. The program is already moving into high gear, as this Update relates.

Patient package inserts for three prescription drugs must be provided to consumers starting in

May 1981. The drugs include: 

Cimetidine, used to treat ulcers. • Clofibrate, used to treat elevated fats in the blood. • Propoxyphene, commonly sold as Darvon, a painkiller. 

FDA published guidelines on November 25, 1980, for the texts of the first three patient package inserts and also established the requirement that these be available in pharmacies in 6 months.

Patient package inserts are leaflets, written in simple language, that describe a drug's proper uses, risks, and side effects. Companies that make the drugs must provide the leaflets to the pharmacist, who must give one to the patient with each new prescription or when a prescription is refilled if requested by the patient. The inserts will be available on request in hospitals and nursing homes. Manufacturers also will be required to provide leaflets in Spanish for pharmacists who request them.

Bendectin is now included in the PPI list. FDA believes there is an urgent need for a Bendectin patient package insert, and it replaces the originally proposed drug, warfarin-a blood thinner used in the prevention of blood clots.

Over the next 3 years, all 10 patient package inserts will be evaluated by FDA, along with alter- 

30 February 1981 FDA Consumer

native means for providing information to patients about prescription drugs. Once that evaluation is completed, FDA will decide whether to proceed with PPI's for other prescription drugs, or adopt an alternate system. A number of drugstore chains and others have indicated interest in working with FDA to test alternate systems of providing drug information.

AFP Tests Limited 

Neural tube defects are crippling and often fatal birth defects in which the brain is malformed or missing or the spinal column fails to develop properly. They are among the most common serious birth defects, affecting about 5,000 of the 3 million babies born in the United States each year. A laboratory test can help detect neural tube defects before the baby is born by measuring the amount of a chemical called alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in the mother's blood. The benefits and drawbacks of this test were discussed in AFP: Sometimes an Ominous 

Clue, in the April 1980 FDA CONSUMER. Here's an update. 

The Department of Health and Human Services 

(HHS) has proposed to restrict the use of AFP test kits, currently under review for marketing approval by FDA.

Laboratories would use a kit to measure the amount of AFP in the blood of a pregnant woman. 

AFP is a substance produced by all developing fetuses and is found in the amniotic fluid surrounding the fetus. Some AFP normally passes into the mother's blood.

A high level of AFP in the pregnant woman's blood can mean that her child will be born with a neural tube defect. But a high AFP level can also indicate the presence of twins, triplets, the death of the fetus, a threatened miscarriage, or an incorrect estimate of the age of the fetus.

The test, therefore, is not conclusive; further tests must be performed before a physician can confirm that the baby will likely be born with a neural tube defect.

AFP test kits have been tested extensively in the 

United States and are in use abroad. Several health professional and consumer organizations and specialists in AFP testing have told FDA that while the AFP test is beneficial, they fear that unrestricted use of the kits could result in serious problems and unwarranted concern. Others have said that the kits are safe and effective and should be made widely available to give women who may be carrying affected fetuses the greatest possible access to this technology to help identify them. 

FDA hopes to balance these conflicting concerns. The Agency will not approve any AFP test kits for marketing until it has determined what restrictions, if any, are necessary for their use. 

In regulations proposed by FDA, the kits' use would be restricted to FDA-approved testing programs that can perform the screening test properly and provide the follow-up procedures necessary to help make a correct diagnosis. These procedures include ultrasound examination of the pregnant woman and analysis of the amniotic fluid. 

The restrictions also would ensure that prospective parents receive adequate professional counseling to inform them about the AFP test and its limitations. The FDA proposal would require, for example, that women be given a brochure explaining the test and what a positive result would mean. 

Physicians would have to obtain written consent before beginning the testing process.

Also, manufacturers of the test kits would have to monitor closely the use of the tests with information provided by the testing programs and participating laboratories and physicians. The manufacturers then would report each quarter to FDA on test results and the outcome of pregnancies in which the test is used. 

Two other HHS agencies, the Center for Dis ease Control and the Health Care Financing 

Administration, proposed complementary regulations that would require clinical laboratories performing the test to adopt additional quality control procedures. 

FDA will review comments from the public on its proposed restrictions before deciding on a final regulation. Any adopted restrictions would remain in effect for 4 years. A new evaluation would then be made on the use of the test kits.

New Rules on Infant Formula 

Nearly 2 years ago a manufacturer's change in an infant formula product had some very serious consequences. How it happened and what resulted was described in Next to Mother's Milk, There's Infant 

Formula, in the July-August 1980 FDA CON- 

SUMER. FDA has taken steps to assure that such mishaps won't occur again, as this Update explains. 

Infant formula manufacturers are now required to submit regular reports to FDA confirming that their products contain all the nutrients essential for normal growth and development.

This notification was mandated by the Infant Formula Act of 1980, and will remain in effect un- 

FDA Consumer / February 1981 / 31

til FDA publishes regulations next fall specifying the quality control procedures manufacturers must follow in making formulas.

The act establishes a nutrient content standard for formulas as well as the requirements for ensuring the safety and quality of the products. Signed into law on September 26, 1980, the act was prompted by the recall in late 1979 of two infant formulas deficient in chloride. The manufacturer had reformulated the products without checking for nutrient content.

Some infants who were fed only the deficient formulas for an extended period suffered a deficiency-induced illness characterized by loss of appetite and failure to gain weight. 

Under the requirements announced in the November 21 Federal ReGISTER, infant formula manufacturers must report to FDA beginning December 26, 1980, and each 90 days thereafter until the quality control procedures take effect.

The law also requires similar reports from manufacturers producing new infant formula products or planning significant changes in formulation or processing. Manufacturers are required to furnish this information to FDA no later than the 90th day before a new product goes into production and before reformulation or change in processing of a product already on the market. 

Manufacturers must also notify FDA immediately when they learn that their products may not contain the required nutrients, or may otherwise present a health risk.

Caffeine Studies Urged 

Caffeine's capability to cause birth defects in rats prompted the Department of Health and Human 

Services to announce a series of actions. What they are was discussed in Caution Light on Caffeine, in the October 1980 FDA CONSUMER. Here are the specifics of two of these measures.

The Food and Drug Administration has pro posed regulations to require new safety studies on caffeine and to encourage the manufacture and sale of caffeine-free colas.

One regulation would make the food industry's continued use of caffeine as an added ingredient in soft drinks and other foods conditional upon its funding of studies of caffeine's effects on children and the unborn. 

The proposal would also remove caffeine from

FDA's list of substances Generally Recognized As 

Safe (GRAS). Current uses of caffeine may con tinue while the studies are being conducted. 

The National Coffee Association and the soft drink industry already have indicated their willingness to support much of the additional research on caffeine, including a study comparing rates of birth defects with the consumption of caffeine by pregnant women. FDA will review the plans for the study to ensure that it can provide useful results. 

The other formal FDA proposal would amend the standard of identity for cola and pepper drinks to permit use of these names for caffeine-free soft drinks.

Under present regulations, a soft drink (except one artificially sweetened) must contain caffeine if it is to be labeled as "cola" or "pepper."

The further studies sought by FDA would determine: • How animals and humans absorb, use, and excrete caffeine, so that animal studies can be applied better to humans.

Whether the birth defects noted in rats were caused by caffeine itself or by a metabolite-a product resulting from the breakdown of caffeine. • How caffeine may affect generations of rats and their nervous systems, reproduction, and conditioning.

Whether caffeine, in long-term feeding studies in rats, causes cancer, or whether other chronic, pathological effects appear. • Whether studies of large populations of pregnant women show an association between caffeine and birth defects. 

Whether caffeine causes adverse behavioral effects, especially in children.

The proposals were published in the October 21, 1980, FEDERAL REGISTER. 

B-15 Fails Court Test 

"Vitamin” B-15 is one of those health fads that have been around for a number of years, as the ar ticle Debunking Pangamic Acid (FDA CONSUMER, September 1978) explained. Here's another court case involving B-15.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern Dis trict of Illinois has upheld FDA's contention that a so-called vitamin B-15 product known as Aangamik 15 is adulterated because it contains the chemically unsafe food additive, N,N-dimethylglycine, or DMG. 

Judge Stanley Roszkowski also found that the 

32 February 1981 | FDA Consumer

product was labeled as containing B-15 and ruled 

October 29, 1980, in Chicago that "there is no scientifically recognized Vitamin B-15." He confirmed the Agency's view that the substance, promoted as a dietary supplement, contains the unsafe food additive DMG, and is adulterated and misbranded under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

He also noted that there are many commercially available products called B-15 or pangamic acid but that they vary in their chemical formulations. 

The ruling followed a 6-day trial during which the Government presented testimony from experts in the fields of nutrition, medicine, and toxicology. 

They testified that DMG is not recognized as safe, that evidence in the scientific literature suggests that it may be dangerous, and that they regard it as unsafe. Judge Roszkowski found that, "after reviewing the considerable amount of expert testimony presented by both parties, it is the court's opinion that N,N-dimethylglycine is not generally recognized among qualified experts as having been shown to be safe under the conditions of its intended use."

The decision was based on six seizure actions taken by FDA against the manufacturer of the substance, FoodScience Laboratories Inc., South

Burlington, Vt. These seizures were consolidated into the case heard by Judge Roszkowski.

Claimed to be a wonder drug and a Russian formula for "Vitamin B-15," products labeled B-15 or pangamates or DMG became a major national fad in 1978.

This is the second major court case FDA has won against so-called "Vitamin B-15" or pangamic acid products. On December 5, 1978, the U.S.

District Court for New Jersey ruled that tablets made by International Vitamin Corp. of Union,

N.J., were adulterated because they contained an unsafe food additive. 

'Generic' List Is Final 

In 1979 FDA published a proposed list of approved drugs that was intended to be the Key to Generic Substitution, according to an article by that title in the February 1979 FDA CONSUMER. 

The proposed list is now in final form and this Update tells how to get a copy.

The Department of Health and Human Services has published a list of more than 5,000 prescription drug products FDA has approved as being safe and effective, along with the names of the manufacturers licensed to market them. The list also provides information on which products are therapeutically equivalent, which are not, and which need further testing before FDA can conclude they are therapeutically equivalent (i.e., which are equally effective in all aspects).

The list originally was prepared to respond to requests from State health agencies for assistance in administering laws that permit pharmacists to substitute lower-cost drugs for higher-priced chemically identical ones.

Forty-eight States permit or require pharmacists to dispense a lower-cost version of the drug when the physician prescribes a higher-cost product; only 

Indiana and Texas prohibit substitution. These

State laws allow the physician to indicate that the higher-priced product may be dispensed if it is in the best interest of the patient.

The 250-page list, published with its first supplement, contains prescription drug products approved for marketing through August 1980 which are still being marketed, according to FDA's records. The list is called "Approved Prescription

Drug Products With Therapeutic Equivalence 

Evaluations." Subscriptions for the list and periodic supplements are available from the U.S. Government Printing Office, Washington, D.C. 20402, for $20. Foreign subscriptions are $25. 

Ban on Mussel Extract 

A wide variety of quack drugs and devices that have been sold as supposed arthritis cures were cited in the article Hocus-Pocus As Applied to Arthritis, in the September 1980 issue of FDA CON- 

SUMER. Here's yet another one.

FDA has issued an Import Alert to stop importation of an extract from the "rare" New Zealand green-lipped mussel, being promoted as a new "remedy" for arthritis by John E. Croft, author of

NATURAL RELIEF FROM ARTHRITIS-A SAFE AND EFFECTIVE TREATMENT FROM THE OCEAN. 

Under the auspices of a public relations firm, Croft has made a promotional tour that was followed by appearance of the extract in health food stores.

The Arthritis Foundation considers the product unproved and fears the campaign could delude arthritis sufferers and raise false hopes. Editors and science writers have been urged by the foundation to avoid giving undue publicity to the product and the book.

The Notebook 

Certain medical devices that have a potential for causing harmful effects or which need collateral measures for their safe and effective use will be restricted under a regulation proposed by FDA. This means that sale, distribution, or use will be restricted to, by, or on the prescription of a health professional. Among the devices to be covered by the regulation are those that penetrate or pierce the skin, the ocular cavity, the ear beyond the external auditory canal, and the mouth beyond the pharynx. Also included are devices to be implanted in the body, and those used to introduce energy into or deliver medicinal gas to the body. Details of the proposed regulation were published in the Octo ber 3, 1980, FEDERAL REGISTER. 

Latest among the medical devices FDA has classified for regulatory purposes are 94 devices for general hospital and personal use. Included in the list published in the October 21, 1980, FEDERAL REGISTER, were 12 monitoring devices, for example, thermometers and scales. Of these, three were put in Class Igeneral controls-and nine were put in Class II-requiring performance standards. Patient scales, rated both a I and a II classification, depending on whether they are mechanical or battery powered (I), or AC

Forty therapeutic devices, such as elastic bandages, infant warmers, burn sheets, and snakebite kits were classified as follows: 19 in Class I, 18 in Class II, and two in Class III, which means manufacturers must have approval prior to marketing. The two Class III devices were cold pack snakebite kits and infant radiant warmers. Support stockings rated Class I designation if they are for general medical use, or Class II, if they are to prevent pooling of blood in the legs. 

Miscellaneous devices, ranging from ice bags to handcarried stretchers, accounted for 29 Class I devices and 

12 Class II. 

FDA tentatively identified eight general medical and personal use devices for which patient information may be required, including liquid crystal forehead temperature strips, suction snakebite kits, and phototherapy units to treat jaundice in newborn infants.
