Investigators' Reports 

Investigators' Reports presents information on inspections, product seizures, court proceedings, and other administrative and regulatory actions by Federal, State, and local food and drug agencies across the country to provide health and economic protection to consumers of foods, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices.

Emergency Protocol 

Hepatitis is a nasty disease, often fatal, and always expensive to treat (medical care costs can run as high as $30,000 per patient). Since 1972, FDA has required that all therapeutic whole blood, blood plasma, and serum be tested for hepatitis B, one form of the disease transmitted through blood transfusions. The number of people contracting hepatitis B has dropped dramatically since then. sit- 

However, there are emergency uations when blood may be transfused or shipped prior to being tested for hepatitis. For instance, in an emergency situation in which the patient might die before the test can be made (the test for hepatitis can take as much as a full day), untested blood may be transfused; but the units of blood should be clearly marked as not having been tested. and the test should be done as soon as possible after the transfusion. Similarly, if there is an emergency need for blood that must be shipped a long distance, untested blood may be shipped. However, all units must be clearly labeled that they have not been fully tested and should not be transfused until the tests have been completed. A doctor must always sign for release of the untested blood, in effect taking responsibility for defining a given situation as a medical emergency.

Last summer FDA's Atlanta Dis trict discovered that the Eliza Coffee

Memorial Hospital Blood Bank, 

Florence, Alabama, was not taking the necessary precautions in its emergency release of blood. Investigators reported the blood bank had collected and transfused 10 units of blood which had not been tested for hepatitis but which did not have labeling stating that tests had not been made. The district sent the blood bank a regulatory letter advising the management to correct these violations (as well as violations concerning the records of blood donors and expiration dates) and to develop the necessary written procedures for emergency release of blood.

The blood bank responded to the regulatory letter within the required 

10-day period and promised to correct the violations. Mixmash 

Last summer a Long Island drug manufacturer made a mistake in formulating a batch of sodium fluoride capsules. The New York City labora tory responsible for analyzing the product failed to catch the error and the product was distributed commercially. An investigator from FDA's 

Hicksville (New York) Resident Post finally caught the mistake and was ultimately responsible for the destruction of a superpotent drug. 

The investigator found the error during an inspection of Private Label 

Packaging and Fulfillment Co., Inc.. 

Long Island. The investigator had checked the calculations in a sample of the batch records. He concluded that if the formulation had been done the way the batch records indicated, one lot (Lot 20580) of sodium fluoride would contain 6.4 milligrams (mg) of the active ingredient instead of the 5 mg it should contain. When 

FDA's New York Regional Labora tory subsequently analyzed a sample from that lot, the results showed the sample was indeed superpotent. 

The firm had told the Hicksville investigator that it did not do the analysis for quality control of its products, that this analysis was done by a firm in New York City-F. L. 

Laboratories, Inc.-before products were released for sale. So F. L. Labs was checked out. 

At FDA's request, the lab manager re-did the analysis on the sample from Lot 20580 and found the same superpotency FDA had found. 

The reason for the error could not be determined. The chemist who had done the original analysis (and had since left the firm) was competent and well-trained, the manager said, and her other calculations and several other analyses were checked by the investigator and proved to be accurate. The instruments used in the analysis were also checked and found to be accurate. 

But if the cause of the error was elusive, the consequence was not. F.

L. Labs contacted Private Label 

Packaging, and Lot 20580 was destroyed.

None of Mom's Apple Pie 

Homecooking should be served in the home. Serving home-cooked foods in restaurants and other commercial food establishments is a no- 

36 February 1981 FDA Consumer

no under local health codes.

So says New York City Health Commissioner Reinaldo A. Ferrar. 

The commissioner warned owners of restaurants and other establishments that serve food that it's illegal under 

New York State law and the city's health code to sell home-prepared foods through commercial outlets. "It may be the best apple pie in town," the commissioner stated. "However, if it's served in a restaurant it had better come from a licensed commercial establishment and not 'Aunt 

Polly's kitchen'." 

FDA does not specifically prohibit the sale of home-prepared foods; but the Agency's 1976 Food Service Sani tation Manual encourages stringent regulation by States and localities of food preparation-regulation that would be difficult to enforce in the case of nonlicensed cooks. The manual includes a format for regulating food service establishments that could be adopted by States, municipalities, counties, or health districts.

Most States do require that food for commercial sale be prepared in a licensed establishment-which excludes private kitchens. (For more information on the model restaurant ordinance, see For Your Dining

Pleasure-A Model Ordinance, in the February 1980 FDA CONSUMER.) 

Health authorities appreciate a good home-cooked meal as much as anyone, but they are more aware than most people that home kitchens rarely can meet the stringent sanitary conditions imposed on licensed foodpreparation facilities. The biggest danger is home-canned goods. While cakes and cookies can wreak only so much damage to your stomach, an improperly processed relish or can of beans can cause botulism, a disease that is frequently fatal. Annual reports from the Federal Center for 

Disease Control indicate that homecanned foods are the most frequently incriminated item in outbreaks of botulism.

Air Tight Case 

Putting too much of one thing into a mixture and not enough of another may be acceptable for a cook or a bartender, but such inexactitude won't do when filling compressed air cylinders for medicinal use in hospitals. The matter could be serious enough to wind up in court. Consider the case involving Manuel Souza and the company of which he is president, Taunton Oxygen Equipment, Inc., Taunton, Massachusetts.

FDA took the company to court on charges it misbranded its medicinal oxygen and failed to test each compressed air cylinder for percentages of oxygen. FDA's Boston District sought Government prosecution for violations of Good Manufacturing

Practice regulations covering mis branding and adulteration. The rea son was the firm's violations endangered the lives of patients in general and specifically the lives of patients at a hospital in Rhode Island.

The district was notified by a 

Rhode Island Hospital administrator that a shipment it had purchased as "compressed air" contained dangerously disparate levels of oxygen. The hospital had decided to test the 30 to 

35 cylinders it had in stock after a respiratory technician complained of problems with one of the cylinders. 

The hospital found that the oxygen content in each varied from 30 percent to 0 percent and that most were outside the acceptable range of 20 to 

23 percent oxygen concentration. 

Compressed air for breathing should approximate atmospheric air, which is 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen. The hospital has no policy of checking the oxygen concentration of compressed air directly from cylinders, but it does check the inspired air which is received by a patient. 

When the technician hooked up a cylinder of pure oxygen and a cylinder of compressed air to an air mixer, to provide oxygen to a patient, she noticed that the oxygen level was over 30 percent.

She adjusted the mixer device but still was unable to obtain the desired oxygen concentration, even with the oxygen cylinder completely turned off. The technician then checked the oxygen level in the compressed air cylinder and found it to be over 30 percent. The hospital alerted other hospitals about the problem and notified the firm.

The firm recalled the problem cylinders and sent the hospital another shipment. But the hospital kept three of the original cylinders and contacted FDA. In the presence of an 

FDA investigator, a hospital administrator tested the three cylinders. One cylinder had an oxygen level of 31 percent, the second had 2 percent, and the third had 0 percent.

The investigator also noted that the cylinders were not coded. All compressed air cylinders are painted white to distinguish them from other medicinal gas cylinders. Inspections of the firm uncovered other GMP violations involving production and controls. 

Medical experts in the field of inhalation therapy advised FDA that if compressed air with 27 percent or 

FDA Consumer / February 1981 / 37

1 more oxygen is used for a period of several hours it could prove fatal to a patient. Compressed air containing no oxygen given to a patient as the sole source of breathing air could result in death by suffocation in less than 3 minutes. 

Taunton Oxygen Equipment, Inc., pleaded guilty, and its president entered a plea of nolo contendere, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. They were assessed fines of $2,000 and $1,500 respectively. 

Good Intentions

There may be an appropriate Confucian moral for this story but the words of Robert Burns come to mind: "The best laid plans of mice and men gang aft a-gley" (often go wrong). 

Early in 1980 an Ohio trade delegation was invited to the Peoples Republic of China. Later in the year 

Governor James Rhodes of Ohio decided to return the invitation. But, things didn't work out as well as had been hoped. 

To promote Chinese business within his State, Rhodes invited some 

Chinese traders to show their products at the Ohio State Fair. An exhibit displaying the wares of that part of the Orient obviously would have been unique to the millions who come each year to browse through the various home and farm product exhibits up and down the midways. 

To handle their affairs in this country, the Chinese hired the China 

Business Corp., a broker in Cleveland, Ohio. For the exhibit, China 

Business sought to import an assortment of arts and crafts, oriental teas, and two types of drug products for display and sale at the fair. 

But the Chinese medical products were denied import entry. FDA alerted the U.S. Customs Service that the importing company had failed to obtain FDA approval to market Chinese medicines, so when the shipment arrived, Customs officials alerted the Cincinnati District. 

At FDA's discretion, an importer may be permitted to bring an illegal imported product into compliance with the law before a final decision is made as to whether it may be admitted. But in this case, the products' labels carried curative claims when no test data had been submitted to FDA for proof of safety and effectiveness.

Thus, they were detained by the district. 

One of the drugs, Chin-Liang

Balm, was labeled for use as a refreshment, and for headaches, skin itch, mosquito bites, scalds, and burns. The label of the other drug,

L-Cystine tablets, made claims of effectiveness in the treatment of chronic hepatitis and hair loss. 

Lots of other Chinese products were sold at the Ohio exhibit but the detention prevented the 51,000 threegram tins of balm and 400,000 tablets from being offered to the 2,700,000 people who attended the fair. The drug products, worth $13,000, were re-exported to China.

To Keep the Heart Beating 

A number of doctors in this country and abroad are watching their heart patients closely and with justified worry. The patients receiving this special attention have implanted pacemakers that were manufactured by American Technology, Inc., a 

California firm that has gone out of business and left behind a significant number of pacemakers implanted in patients with a failure rate that's of concern to the heart specialists.

FDA's Los Angeles District had inspected the firm several times since 1977 and had observed objectionable manufacturing practices. The investigators had advised the firm to correct the problems, and the firm had promised corrections. The firm also had recalled 782 pacemakers that were in danger of premature failure, which the firm claimed had resulted from one lot of defective components.

A pacemaker recall is unlike a recall of food or drugs. Pacemakers are surgically implanted in the human body-under the skin in the upper chest or abdominal wall-and the electrodes are either attached to the outside of the heart (on the muscle) or threaded through a vein and lodged inside the heart. Since any operation involves some risk, the surgical removal of a possibly defective pacemaker can be, in some cases, of more serious risk than leaving it in, depending on the patient's condition. 

So the recall by American Technology involved notifying its doctor customers that the pacemakers were in danger of premature failure and patients using them should be carefully monitored. 

At the time of the first inspections the "objectionable manufacturing practices" were not legally violations of FDA regulations. Congress had approved amendments to the FDC

Act-the Medical Device Amend ments of 1976-that would make such conditions a violation of the 

38 February 1981/ FDA Consumer

law; however, regulations necessary to enact the new legislation, i.e., Good Manufacturing Practices regulations (GMP's) for medical devices, had not yet gone into effect. In order to take action against American 

Technology's pacemakers, FDA would have had to prove in court that the devices were, without doubt, defective and dangerous to health.

Simply showing that they were manufactured under conditions that might render them hazardous was not sufficient. 

In December 1978 the GMP's for medical devices went into effect. The 

Los Angeles District made subsequent inspections of the firm. After an extensive investigation, FDA determined that the firm's previous recall notification of pacemakers should extend to all pacemakers manufactured by the firm prior to May 1977, since they were all subject to premature failure. FDA then ordered the firm to notify all consignees of these pacemakers concerning the problem under a new provision of the Medical

Device Amendments. 

Later, during an inspection of the firm, the Los Angeles District learned that two other models, currently being manufactured by the firm, were failing prematurely as a result of defects in these pacemakers.

The district also learned that the firm had not adequately complied with the 

FDA-ordered notification, and that the firm appeared to be marketing two other new models as "investigational" devices without adequate controls and without FDA approval. The 

Los Angeles District immediately issued an administrative detention order (another new provision under the

Medical Device Amendments) to prevent the firm from distributing the two models which were failing prematurely. At a subsequent meeting at the Bureau of Medical Devices, the firm's new management (the firm had changed hands several months earlier) agreed to stop production of the two models that were failing prematurely, and to immediately recall one of those models. The firm also agreed to correct the previously noted GMP violations, to comply with the FDA-ordered notification, to correct problems associated with their "investigational" devices, and to indefinitely detain (per a written agreement) all pacemakers already under a limited FDA detention. 

The Los Angeles District returned shortly to inspect the firm. More poor manufacturing conditions were documented. Investigators reported that employees were seen handling the fragile pacemaker components carelessly and that production and calibration procedures were either inadequate or nonexistent. The entire operation was labeled "sloppy" and "negligent." At the conclusion of the inspection, the investigators gave the firm's chief executive officer a ninepage list identifying at least 65 violations of GMP regulations. The executive officer expressed regret about the poor conditions, but said that since the management was new, more time was needed to make the necessary changes. He said the firm could not afford to "close its doors" until corrections were made and that although he would consider stopping current remaining production, he needed to sell the stock on hand.

The district and the Bureau of Medical Devices, however, believed the firm had had more than enough time. to deal with the problems. FDA filed for-and obtained-an injunction prohibiting the firm from selling and distributing pacemakers. The U.S. 

District Court for the Central District of California ordered American

Technology, Inc., to stop all distribution until it complied with GMP regulations, recalled pacemakers as 

FDA deemed necessary, destroyed or brought into compliance all pacemakers on hand as FDA deemed appropriate, and received FDA approval prior to distributing "investigational" devices. 

About the same time, the Internal 

Revenue Service had seized the firm's assets for overdue tax obligations. The IRS action was then stayed because of a larger lien against the firm by a bank. The firm's assets were turned over to the bank, and American Technology went out of business as a pacemaker manufacturer. These assets were subsequently purchased from the bank by another firm which, under an agreement with the district, voluntarily destroyed all of American Technology's stock of pacemakers along with related components. 

However, a large number of pacemakers many which were subject to premature failure-had been distributed and implanted and could endanger the heart patients using them. 

FDA sent letters to American Technology's consignees-over 800 physicians and 73 distributors, both foreign and domestic. The letters advised the consignees not to implant any pacemakers manufactured by 

American Technology, Inc., and requested status reports about the pacemakers the consignees had received.

Seizures and Postal Service Cases 

FILED SEIZURE ACTIONS charge violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and are initiated based upon FDA recommendations. A seizure action is commenced by the filing of a complaint in the U.S. district court where the goods are located. A U.S. marshal is then directed by the court to take possession of the goods, removing the product from commerce, until the matter is resolved. 

A total of 32 actions to remove from the consumer market products charged to be violative was reported in December. These included 7 seizures of foods: 1 involved a charge concerning poisonous and deleterious substances, 5 involved charges concerning contamination, and 1 involved a charge concerning economic and labeling violations. Other seizures included 2 of animal feed, 20 of drugs (including 11 of veterinary), and 3 of medical devices.

Selenium tablets, RNA with brewer's yeast tablets, Arthril selenium, copper & yucca plant combination tablets, Head Start vitamin-mineral & chromium proteinate tablets, and Earthquest oriental ginseng tablets, at 

Atlanta, N. Dist. Ga. 

Charged 9-13-77: while held by Braswell, Inc. (t/a Cosvetic Laboratories Inc., Earthquest Ltd., and Quest Research Inc.). Atlanta, Ga., the articles, labeled in part "Selenium . . . tablets. . . 25 mcg of Selenium from a special primary yeast Quest Research, Inc. 

Atlanta, Georgia," "Earthquest Oriental Ginseng tablets. . .Distributed by Earthquest Ltd. . . . Atlanta, Ga.." "RNA | 

RNA RNA with Brewers Yeast. . . tablets. . . 200 mg RNA 400 mg 

Brewers Yeast . . . Earthquest, Ltd. . . . Atlanta, Ga.." "Arthril vitamins. . . tablets. selenium (bound in yeast). copper (as

Copper Proteinate) Dried Yucca Plant Quest Research 

Atlanta, Ga.," and "Vitamins For Your Hair. . .Head Start tablets...Distributed by Cosvetic ... Atlanta, Georgia

Phase 1 Natural Vitamin-Mineral Complex. Plus: Brasium-273 

(A specially processed compound containing Chelated Trivalent Chromium Proteinate)," contained one or more of the following nonconforming food additives: ginseng, selenium, RNA, copper proteinate. dried yucca plant, and chelated trivalent chromium proteinate- 402(a)(2)(C); and the labeling of the Head Start vitamin-mineral tablets contained false and misleading claims that vitamins in general and the vitamins in the article per se would increase hair growth and would supply nutrients specifically and directly to the hair-403(a)(1). 

The Selenium tablets and the Arthril tablets were claimed by Quest 

Research Inc., Atlanta, Ga., and the Ginseng tablets and the RNA tablets were claimed by Earthquest Ltd., Atlanta, Ga. The claimants denied the charges. Cosvetic Laboratories Inc., also moved for a preliminary injunction against the Government, charging that the Government had seized a quantity of Head Start vitamins plus Brasium; that such claimant manufactured and distributed three formulations of Head Start vitamins, only one of which formulations contained Brasium-273; that FDA published and circulated the FDA 

Enforcement Report which referred to the seized product as "Head Start Vitamins for Your Hair," which confused such claimant's wholesale and retail customers into believing that all formulations for Head Start vitamins were subject to seizure, causing cancellation of purchase orders and product retainers. FDA promised a correction printed in later FDA Enforcement Report and the parties stipulated to the dismissal of the injunctive motions of Cosvetic Laboratories Inc. Subsequently, pursuant to stipulation of the parties, the action was dismissed without prejudice as to all products except the ginseng and the seized Head Start vitamin tablets, and the charges were dismissed except for the food additive charge against the ginseng and the charge of false and misleading labeling as to such Head Start vitamin tablets. 

Accordingly, the selenium tablets, RNA tablets, and Arthril tablets were ordered released to the claimants.

The parties served written interrogatories on each other. Subsequently, the parties entered into an agreement concerning "Earth quest Oriental Ginseng" and "Head Start Vitamins For Your Hair Phase 1 Natural Vitamin-Mineral Complex Plus: Brasium-273 Che lated Chromium Proteinate".

As part of the agreement, it was agreed 

44 February 1981 FDA Consumer

as follows: that "Head Start" was a valid trademark as used in connection with the marketing and distribution of the seized Head Start vitamin-mineral tablets; that hair follicles had specific nutrient requirements for cell division and growth; that the Head Start product's vitamins and minerals were presumed to be absorbed from the intestinal tract and available for use by body tissues, including hair follicles; that the Head Start product was marketed and distributed as a vitamin/ mineral product and should be so marketed and distributed in accordance with applicable FDA regulations; that Cosvetic Laboratories 

Inc. agreed that future labeling of the Head Start product would not make reference to the product's benefit to the hair in a misleading way; that Earthquest Ltd. conceded that the Ginseng capsules were adulterated as alleged and agreed to their destruction, but such agreement was not to preclude the sale of Ginseng Tea by Earthquest Ltd.: that one unresolved issue concerning the Head Start product remained in the case; and that such remaining issue was submitted to the court for determination. A consent decree of condemnation ordered the ginseng capsules destroyed.

In deciding the remaining issue in the case in favor of the Government, the court ruled as follows: "On September 13, 1977 the United States filed a complaint against 

'Earthquest Oriental Ginseng' and 'Head Start Vitamins for Your 

Hair' (hereinafter 'Head Start'), alleging that the former is an adulterated article of food within the meaning of 21 U.S.C. §342(a)(2)(C). and that the latter is a misbranded article of food within the meaning of 21 U.S.C. $343(a)(1). The United States, Earthquest Ltd. and 

Cosvetic Laboratories, Inc. (hereinafter the 'parties') have agreed to the entry of a final judgment in this action. "As to the 'Earthquest Oriental Ginseng. the parties have submitted to the Court a consent decree of condemnation and destruction. 

As to the 'Head Start,' however, an issue of fact remains to be decided. 

That question is before the Court for determination on the basis of affidavits of experts. The issue is described as follows by the parties: 'Claimant, Cosvetic Laboratories, Inc., contends that the human body has priorities in its use of nutrients and that the life sustaining organs such as the brain, heart. kidneys and etc. get priority for nutrients over and above non-life sustaining tissues, such as hair follicles. Because of the hair follicles' low priority, nutrients which are in short supply are shut off from the hair follicles and shunted to other areas of higher priority. The United States of America disagrees with this principle and is of the belief that this principle is scientifically wrong. 

Consequently, the United States cannot agree to labeling information based upon this principle.' The contention of the United States as to 'Head Start,' is set forth in the complaint in this action. . . . "The affidavit of Robert B. Bradfield, and the articles which accompany it, provide sufficient evidence for the Court to find (1) that the human body does establish priorities for use of nutrients when nutrients are in short supply and that preference is given to the more important life-sustaining tissues and processes in such a case, and (2) that hair follicles are among the first of tissues to be affected by protein-calorie malnutrition because they have a low priority relative to other tissues and processes and because they are tissues with a very high rate of protein synthesis. The affidavits of Eugene J. Van Scott and Alfred Jay Bollet, submitted in support of the United States' position, do not dispute such a finding. "The Court is not satisfied, however, that a finding that the human body has priorities in its use of nutrients and that preference is given to tissues and processes other than hair follicles when nutrients are in short supply is dispositive of the issue of whether 'Head Start' is a misbranded article of food. First, there is evidence before the Court that the most common types of hair loss in the United States are unrelated to dietary intake. Second, it appears that it is only in circumstances of extreme nutritional deprivation that hair follicles are affected by lack of nutrients and that in such cases an improved diet, rather than a formulation such as 'Head Start, is necessary. There is no evidence of a situation in which the body has enough nutrients for all tissues and processes except hair follicles, even though the logic of Cosvetic's theory might suggest that to be a possibility. Third, the studies described by Robert B. Bradfield concern protein-calorie malnutrition. The product which is the subject of this action purports to be a vitamin-mineral supplement. Even if Cosvetic's general premise is true, there is no evidence that hair follicles are among the first tissues to be deprived of vitamins and minerals when those nutrients are in short supply. Finally, the percentage of the normal daily requirement of the nutrients present in 'Head Start' is very low, and there is no evidence of what nutrients are in fact essential to the health of hair follicles. "Accordingly, this Court finds that representations that 'Head Start' will increase hair growth and will supply needed nutrients specifically and directly to the hair are false and misleading. This Court further finds that Head Start' is a misbranded article of food within the meaning of 21 U.S.C. $343(a)(1). . . ." (F.D.C. No. 61389; S. No. 

77-31-425 et al.; N.J. No. 18)

Subsequently, the parties consented to an order that adjudged that the inspection warrant had been disobeyed previously, that such disobedience was a contempt of court, that the costs of FDA's attempts to obtain compliance were taxable to the party in contempt, and that, accordingly, FDA was to be paid $1,750. Shoals Cheese Corp., and William H. Jones, president, Florence, N. Dist. Ala.

The court issued a temporary restraining order enjoining the complained of violations. Upon the proceedings' findings, the court issued a permanent injunction enjoining the complained of violations. (Inj.

medicine; that the regulations and accompanying text unconstitutionally interfered with the physician-patient relationship and deprived the plantiffs of their rights to practice medicine in accordance with their best medical judgment; that the regulations and accompanying text were promulgated without any rational basis for a finding that current regulations were inadequate or that physicians had not adequately informed patients of the advantages and risks of particular estrogenic prescription drugs and created the inconsistent presumption that patients were not presently receiving adequate information; and that the regulations were therefore arbitrary, capricious, and an improper exercise of rulemaking authority.

This action, along with a similar action in the District of Delaware. were litigated until the court stayed this action, saying: "The action was filed in this Court on July 25, 1977. On July 29, 1977, an action was filed in the United States District Court for the District of Delaware seeking declaratory and injunctive relief from the same regulation that is at issue in this case. The complaint in the 

Delaware action was filed by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association against Defendants Food & Drug Administration; Joseph 

A. Califano, Jr.. Secretary of Health. Education & Welfare; and

Donald Kennedy, . 

"On August 12, 1977, the defendants in the Delaware case moved to transfer that action to this district, or, in the alternative, to stay or dismiss said action with leave to the plaintiff therein to resume its litigation upon final determination of this case. The plaintiff in the 

Delaware case filed a motion for preliminary injunction on September 12, 1977; a similar motion was filed in this case by the Plaintiffs herein on September 13, 1977. On October 5, 1977, the Delaware court rendered its opinion denying the defendants' motion to transfer, dismiss or stay the Delaware case in favor of the case in this district and denying the Delaware plaintiff's application for preliminary injunction. On October 7, 1977, the Defendants in this case filed a Motion and Brief to Dismiss or Stay, requesting that the Court dismiss this proceeding or stay the same pending conclusion of the Delaware litigation. The aforementioned October 5, 1977 opinion of the Delaware court is attached to Defendants' Motion. Plaintiffs have filed a Brief in Opposition to Defendants' Motion and Brief to Dismiss or Stay. 

"The basis of the Motion to Dismiss or Stay filed herein is that there are now pending in the District of Delaware and the Eastern District of Louisiana actions involving the same issues as are involved in this case. Defendants claim that all groups affected by the challenged regulation, to include manufacturers, retailers, pharmacists, physicians and consumers, are represented in the Delaware litigation. "In opposition to Defendants' motion, Plaintiffs claim that there are factors existing in this case which mitigate against it being stayed while the Delaware action goes forward. Plaintiffs state that this 

Court, as the Court whose action was first filed, has priority: that the parties in the Delaware and Oklahoma cases are not identical: that simultaneous litigation in Delaware and Oklahoma would not tax FDA's manpower abilities; that where the question is one of national importance, the appellate court may welcome the interim expression of views by more than one lower court; that there is no reason to expect protracted litigation in this case whereas it would appear that it would be four to nine months before a decision in the Delaware case would be rendered; that the rights of the Plaintiffs in this case are not receiving attention in the Delaware litigation; that the issues presented in this case are apparently not being considered by the Delaware court; and that Plaintiffs are unable to intervene in the 

Delaware case as venue would be improper. "Defendants' Motion, insofar as it seeks dismissal of this action. is denied for the reason that it does not assert any of the defenses enumerated in Rule 12(b), Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. . . . 

"However, inherent in the power of every Court to control its docket is the power to stay proceedings in the interest of justice. ... The granting of a stay ordinarily lies within the sound discretion of the district court. "In exercising its discretion in determining whether a stay of this case pending the conclusion of the Delaware litigation would be proper, the Court notes that the Oklahoma and Delaware cases involve the same issues; that a full airing of the issues in this case is occurring in the Delaware litigation; that the Plaintiffs involved in the 

Oklahoma and Delaware cases represent substantially the same viewpoint; that the Delaware court has spent considerable time and effort in advancing the Delaware litigation to its present stage and has clearly indicated that it will proceed with its case notwithstanding the first filed rule; that the interests of judicial economy seek to avoid duplication of effort; that the Delaware litigation is now at a more advanced stage than this case; that the Plaintiffs herein may intervene and share prosecution costs in Delaware without objection from Defendants; and that, though there is a stay of this action, Plaintiffs herein will still be entitled to their day in Court. "Accordingly, the Court finds and concludes that in the interest of judicial comity and economy, this Court should exercise judicial restraint and stay the instant action subject to the trial judgment on the action pending before the United States District Court for the District of Delaware. Accordingly, Defendants' Motion to Dismiss should be overruled and their Motion to Stay should be sustained."

The plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal and moved for an injunction pending the appeal. In denying the motion for an injunction pending the appeal, the court said: 

"The Plaintiffs' Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal from Order in the District Court is hereby denied. It is not believed from the exposure of the Court to this case that Plaintiffs have demonstrated a strong showing of prevailing on the merits on appeal, that irreparable injury to Plaintiffs is present if the Motion is not granted, that if the Motion is granted substantial harm could come to the users of estrogen and the public interest dictates against granting the Motion. The Court by an Order of this date has stayed this proceeding for the reasons set out therein. The Court is not inclined to disturb this stay Order which is the thrust of the above mentioned Motion. Virginia Petroleum 

Job. Ass'n v. Federal Power Com'n, 259 F.2d 921 (D.C. Cir. 1958)." 

However, the plaintiffs were granted their application to intervene in the action in the District of Delaware. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed upon stipulation of the parties; and, upon motion of the plaintiffs, this action was dismissed for the reason that the claims and contentions raised in this case would be realleged in the action in the 

District of Delaware. (Misc. No. 443; N.J. No. 37)

FDA Consumer / March 1981 / 1

Hearing Aids Tested 

Update How to recognize and treat hearing loss was discussed in Tuning In On Hearing Aids in the May 

1980 FDA CONSUMER. The article pointed out that most hearing problems can be helped by drugs, surgery or, in some cases by hearing aids, which are regulated as medical devices by FDA. Here's an update.

A special FDA study of hearing aids has found that of 21 models tested, 4 had performance problems serious enough to warrant special manufac turing inspections by the Agency. Twelve others had only minor performance or labeling deficiencies judged not serious enough to impair the effectiveness of the aids. Five models presented no problems.

The testing was conducted in a specially designed "quiet room" at the Agency's Winchester Engineering and Analytical Center (WEAC) in Winchester, Mass. FDA asked 21 manufacturers to lend three units of their most popular nondirectional behind-the-ear model to WEAC for the tests. (Nondirectional behind-the-ear models account for 30 to 35 percent of hearing aids sold in the United States.) All 21 firms representing all foreign and domestic companies selling this type of hearing aid in the United States agreed.

The tests measured the devices according to procedures set by the Acoustical Society of America and adopted by FDA in its 1977 hearing aid regulations. WEAC also checked to see if labeling information required was complete and accurate.

FDA informed all the firms of the test results. 

Besides the five models with no performance or labeling problems, four models had only minor labeling problems, such as a hard-to-read marking of the year of manufacture or improperly marked battery poles.

The remaining 12 models-6 foreign and 6 domestic-failed to measure up to values listed in the labeling. (Although FDA has not set performance specifications for hearing aids, manufacturers must test their products for certain factors and list the results in the labeling.)

Two models showed excessive distortion. Three had unsatisfactory output of the induction coilthe part that helps the user hear over the telephone. One model took too long to respond to abrupt changes in sound levels. FDA concluded that the failure of these models to function as labeled would not adversely affect their performance. 

Hearing aids from two U.S. and two foreign firms, however, were found to be so seriously flawed that FDA conducted special manufacturing plant inspections. The inspections turned up deficiencies in the manufacturing process and methods of product testing. As a result, FDA sent regulatory letters to three of the firms, warning of legal action unless the deficiencies were promptly corrected.

In addition to the inspections and regulatory letters, six letters of adverse findings were issued for the less serious deficiencies. (The Agency was prepared to send a seventh letter but the firm had stopped making the model in question.) All manufacturers notified of deficiencies by FDA have promised to correct the problems. 

FDA's Bureau of Medical Devices, which regulates hearing aids, found the study results so useful that it intends to work with WEAC to conduct similar tests of all in-the-ear hearing aids, which account for about 40 percent of the aids sold in the United States. Those tests should begin later this year.

Consumer Forum 

"Update" (FDA CONSUMER, July-August 1980) 

quotes Dr. Lester Crawford on the alleged dangers of using DES implants in beef production, because DES "was long ago shown to be carcinogenic" (in 

1944). Natural estrogens were even earlier (1939) shown to be carcinogenic by the same test (mammary tumors in mice). The exclusion of DEStreated beef by Canada, Argentina and Australia kept out foreign competition, just as did the ban on Argentine beef from entering the U.S.A. 

The "myth of the pioneering spirit" that Dr. 

Crawford blamed for using DES was actually the manifestation of skepticism, because the FDA authorized the implantation procedure more than 15 years ago, and suddenly decided that it should be banned. The decision was highly controversial because DES could not be detected in the muscle meat of implanted animals; its detection in liver was dubious, and estrogens are produced in the body and are ingested in all diets in quantities that, in sum, are orders of magnitude higher than the amounts that would be obtained by consuming meat from implanted cattle.

The dose-response curve is not a myth. Carcinogenic hazard is dose-dependent, and this has specifically been shown for DES in animal tests. 

FDA CONSUMER does not do consumers a service by quoting Dr. Crawford's petulant and rhetorical press release, to arouse fears of cancer from previous consumption of beef. In a letter, Dec. 12, 1975, Dr. W. Gary Flamm, National Cancer Institute stated that "the upper limit of risk attendant to 1.5 mg of DES is equivalent to a lifetime exposure to one puff from a single cigarette". At 0.25 parts per billion, which is a pessimistic estimate of the DES content of liver from implanted cattle, 1.5 mg would be present in 6 tons of such liver. 

Thomas H. Jukes

Department of Biophysics and Medical Physics 

University of California at Berkeley 

Berkeley, Calif.

Dr. Jukes is an eminent nutritionist, who disagrees with FDA on the safety of using DES in animals. He testified on behalf of the DES manufacturers in the 1977 FDA hearings, and appeared this past fall as a witness for a feedlot whose beef had been seized by USDA because it was alleged to have been the product of animals illegally implanted with DES after the DES withdrawal took effect. 

FDA's actions against DES in food have not been, as Dr. Jukes alleges, "sudden". They began in 1959 with the discovery of DES in chickens, which resulted in the Bell v. Goddard decision in 

1966; and continued in the 1970's, culminating in the Commissioner's decisions to withdraw all DES 

New Animal Drug Applications in 1972 and 1973.

These decisions were set aside in January 1974 by the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which held that FDA had not afforded the DES manufacturers enough of an opportunity for a hearing. The FDA held a full evidentiary hearing in 1977-1978, which included Dr. 

Jukes' testimony, both written and oral. Dr. Jukes' views on the risk of DES in food were considered and rejected by FDA Commissioner Kennedy in his decision (published in the September 21, 1979 FED- 

ERAL REGISTER). Two of the manufacturers, Hess & Clark division of Rhône-Poulenc and Vineland, appealed the Commissioner's decision to the United

States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which affirmed the Commissioner's decision and the DES withdrawal in its opinion issued on November 24, 1980. (The manufacturers have requested a reconsideration by that court.)

Dr. Jukes' quotation of Dr. Flamm's comparison of the risks of occurring DES in beef and the risks of smoking is accurate, but that comparison was based on pre-1975 data. Subsequent risk estimates indicate that DES exposures as low as one part per trillion may be associated with risks of one cancer per million consumer lifetimes. Dr. Crawford's point on dose-response was not to allege that there is no dose-response curve, but that it provides little comfort for those who involuntarily consume substances such as DES. ! 1 1

MEDICAL DEVICE Home Is Where The Heart Is 

For a number of reasons, consumers are becoming less willing to rely solely on physicians and other health professionals for medical care. As these consumers swell the ranks of the self-care movement, they provide a growing market for a wide variety of home-use medical deviceseverything from blood pressure monitors to cancer screening kits. These products can be valuable tools in self-care, but their use by laymen is not without limits. 

Sw ixty-eight-year-old Harvey Aspen and his 65-year-old wife, Sarah, sat down at the kitchen table and began their daily ritual. Harvey rolled up his left sleeve. Sarah, following the directions that came with the instrument (and remembering some helpful tips supplied by Harvey's doctor), wrapped the cloth-covered rubber cuff around

Harvey's arm and began squeezing the rubber ball to inflate the cuff. Then, opening the valve, she listened through the stethoscope for the sound of blood rushing through the artery and then for the sudden weakening of the sound as Harvey's heart rested between beats. 

The ritual went just the same as it did every day, but today the results were different. The instrument showed that Harvey's blood pressure was considerably higher than usual. But Harvey knew what to do and what not to do. His doctor had told him that monitoring his blood pressure daily could be a big help in the control of his hypertension but that he should not be tempted to "play doctor" himself and change the dose of his medication. 

Instead, Harvey called his doctor, reported the unusual reading, and made an appointment to have the doctor double check to see what should be done. 

Judy Thomas, 38 years old and mother of three, was caught by the headline of the full-page magazine ad: "Millions of women find it easier to face cancer of the cervix than face a Pap test in a doctor's office.' 

The ad drew Judy's attention; she had been troubled for some time by "spotting" between her menstrual periods. She had heard that this could be an early sign of cancer of the cervix or uterus. Although she was concerned, money was tight and she hated to pay $20 or $25 to visit a gynecologist for a Pap test. She also didn't relish the thought of subjecting herself to such an “intimate" exam anyway.

So the ad seemed to be written just for her. For only $9, it offered a mail-order "Pap test" that could tell her whether she had cervical cancer. She could do the test herself. And it must be all right, she thought, for the ad said it was approved by the Government and "leading" doctors. 

Judy mailed her check and a few days later received the test kit with instructions on how to collect a vaginal specimen. She completed the procedure with ease and mailed the specimen back to the company. In a few more days, she received a report in the mail from the company's laboratory: The test was negative. Judy was relieved, for now she knew that whatever her problem was, it was not cervical cancer.

What Judy did not know was that, despite the assertions in the ad, the test was not a Pap test at all. And it was not approved by the Government because, unlike the medically accepted Pap test, it too often gave false negative results, which could lull women like Judy Thomas into a false sense of security and, despite warning symptoms such as spotting, cause them to delay seeking the medical attention they urgently needed. 

Harvey and Sarah Aspen and Judy Thomas are not real people. But their health problems and the ways they dealt with them are very real for many Americans. In fact, more and more of us are beginning to do what the Aspens and Judy Thomas did: Acquire devices and diagnostics-tools of the medical trade, as it were for our own use so we can have a greater hand in our own health care.

The self-care movement has many benefits for health, and for the pocketbook. But there are limits to the kind and degree of self-care a layman should undertake. Even though many of the "tools" are easy to obtain, the same cannot always be said of the skill and knowledge needed to use them properly. And consumers must beware of quack devices such as Judy Thomas's so-called Pap test —that falsely claim to be just what the doctor ordered.

The growing use of medical devices by laymen is not surprising, considering that consumers have long used over-the-counter drugs to help relieve a variety of health problems. In 1977, the public spent more than $4.2 billion for aspirin, cough syrups, and countless other nonprescription medications.

The medicine cabinets and closets of American households have always contained a few basic medical devices certainly a fever thermometer and often a hot water bottle, a heating pad, and perhaps even a vaporizer to help ease the misery of colds and the flu. But in recent years a good many medical devices and test kits that traditionally had been found only in doctors' offices, hospitals, or clinical laboratories have found their way into millions of homes. Consumers with little or no medical training are buying and using not only blood pressure monitors and stethoscopes but also speculums for vaginal examinations, otoscopes (flashlight-like devices for looking in the ear), pregnancy test kits, and even cancer test kits (which generally call for the consumer to mail a specimen to a laboratory and receive results, by mail, a few days later). At least one firm is marketing, to the general public, a complete doctor's black bag with just about everything you'd expect to find inside except a prescription pad.

The growing popularity of home medical devices is creating a big business. Sales of home blood pressure kits 1 

FDA Consumer / March 1981 / 5

WARSBALLT HEALTH 

A Family "Black Bag," marketed by Marshall Electronics, Inc., exemplifies the growing use by consumers of medical equipment once found only in doctors' offices, hospitals or clinics. The bag contains many of the same instruments found in the familiar kits carried by physicians: an otoscope for ear and nose exams, oral and rectal fever thermometers, exam light, a dental reflector/ tongue depressor, stethoscope and sphygmanometer for measuring blood pressure. Self-help medical information also is included. were expected to reach more than $30 million last year, according to AMERICAN DRUGGIST magazine. Pregnancy test kits were heading toward record sales of some $40 million, with a prediction of about $100 million a year by 1984.

The trend is not limited to doctors' "tools"; even dentists instruments are being promoted to the general public. Electric tooth buffers and plaque detection kits, that temporarily stain the areas of plaque buildup on the teeth to aid in brushing (and are regulated as drugs by FDA), are two such products that can be used safely with fairly good results. The same cannot be said of do-it-yourself denture repair kits. They may be useful for a "quick fix" until the individual can see a dentist, but it's almost impossible to get a fit good enough for continued use without making a dental mold to assure proper shape of the repaired bridge.

What accounts for this surge in popularity of home-use health instruments? Probably the most important factor is the growing public interest in health matters, particularly increasing awareness of the benefits of preventive medicine. People are realizing more and more that their health is largely in their own hands. Lowell Levin, professor of public health at Yale University, stressed the importance of this trend during a symposium on self-care last year in Washington, D.C.: "Probably the most significant event in health care since the discovery of the germ theory of disease is the discovery of the 'self,' he said. "This discovery portends a revolution, a movement from the professional construction of the health reality to lay, or social, control." 99 

Money, too, is a factor in the self-care movement.

Many consumers have reacted much the same to rising health care costs as to higher prices for other goods and services: they've decided to do-it-themselves-and-save. By purchasing a few tools, many a driveway mechanic figures to save the cost of automobile tuneups and oil changes. 

Likewise, some consumers have turned to self-care-with home-use medical devices-to help cut the costs of office visits and lab tests.

Convenience plays a part in the self-care movement, too, of course. For example, diabetics have for many years been able to care for themselves by using chemically treated test strips to measure the level of glucose in their urine. (Although the procedure is simple and relatively inexpensive, diabetics are cautioned to use the test strips only under the advice and supervision of their physicians; many factors can interfere with the performance of the strips and physicians should discuss these limitations with their patients.)

More recently, diabetics have been able to measure their glucose more accurately by testing samples of blood rather than urine. Although the equipment is more expensive and the technique a little more difficult, studies have shown that many diabetics can perform the tests quite adequately with results as accurate as those obtained in laboratories.

Although the blood and urine glucose tests can be very helpful in controlling diabetes, they are not intended to diagnose the disease. FDA has taken action against test kits that have made such diagnostic claims in their labeling. 

Such actions point out the limits to the use of medical devices by consumers. Self-care and self-treatment are not the same as self-diagnosis and self-cure. The old adage that anyone who treats himself has a fool for a doctor and an ass for a patient-is too extreme, considering today's educated consumers. Nonetheless, the Biblical advice, "Physician, heal thyself" should not be updated to read, "Patient, heal thyself."

Accurate diagnosing of an illness requires not just medical instruments and laboratory test kits. It also demands the training and knowledge necessary to conduct the procedure properly and to interpret the results. Even something like swabbing a throat to check for a strep infection is not as easy as it seems. Untrained consumers could use the swab and obtain nothing more than a sample of saliva instead of the bacterial culture needed to make a diagnosis.

At-home use of even simple devices such as otoscopes has limitations, too. It's easy enough to peer inside the ear, but a doctor's instruction is needed to tell the layman what to look for and how to interpret what's seen. 

Laboratory diagnostic products are generally used by trained individuals. However, the consumer can use products that detect the possible presence of a disease. For instance, kits consisting of special containers-can be purchased to screen for the presence of "occult" or hidden blood in the feces-a tipoff of possible cancer of the colon or rectum. A small fecal sample is sealed in the special container and mailed to a laboratory. If occult blood is detected, the person is advised to see a physician for further tests to determine whether the problem is due to cancer or some other condition, such as ulcers or colitis. 

Although the test is useful as a screening procedure, those using it should be aware of its limitations. A West 

German study found that one such test kit failed to detect the presence of blood in more than 58 percent of samples from patients who did, in fact, have colorectal cancer. Another study showed 35 percent of false negatives. 

6 March 1981 / FDA Consumer

The main reason for the high rate of false negatives is that even those with colorectal cancer may not have occult blood in the feces at all times. For best results, three successive fecal samples should be analyzed. 

Because of its extraordinarily high rate of false negative results (not to mention the false statements in its advertising), a mail-order test that claimed to be able to detect cervical cancer (the same so-called Pap check used by "Judy Thomas") was recalled from the market at

FDA's insistence. The Agency was concerned that the incorrect results could cause the patient to delay getting a medical examination that could provide an accurate diagnosis of cancer.

Even the best screening tests are occasionally wrong. 

So a negative result should never be taken as assurance that a serious disease is not present. It can be dangerously foolish to trust test results to the point of ignoring troublesome symptoms. Physicians use lab tests as only one kind of information in making a diagnosis; usually more important is the patient's medical history, particularly the current symptoms, and a physical examination. 

Early detection and treatment of serious illness can be delayed not only by incorrect test results but also by the use of devices that may treat symptoms while masking the actual disease. Hearing aids can be extremely helpful to many who are hard of hearing. But they should be used only after a physician has determined that the hearing loss is not due to a condition that requires medical treatment. For that reason, FDA requires that before a person can be sold a hearing aid, a physician must evaluate the hearing impairment. The patient may waive medical evaluation, but hearing aid sellers are prohibited from encouraging a person to do so and must advise the patient that it is not in his or her best health interest. 

Tinnitus is another hearing problem that can cause similar difficulties in self-treatment. Tinnitus is a ringing or buzzing in the ear and affects many people from time to time, especially after they've been subjected to loud noises. But for an estimated 2 to 6 million people, it is a serious, chronic, and extremely distressing condition. 

Medical devices called tinnitus maskers have been developed that emit a single or varying tone. Some are as small as a hearing aid (and can be worn inside the ear); others are the size of table radios.

Tinnitus maskers have been promoted for sale directly to the public. Although they can provide relief, they also in some cases may be masking a serious disease, a tumor in the ear, for example. Also, most tinnitus sufferers experience some hearing loss, which can grow worse if left untreated. For those reasons, tinnitus maskers should be used only on the advice of a physician. 

Likewise, home-use blood pressure machines can be valuable when used as recommended by a physician, with proper instruction by a health professional. But FDA cautions against using results obtained from blood pressure monitors as the basis for self diagnosis. Therapy should not be altered on the basis of a self-reading, nor should the physician's instructions be ignored. Not only is there the possibility that the machines may not be accurate, but also an individual's blood pressure can vary due to a number of factors, such as age, emotions, and exertion. Thus, a single casual reading may not accurately characterize a person's condition. 

Some medical devices used for legitimate medical purposes by health professionals are advertised for sale to laymen for unproven and sometimes even unsafe purposes. Muscle stimulators, for example, are used with good results by health professionals to prevent muscle deterioration in stroke patients and for several other proven purposes. But some companies have been promoting their use in figure and beauty salons for weight reduction, "cellulite" removal, bust development, and other quack cures. FDA has declared that muscle stimulators are prescription medical devices and has taken action against those promoted for lay use, including use in beauty salons.

Whether a device can be sold directly to consumers without a prescription generally depends on whether adequate directions can be written for safe and effective use of the product by a layman, or whether specialized training or supervision is needed. Claims that the product is useful in treating specific medical conditions also weigh in 

FDA's decision. For example, biofeedback equipment can help a person alter a physical condition by monitoring and mentally adjusting a certain body function, such as heartbeat or brain waves. FDA has determined that if a biofeedback device is labeled solely for monitoring or for helping a person simply to relax or exercise better, it may be sold directly to consumers. Such is the case with electronic pulse monitors sold to joggers to help them set a proper pace to get the most out of their running. 

But if claims are made that a biofeedback device is useful in treating specific medical conditions, such as relieving migraine headaches or asthma, then it is considered a prescription device. Prescription devices are to be used only by or under the supervision of a health professional trained to achieve the intended result and able to provide information to the patient about the device, its benefits, and its risks.

As the self-care movement continues to grow, patient information about medical devices will become more and more important. Dr. John Fry, of Great Britain's Royal

College of General Practitioners, speaking at last year's self-care symposium, said that “self-care . . . must be taught and learned. It is an integral part of health care; teaching self-care should start in school days and continue through life."

There is every reason to believe that the self-care trend, including the use of more and more "tools of the trade," will continue its upswing. Recent reports in the medical press tell of plans by medical device firms to market to consumers emergency medical equipment, midwife kits, and tests for anemia, for cholesterol, and for urinary tract infection. Yale's Levin predicts that "with increasing interest in home care and lay self-care for minor illnesses and injuries and in routine care of chronic disease, we can expect to see more testing of this technology and its vigorous marketing. Indeed, the home itself is being newly appreciated as a medical care facility." 

We can't all become staff physicians and nurses in this hospital-of-the-home, of course. But, with the right "tools" and proper instruction, we can become active members of the medical team, instead of mere spectators in our own health care. 

Bill Rados is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

Coughing: Beneficial Misery 

Coughing can be irritating both to the cougher and to those around him. But there are times when a cough should not be suppressed, for it is a vital reflex action-nature's way of keeping the body's airways clean. by Annabel Hecht 

The conductor lowers his baton, the music fades, and the inevitable begins. A barrage of staccato coughs breaks the stillness of the concert hall. Is this a show of disrespect for the performers or just plain rudeness? Actually neither, for despite the glares and "shsss's" of other music lovers, once some coughs have started they are beyond the cougher's control. They simply have to all come out. 

Coughing is a vital reflex actionnature's way of clearing the airways of some irritating substance. Coughing can occur in perfectly healthy people and be nothing more than the body's response to a tickle in the throat. It also is a symptom of a variety of diseases, and in some cases, a person's inability to cough can be life threatening.

It is generally believed that a cough starts when "receptors" or nerve endings in the respiratory tract are irritated. The receptors send a signal to the cough center in the brain which in turn sends a signal to the muscles in the chest which produce the cough. An alternative, though not widely held theory, holds that the cough reflex is not triggered directly by the irritation, but rather by a constriction of the bronchial tubes that were stimulated by the irritant. 

However the cough reflex is stimulated, the act of coughing occurs in three phases. First there is a deep inhalation of air, filling the lungs. The glottis, the upper part of the larynx containing the vocal chords, opens wide to allow this air to get into the lungs quickly. In the second phase, the glottis closes while air pressure within the chest builds up. In the final phase, the glottis opens and the trapped air is expelled explosively, at speeds up to 500 or 600 miles an hour, carrying with it the material that caused the irritation. While this is happening, the vocal chords and the lining of the larynx vibrate, helping to shake loose the irritating material. 

Not all coughs originate in the respiratory tract. Receptors that can stimulate the cough reflex also are located in the nose, sinuses, stomach, heart, and even the ear. Tickle the outside of the ear and you may get a cough. 

There are two general types of cough. One is the dry, irritative, nonproductive cough, so called because there is no mucus or phlegm to spit out. The other is the loose, productive cough that gets its name from the fact that it is triggered by large amounts of secretions in the bronchial passages. Coughs can be transient and self-limiting-that is, they will disappear in a short time, usually without help from medication. On the other hand, coughs can hang on for a long time and become persistent and chronic.

A dry nonproductive cough can develop from breathing the dry air of overheated rooms as well as from inhaling irritating gases, dusts, or other foreign substances that sneak past the body's primary defenses in the nose and mouth. This type of cough is generally not long lasting, but it can be prolonged because the rapid expulsion of air during the act of coughing continually irritates the throat.

The common cold is probably the most frequent cause of short-term coughs, which can be either nonproductive or productive. Smoking is considered the most common cause of the persistent, chronic cough that can come from direct irritation of the bronchial passages or from damage to the lung's cleaning mechanism.

Thus the smoker is more likely to get upper respiratory infections that pave 

8/ March 1981 / FDA Consumer

the way for more serious respiratory diseases. Nonsmokers also can develop a chronic cough if they have postnasal drip from sinus and allergy difficulties or from enlarged adenoids.

A cough also may be a symptom of a number of serious illnesses, including measles, influenza, psittacosis (a disease carried by infected parakeets or parrots), and both types of pneumonia-mycoplasmal and pneumococcal. Chronic bronchitis and emphysema may get their start in several ways, but usually the first symptom is a chronic productive cough. Some bronchitis and emphysema patients may have a chronic cough for years with no other symptoms.

Coughing is also associated with tuberculosis, and when the heroine of a play or opera coughs delicately behind her fan chances are the luckless lady will die of the disease before the final curtain. Actually, the early stages of TB may be without symptoms or, if there are any, they may be no more than fatigue, weight loss, vague chest pains, and a mild cough.

The persistent, productive cough of tuberculosis comes in the advanced stages of the disease. 

As the name suggests, cough is a prominent feature of the once devastating disease of childhood-whooping cough. The "whoop" itself is not a cough, but the sound made by a deep inhalation of air following a series of 15 to 20 short coughs of increasing intensity. 

Patients with cardiac failure often experience coughing stimulated by congestion in the lungs and bronchial tubes. 

A cough may be initiated by a physical condition such as nasal polyps or infected tonsils. Impacted earwax or irritation of the eardrum by hair also have been associated with chronic nonproductive cough. Rare cases of cough have resulted from irritation of receptors in the pleura (the sac surrounding the lungs), diaphragm, pericardium (the sac surrounding the heart), and the stomach. 

Then there is the cough that's "all in the mind," the so-called psychogenic cough often seen in older children and adolescents. This cough usually develops when the child has some emotional or school problem. It is described as "barky and brassy," with a sound resembling a fog horn. 

Psychogenic cough is not exclusive to children, however, and adults under emotional stress also may experience the characteristic paroxysms of dry nonproductive coughing that leave them exhausted. Fortunately, the psychogenic cough does not occur during sleep. 

Although coughing serves a useful purpose in helping rid the lungs of irritants, complications such as vomiting, loss of sleep, loss of appetite, fever, and headache can result. 

Because of the tremendous pressure that builds up in the chest and the force with which the air is expelled, severe coughing can lead to ruptures of the muscles that support the abdomen, rupture of some blood vessels, rib fractures, and sometimes loss of consciousness.

On the other side of the coin, the inability to cough also is a serious matter. If the lungs are not cleared of foreign matter, the individual will be open to respiratory infection.

Some patients with debilitating diseases may be unable to get up the strength to cough. Those with chronic obstructive lung diseases may have difficulty coughing because of lung damage. Such patients may need special treatment to help them get rid of secretions in their lungs. Unconsciousness or a head injury can pose a special threat by causing loss of the cough reflex capability. 

What to do about a cough depends on what causes it. A smoker's cough, for instance, usually will stop when the smoking habit is kicked. Removing a tickling hair in the ear will solve that kind of cough problem. An antihistamine will put an end to postnasal drip. The dry, nonproductive cough that goes along with the common cold should disappear when the cold gets better and in many cases can be controlled without any drugs at all. 

Nonmedical cough remedies that many experts recommend include sucking on a hard candy or lozenge to increase the flow of saliva or drinking liquids to keep the throat lubricated. Steam from a vaporizer, hot shower, or a tea kettle helps loosen secretions in the bronchial passages and makes them easier to cough up.

Keeping moisture in the air indoors with various humidifying devices can help keep throats from becoming dry.

When the dry nonproductive cough becomes too annoying, exhausts the cougher or robs him and his family of much needed sleep, relief may be obtained from nonprescription medicines, called antitussives (from the 

Latin word tussis, meaning cough).

An antitussive works by depressing the cough center in the brain. Codeine is one of the most commonly used antitussives. Although it is a narcotic, there is no danger of psychological and physical dependence when codeine is used in the recommended dose for cough control. 

Stringent controls have been put on the sale of codeine in nonprescription cough medicines to assure that it is not misused. 

An expert advisory panel, set up by FDA to review ingredients in over-the-counter (OTC) cough and cold remedies, reported in September 1976 that codeine is a safe and effective OTC antitussive, but warned that it may cause or aggravate constipation and should not be given to children taking other drugs except on the advice of a physician. Cough remedies containing codeine should not be taken by people with chronic pulmonary (lung) disease except on the advice of a physician.

A non-narcotic antitussive considered safe and effective by the expert advisory panel is dextromethorphan which-like codeine-acts on the 

10 March 1981/ FDA Consumer

cough center in the brain. Taken at the recommended dose, dextromethorphan produces few adverse reactions and these are usually mild and limited to drowsiness and upset stomach. 

Diphenhydramine hydrochloride, the first antihistamine to be developed in the United States, was a third ingredient the cough-cold advisory panel said was safe and effective in OTC cough remedies. FDA, however, has not given its final approval for over-the-counter sale of this drug, and it is currently available by prescription only. Drowsiness is a major side effect associated with diphenhydramine hydrochloride, which also tends to have a drying effect, creating problems for those who need to cough to clear bronchial passageways. 

While antitussives are useful in stilling the dry, nagging kind of cough, they should never be used to control a loose, productive cough, such as that associated with asthma, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema.

In these diseases it is important to keep the airways clear. Suppressing the cough reflex will only make matters worse by slowing down or preventing the natural clearing process. 

Another type of cough medicine is the expectorant, used to encourage removal of secretions from the bronchial airways by reducing their thickness or by increasing the amount of respiratory tract secretions. There are many ingredients in cough remedies that are claimed to be expectorants, such as guaifenesin, terpin hydrate, iodides, or syrup of ipecac, but none is really effective, according to the cough-cold advisory panel. Further testing was recommended to establish whether these drugs can do the job.

Many over-the-counter cold remedies are combinations of several ingredients. They may contain an antitussive, an expectorant, a nasal decongestant, and an antihistamine. 

Sometimes a bronchodilator for clearing the bronchial tubes or a fever reducer is included. Generally these products are intended to treat the various symptoms associated with the common cold-sore throat, runny nose, stuffed-up nose, headacheand should not be taken for a cough alone. In fact, the cough-cold panel noted that at the present time the public has too little choice in selecting an appropriate drug for a cough because there are too few single drug ingredient cough preparations on the

OTC market. 

Many OTC cold remedies contain alcohol, suggesting that parents would be wise to read the labels carefully before giving cough medicines to young children. On this point, the panel recommended that cough and cold preparations containing alcohol in excess of 10 percent by weight be labeled with directions that they not be used by children under 6 years of age except under the advice and supervision of a physician.

The average self-limiting cough usually lasts about a week. Anything longer can be a sign of more serious problems. Thus the cough-cold advisory panel recommended that labeling for antitussive products bear the following label: "Caution: A persist ent cough may be a sign of a serious condition. If cough persists for more than 1 week, tends to recur, or is accompanied by high fever, rash or persistent headache, consult a physician." 

According to the National Heart and Lung Institute and the National

Tuberculosis Association, a cough that lasts more than a month is a chronic cough that could be a symptom of a chronic lung disease. A person who buys a lot of cough medicine and is constantly "popping" cough drops, or who seems to cough a lot at bedtime or when waking up in the morning may have a chronic cough. 

If this is the case, the cougher should not undertake self-treatment but should be checked by a physician. 

Annabel Hecht is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.
