Please Don't Stop Publishing This Waste Of Taxpayers' Money 

ONEA WARNING SAFE 

GANAER GANOR 

CONNUMER CONSUMER 

Half of the domestic subscribers to this magazine received a letter in the mail a while back that included a selfaddressed postal card containing questions about the magazine. More than half of those who received the card filled it out and returned it. The following article tells the results. 

If the f there's one generalization that can be made about FDA CON SUMER readers, it's that they are "highly interested and articulate." 

That's what Richard Barton of the

Direct Mail Marketing Association said when he learned how many sub scribers responded to CONSUMER'S 

recent readership survey. 

Last October, half of our subscribers (every other one) were sent a questionnaire on a self-addressed, postage-free return card, asking for information about the people who read the magazine and what their preferences and interests are..

In less than 3 weeks, more than half the cards had been returned, a response called "fantastic" by Kent 

Rhodes, former chairman of the board of READER'S DIGEST and now president of the Magazine Publishers 

Association. Experts say a return of 

15 to 20 percent would have been enough for an adequate mail survey and some magazines have to be content with 7 to 8 percent.

The survey has proved far more valuable than originally expected, for not only did our readers send in their cards promptly, but more than a third took the time to comment specifically on the general quality of the magazine and on the writing and graphics. Many offered suggestions as to what they would like to see in the way of subject matter or changes in format. And, regrettably, some subscribers let us know that the magazine wasn't reaching them at all. 

Better than one out of five (22.7 percent) of the people who responded had a favorable comment about the magazine. And the favorable comments outnumbered the negative remarks 10 to 1.

Information taken from a representative sample of the responses (from a total of 834 cards) was fed into a computer to provide a profile of the readers and their interests. 

The computer told us that an average of eight people share an issue. We also learned that subscribers are from all walks of life. In addition to people who described themselves as housewives, interested consumers, homemakers, and farm wives, there were corporation executives; health professionals; newsmen; State, local, and Federal Government officials; lawyers; lobbyists; quality control personnel; insurance underwriters; lab technicians; students; teachers; retailers; and retired people.

Those who expressed their satisfaction with the magazine used terms such as "excellent publication," "useful," "unique," "I love it," "I salute you," and "keep up the good work".

On the question of the writing style of the magazine, 93.3 percent marked the box "about right"; only 

4.3 percent said it was "too simple"; and only 1.3 percent thought it was "too technical."

Although the vast majority did like the way the articles were presented, آرت 

12 March 1981 / FDA Consumer

some readers found them bureaucratic, inaccurate at times, too simplistic, or too general. One said the information is too meager and the writing style dull; another called the magazine a "waste of taxpayers' money. 99 On the other hand, a journalist wrote: "I think that FDA CONSUMER 

is one of the finer publications emanating from gov't. Well-written, nicely laid-out and certainly filled with timely material."

Some readers accused CONSUMER 

of being biased or opinionated rather than factual, a "propaganda tool for 

FDA." But others found the magazine "the only reliable source of information in this field . . ." and "the best consumer publication available."

The magazine was commended for maintaining a healthy balance between the consumer and industry and for having an unbiased viewpoint. A lawyer penned on his questionnaire: "The magazine is well-written and timely. It also tries not to root for the FDA while still espousing the official view. My compliments.' 99 

Despite the name of the magazine, one reader could find nothing in it of interest to consumers. However, a number of readers reported that they and their families use CONSUMER to keep abreast of current trends in foods and drugs. A farm wife said, "FDA CONSUMER is essential for my self-education program." A veteran of 22 years as a hospital worker suggested that "every family should read it." The host of a syndicated TV program uses the magazine on his show. 

Any number of comments said the publication should be more widely publicized.

In assigning ratings to subjects that interested them most, readers gave top priority to food with a 1.4 rating, according to the computer ("1" being the highest rating and "6" the lowest). Drugs weren't far behind, with a 1.8 rating. Ratings for other subject areas were medical devices 

3.5; cosmetics 4.2; x-ray and other radiation 4.6; and "other" subjects (those written in by the readers) 5.9.

FDA CONSUMER articles, which usu ally appear at the front of the magazine, were rated most useful by 58.3 percent, while 40.3 percent found

The Notebook section useful. Ratings for the Investigators' Reports and 

The Notebook turned up surprisingly high inasmuch as the titles of those sections had been changed in the past year. 

One group of respondents, accounting for about 11 percent of those who added comments to the questionnaire, made specific sugges tions about what they'd like to see in the magazine. Suggestions included an "op-ed" page with comments from non-Government contributors, book reviews, compilations of FED- ERAL REGISTER notices, and lists of upcoming seminars and workshops.

As for the articles themselves, a few readers would like to have bibliographies, or at least suggested additional reading. An annual index would be helpful to others.

As to content, readers would like more information on food and nutrition, dangers of fluorescent lighting, and product recalls and imported foods, among other things. A number of consumers want to have more articles "about the things we have to live with" and "more ideas and resources for consumers to fight for our rights.' 99 

Clearly, FDA CONSUMER is doing a good job for many people, judging from what the readers are saying.

But there is always room for improvement and the editor and staff will take to heart many of these suggestions, even the most disparaging.

FDA Consumer / March 1981 / 13

Yesterday's Additives = 

Generally Safe

The title of this article might be: "Let 

Them Eat GRAS," for the piece is about a review of items that have been on the GRAS, or Generally Recog nized As Safe, list for 23 years. As the article points out, the extensive review found no items should be banned but it did raise questions about some.

Ha ow safe were food ingredients of generation ago? Pretty safe, according to a comprehensive review just completed on 415 substances that had been in use prior to the 1958 food additives amendment to the 

Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. 

A group of experts who reviewed the 415 items for the Food and Drug 

Administration didn't find the need to ban immediately any of the substances, but it did call for more study on quite a number. The 415 food ingredients had been on the FDA's "generally recognized as safe" list, also known as the GRAS list. They had been in use and apparently had been in use safely when the food additives amendment was passed in 1958. 

However, in 1969 problems developed with one of the items-cyclamate, an artificial sweetener. As a result, cyclamate was removed from the GRAS list and banned from use in foods. President Nixon then ordered a reevaluation of the safety of all GRAS list substances to determine their continued eligibility for listing as Generally Recognized As 

Safe. 

FDA contracted with the Federation of American Societies for Exper imental Biology (FASEB) to provide the Agency with expert opinions on the safety of the substances.

FASEB's Select Committee on GRAS Substances recommended that more study be done on a total of 110 items. Included in those "more study" items were caffeine, BHA, and BHT. For salt, the report recommended that FDA establish stricter rules for its use. 

The FASEB committee broke the 

415 ingredients into five categories (see chart). By far the most items- 

305-went into Class I status, meaning that they are considered safe for use at current levels and future anticipated levels under conditions of good manufacturing practices. The

Class I items would remain on the 

GRAS list. 

Sixty-eight items were placed in 

Class II. They are ingredients consid ered safe for use at current levels but needing more research to determine whether a significant increase in consumption would constitute a dietary hazard. 

Class III was another "more study" category for 19 substances. In this case, current use may be safe but additional studies were recommended because of unsolved questions in research data. Caffeine and the two common antioxidant preservatives, BHA (butylated hydroxyanisole) and 

BHT (butylated hydroxytoluene), were included in this category. 

Salt and four modified starches were placed in Class IV, which means that the committee recommended that FDA establish safer conditions of use or prohibit addition of the ingredients to food. The committee said there is no evidence that salt hurts most people. However, it suggested that a reduction of salt in processed food would benefit the 10 to 30 percent of the U.S. population genetically predisposed to hypertension. 

Class V was for 18 substances that the committee said it had insufficient data upon which to make an evaluation. FDA will propose removing these substances from the GRAS list unless sufficient data become available for evaluation. 

The committee's evaluations were based on a review of medical and scientific literature and unpublished reports. In some cases the research reports were as long as 60 years ago.

The number of references obtained for a given GRAS substance ranged from 23 reports (carnauba wax) to 

20,000 (Vitamin A).

The Agency has already implemented some of these recommendations by publishing new regulations for GRAS ingredients and is preparing to act upon the remaining recom mendations. Completion of Agency action will probably require an additional 2 to 3 years.

Copies of the select committee's final report and 118 individual reports that went into it are available from the National Technical Information 

Service, Springfield, Va. 22161.

Taking The Bite Out Of Rabies 

Time was, and not long ago, that a bite by an animal known or suspected to be rabid meant the victim had to take a prolonged series of painful shots to prevent rabies-with no absolute certainty it would prevent onset of the disease. But a new vaccine approved by FDA and now coming into use promises a much less traumatic immunization experience and a more effective one. by Harold Hopkins abies is so uncommon that the 

Rordinary person never encounters a case in a lifetime, either in a human or an animal. Only 153 human cases were reported in the three decades from 1950-79. Yet it is a disease that evokes the most profound dread. 

Practically everybody has heard enough about rabies to understand that as the disease runs its course, it inexorably ravages the brain and body until death mercifully intervenes. The thought of a loved one or oneself or even a favorite pet suffering from rabies can cause a shudder.

One reason this is so is our knowledge that we are so vulnerable. Rabies can be transmitted to a child or to an adult by the family pet, a barnyard animal, a stray animal, or a wild creature. Anybody can be scratched or nipped by an anguished puppy, a tormented stray cat, or a fox, skunk, raccoon, bat or other wild animal driven into the open or rendered uncomprehending by the effects of rabies. It can happen despite all the care and precautions the average person can devise. 

In the past the only hope held forth to persons who were exposed or believed exposed to rabies was from a vaccine that required a prolonged and painful series of 23 immunization shots-and even then there was no certainty that it would be successful. The shots were usually injected under the skin on the stomach or in other unlikely spots and were highly traumatic, especially for children. They were dreaded almost as much as the threat of the disease itself, and they often produced undesirable side effects or adverse reactions or, in rare instances, even death. 

And that's the way things were until 1980. That year has suddenly become a time to remember in the long history of rabies vaccine treatment, which dates back a hundred years to Pasteur. 

On June 9, 1980, the Food and 

Drug Administration approved a license for Institut Merieux of Lyon, France (which also has offices in 

Miami, Florida) to manufacture for marketing in this country a new immunization product-human diploid cell strain rabies vaccine (HDCV).

Since then HDCV has been widely distributed to and stocked by State and local government health departments, where it can be made available to physicians on short notice. 

Wyeth Laboratories, Radnor, Pa. also has an application before FDA for a license to manufacture a similar form of HDCV. HDCV was developed by the 

Wistar Institute, Philadelphia, in 

1962, using the Pitman-Moore strain of fixed rabies virus, which it adapted to grow in human cell culture. Trials in humans were conducted beginning in the 1970's in Europe and the United

States and it has been used since then in several European countries. 

Produced from human embryonic lung cell cultures, HDCV seems certain to eventually replace the vaccine known as DEV (duck embryo virus), made from embryonated duck eggs and in use since 1956. HDCV produces an antibody response quicker and in greater strength than DEV. It also causes fewer and apparently less

serious side effects in humans, largely because the protein it introduces into the system is of human instead of animal origin, and is present in a smaller amount.

HDCV requires only 5 shots to produce acceptable protective immunity, compared to 23 shots for DEV.

These shots are less painful than 

DEV shots and typically are injected into the upper arm or shoulder instead of the abdominal wall and other places recommended as rotation sites for DEV injections. The five shots can be completed within 30 days, followed by a check done routinely to verify that enough antibodies are present in the patient.

One of the best bits of news about the new vaccine is that so far, after extensive use world-wide, there is not a vaccine failure on record, that is, of rabies developing after treatment with HDCV. 

The Immunization Practices Advisory Committee of the U.S. Public Health Service (known as ACIP 

under its former name, Advisory

Committee for Immunization Practices) has issued a recommendation for rabies prevention that amounts to an optimistic endorsement of HDCV. 

It appears in the June 13, 1980 issue of the Center for Disease Control's 

"Morbidity and Mortality Weekly 

Report." ACIP reports that although there is not enough information to permit a direct comparison of HDCV 

and DEV in actual prevention of rabies, the superiority of HDCV was clear in tests. In the tests, HDCV produced adequate antibody response 

100 percent of the time. The strength of the response was 10 times that produced by DEV. Adequate antibody response was produced by DEV in only 85 to 90 percent of patients even when all 23 shots were tak

ACIP reports that adverse reactions from HDCV are less common than from DEV. In tests, local reactions such as pain, inflammation, and swelling or itching at the injection site were reported in about 25 percent of HDCV recipients and mild systemic reactions such as headache, nausea, abdominal pain, muscle aches, and dizziness in about 20 percent. No serious neuroparalytic reactions (paralysis caused by nerve damage) have been reported, although 

ACIP feels more experience is needed with HDCV for better assessment of risks. 

Local reactions to DEV are so frequent as to be considered "very common," says ACIP. Most patients experience pain, inflammation, and tautness of the flesh around the injection site. About 13 percent have itching and 33 percent develop systemic symptoms such as fever. There are occasional allergic reactions, sometimes serious, but neuroparalytic reactions occur only rarely. 

In postexposure rabies treatment, an immune serum preparation is used routinely with the first injection of either HDCV or DEV. It is either human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) or antirabies serum (ARS) of equine origin. HRIG is made from the plasma of human donors and ARS from the serum of hyperimmunized horses. Both provide protection during the several days it takes the vaccines, HDCV or DEV, to develop an antibody response in the system. 

HRIG is considered better because it has a lower risk of adverse reactions.

ARS is much riskier and is recommended only when HRIG is not available. If the patient has any rabies antibodies from a past immunization, the immune serum shots are not needed. HDCV may also be used for immunization of veterinarians or other persons subject to rabies exposure because they handle or work with animals. 

Rabies has declined in the United

States from an average of 22 cases a year during 1946-50 to 1 to 5 cases a year since 1960. Wild animals-particularly skunks, foxes, raccoons, coyotes, bobcats, and bats-are now the most frequent source of rabies, apparently because of improved preventive vaccination programs and veterinary care for dogs and cats. 

Carnivorous animals including dogs and cats are more often infected than animals such as deer or barnyard beasts. Rodents (squirrels, guinea pigs, hamsters, gerbils, chipmunks, rats, mice) and lagomorphs (hares, rabbits) are rarely found to be infected. It is recommended practice for private physicians to check with 

State or local health authorities before making decisions to treat persons who have been bitten by these animals. An unprovoked attack by an animal is more likely to indicate it is rabid than when an attack is provoked, as when handling or feeding an animal. 

Rabies is transmitted only when the virus, which occurs in saliva or other infectious materials from rabid animals, gets into open cuts or wounds in skin or on mucous membranes. Bites and scratches are the most common ways exposure occurs. 

Prompt cleansing of such bites or scratches with soap and water as soon as possible is most important. 

Handling or petting rabid animals is unlikely to transmit rabies if the person doing the handling isn't bitten or the mucous membranes are not exposed to the animal's saliva. Transmission of viruses through the air is remotely possible, but unlikely.

In case of possible exposure, a physician's close examination frequently negates the need for vaccination. But if it's decided that immunization is needed to be on the safe side, the promise offered by the new HDCV product is of utmost significance to the estimated 25,000 to 

30,000 persons who each year would otherwise have to accept the uncertain benefits and the painful experience of the immunizations of the past. 

Harold Hopkins is editorial director of FDA CONSUMER.

A Healthy Look At China 

DD A member of FDA's public affairs staff recently took a vacation trip to China. Trips to China are no longer that unusual, but our man looked at the big nation through the eyes of a person interested in food, drugs, and public health. This article details his impressions. 

by Emil Corwin

China is that the food is nothing like what you get at your favorite Chinese restaurant back home. When was the last time your neighborhood Chinese menu offered partridge soup; musk deer and anteater meat; pigeon stuffed with swallow meat; whole, steamed fish; pigeon eggs; sea slugs; fried lotus flowers; taro cakes; and a variety of dumplings? 

I was one of 32 Americans on a study tour of China, recently, and those were only some of the unusual dishes served routinely in our tourist dining rooms. What must be one of the most remarkable ironies of gourmet dining is that these dishes, now considered delicacies, were invented in times of famine. On the few occasions we really splurged at outside restaurants, the fare was more elaborate, and included Peking duck, suckling pig, sweet and sour croaker, frog legs with mushrooms, sea cucumber, pickle-peanut relish, something called eight jewel rice, and several unfamiliar pork and chicken dishes. These big smelled like carbon tetrachloride. If this is what was in those little glasses President Nixon hoisted at State dinners in Peking, was it ever recorded that he actually drank the stuff? For our group, the beverages of choice were Chinese laurel wine and beer and, of course, tea, and all were excellent.

There were eight of us at the table as a rule. Food was served in ten or more heaping bowls, one right after the other, by young waitresses who somehow managed to fit them on our round table even if it meant stacking a few 

FDA Consumer / March 1981 | 19

Parel Falings 洪​椒​国​万岁 ​世界​人民​大​团结​万岁

of the bowls. From that point we were on our own. Passing the bowls around was good exercise, but trying to find room for our selections on a plate no larger than a butter dish took a little practice. I thought this systemthe idea of a little plate for all that food-could be a sensible but subtle Chinese custom to control the amount of food one might be tempted to put away at one sitting. Incidentally, if you happen to be fond of soup, you had better leave room for it, since it is served last, arriving at about the same time as dessert, which was usually a bowl of apples or pears.

In Szechwan province, where food is traditionally hot and spicy, and seasoned with medicinal herbs, I was unable to learn whether any of it was made with mo-er, a black tree fungus that an American scientist recently found could reduce the chance of heart attacks. A "longevity tonic," one press report called it.

Notwithstanding these healthful ingredients, a number of us came down with debilitating colds, a not uncommon occurrence among visitors to China who seem vulnerable to a particularly hardy strain of Asian virus. For my cold, a sympathetic Chinese acquaintance introduced me to a preparation popularly known as "tiger balm," a strong mentholated ointment dispensed in a tiny flat red tin. As my friend instructed, I dabbed a bit of it on my temples and under my nose. A miracle cure it's not. (Neither, for that matter, was the antibiotic my Washington doctor prescribed for respiratory infections.) 

That respiratory ailments might also be a problem with some Chinese is suggested by the hawking and spitting often seen in the streets. I have the feeling much of this is due to the heavy cigarette smoking among men and teenagers. At a briefing in a large city hospital in Kunming, the physician-director (in his blue Mao cap and jacket he could be easily mistaken for an orderly) told us that cigarette smoking is a serious health problem and that a nationwide educational program has been launched to discourage the habit. I saw evidence of the campaign in a postage stamp issued this year. It shows back-to-back profiles of two men, one smoking a cigarette, the other with a daisy between his lips-and looking a lot healthier and happier. The legend beneath simply says, "Don't 

Smoke." In another step to discourage smoking, the national airline, the Civil Aviation Administration of China, has stopped handing out cigarettes to passengers; it has not yet, however, set aside sections for nonsmokers. 

To me, the Chinese appear to be physically fit. Nowhere in the crowds encountered in the streets and stores did I notice any overweight people. Perhaps that lean and wiry look comes partly from riding bicycles, which everyone seems to be doing most of the time. There are probably more bike riders in any given block of a wide city street in China than there are runners at the start of the 

Boston Marathon.

The people take their exercise and sports wherever and whenever they can. One morning, during a pre-breakfast stroll through Green Lake Park in Kunming, I was surprised to see so many elderly people jogging (in street clothes) or performing, solo and in groups, the graceful, slow motion blend of ballet and calisthenics known as T'ai Chi Ch'uan. Whether this daily ritual builds body tone by bringing vital forces in harmony with nature, as the Chinese believe, I don't know, but it is delightful to watch. 

I saw evidence of sports interest in an unlikely place: a filigree factory. The most conspicuous feature of a large workroom was a ping pong table placed in the middle of the room. The table looked as if it had been given a lot of hard use, presumably by employees on their tea breaks. 

Although these observations reflect the government's emphasis on exercising to maintain good health as part of its preventive medicine program, there are serious health problems in China. Two of the biggest, according to the hospital director, are air and water pollution. In a step to reduce air pollution in cities, he said, some factories are being moved to less densely populated areas. The water pollution problem was obvious to me the moment I entered my hotel room. On a table was a huge Thermos bottle of boiled water for tea (a cannister of tea and cups were also provided), and a carafe of cold water that had also been boiled. In rural areas the "barefoot doctors" (paramedical personnel) deal with problems of sewage and disinfecting wells. 

The director of the 300-bed Kunming hospital permitted us to observe a diagnostic session and an acupuncture treatment clinic in the outpatient department.

The bottom photo shows the botanical garden near Nanning, where more than 3,000 herbs are cultivated for use in treating a wide range of diseases and for controlling common household pests. In the top picture, a patient rests on an examining table after acupuncture needles are inserted in various parts of his abdomen. The small acupuncture room is dominated by wall charts of the human body showing 500 to 800 acupuncture points. A relaxed patient lying on an examination table had needles protruding from a number of acupuncture points in his abdomen. A man sitting on a chair, with the trouser of one leg rolled up, was holding a smoldering item over several needles in his leg. The item he held appeared to be a slow-burning roll of paper about the size and shape of a cigar. The smoking object, impregnated with moxa, a powdery medical herb, is intended to intensify the effect of the implanted needles. 

The procedure, called moxibustion, represents a combination of two basic elements of traditional Chinese medicine-acupuncture and herbal medicine.

Our tour included a visit to a large herbal park near Nanning, where some 3,000 herbs were being cultivated. 

Signs in English identified herbs that were used for "prevention and treatment of common dermatopathy"; "diseases of the eye, ear, nose, and throat"; "gynecological disease"; "vascular and nervous systems", "digestive systems"; "common epidemics, contagious, and parasitic diseases"; "killing pests, mosquitoes, flies, rats, and bedbugs," and so on. 

Although most Chinese prefer traditional medicine,

Western medicine has been making inroads in recent years, and the two are increasingly combined. There was some indication of this blend in an agricultural commune's medical service store. On one side were cabinets stocked with hundreds of herbs. In the room across a passageway was a cabinet stocked with vaccines, antibiotics, hormones, and other modern medicinals. Many of these, according to the labels, were imported from Hungary. 

We left China on the Canton-Hong Kong express, a crack train with such appurtenances as double swivel seats for the convenience of parties of four, television screens above the doors at each end of the coach, extrawide windows, leg room to accommodate the tallest basketball center, and a porter with a sawed-off straw broom who kept a watchful eye on the immaculate floor, lest anything spill or fall on it.

I was late for lunch in the dining car, but a pre-prepared dish of rice and chicken, eaten from a plastic container, was satisfying enough. For my beverage, I tried something called Vitasoy, a sweetish soy milk drink in a half-pint container. The labeling on it would have pleased 

FDA for its detailed information. It listed the ingredients (extracts from soya beans, vegetable fat, cane sugar, and other ingredients, plus several vitamins), and advised that the drink keeps fresh without refrigeration. The label also had a "consume before" date and a notice printed in 

Chinese and English, "please do not litter. 99 At our group's get-acquainted dinner in Los Angeles before our trip began, an old China hand paraphrased a saying attributed to Chairman Mao: "To see China briefly is like picking flowers from a galloping horse."

The chairman was right. Three weeks is not enough to see and to savor the many delights to be found in China and its people. The flowers gathered, as far as I am concerned, are all forget-me-nots. 

Emil Corwin is on FDA's public affairs staff.

Kelsey's Kops: 

They Investigate The Investigators 

The law requires that drugs be tested for safety and effectiveness before being marketed. But that requirement is only as good as the care with which the tests are made and the honesty with which they are reported. That's why FDA investigates and sometimes disqualifies-drug researchers.

by William Grigg Officially, they're the Division of 

Scientific Investigations in 

FDA's Bureau of Drugs, but informally they're "Kelsey's Kops." Their boss is the heroine of the thalidomide episode, Dr. Frances O. Kelsey, and their job is to police drug testing to make sure it's honest.

They investigate drug investigators. 

They want to know if Doctor X really treated the patients he said he did, whether he gave them the drug he said he did, and whether the results he got were what he reported. (They've found "patients" with addresses in drug investigators' files that turned out to be vacant lots.) 

They want to know if Researcher 

Y's white mice were properly handled so that the results of pathological examinations are of value. (They've found cases where large numbers of animals died and researchers didn't even discover the deaths until too late for their tissues to be examined; they had decayed.) 

Sometimes, "research" claimed to have been done by a drug investigator on animals or people has proved to be no more than pencil marks on a piece of paper. Speaking of one researcher's work, Dr. Kelsey said, "He just graphited it.' 

Drug applications today are quite a contrast from 20 or 30 years ago. The application files from the 1950's and 

1960's were but an inch or two thick-tiny by today's standards but more complex than those of the 

1940's when the Food, Drug, and

Cosmetic Act of 1938 was new. The early proofs were somewhat informal, and an FDA physician back then might drop in on an investigator and get a first-hand view of a drug tested. Similarly, FDA personnel might informally consider one or another drug researcher's work to be poor or even fraudulent-and look at his report with that in mind. 

However, by the early 1960's, drugs, drug research, and drug applications were becoming increasingly sophisticated and complex. Medical officers reviewing these applications noted that a small number of researchers were doing an awful lot of studies for various drugs-and that some of this research seemed out of the fields of competence of these doctors.

In late 1961, FDA began its first real "investigator investigation." It ended successfully and spectacularly, the physician pleading "no contest" to an indictment charging him with making "false, fraudulent and fictitious reports" on five new drugs. He had fabricated the names of patients, their symptoms, the doses of medicine given them, the time of administration-and the patients' reactions.

The physician was fined and given a suspended sentence, and later was barred from medical practice in Maryland. 

About that same time, a major drug manufacturer was making a similar no contest plea after a former employee reported she was instructed to falsify animal data on MER/29, a drug that FDA had approved for marketing in 1960. After severe toxic reactions were reported, FDA ordered the drug's sales suspended. 

Dr. Kelsey came to Washington in 

1960 to join FDA's drug review staff, which was expanding from 3 medical officers to 13. Six months later she was handed a New Drug Application for a product called thalidomide, a sleeping pill. She questioned some of the information supporting the application and held up the drug's sale in the United States-thus sparing the 

Nation the epidemic of crippling birth defects experienced in other countries. 

Like the prosecution of the physician and the MER/29 case, thalidomide focused attention on the authenticity of drug research. It was discovered that thalidomide's manufacturer had distributed the unapproved drug to 1,248 physicians for their experimental use-a distribution that smacked more of promotion than legitimate drug investigation. 

The thalidomide case helped deliver the votes for enactment of the 

1962 Kefauver-Harris drug amendments that expanded FDA's monitoring of drug research. Those amendments required that manufacturers report on animal studies and gain 

FDA's approval before starting drug experimentation on patients. They also required that a drug be proved not only safe but also effective before its sale could be approved.

Dr. Kelsey, after a short stint directing the review of applications for new anticancer drugs, became assistant to the director of the Bureau of 

Drugs "to start looking for poor investigative work," as she put it. Her first "detective" was Dr. Alan B. Lisook. Then, in 1967 a small investigative unit was formed, with Kelsey,

Lisook, and two support staffers. 

Progress was slow, at first, because 

FDA thought an Agency physician should be on hand for every field investigation-which meant that the cases were limited by how much time 

Dr. Lisook had for travel. Field staffers are now specially trained and the physician-present requirement has been eliminated. Today the headquarters staff numbers 38 with 16 of these concentrating on physicians investigating drugs in humans-both here and abroad.

The rest of the staff is divided between those checking up on animal research through 60 inspections a year and those conducting a procedural review of about 200 institutional review boards each year. 

These boards, composed of local professional people, are required in nursing homes, hospitals, and other institutions where drug research is performed. They are charged with assuring that patients getting experimental drugs have given their consent-and that the potential benefits to the patients are worth the risks. 

When FDA began visiting the boards in 1977, more than half were delinquent in such matters as assuring that patients know they are receiving experimental therapy and have freely consented.

The Kelsey Kops disqualify five or six drug researchers a year, with each case requiring hundreds of hours of work. These disqualifications, and the 200 random and 70 "for cause" investigations conducted among clinical researchers each year, have a healthy "ripple effect" in the pool of 

9,000 physicians doing drug research. 

Not all of the information on spu- 

24 March 1981/ FDA Consumer

The line-up, seated left to right, Frances O. Kelsey, Ph.D., M.D., deputy director Heinz G. Wilms and George Sharpe, M.D., chief of the institutional review branch; standing, branch chiefs Walter H. Hansen, nonclinical laboratory studies, George Blatt, regulatory management, and Alan Lisook, M.D., clinical investigations. rious research is developed in-house. 

There are "sources" and tipsters.

One source may be the drug manufacturers themselves-burned by inferior work from a researcher. 

Among the players who have been thrown out of the research/investigating game are:

The clinical investigator who reported very routine reactions to a new hypnotic. That wouldn't have surprised anyone ordinarily but this batch of the experimental drug had been made too strong accidentally, and another researcher who used it had reported a dry mouth, flushed skin, and excitement in his patients. 

Why hadn't Dr. Q seen these effects?

Well, as a matter of fact, some of the doctor's patients hadn't been in the hospital when they supposedly got the drug there. Indeed, some were dead. 

The researcher who swore he had once had all the patient records and data to back up his reports. And he'd still have them, he said, if he hadn't taken them with him on a picnic and then for a ride on a boat-which sank.

The doctor who claimed to have given Company A's drug to a batch of patients, while reporting to Company B that he was using its drug on them.

The physician who claimed to have taken smears and cultures from patients being treated with an experimental antibiotic for gonorrhea.

After a visit, the FDA's inspector realized that he had seen no incubator for the cultures to grow in. Returning the next day, the inspector found a shiny incubator in place, but so new it still had the packing material in it. "But don't make it out that we're just cops," Dr. Kelsey says. "We're also teachers and preachers. "We like to think we help researchers-the vast majority who are trying to do their work well. We like to think we help them, through our visits and suggestions, to do a better job." 

True. And most drug investigators, as Dr. Kelsey believes, do want to do a good and honest job. Nevertheless, there is that human trait that British statesman Edmund Burke observed, "Early and provident fear is the mother of safety." 

That might well be inscribed over the doorway to the Division of Scientific Investigations. 

William Grigg is on the staff of 

FDA's office of public affairs.

The Notebook 

Natural sea sponges are being promoted as alternatives to menstrual tampons as a result of the recent outbreak of toxic shock syndrome associated with tampon use. However, FDA has not approved the sale of sea sponges because their safety and effectiveness have not been established. Anyone wishing to sell natural sea sponges in interstate commerce legally would have to comply with FDA's medical device regulations. To date, the Agency has received no requests to conduct investigations of sea sponges as menstrual tampons. 

FDA has issued class labeling guidelines for the professional labeling of prescription single-entity barbiturate drug products, the first of 32 such documents to be developed. The guidelines are intended to promote the use of identical professional labeling for various classes of drugs to help FDA monitor drug labeling, aid manufacturers in preparing professional labeling, and eliminate the need for prescribers and dispensers to compare labeling for drug products in the same class.

The barbiturate labeling, made public in the November 18, 1980 FEDERAL REGISTER, is the only guideline to be published. In the future only a notice of availability of a guideline will be published. The 32 classes of drug products in the class labeling program accounted for more than 500 million prescriptions in 1979 at more than $2 billion in retail costs to consumers. 

Add to the list of FDA's standing advisory committees the Anti-Infective Drugs Advisory Committee, the Dermatologic Drugs Advisory Committee, and the Ophthalmic Drugs Advisory Committee. Es tablishment of the three committees and a call for nominations for members were announced in the No vember 28, 1980 FEDERAL REGISTER. Each commit tee will have 11 members who will review the data on the safety and effectiveness of prescription drugs in these areas.

1976, devices are classified as Class I, calling for general controls; Class II, calling for performance standards; or Class III, requiring premarket approval.

Prosthetic devices including crowns and false teeth accounted for 70 of the class ifications. Six were Class I, 53 Class II, and 11 Class 

III. Needing premarket approval will be denture adhesives, denture cushions and pads, repair kits, and an implant surgically placed in the jaw to provide support for prosthetic devices. Thirty-four surgical devices-drills, lights, bone cutters, scalers-were classified as follows: 6 in Class I and 28 in Class II. 

Thirteen therapeutic devices, such as braces, were put in Class II, while 7 were in Class I. One of these, teething rings, rated a dual classification: I for nonfluid-filled rings and II for fluid-filled rings.

■ Elderly patients in a Wauwatosa, Wis. hospital routinely received double the prescribed dose of radiopharmaceuticals during diagnostic tests from 1976 to 1980, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) revealed in an abnormal occurrence report in the De cember 31 FEDERAL REGISTER. Alerted in July 1980, the NRC investigated the hospital and found that the nuclear medicine staff had been giving the overdoses to patients, most of them 65 and older, for diagnostic scans of brain, bone, liver, spleen, and lung in which technetium 99m (Tc-99m) was part of the scanning agent. The dosage had been increased to cut down on the scanning time and to obtain brighter images before the patients moved, although there are other means to accomplish this without subjecting patients to unnecessary radiation. In addition, the technetium utilization log was falsified to indicate that proper dosages had been given. The two employees involved were discharged.

Investigators' Reports 

Blinded Eyes

Seven elderly cataract patients who had intraocular lenses implanted to improve their vision ended up completely losing the sight in the affected eye. The seven developed eye infections because the sodium bicarbonate neutralizing solution, used to rinse the lenses prior to surgery, had been inadequately sterilized and contained bacteria and mold. FDA's San Francisco District investigated the case and brought criminal charges against Dr. 

Francis J. Kanofsky, president of Luminex International, Inc., the Las Vegas, Nevada, manufacturer. The prosecution's case rested largely on the case histories of the seven patients, one of whom was permanently blinded and six whose eyes had to be removed because of the infection. 

Joseph Smith (not the patient's real name) was 87 and suffering from cataracts when his doctor suggested he have an intraocular lens (IOL) implanted in his left eye. IOL's are surgically implanted in the eye as permanent replacements for damaged natural lenses. The patient agreed to this, and shortly afterward underwent the operation in which the lens was sewn onto his eye. The lens was manufactured by Luminex International, Inc.

The operation itself was successful, but after about 3 weeks the patient complained that the eye felt sore and "scratchy." These were, however, fairly typical reactions. Then began the pain, deep and unabating. Smith's doctor prescribed three types of drugs (including steroids) to combat what he diagnosed as inflammation. Application of the drugs to the eye was required every hour. The doctor also prescribed a painkiller. Lab tests and examination of the eye and lens showed signs of inflammation but no unusual complications.

A month and a half after the operation the patient was still having pain, and his doctor was worried. Then, during one of many examinations, the doctor saw a fluffy, white mass on the newly implanted lens. In the next few days the mass gradually increased. 

Smith's doctor began to suspect that the patient's eye had become infected with a fungal endophthalmitis, a condition that causes inflammation of the eye cavity and adjacent structures. He hoped he was wrong.

Fungal endophthalmitis following routine cataract surgery is uncommon, occurring in less than 0.60 percent of the cases. It was, therefore, unusual that Smith should develop the condition. It was even stranger that, about the same time, five other people—all elderly patients with cataracts-also developed fungal endophthalmitis after implantation of Luminex IOL's. 

It was also obvious to the two physicians who did the implantations for those five patients that something was wrong with the Luminex products.

The physicians, who worked together at a California clinic, called both

Kanofsky at Luminex and a prominent California medical center. They sent a bottle of the neutralizing solution and a culture from one of the patient's eyes to the medical center for analysis. There was foreign matter floating near the bottom of the bottle that was identified as a fungus. The culture from the eye also contained a fungus.

The medical center called Kanofsky and was told by the latter that he had already learned of the problem from the California physicians. Kanofsky said he had sent telegrams to all purchasers of Luminex products, warning them of the danger. 

One telegram went to Smith's doctor. It confirmed the doctor's suspicion that his patient had a fungus infection. The telegram said there was a problem with lot 128 of the sodium bicarbonate neutralizing solution that had been shipped with the lenses (the lenses were supposed to be rinsed in the solution just before surgery to neutralize the liquid they were packed and shipped in). The telegram stated that a patient who had been fitted with a lens rinsed in solution from lot 128 had developed fungal endophthalmi- tis. 

Lot 128 had also been used to rinse 

Smith's lens. The doctor, with his patient's concurrence, surgically removed the lens and as much of the fungus as he could. But several days later it became apparent that some of the fungal mass was still in the patient's eye, and growing. 

Fungal endophthalmitis leads to widespread festering inflammation within the eye. The fungus grows rapidly and can spread to other parts of the body. Drugs specifically used to treat fungal infections are generally ineffective with this disease, as are antibiotics. Steroids, which are often used to treat other types of eye inflammation-and which were used to treat 

Smith-exacerbate fungal endophthalmitis. Currently the best treatment is surgical removal of the eye and the infected tissues to prevent the fungus from spreading. 

Smith's condition, and his pain, worsened. His doctor called in several other physicians. Smith was told that the cultures of the fungus were resistant to the antifungal drugs; that they could try treating him with the drugs anyway, but that therapy would probably be quite long and painful, and it was unlikely that useful vision could be saved in the affected eye. The doctors explained that, if left untreated, the fungus might burn itself out, but there was a chance it would not and might metastasize through the bloodstream to other organ systems and result in a fungus infection throughout the body. The safest thing, the patient was told, was enucleation-removal of the eye. 

Meanwhile, other doctors who had purchased Luminex lenses had received the letters sent by Kanofsky, and the products were returned to the manufacturer. The California Department of Public Health had also been contacted, and the State called FDA's 

San Francisco District and relayed the 

FDA Consumer / March 1981 / 29

background of the case. Although the problem had been traced to lot 128 of the neutralizing solution, a question remained: How had the solution become contaminated?

The San Francisco District in spected the firm and found the answer. The district found that Kanofsky had failed to take reasonable precautions to ensure the sterility of his firm's products. Investigators reported that the doctor's sterility testing procedures were inadequate, the room used for sterilizing the solution had inadequate facilities, and the sterilizing process itself was inadequate.

Kanofsky, district investigators learned, was using a filtration method for sterilizing the neutralizing solution. This is a simple and inexpensive method for sterilizing small amounts of liquid that will be used immediately. But it is inappropriate, the district believed, for sterilizing materials intended for use at a much later date.

A more appropriate method-and more expensive-would be autoclaving (heat treatment), which definitely kills all contaminants. 

The district recommended that criminal charges be brought against

Kanofsky, supporting its request with inspection reports, laboratory analysis, and evidence provided by the State and the doctors of the affected patients.

Kanofsky was charged with five counts of misbranding and adulterating devices. He pleaded guilty to two counts in the U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada and was fined $1,000. He also entered into an agreement with FDA never to engage again in the commercial manufacture, distribution, or sale of intraocular lenses and accessories. He may continue to dispense the lenses within the ordinary course of his medical practice if they are manufactured by other firms. -Carol Ballentine

Investigators' Reports presents information on inspections, product seizures, court proceedings, and other administrative and regulatory actions by Federal, State, and local food and drug agencies across the country to provide health and economic protection to consumers of foods, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices.

Drug Cache in Storage 

People who rent mini-storage lockers usually use them to hold unneeded household goods, seasonal recreation equipment, or antiques. 

So when an Omaha, Nebraska, mini-storage owner opened the locker of a renter who had fallen behind in his rent, he never expected it to be filled with an assortment of drug products. 

Suspecting something was amiss, the owner immediately called the 

Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) to report what he had discovered. When he described most of the drugs as prescription drugs bearing the labeling of a major drug firm, DEA contacted FDA's Omaha Resident Post.

A visit to the locker by an FDA investigator confirmed the presence of a large quantity of old physician samples bearing the labeling of 

Searle Laboratories and an assortment of nonprescription drugs. After obtaining the name of the former renter from the owner, the investigator contacted Searle and was told that the man was a former salesman who had been fired for falsifying records, which may have resulted in his ability to accumulate such a large quantity of physician samples. 

The entire quantity of drugs was destroyed in the presence of an FDA investigator, a Nebraska State inspector, and a representative of Searle 

Laboratories. Searle estimated the drugs' value at $20,000. 

After Dinner Event 

The poison was in the meatballs. 

That's what investigators from the

Suffolk County Department of Health 

Services (New York) concluded after thoroughly investigating a food poisoning incident. The department was called in by the principal of a Suffolk 

County elementary school after 102 people became ill following the school's PTA dinner. 

Approximately half of 200 diners experienced nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and other symptoms of gastrointestinal upset. The investigators asked what the victims had eaten, and what those who didn't get sick had eaten. They checked the preparation area and questioned the staff about techniques. Was everything refrigerated that should have been? 

Had foods been cooked adequately? 

Where had the raw ingredients come from?

They reconstructed the event and narrowed the field of possible culprits. They learned that a dish of meatballs had been left at room temperature for some time, long enough for any of several types of bacteria to multiply. 

The conclusive evidence came from the department's laboratory. Samples of meatballs and specimens from patients were analyzed and Clostridium perfringens identified. This organism is widely distributed in soil, air, water, and feces. Investigators concluded that one of the workers handling the meatballs had not observed proper sanitary procedures and thus was responsible for the bacterial contamination. The meatballs, left at room temperature, then provided perfect conditions for the bacteria to form harmful toxins.

Stronger Medicine 

Frequently, State agencies help

FDA deal with firms that violate food and drug laws. At FDA's request and based on convincing evidence, for instance, a State agency might use its own statutory authority to suspend a firm's license or embargo an adulterated product. Similarly, if a State agency needs help dealing with an offending firm, it might turn to FDA. This was recently the case in upper New York. 

Under a contract with FDA, the

New York Department of Agriculture and Markets inspects manufacturers of medicated animal feeds. One man ufacturer-Floyd Collins & Son Feed 

Mill, of Newfane-had been causing problems for the State for some time. 

A string of inspections showed the firm was violating FDA's Good Man ufacturing Practice regulations. In spectors reported that company employees were not assaying the feeds for potency, were not ensuring that the feeds were uniformly mixed, and were generally being careless. The 

State's warnings and fines failed to impress the firm's management—at least, not enough to cause them to halt the violations-so the State asked the Buffalo District to lend a hand. District investigators confirmed evidence in the State's inspection reports and a regulatory letter was sent, advising the firm to cease the violations. The feed manufacturer failed to heed the advice. The district then took more stringent measures, filing for an injunction. The firm was subsequently enjoined by a Federal district court from manufacturing violative medicated feeds and has since gone out of the medicated animal feeds business.

A Recall Is a Recall Is a... 

Recalls can come in several forms.

The main idea is to get the job done. 

Several shipments of canned mushrooms were recalled by a New York 

City firm because of underprocessing. 

FDA's Baltimore District laboratory originally discovered the cans were underprocessed-and contaminated by bacteria-while checking import samples. The mushrooms, canned in 

Korea, were being imported and distributed by Won International, Inc.,

New York City. FDA's New York 

District office contacted the firm, which began a recall of the sampled shipments. The Newark District office was asked to get samples from shipments that had been canned at another of the firm's Korean canneries. These lots, analyzed by the New 

York Regional Laboratory, were also found to be underprocessed. The firm extended the recall to include these shipments.

In this instance, the recall meant that the mushrooms were physically returned (or "called back") to the responsible firm. In FDA parlance, however, a recall can mean other things as well. 

For instance, Foregger Co., Inc., a 

Smithtown, New York, manufacturer of anesthesia equipment submitted a recall plan to the New York District office after learning of a defect in some of its machines. The firm reported that 105 anesthesia machines had a defective part that would probably malfunction several hours after being in operation. This malfunction would interfere with the release of the anesthetic gas. The firm said it had contacted all the owners but had not asked that the machines actually be returned; instead, the company sent out a number of staff people to replace the malfunctioning parts.

In another recall plan, submitted to the Newark District, Ortho Diagnostics, Inc., Raritan, New Jersey, asked its customers to make a correction in the labeling of an in vitro diagnostic test kit. The kit, used to detect sickle cell anemia or sickle cell trait, was composed of a reagent powder and a test solution. The firm discovered that one of the reactive ingredients degraded too rapidly after being reconstituted. The expiration date on the product was, therefore, inaccurate. The firm wrote to its customers-including 168 Government accounts and 44 foreign consigneesrequesting that they discontinue using any of the materials that had been reconstituted for longer than 21 days. 

The firm also sent stickers for the customers to put on the labels changing the expiration time of the reconstituted solution from 60 days at room temperature to 21 days at 2 degrees Celsius. 

Inspector Assaulted

When Wisconsin dairyman Donald 

Zeien learned that his grade A milk farm would be downgraded, Zeien and his son Larry decided they would rather fight than switch. 

The two men, who live in Green

County, were each fined $500 by Circuit Judge Franz Bran, in Green

County Circuit Court, after they had entered a plea of no contest to a statutory disorderly conduct charge.

Both had been charged with physically assaulting a food inspector with the Wisconsin Department of Agricul ture, Trade and Consumer Protection during an inspection of their farm under the State's Grade A milk inspection program.

The Zeiens became angry at the inspector after he inspected and degraded their farm from A to D. The change meant the Zeiens would be getting less money for their milk on the dairy market, because it would be used in the production of cheese, butter, ice cream, and other products of lesser demand.

In the court action, the charge of obstructing an officer was held open by the court for 8 months following the incident, and the Zeiens agreed to make restitution to the State of 

Wisconsin for the inspector's doctor and hospital fees.

Public Disservice Announcement "Your Child Does Not Have To 

Be Immunized For School," read an advertisement in a metropolitan Detroit newspaper. "Would you let your child have live puss from sick animals or the use of dead bacteria put into their veins?" 

The ad horrified the health officials who saw it, and not just because of the bad grammar and poor spelling, such as pus with two s's. An investigator in FDA's Detroit District showed it to the district's consumer affairs officer (CAO), and she called the newspaper. None of the editors could fathom how an ad so misleading and grossly inaccurate had gotten onto the "Back-To-School" pages.

Not only were the statements about vaccines completely false, but the ad falsely claimed to be a public service announcement. The name Taylor 

Straight Chiropractic Center was in large type (along with the phone numbers and office hours) and the copy read: "Health comes totally from the body. Take care of your health and your family's health through a spinal exam today." The editors agreed with the CAO that the ad was a disservice to the paper's readers. At her suggestion, they printed an editorial rebuttal based on an interview with the director of the 

Wayne County Department of Public

Health. The editor also had a few words with the newspaper's advertising staff. 

The CAO contacted the Michigan 

Department of Health, which promptly wrote a "letter to the editor," which, when published, termed the chiropractic ad "a flagrant distortion of facts. . . . No vaccine is produced for, required of, or given to children which uses pus or dead bacteria from sick animals. All vaccines are given intramuscularly or subcutaneously, not into veins as the ad implies."

The letter pointed out that before vaccines were available, thousands of children were crippled-or killed-by diphtheria, whooping cough, rubella, measles, and polio. Before polio vaccine was licensed in 1955, for instance, 30,000 to 60,000 cases of polio were reported each year. Now there are fewer than 25 cases per year. 

The letter added: "Ironically, one of the few cases of diphtheria reported in 1979 occurred in the 5year-old son of a California chiropractor, who had signed a waiver against immunizations. The boy was the only unimmunized child in his class. He subsequently died of the disease." 

What worried both Federal and 

State agencies was that the Detroit newspaper was part of a large chain of weekly papers. The health depart ment contacted all county and local health departments across the State, advising them to watch for similar advertisements. The department also contacted the State Attorney Gen eral's office and the Department of 

Licensing and Regulation. Those agencies are investigating the matter and are considering taking action against the chiropractor for unethical conduct. 

Too Close to 2,4,5-T 

A Wisconsin milling firm was fined $8,750 in a Brown County Court on 

37 counts of violating State law and administrative codes covering the storage, sale, and labeling of pesticides, food-grade salt, animal feed, and seed products.

The Wisconsin Department of Agri culture and FDA's Minneapolis District brought charges against the 

Osen Milling Co. of De Pere after a number of inspections of its warehouse. Despite many orders to clean up spilled pesticides and other products, Osen had failed to comply.

The most serious charge brought against Osen was the potential contamination of bakery salt and animal feed by storing them too close to a product containing 2,4,5-T. A weaker form of Agent Orange, 2,4,5,-T is a herbicide suspected of causing harmful effects. Its use is restricted domestically by the Environ mental Protection Agency. 

Other charges brought against

Osen included storing table salt under insanitary conditions, contaminating animal feed by storing it too close to pesticides, storing pesticides in broken or defective containers, and selling 443 bags of improperly labeled animal feed products after the department had ordered a halt to their movement. The firm pleaded no contest to the 37 charges.

Osen, a family-owned operation, is a wholesale distributor of salt products for human and animal use, animal feeds, fertilizers, pesticides, lawn and garden supplies, seeds, and animal health products.

Bad Blood 

The first letters from FDA's At lanta District were congenial and matter-of-fact. Sent to two hospitals in Alabama, the letters stated simply that the hospitals had failed to register with the Bureau of Biologics, a procedure required annually for firms. shipping or manufacturing blood or blood products. The district enclosed the necessary registration forms.

The next letters-this time regulatory letters from the district-were still matter-of-fact, but not so congenial. The messages, hand delivered by an investigator from FDA's Mobile office, noted that the hospitals still had not registered even though 5 months had passed since the initial letters had been sent. If the hospitals failed to correct this oversight, the regulatory letters said, the district was prepared to take legal action, such as seizures or injunctions. 

Both hospitals promptly submitted the required registration forms. 

Made for Each Other 

The long, hot summer of 1980 doubly afflicted FDA's Atlanta District.

The staff had to deal both with the sweltering heat and with a growth in the insect population in the district. 

The insects that thrive in warm, humid conditions are unfortunately the same as those that infest grains, cereals, packaged mixes, flour, and dried fruits and vegetables. Whole grain kernels can become infested with larval forms of these insects, which remain intact during the milling process. They then develop into hardy and mobile adults and spread to other susceptible products during storage. 

Atlanta District investigators advised local firms against keeping finished products too long in storage, 32/ March 1981 FDA Consumer

and said infested goods should be segregated quickly from clean products to prevent the insects from spreading. Nonetheless, many firms experienced serious insect problems, including several warehouses, a cannery in Port Royal, South Carolina, and a bakery supply firm in Atlanta. 

Following district inspections, the firms destroyed the insect-infested products.

Half-baked Sanitation 

It took a court order and $100,000 for a Washington State bakery to put the "good" in Good Manufacturing Practices. 

Ruth Ashbrook Bakeries Corp. of 

Seattle has been manufacturing bakery products for customers in Washington, Oregon, and Alaska since 

1946. The firm bakes private brand bread, buns, rolls, and sweet goods for retail outlets under its own labels, as well as a number of other labels.

Inspection records by FDA's Seat tle District and the Washington State 

Department of Agriculture show that for the past several years these products were made under unsanitary conditions. 

Repeatedly these inspections disclosed live and dead insects in and on the firm's raw materials and food processing equipment, improperly cleaned equipment, structural defects which provided insect and rodent harborages, and mold on the walls. 

At the conclusion of each inspection, the insanitary conditions were discussed with the firm's management, and subsequent letters were issued to reiterate the problems. But despite the management's promises to improve sanitation and eliminate other unsatisfactory conditions, there was no lasting compliance with Good 

Manufacturing regulations.

After the Seattle District's most recent inspection found continuing sanitation problems, the district filed a complaint for injunction in the U.S.

District Court for the Western Dis trict of Washington in Seattle. The firm subsequently agreed to enter into a consent decree of permanent injunction, under which it ceased distribution of all food products until the facility was cleaned, renovated, and made suitable for the production and storage of contamination-free food. 

After a concerted effort by the firm, including contracting a sanitation consultant and spending $100,- 

000 on improvements, the firm was again inspected by the district, was found to be in compliance, and was allowed to resume its normal operations. 

Getting Along Without Morels?

In spring the morels come out, and many wild mushroom connoisseurs comb the forests for this delicacy. All true morels, which belong to the genus Morchella, are edible and choice, according to Orson Miller in Mushrooms of North America. The discreet mushroom hunter, however, is careful not to confuse the true morels with their look-alike relatives, the false morels. Although both the true and false are members of the same family (Ascomycetes), many of the false morels are toxic, and some can kill. 

Some mushroom hunters in Europe evidently have been having problems identifying their morels in recent years. The mushroom hunters have attracted FDA's attention because they are in the business of harvesting morels for commercial canners in France and Switzerland. In 

1977 and 1980, FDA issued import alerts directing Agency inspectors to collect samples of all mushrooms offered for import from either Cie

Franco of France or Lankor Interna tional, Inc., of Switzerland, because cans from these firms were labeled as "morels" but in fact contained Gyromitra esculenta, a type of false morel. An alert was issued in 1977 when four people in New York City got sick after eating these mushrooms in a dish called Veal Morel. In 1980, an 

FDA alert was sent out when the 

Denver District collected import samples of canned mushrooms, and analysis by the Bureau of Foods and 

U.S. Department of Agriculture re vealed the presence of G. esculenta. 

G. esculenta contains the toxin monomethylhydrazine (MMH), which can cause severe gastrointestinal disturbance and sometimes death, notwithstanding that the name is Latin for "edible." This species is similar in appearance to some species of Morchella, and harvesting errors could account for part of the problem. Imported morels are also quite expensive, and some FDAers believe that the $23-a-can price might encourage some intentional "mistakes." 

One brand of canned mushrooms, however, was labeled "Wyco Round 

Morels Extra Gyromitras Au Naturel 

Morels," indicating that the Gyromitras were intended to be added. 

There is some debate among wild mushroom aficionados as to the edibility of G. esculenta. Many people claim that certain methods of preparation will destroy the toxin; others say that the toxin is more concentrated in summer and fall, and that the mushrooms picked in the spring are safe to eat.

FDA, however, is firm in its position that any product labeled "morels" must contain Morchella and only Morchella. The Agency prohibits commercial distribution of all false morels. Including mushrooms other than Morchella in a can of morels can present a health hazard as well as an economic deception of consumers, the Agency maintains. 

FDA also firmly advises against amateur collectors gathering wild mushrooms. It is often almost impossible to distinguish toxic from nontoxic species, according to the Bureau of 

Foods, and even experts make mistakes. Wild mushroom lovers who fancy false morels therefore must take their gastronomical chances without protection from FDA.

Seizures

FILED SEIZURE ACTIONS charge violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and are initiated based upon FDA recommendations. A seizure action is commenced by the filing of a complaint in the U.S. district court where the goods are located. A U.S. marshal is then directed by the court to take possession of the goods, removing the product from commerce, until the matter is resolved. A total of 20 actions to remove from the consumer market products charged to be violative was reported in January. These actions included 5 of foods: all involved charges concerning contamination. Others included 1 of animal feed, 12 of drugs (including 6 of veterinary), and 2 of medical devices.

Chlordiazepoxide HCl & clidinium bromide capsules, at Hollywood, S. 

Dist. Fla. 

Charged 9-15-77: when shipped by Premo Pharmaceutical Laboratories, Inc., South Hackensack, N.J., the article, labeled in part 

36 March 1981 / FDA Consumer

"Goldline c.d.p. plus capsules brand of chlordiazepoxide hcl. and clidinium bromide . . . Manufactured by Premo Pharmaceutical Laboratories, Inc., So. Hackensack, N.J. . . . distributed by Generix Drug

Corp., Hollywood, Fl.," was a new drug without an effective approved 

New Drug Application; 505(a). The article was claimed by the shipper who denied the charge and asserted, among other things, that the Government had been arbitrary in the classification and treatment of the claimant's drug. The Government moved to strike five of the seven defenses raised by the claimant. 

The claimant served written interrogatories on the Government and moved for the production of certain documents. The Government objected to such discovery on the ground of relevance. Upon the consideration of the record of the action, the court found that the claimant was entitled to discover facts pertaining to its defense of arbitrary conduct by the Government, but found that the claimant's 

45 interrogatories were burdensome and unnecessary. Accordingly, the motion to compel answers to the interrogatories was denied. However, the motion to compel the production of documents was granted and the claimant was authorized to propound no more than 20 new interrogatories.

Subsequently, a motion to dismiss the complaint was filed by the Government due to the February 17, 1978, Federal Register notice, entitled "New Policy Concerning Drugs Allowed To Remain On Market Pending Completion Of Studies Of Effectiveness ("Paragraph 

XIV" Drugs)". As a result of the notice, the seized article was not considered by the Government to be a violative new drug at that time, the allegation against the article was no longer applicable, and the action was thereby rendered moot. Accordingly, the action was dismissed and the article was ordered released to the claimant. (F.D.C. 

No. 61370; S. No. 77-28-262 et al.; N.J. No. 15)

No. 31)
