No. 32) 

Elbert A. McCracken, M.D., Stuttgart, E. Dist. Ark. 

Charged 11-8-77 by grand jury: (count 1) that, in a matter within the jurisdiction of a department and agency of the United States, a Statement of Investigator (FD 1573) was willfully and knowingly made which contained false material statements and entries (i.e., that a study of the investigative new drug, Live Attenuated Intranasal Influenza A/B Vaccine, was to be conducted only on healthy, noninstitutionalized adults from whom written informed consent would first be obtained), when many of the persons the defendant intended to use in the study would not be healthy and could not give the required written informed consent-18 U.S.C. 1001; and (count 2) that, in a matter within the jurisdiction of a department or agency of the United States, clinical test reports were knowingly and willfully filed for submission to FDA, which reports falsely stated and misrepresented data as accurate results of clinical trials of the investigational new drug, Live Attenuated Intranasal Influenza A/B Vaccine, when the defendant knew the data was inaccurate and fabricated; 18 U.S.C. 1001. 

The defendant pleaded not guilty. The defendant moved to dismiss on the grounds that count 1 of the indictment failed to state an offense against the United States and that proper venue was lacking since it would lie, if at all, in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania or the District of Columbia. The defendant moved for a bill of particulars and for discovery of Government documents. The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss, saying: "Pending before this Court is a motion to dismiss filed by Elbert A. McCracken, the defendant in the above captioned case. The defendant is charged under a two count indictment which alleges that he submitted documents containing false statements regarding his study of a 'new drug' to Smith, Kline & French Laboratories in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 101. The defendant's motion seeks the dismissal of the indictment on two alternative theories. First, the defendant contends that Count I of the indictment should be dismissed because the government failed to allege that the Smith, Kline & French Laboratories 'is an agency of the United States.' Second, the defendant argues that both counts of the indictment should be dismissed because the government lacks proper venue to prosecute either offense in the Eastern District of Arkansas. Specifically, the defendant contends that the only proper venue for the aforementioned offenses would be either Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, the place the allegedly false reports were received, or Washington, D.C., the headquarters of the government department which ultimately received the allegedly false reports. "Section 1001 of Title 18 does not require that the allegedly false statement be submitted 'to' an agency of the United States. It requires that such statement be made within a matter 'within the jurisdiction' of a department or agency of the United States. An allegation to that effect is included in Count I. "Although Count I of the indictment does not specifically set forth the relationship between the Smith, Kline & French Laboratories and the affiliated government agency or department, it does contain sufficient information to constitute a 'plain, concise and definite written statement of the essential facts constituting the offense charged' under Rule 7 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure. Thus, the Court concludes that, while it would have been preferable for the government to set forth the federal agency or department that would ultimately receive the report and its relationship to Smith, Kline & French Laboratories, this omission is not fatal to Count I of the indictment. 

However, the government will be required to provide the defendant with the omitted information in a Bill of Particulars. "In regard to the defendant's second grounds for dismissal of the indictment, a closer question of law is presented. In pertinent part, 18 U.S.C. § 3237(a) provides the following: 'Except as otherwise expressly provided by enactment of Congress, any offense against the United States begun in one district and completed in another, or committed in more than one district, may be inquired of and prosecuted in any district in which such offense was begun, continued or completed.' The defendant appears to contend that the offenses alleged in this case do not fall within the ambit of § 3237(a). In support of this contention, the defendant relies on the courts' decisions in 

Travis v. United States, 364 U.S. 631 (1961), and Mischlich v. United 

States, 310 F.Supp. 669 (D. N.J. 1970), aff'd without opinion, 455

F.2d 1194 (3rd Cir. 1971). 

"The former case involved the proper venue for an offense under 

18 U.S.C. § 1001 in the context of the National Labor Relations Act. 

Numerous courts have held that 'this decision was surely meant to be confined to the facts based on the unusual statute involved [Section 

9(h) of the National Labor Relations Act].' United States v. Slutsky, 

487 F.2d 832, 839 n.8 (2nd Cir. 1973); United States v. Ruehrup, 333 

F.2d 641, 643 (7th Cir. 1964); Imperial Meat Company v. United States, 316 F.2d 435, 440 (10th Cir. 1963). The court in Mischlich failed to recognize this distinction by relying on the Travis decision to support the general proposition that venue under § 1001 was in the district where the documents containing the false statements were delivered. "In contrast, numerous other courts in interpreting statutes closely analogous to § 1001 have held that venue for the prosecution of such offenses exists in the district where the false statements were made. 

For example, in United States v. Ruehrup, 333 F.2d 641 (7th Cir. 

1964), the defendant appealed his conviction for making false statements for the purpose of influencing an agency of the Farm Credit 

Administration in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1014. The defendant was convicted in the Southern District of Illinois. On appeal, the defendant argued, inter alia, that since the alleged false statements and reports 

38 March 1981/ FDA Consumer

were submitted to the St. Louis Bank of Cooperatives in St. Louis, Missouri, venue was solely in the Eastern District of Missouri. In rejecting this argument, the Court stated the following: 'We agree with the Tenth Circuit that Travis is not controlling and is limited to the statute there involved. Imperial Meat Company v. United States, 316 F.2d 435, 440 (10th Cir. 1963). We conclude, as did the district court, that 18 U.S.C.A. § 3237(a) is controlling. The following events occurred in Illinois in the instant case. Defendant prepared rough drafts of the statement in issue. A stenographer typed the statements and submitted them to defendant for approval. The stenographer deposited the statements in the mail. 'These events were the beginning of the offenses charged and the offenses were completed when the statements were received by the bank. See DeRosier v. United States, 218 F.2d 420, 422 (5th Cir. 1955), cert. denied, 349 U.S. 921 (1955).' 

See also, United States v. Natelli, 527 F.2d 311, 326-27 (2nd Cir. 1975).

Thus, the Court concludes that venue in this case may properly be maintained in the Eastern District of Arkansas. "It is therefore Ordered that the defendant's motion to dismiss be, and it is hereby, denied."

The court also denied the defendant's motion to take depositions, saying: "Pending before this Court is a Motion for Deposition filed by the defendant in the above captioned case. This motion seeks to have the 

Court order the taking of the depositions of certain individuals so that their testimony will be preserved and introduced at the trial of this case. The apparent need for the taking of these depositions is that the deponents reside a great distance from the site of the trial, and, therefore, their availability at trial is 'uncertain.' Finally, the defendant asserts that the testimony of each deponent is relevant, material and essential to his defense. "In pertinent part, 18 U.S.C. § 3503 provides the following regarding the taking of depositions to preserve testimony in a criminal trial: 'Whenever due to exceptional circumstances it is in the interest of justice that the testimony of a prospective witness of a party be taken and preserved, the court at any time after the filing of an indictment or information may upon motion of such party and notice to the parties order that the testimony of such witness be taken by deposition and that any designated book, paper, document, record, recording, or other material not privileged be produced at the same time and place.' This statutory language is almost identical to that used in Rule 15(a) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure. In 8 

Moore's Federal Practice ¶15.02, 15-15, the author sets forth the following requirements which must be established in order to invoke the discretionary power of the court to order the taking of a deposition for use in a criminal case: (1) that the 'prospective' witness may be unable to attend or will be prevented from attending a trial or hearing; (2) that the testimony of the witness will be material; and (3) that the taking of the testimony by deposition is necessary in order to prevent a failure of justice.' See also, United States v. Singleton, 460 F.2d 1148 (2nd Cir. 1972). "The defendant's motion and accompanying memorandum of law merely set forth that the availability of the listed deponents for trial 'is not subject to being presently ascertained.' This statement, however, is not supported by any facts which would buttress the alleged unavailability of these potential witnesses. In United States v. Rosenstein, 474 F.2d 705, 715 (2nd Cir. 1973), the Court made the following statement regarding the trial court's denial of the defendant's rule 15 motion: 'The defense motion to depose Batliner before trial under 

Fed. R.Crim. P. 15 was properly denied by Judge Tenney (United 

States v. Rosenstein, 303 F.Supp. 210, 212 [S.D. N.Y. 1969]) since the only allegation made to support the motion was that counsel had 'reason to believe' that Batliner would not attend any trial in the United States. This was deemed insufficient to establish factually that the witness could not be present.' [Emphasis added.] The defendant fails to provide any supporting factual justification for the unavailability of these potential witnesses. Thus, the Court concludes that unless the defendant can provide some factual justifications to support his motion the requested depositions should not be taken. "It is therefore Ordered that the defendant's Motion for Deposition be, and it is hereby, denied."

The case came on before court and jury. After 3 weeks of trial and at the close of the Government's rebuttal, the court Dismissed count 1 on its own motion. The jury thereafter found the defendant Not 

Guilty of count 2. (Misc. No. 423; N.J. No. 33)

DES Ban Is Upheld 

DES-diethylstilbestrol-is a synthetic hormone used from the 1950's to make animals grow faster on less feed. The history of FDA's attempts to ban this use of DES was given in DES in Feed: Promoting Growth and Problems, in the May 1979 

FDA CONSUMER. Here's an update: 

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of 

Columbia Circuit has affirmed FDA's ban on the use of DES in livestock. The ban was effective November 1, 1980.

A suit seeking to overturn the ban had been filed in 1979 by two manufacturers of DES, Hess 

& Clark Division of Rhone-Poulenc, Inc., and Vineland Laboratories, Inc. 

In its opinion November 24, 1980, the court found that the FDA Commissioner in his June 29, 1979, decision to ban the animal growth promotant had "satisfied his burden of coming forward with new evidence concerning the safety of DES. His conclusion that the drug is 'not shown to be safe' is supported by substantial evidence. We therefore hold that he acted properly. . . in banning DES." 

The ban does not affect the uses of DES as a human drug.

Long Wear Lenses OK'd The February 1980 FDA CONSUMER took a close look at the various alternatives to use of eveglasses in The ABC's of Contact Lenses. The article noted that FDA had recently approved special soft contact lenses for extended wear (up to 30 days without removal) by those who had undergone cataract surgery for removal of damaged natural lenses. 

FDA said it would evaluate the success of the extended wear lenses in cataract patients to help decide whether to approve them for routine vision correction. The outcome is reported in this update: 

FDA has approved the first extended wear contact lenses for general use up to 2 weeks at a time-without the need to remove the lenses even while sleeping.

The lenses are made of a water-absorbing material that allows oxygen to reach the cornea even when the wearer is asleep. The lenses must be cleaned and disinfected just as do daily-wear soft lenses, but less frequently. 

The long-wearing lenses, called Hydrocurve II, are manufactured by Soft Lenses, Inc., of San 

Diego, Calif. (Soft Lenses, Inc., uses the name 

Hydrocurve II for three types of soft contact lenses: daily wear, extended wear for patients who had cataract surgery, and the newly approved extended wear lenses for routine vision correctionthat is, for general use. The three are not interchangeable and no change in wearing habits should be made without first checking with an ophthalmologist or optometrist.)

The lenses were recommended for approval by 

FDA's Ophthalmic Device Section, a panel of non-FDA ophthalmologists, optometrists, and representatives of consumer interests and regulated industry. The panel advises FDA on the safety and effectiveness of ophthalmic medical devices.

FDA recommends that extended wear contact lenses be prescribed and fitted only by an ophthalmologist or an optometrist. As part of its approval, FDA is requiring that the manufacturer monitor at least 500 people wearing the lenses for years to uncover any adverse effects. Before approving the lenses for extended wear for general use, FDA evaluated the results of several studies of Hydrocurve II lenses for daily and extended wear. More than 2,100 people participated in the studies, including patients who had undergone cataract surgery and people who had healthy eyes that required vision correction. 

A summary of the safety and efficacy data upon which FDA based its approval is available from the Dockets Management Branch (HFA-305), 

Food and Drug Administration, Rm. 4-62, 5600 

Fishers Lane, Rockville, Md. 20857.

Caffeine in Baked Goods?

In your article on caffeine in the October 1980 issue, you refer on page 6 to several food products-baked goods, frozen dairy products, soft candies, gelatins, and puddings-containing caffeine. Can you please notify me of your sources of information for such a statement? Furthermore do you have references detailing the actual caffeine content of such food products?

There is intense consumer interest in caffeine, at least in Iowa, and we are constantly seeking more information. 

Elisabeth Schafer, Ph.D.

Extension Nutritionist Iowa State U. 

Ames, Iowa

The references to caffeine's presence in such food products as baked goods, frozen dairy products, soft candy, gelatins, and puddings are based on a 1970 survey of food manufacturers. The survey was done as part of the Agency's GRAS review by the 

National Academy of Sciences. 

The survey also contained data on caffeine content-that is, caffeine that was added to the food items, not that which was naturally occurring. For the four categories of foods listed above, the maximum caffeine content was 0.04 percent.

The survey indicated that the main purpose for the added caffeine in those food categories was as a flavor enhancer or to impart a coffee flavor (coffee ice cream, etc.). "Subtle" Error Cited

I was very much interested in your article "A 

Food Poisoning Whodunit" by Emil Corwin in the

November 1980 edition of FDA CONSUMER. Com ing from a microbiological background by degree, and having worked for several years in the food industry, the case review was interesting and an enlightening review of the efforts exerted to research such food related circumstances. 

I did want to point out, however, a subtle error appearing at the end of paragraph 10, ". . . and seal live spores in the oxygenless environment necessary for them to sporulate and begin producing their deadly toxin." As you correctly point out elsewhere in the article the toxin elaborated by C. 

Botulinum is a metabolic by-product, accurately called an exotoxin. Metabolizing organisms "sporulate" when they assume their dormant state. 

Spores on the other hand are correctly said to "germinate" when they become metabolizing reproducing units. This is a rather common error, but one which should not be perpetuated in a government technical publication.

C. P. Land 

Cincinnati, Ohio

Tracking The Skin's Reactions To Drugs 

A rash on the face could be an allergic reaction to a food; or it could have been caused by a drug. No one knows exactly how many people develop such drug-induced skin reactions, but FDA would like to find out. 

In order to learn more about these drug reactions and who gets them, the Agency has established a National Registry of Dermatological Reactions to Drugs. by Annabel Hecht 

Tf you woke up one morning and 

Idiscovered a rash on your hands from an unknown cause what would you think? 

Measles? No, you decide, you had them when you were a kid. 

That new dishwashing detergent that the commercials said was gentle on the hands? 

The paint thinner you were using? 

The insecticide you sprayed on the tomatoes? Poison ivy, or something you ate? 

Any of a number of commercial products might have caused those red and itchy spots, but would you ever think to put the blame on the medication you started taking last week?

Skin eruptions are the most common reactions people experience when they are taking drugs. They can be caused by both nonprescription (over-the-counter) and prescription drug products. A drug-related skin reaction may be just a mild rash, or it could be a severe form of eczema that threatens life. One dermatologist has estimated that 10 percent of hospital patients suffer drug-caused skin eruptions, and that the percentage of sufferers in the general population may be higher.

At present, it can only be estimated how many people experience such drug reactions. Although FDA collects information on adverse drug reactions, little has been reported on those occurring on the skin. Often the reports that do come in are incomplete or inaccurate because the physician or other health professional making the report doesn't have the training and background to describe the reaction in all its specifics or to recognize the origins as drug related. 

To improve the reporting of drugcaused skin reactions, FDA has turned to the professionals who know what they're looking at—the nation's dermatologists. Under a contract with the American Academy of Dermatology, the Agency has established a National Registry of Dermatologi cal Reactions to Drugs, providing a central point for reporting adverse reactions. A 24-hour toll free telephone reporting system began operation in the academy's Evanston, Ill., headquarters last December. 

Rashes and blisters on the skin of drug takers can be more than an allergic reaction peculiar to an individual patient. What happens on the skin often is the first clue that a patient is reacting to a drug. Although it may seem simple, accurately diagnosing the cause of a skin eruption is not easy for a variety of reasons. The same drug may cause different reactions in different patients or even different reactions in the same patient on different occasions. A drug-induced skin reaction doesn't necessarily appear with the first dose and in fact may not crop up until the patient has stopped taking the drug. 

A particular drug might not be considered as the source of a skin eruption because the patient took it for years without problems. Yet it is possible for a person to develop sensitivity to a drug over time. Polypharmacy-namely, taking several drugs at one time-presents still another problem. How do you determine which is the culprit? A mild rash may be completely overlooked. And there is always the possibility that the skin condition was not caused by a drug at all. 

Fortunately, some skin eruption patterns appear fairly consistently when certain drugs are taken so that a diagnosis of a drug reaction can be made with a degree of certainty. For instance, inflamed pimples looking like acne can be caused by drugs such as corticosteroids, bromides, dantrolene sodium, haloperidol, isoniazid, lithium, phenytoin, and trimethadione. These reactions, called "acneiform eruptions," also develop in the skin of people who have taken iodides for a long time. Iodides are among the ingredients found in some over-the-counter drug products such as vitamin and mineral preparations, sedatives, and asthma and cold remedies. Health food enthusiasts who eat kelp, another source of iodides, may experience these acne-like skin eruptions.

A rash resembling measles or scarlet fever, known as an exanthematous eruption, can indicate a reaction to a variety of drugs. Topping the list of offenders are antibiotics including penicillin, streptomycin, tetracycline, kanamycin, and neomycin. Other drugs associated with this reaction are allopurinol, barbiturates, mercurial diuretics, phenothiazines, and thiazides. 

Eczematous eruptions, which look like a contact dermatitis, may appear on the skin when a patient takes some antibiotics and phenothizines as well as sulfonamides and thiamine. 

The medical term urticaria comes to us via the Latin urtica, which was

XII Hirsutism 

(Abnormal growth of hair)

An ingredient found in many drug products 

Generic Name of Drug 

Dantrolene sodium Phenytoin Thiazides 

Oral contraceptives ** In Germany Aspirin is a trade name. In the U.S. aspirin is a generic name. Aspirin is found in many drug products. what the ancient Romans called nettles. What could be a more appropriate name for the skin eruption known popularly as hives. The red and itchy patches of hives can be caused by practically all drugs. Most often hives, or urticaria, appear after a person has taken barbiturates, codeine, insulin, isoniazid, penicillin, and even aspirin.

The lesions of erythema multiforme, in its simplest form, look like small targets and may be caused by barbiturates, phenytoin, penicillin, phenylbutazone, sulfonamides, and thiazides. The most severe form of erythema multiforme, called the Stevens-Johnson syndrome, produces blisters on the skin and in the mouth. 

Long term use of sulfonamides has been linked with this syndrome, which can be fatal if not recognized and treated appropriately. 

Women more often than men can suffer from erythema nodosum, which is not surprising because oral contraceptives are the leading cause of this condition. The painful red-violet colored swelling also may result from taking sulfonamides, bromides, iodides, opiates, penicillin, or salicylates. 

Not serious, fortunately, are the "fixed drug eruptions," which develop the habit of recurring in exactly the same spot each time the patient takes a particular drug. The reaction consists of well-defined round or oval plaques that often leave a persistent brown color after they heal. Diazepam, barbiturates, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, and phenolphthalein (a frequent ingredient in laxatives) are among the drugs known to cause the fixed drug reaction. 

Pigmentation is another type of skin reaction associated with drug use. Most common are the yellowish- 

8 April 1981 FDA Consumer

brown patches, or chloasma, that sometimes appear on the forehead and cheeks of women taking oral contraceptives. Chlorpromazine and related phenothiazines cause a bluegray discoloration on areas of the skin that are exposed to light. Heavy metals-silver, gold, bismuth, arsenic can leave the skin a brown or blue-gray color.

A rash reminiscent of a sunburn may be the price some people pay when they venture out into the sun after taking tetracyclines, chlordiazepoxide, griseofulvin, sulfonamides, or thiazides. Whatever parts of the body are exposed to the sun or other sources of ultraviolet (UV) light may break out, because these drugs make the patient especially sensitive to UV light. Loss of hair is expected with some anticancer drugs, but also can plague the person who is taking anticoagulants and antithyroid drugs. 

Hair loss also occasionally occurs with use of the popular antihypertensive drug propranolol, but the condition is reversed when the drug is discontinued. The opposite reactionappearance of hair in areas where it does not usually grow-has been seen in patients taking phenytoin and streptomycin.

These are just some of the skin eruptions that can develop after certain drugs have been taken. Happily, many of them disappear when the drug is stopped. Others can be treated with alternative drugs and other supportive measures. 

The academy's new reporting system not only will provide a better idea of how many drug-induced skin reactions are occurring, but also will make it easy for dermatologists to report new, unusual, or serious drug reactions at the time they observe them. The telephone system will serve as a first step in alerting the medical community to possible adverse reactions to drugs. Reports of these reactions will be carried in a regular column featured in the JOUR 

NAL OF THE AMERICAN ACADEMY OF DERMATOLOGY. Ultimately, the program will help practicing dermatologists provide better care for their patients. The information that will be gathered also will be useful in modifying or updating drug labeling.

In at least one respect, the dermatology registry is one of a kind. Although the idea of contracting with a nongovernment unit to collect and document drug-related problems and using specialists in their fields to gather this information is not new, no other reporting system at this time is administered by a professional or specialty medical organization.

This arrangement allows FDA to utilize the expertise of an important medical subspecialty and increases the probability of shedding light on many drug-induced skin eruptions that might not have been reported.

Many people, including physicians, are reluctant to report directly to a government agency, but do not hesitate to communicate with their own professional organizations. As an added inducement, the new system guarantees physician and patient confidentiality.

Typical drug-induced skin reactions that have been observed in patients include the severe rash produced by lincomycin (above, left and right), and urticaria or hives (below, left) that sometimes develop following ingestion of aspirin, penicillin, phenothiazines, coumarin, or isoniazid. (Photos taken from slides provided by Dr. Laurence H. Miller, National Institute of Arthritis, Metabolism and Digestive Diseases, National Institutes of Health.)

The dermatology registry is the fifth FDA-funded program set up to gather information on specific drug reactions. Already operating are registries for drug effects on the eyes, effects of contrast media such as dyes used in radiography, tissue reactions to drugs, and drug-induced effects on the liver. The dermatology program, scheduled to run 3 years, will not only provide an enlarged fund of information on drug-induced skin problems, but will prove the feasibility of using a specialty society in medicine as the focal point for collecting drug experience data. 

Annabel Hecht is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

VDT's 

Pass Medical Tests 

Offices have traditionally been thought to be among the safest workplaces. But over the past few years some office workers have become concerned that a new piece of high technology office equipment-the video display terminal, or VDT-could be causing a variety of health problems. 

Tests have been made of the devices for potential health hazards, including radiation leakage. Here are the latest findings.

The technology of the future sometimes has a way of becoming commonplace almost overnight. First, secretaries in more and more offices begin using new typing machines, where the words are displayed not on paper but on a "TV" screen above the keyboard. Next, newspaper reporters and editors are trading in their paste pots and pencils for these typewriter-TV hybrids. Then the technology creeps from the office to the home, where micro-computers help balance the household budget, displaying income and expenses for the family to fret over on a video screen. Office and home alike begin to resemble the bridge of the Starship Enterprise. The future is now. 

It's a fact that these "high tech" computerized typewriters are hardly a novelty anymore. According to the

National Institute for Occupational 

Safety and Health (NIOSH), more than 7 million Americans now work at these video display terminals-or 

VDT's, as they've come to be known. And that doesn't count those who have bought VDT's for home use.

A typical VDT has a keyboard similar to those on "old-fashioned" typewriters but with a few extra keys for special instructions to a computer that can rapidly store, transmit, retrieve, or edit information. The information is displayed on a video screen, similar to a television screen, greatly reducing the need for paper, pencils, and files. 

Because of their potential for increasing productivity, VDT's are being put to work in banks, libraries, airline reservation offices, newspapers, government agencies, and countless other workplaces. Students use them in school; consumers use them at home to balance checkbooks or keep an inventory of household items. Some experts predict that

VDT's may soon be as commonplace as telephones. 

But as the use of VDT's has increased, so have reports of a variety of health problems among those who operate the machines. VDT workers have complained of eyestrain, blurred vision, sore necks, backs and legs, fatigue, insomnia, headaches, tension, nausea, and irritability. 

There also have been isolated reports alleging serious, permanent injuries from VDT's. In 1977, for example, two newspaper employees, aged 29 and 35, were diagnosed as having cataracts-an eye disease, usually afflicting the elderly, in which parts of the lens become opaque, leading to partial or total blindness.

Cataracts can be caused by a variety of factors, including exposure to certain forms of radiation. Because the two employees worked at VDT's, their newspaper and their union asked NIOSH to test the machines for possible radiation leakage. After testing the units, NIOSH concluded that the VDT's did not appear capable of producing high enough levels of radiation to cause cataracts. 

But in 1979 radiation worries welled up again when four women who worked at VDT's in the classified advertising department of a Canadian newspaper had babies with birth defects. The provincial government checked all of the newspaper's VDT's but could find no levels of radiation that could account for the birth defects.

Nevertheless, the results of these tests by NIOSH and Canadian health officials were not enough to relieve the growing concern among VDT workers that many health problems were being caused by radiation from their machines. 

VDT's can, in fact, produce several types of radiation: x-rays, radiofrequency, microwave, ultrasound, ultraviolet, infrared, and visible light. 

At low enough levels, these forms of radiation would have no significant health effects. But can VDT's emit levels high enough to harm users? 

FDA's Bureau of Radiological 

Health decided to find out. The bureau, under the Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act, is responsible for assuring the safety of numerous radiation-emitting products, from television sets to microwave ovens to x-ray machines. Numerous inquiries about possible hazards from VDT's prompted the bureau to test a representative cross-section of VDT models from all known manufacturers. 

Most of the tests were done at 

FDA's Winchester Engineering and 

Analytical Center in Winchester, Mass. One-hundred and twenty-five machines were checked for x-ray leakage; 34 for other radiation. The testing was done under "worst-case" conditions; the machines were adjusted to produce the most radiation possible and safety circuits designed to protect against x-ray leakage were purposely made to fail. 

Because there are no performance standards setting permissible radia- 

FDA Consumer | April 1981 | 11

"It's a fact that these 'high tech' computerized typewriters are hardly a novelty anymore... more than 7 million Americans now work at these video display terminals. . . tion levels for VDT's, the test results had to be compared to occupational exposure standards or to performance standards for other products. 

The testing found radiofrequency (RF) and microwave emissions from some of the electronic components and circuits in the VDT's. But, while high levels of microwave and RF radiation have been associated with cataracts, those levels were not detected in any of the machines tested. 

Microwave emissions were more than 100 times below the maximum level allowed under exposure guidelines set by the American National Standards Institute. Almost all of the RF radiation was in a frequency range of 

15 to 125 kilo Hertz (thousands of cycles per second). In this range the body absorbs so little radiation that no public exposure standards have even been thought necessary. The levels of higher frequency RF and microwave radiation measured from the machines were so low as to be insignificant.

As with low-frequency RF radiation, no mandatory standards exist for public exposure to ultrasound (sound above the frequency range that humans can hear). So a highly conservative voluntary standard, widely accepted in Great Britain, was used as a basis of comparison with the ultrasound measurements from the VDT's. 

Ultrasound can be produced by vibrations in a VDT's transformer. Industrial workers exposed to high levels of ultrasound, such as those produced by ultrasonic welding equipment, have suffered headaches, fatigue, ringing in the ears, nausea and irritability. Scientists are concerned that long-term exposure to such high levels of ultrasound may also promote subtle adverse changes in the cardiovascular and nervous systems, although this has not been proven.

But FDA's testing of the VDT's did not find high levels of ultrasound. 

The maximum emission was 68 db., four times below the permissible levels set in the voluntary British standard. 

To measure light radiation, FDA's scientists focused their instruments on the VDT's display screen. The screen's flourescent coating not only produces visible light in the form of letters, numbers and symbols, but may emit ultraviolet and infrared radiation as well. High levels of ultraviolet radiation, such as a person might receive from years of exposure to the sun, have been associated with skin cancer and cataracts. High levels of infrared radiation can cause cataracts and damage to the eye's retina. Even exceedingly bright visible light can produce eyestrain and retina damage.

Measurements of visible and infrared radiation from VDT's were compared to FDA's performance standard for lasers, which allows no more than 2 milliwatts per square centimeter. The worst of the VDT's emitted less than half that amount. 

The highest level of ultraviolet radiation from the machines was about 5 microwatts per square centimeter, some 200 times below occupational exposure guidelines set by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists.

While radiofrequency, microwave, sound and light radiation emissions were all well below levels that would cause concern, problems were discovered in testing for x-ray leakage. Xrays can be given off by several components of a VDT, particularly the cathode ray tube (similar to those in television sets) used in some of the machines. Exposure to x-rays in sufficient amounts can increase the risk of cancer, genetic damage, and birth defects. 

X-ray leakage from VDT's can be controlled by proper circuit design 

12 April 1981 / FDA Consumer

"X-ray leakage from VDT's can be controlled by proper circuit design and the use of shielding in or around the cathode ray tube. and the the use of shielding in or around the cathode ray tube. FDA's testing found that all but 8 of the 125 units checked emitted no more than 

0.4 milliRoentgens (mR) per hour. 

This is below the 0.5 mR per hour permitted by FDA's performance standard for television sets. 

Of the eight problem units, the worst reading was 2.0 mR. The three firms that manufactured these machines were notified of the findings and either corrected the problem or took the model off the market.

Overall, the results of FDA's radiation testing generally agreed with those of earlier studies done by 

NIOSH and other organizations here and abroad. The consensus of the studies is that VDT's emit little or no harmful radiation under normal operating conditions; the emissions that are detectable are well below any existing national and international standards. Compared to some other common sources of radiation, VDT's present a much lower risk. Fluorescent lamps, for example, emit more visible and ultraviolet light. Space heaters give off more infrared radiation, with no known ill effects. And

VDT's normally omit less x-radiation than TV sets. 

If radiation from VDT's is not a public health hazard, what then accounts for the many health complaints among VDT users? The answer may lie in what occupational health experts call ergonomics-factors that affect the way a worker adjusts to working conditions. The factors have to do with the work environment, the demands of the job, and the worker's physical condition to begin with. Several studies have identified ergonomic factors that could bring about some of the health problems reported by VDT workers: poor room lighting and glare from the display screen could cause eyestrain; incorrect equipment layout could cause sore necks, backs, and legs. 

Last year NIOSH surveyed about 

250 VDT workers at two newspapers and an insurance company and found a prevalence of ergonomic problems at all three sites. These included screen glare, room lighting problems, improper screen and keyboard heights, and poorly designed tables and chairs. The study also found that pressure for higher productivity appears to be responsible for a significant portion of the stress and health complaints of VDT operators. 

Those findings led NIOSH to make several recommendations to help reduce health problems among VDT users. Among them: • Workers should be able to adjust the height of their keyboard, screen, chair seat, and backrest; screen brightness and contrast; leg room; viewing distance; room lighting levels; and chair tension. 

Screen glare should be controlled by using drapes or blinds on windows, hoods and glare shields over screens, and proper positioning of machines with respect to room lighting. • Workers should take rest breaks of at least 15 minutes every 2 hours. • Workers should undergo a complete eye exam before they begin working with VDT's and limited exams periodically. 

NIOSH and health agencies from other countries are continuing to study health problems associated with the use of VDT's. FDA's findings confirm earlier reports that radiation does not appear to be a cause for concern. But research still needs to be done to determine the best working conditions and machine design for VDT operators, to make sure that tomorrow's technology doesn't bring with it today's headaches.

Bill Rados FDA Consumer | April 1981 / 13

IODINE 

Going From Hypo To Hyper 

The body needs iodine, and not enough occurs in food naturally. So it must be added to foods. Some years ago, salt was selected as the best conveyor of iodine, and today most of the table salt that is sold contains the added nutrient. However, recent indications are that we Americans are getting several times the necessary iodine. The findings have started a new debate. 

When It Rains It Pours." So 

With the Morton salt box.

It's a sentiment echoed by many these days as we find that one food after another contains something we wish it didn't. One of the most disturbing new surprises is that many foods now have too much iodine in them. 

It is particularly surprising to find an oversupply of iodine in food, because a lack of dietary iodine was a major public health problem 75 years ago. Iodine is essential for normal nutrition and the consequences of a deficiency can be serious. The thyroid gland uses iodine to make thyroid hormone, which regulates body heat, influences protein synthesis, keeps connective tissues healthy, and promotes physical and mental development. If there isn't enough iodine in the diet, the thyroid gland will enlarge itself so that it can use what iodine is available as efficiently as possible. That enlargement is called goiter. When iodine inadequacy persists, hypothyroidism may also develop, a condition characterized by mental and physical sluggishness and subnormal body temperature. Hypothyroidism in a pregnant woman can result in the mental and physical retardation of her child. 

The ultimate source of iodine is the ocean. Seafood is usually rich in iodine, as is food grown on soil that was once covered by the sea. But the effects of glaciers and other weathering of the soil have removed much of the iodine from the soil over large portions of the Earth's surface. Food grown on that soil doesn't contain by Flora Taylor enough iodine for nutritional needs; the result has been widespread endemic goiter among the natives of those regions. In the United States, endemic goiter was a prevalent public health problem in the early 1900's in the States bordering the Great Lakes and to the northwest. Once it was recognized that goiter was caused by iodine deficiency, the remedy was clear: iodine must be added to food in some way. Iodization of table salt was begun in the State of Michigan in 1924 to prevent endemic goiter in that region, and such salt eventually became available throughout the 

United States, solving a public health problem of some magnitude. But public health officials were unable to make iodization of salt mandatory, so the fear persisted that some people who weren't using iodized salt might develop deficiencies. For that reason,

FDA adopted regulations requiring that salt manufacturers state on the label whether or not the salt supplies iodine, thus warning consumers that if they choose noniodized salt, they are passing up a way of obtaining a necessary nutrient.

But in the early 1970's, it began to appear that iodine deficiency was no longer a public health problem. Physicians noticed that in clinical tests of patients with radioactive iodine, their thyroid glands were taking up less of it, which suggested that their thyroids were already saturated with iodine.

Some thyroid specialists became concerned that some people might be getting too much iodine. In 1974,

FDA sought more information by in cluding iodine in its Total Diet Study 

(TDS), which estimates residues of pesticides and certain heavy metals in 

American diets. 

The results were startling. Analysis of the foods sampled revealed that a growing teenage boy consuming 

2,850 calories per day received an average of 830 micrograms of iodine.

That's about 5½ times the current 

Recommended Daily Allowance 

(RDA) of 150 micrograms thought to be needed for normal growth and good nutrition. In the TDS, salt added at the table and used in cooking was not iodized. Thus, use of an average amount of iodized salt would have added another 300 micrograms of iodine per day to the intake. 

Iodine in the adult diet decreased in 1975 to 550 micrograms a day (about four times the RDA) in a 

2,850 calorie diet and rose again in 

1978 to 700 micrograms a day, or about 4½ times the RDA. 

The large amounts of iodine weren't the only surprise: the iodine was turning up in unexpected places-for example dairy products contributed up to 38 percent of the iodine. To find so much iodine (about 320 micrograms a day) being furnished by dairy products was also a cause for additional concern, because milk is the dietary staple of babies. 

In 1975, FDA expanded its TDS to include the typical American diets for 

6-month-old infants and 2-year-old toddlers. The study revealed that iodine intakes of infants and toddlers were even greater than adults in relation to their RDA's. The typical infant diet supplied an average of 380

FDA Consumer April 1981 | 15

micrograms of iodine a day in 1975, although the RDA for 6-month-old infants is only 45 micrograms. In 

1976 and 1978 the levels were even higher, 10 and 13 times the RDA, respectively. Typical toddler diets also showed very high levels of iodine ( 6 to 10 times the RDA) during 1975 through 1978. About one-half to twothirds of the iodine in the infant and toddler diets was from milk. Preliminary data from the 1979 and 1980 FDA studies indicate that levels of iodine in our food supply, particularly milk, are decreasing, though daily intake still remains several times higher than the RDA. 

Iodine can get into milk in a number of ways. Some occurs in milk handling, via use of iodophors, a group of iodine-containing chemicals. 

Because they kill bacteria, fungi, and viruses, iodophors are used to clean, sanitize, and disinfect. Teat dips used to control mastitis (udder inflammation) sometimes contain iodophors, as may udder salves. Some farmers use iodophors to clean the udders before each milking, or to clean milking machines, refrigerated farm vats, road transport tankers, raw milk tanks, pasteurized milk vats, and bottle filler sealing rubbers. 

Indiscriminate use of iodophors can add significant amounts of iodine to milk-up to 740 micrograms per liter according to one study (that's about 180 micrograms per cup, because a liter is just over a quart). But iodophors aren't the major source of iodine in milk. The biggest problem is that cows are being fed too much iodine. 

Cows have thyroid glands and, like humans, their bodies need a certain amount of iodine to prevent goiter.

Some iodine may occur naturally in cattle feed. Farmers-to be sure their cows will not develop goiter-often provide iodized salt licks, or add iodine to feed in the form of ethylene diamine dihydroiodide (EDDI). Add ing about 10 milligrams of EDDI per cow per day will usually prevent iodine deficiency. But many dairy farmers are adding at least five times that much in the belief that the extra iodine will help to prevent a disease known as foot rot-though there is no scientific evidence to support this. 

FDA's Total Diet Study assumed that infants were being fed fresh whole milk. Prepared commercial formulas weren't given much weight, and breast milk wasn't included at all. Current data indicate that milkbased infant formulas often contain as much iodine as fresh milk does.

The iodine content of breast milk will depend on how much iodine the mother consumes. The few figures available suggest there's an average content of about 139 micrograms per liter in mothers' milk, which is far lower than the 500 micrograms of iodine per liter found in commercial milk. 

Dairy products accounted for larger amounts of iodine than any of the other food groups analyzed in the 

TDS. But other foods were found to contain unexpectedly large quantities. 

In 1974, grain and cereal-based products accounted for 28 percent of the iodine in the typical adult diet, and sugars and adjuncts (such items as jam, jelly, pudding mixes, and candy bars) supplied another 23 percent.

Iodophors are also widely used in general food processing to clean and sanitize equipment and are probably contributing to the high iodine content in both of these food groups. 

Many foods in both groups also contain milk and milk-derived products, such as whey. Significant amounts of iodine are probably contributed by the red food color erythrosine (FD&C Red No. 3), which is more than 50 percent iodine. The use of

Red No. 3 has almost doubled since two other red food dyes were taken off the market by FDA in 1976. Concentrations of iodine up to175 micrograms per gram of food, presumably due to erythrosine, have been as-

A single serving of erythrosine-colored dry cereal can increase the daily iodine intake by as much as 400 micrograms. (However, scientists are not sure yet if the iodine in red dye is absorbed and utilized by the body.) 

Another possible source for the iodine in grain and cereal products is the iodine found in compounds sometimes used as dough conditioners; these can produce bread containing from 28 to 140 micrograms of iodine per ounce. Most major baking companies have voluntarily switched to other conditioning agents since being made aware of the problem.

Fast foods and many of the highly processed convenience foods of today were not included in the typical daily diets prepared for analysis in FDA's 

Total Diet Study, but recent research indicates these may contain large amounts of iodine. A typical meal at 

MacDonald's (a Big Mac, french fries, and a milkshake) contains almost 3 times the RDA of iodine for adults. Frozen fried chicken dinners analyzed in one study contained an average of 970 micrograms of iodine, with a range of up to 4,300 micrograms, or almost 29 times the RDA. 

Food additives derived from algae, such as carrageenan, contain iodine and are widely used in food processing. Iodine-rich kelp is often used in seasoning mixes; the iodine content of 1 gram of this dried seaweed can be as high as 4,500 micrograms. 

Dietary supplements are another possible source. Many multivitamins with minerals supply 100 to 150 micrograms of iodine, but if they are colored with Red No. 3, they will contain more than the label indicates. 

One brand contained 375 micrograms per tablet.

In some small towns, or farms, and in remote areas of our national forests, iodine is sometimes used instead of chlorine to purify drinking water. 

This can add another 1,000 to 2,000 micrograms to the daily iodine intake of the people who drink this water. 

The Environmental Protection 

Agency has recommended against iodization of drinking water for communities except on a temporary basis.

The American Medical Association's Department of Food and Nutrition Workshop Committee on Cur rent Exposure to Iodine recently stated that current evidence indicates there are no adverse physiologic reactions from iodine intakes up to 

2,000 micrograms per day in healthy adults, and 1,000 micrograms per day or more in some children. Average intakes as measured by the TDS are obviously within this range. The 

AMA committee admits that additional information is needed on the long-term effects of iodine before a maximum "safe" level of intake can be established. Because there has not been enough research, the effects of moderately high levels of iodine in the diet are not known. 

Although the usual cause of goiter is inadequate iodine, excessively large intakes can also cause goiter by reducing hormone release from the thyroid gland. Very high levels of iodine (10,000 to 200,000 micrograms per day) among seaweed fishermen in Japan have been found to cause goiter in 6 to 12 percent of those exposed. 

Repeated large doses of iodinecontaining medications during pregnancy can cause goiter in newborns.

This is particularly dangerous because the goiter can block the airways and cause suffocation. Iodinecontaining asthma medications taken by the pregnant mother have been reported to cause goiter in her newborn infant. Those medications may provide daily doses of 12,000 micrograms of iodine. 

A disease known as Hashimoto's thyroiditis appears to have become increasingly common in this country in the last few decades. Its yearly incidence is now thought to be 3 to 6 cases per 10,000 people. The higher incidence may be due to increases in dietary iodine, though supporting evidence is circumstantial and incomplete. People suffering from Hashimoto's thyroiditis can be affected adversely by high levels of dietary iodine, which may disturb their hormone synthesis and cause enlargement of the thyroid gland. Daily doses of 2,000 micrograms can block their thyroid function. 

Rising iodine intakes may also be responsible for decreased remissions in the treatment of hyperthyroidism with anti-thyroid agents. The rate of therapeutic success reportedly has declined from 60 to 17 percent.

Experts differ as to the need for concern about these hazards. But there is general agreement that we certainly don't need any more iodine than we're currently getting. For this reason, in 1977 FDA's Bureau of 

Foods said it would approve no new iodine compounds for use in foods or food processing. As noted, bureau officials have also urged industry to eliminate indiscriminate use of iodophors, and dairy people and feed manufacturers have been cautioned about the overuse of EDDI. The

JOURNAL OF THE AMERICAN MEDI- CAL ASSOCIATION has asked physi cians to be on the lookout for any problems that may be attributable to dietary iodine.

Flora Taylor wrote this article while an intern in FDA's public affairs office.

X'ing Out Unneeded X Rays 

The he Federal government is saving an estimated $4 million a year by eliminating unnecessary chest x-rays formerly required for many employees. 

The savings result from a 1978 presidential directive that set guide-. lines for Federal agencies to reduce unnecessary diagnostic x-rays. One of the guidelines was that x-ray screening should only be done when it significantly helps detect health problems among those screened. 

The directive assigned responsibility for implementing the x-ray guide lines to the Public Health Service 

(PHS). On May 29, 1980, PHS sent letters to all its agencies, to all other agencies within its parent organization, the Department of Health and 

Human Services, and to 28 other 

Federal departments and agencies. 

They were asked to review their current procedures, eliminate chest x-ray screening not supported by the guideline, and justify any screening that would be continued. 

The letter emphasized that the guidelines are not intended to prevent or discourage any physician from ordering an x-ray when it is believed necessary for the care of a patient. Only "unproductive, routine screening programs originating from long-time, standing order administrative requirements in which otherwise healthy people are given chest x-rays without prior physician examination or specific indications," should be ended, PHS said. 

The agencies were asked to report their results to FDA's Bureau of Radiological Health. The reports indicate that about 32,000 yearly chest xrays within PHS and 128,000 in other 

Federal agencies have been eliminated. At an estimated cost of $25 each, the annual savings amounts to about $800,000 within PHS and $3.2 million in other agencies. 

Besides the monetary savings, elimination of 160,000 chest x-rays a year also reduces unnecessary radiation exposure.

Among the actions taken by Federal agencies in response to the directive: 

The Department of the Navy has discontinued routine chest x-rays for annual, reenlistment, and extension physical examinations and for occupationally exposed radiation workers.

The Navy also has reduced the frequency of x-ray screening for divers from once a year to once every 3 years. The result of the Navy's efforts: more than 100,000 chest x-ray exams eliminated per year at an annual savings of $2.5 million. • The National Aeronautics and

Space Administration has ended all yearly chest x-ray screening exams for asymptomatic employees. The result: 17,000 chest x-ray exams eliminated at an annual savings of about $425,000.

To help assure that the savings achieved by the agencies remain permanent, the bureau will monitor PHS facilities periodically to see that the guidelines in the presidential directive continue to be followed.

To achieve even greater reductions in cost and x-ray exposure throughout the country, the bureau is working with medical associations and expert panels of physicians to develop x-ray referral criteria. These criteria. will serve as guidance for physicians in deciding when a particular x-ray procedure is needed. The bureau expects to publish referral criteria for chest x-rays, with the endorsement of medical groups, later this year.

Cervical Caps-The Perfect, 

Untested Contraceptive

There has been growing discussion, but little scientific data, on the cervical cap, a recently rediscovered form of birth control. Clarification of the cap's effectiveness and safety as a contraceptive may be forthcoming from studies now underway, but for the present the device remains investigational. by Judith Willis 

The search for a safe, effective, and convenient contraceptive has led down paths of panacea that often end in blind alleys.

In the 1960's, millions of American women climbed aboard the birth control pill bandwagon, believing that they had found a convenient contraceptive that was risk-free in terms of both conception and side effects. The 

Pill's success in preventing pregnancy remains uncontested. But today, most medical authorities would agree that the Pill is a medication whose risks and benefits should be carefully weighed. 

Frightened off the Pill by new information on its side effects, many women in the 1970's thought they had found the safe, effective answer in the intrauterine device (IUD). But then came information about its dangers, the most dramatic of which were associated with the Dalkon 

Shield, now off the market. Many women turned back to the diaphragm, but some found it fell short of the efficacy and convenience goals, although it appears to be among the safest of choices in terms of health. 

Enter the cervical cap which, in the 1980's, may well turn out to be the eternally sought safe, effective, and convenient method of birth control, but about which relatively little is currently known.

A small, thimble-shaped device made of rubber, the cervical cap fits over the cervix, or neck of the uterus (womb), that protrudes into the top of the back of the vagina. In contrast to the diaphragm, which is held in place by the pressure of its rim against the vaginal wall, the cap fits directly around the cervix. A groove on the inner lip of the cap helps to form an airtight seal that holds the cap in place through suction. 

For contraceptive purposes, the cervical cap is used with a spermicidal cream or jelly, like that used with the diaphragm. Some researchers theorize that spermicide may not be necessary if it can be shown that the seal of the cap around the cervix is sufficient to prevent entry of sperm. 

At present, there are no data to either substantiate or repudiate this theory. 

What is known is that a lot less spermicide is needed with the cap than with the diaphragm. Thus, part of the appeal of the cap is that it is less "messy" and more convenient than the diaphragm to which spermicide must be added before each intercourse. In contrast, the cap need only be filled one-third with spermicide before insertion and no more need be added for several days, regardless of sexual activity.

It is not known exactly how many days the spermicide will stay effective inside an inserted cap. Nor is it known how long a cap can be left in place without ill effect. There are some reports of an odor developing after a few days. Some researchers suggest adding chlorophyll to the spermicide to prevent odor. However, other experts believe that the cap should be taken out and cleaned every day or every few days. There are no studies to verify what, if any, is the optimum safe and effective duration of insertion.

In the United States there is now only one cervical cap manufacturer (Milex Co.). However, this cap has not been approved for contraceptive use and is marketed only as an aid in artificial insemination or for collection of menstrual fluid.

Cervical caps used as contraceptives here are imported from an English Company (Lamberts, Ltd.).

When shipped to this country they must be clearly marked, "for investigational use only. 

Although the imported cap comes in four sizes, attaining a proper fit has been a problem. To overcome this problem, a Chicago dentist and a physician have collaborated on an in novative cap. The dentist, Dr. Rob ert A.

Goepp, director of the Uni versity of Chicago's Zoller Dental 

Clinic, came up with the idea of making an impression of each individual cervix in much the same way and with the same material that dentists use for making impressions of teeth. Dr. Ewe Freese, chairman of

Obstetrics and Gynecology at Chicago Medical School, works with Goepp in making custom-fitted caps from the individual molds of cervixes. The Goepp-Freese cap also has a valve which can be opened to allow secretion of menstrual fluid, so that the cap could be left in place for several months. In contrast to other available caps, the Goepp-Freese cap, with its unique features, may be patentable.

Difficulty of insertion is another problem of the cap. Measuring less than 2 inches in diameter, the cap containing spermicide is inserted into the vagina by grasping it, dome down, between two fingers of one hand, and compressing the rim. The cap is pushed as far as it will go along the back wall of the vaginal canal, and then the rim must be pressed around the cervix until it forms a seal. The cap is removed by tilting the rim away from the cervix, thus breaking the suction; or it can be grasped between two fingers and pulled downward. Thus, insertion and removal require manual dexterity and knowledge of anatomy, which may be difficult for some women, even after detailed instruction. 

However, to many women the cap is appealing because it is smaller and more aesthetically acceptable than the diaphragm, yet, unlike the IUD which must be inserted and withdrawn by a physician, the cap can be 

20 April 1981 FDA Consumer
