Tube 

Cervical Cap Cervix Ovary 

Uterus

This drawing shows how the cervical cap fits over the cervix to serve as a contraceptive device. inserted and removed by the woman herself.

Like the IUD, whose history apparently goes back to the ancient Middle East when stones were inserted into the neck of the female camel's uterus to prevent conception during long treks across the desert, the cervical cap has a long history dating back to at least the 1700's and possibly to ancient Sumeria. It has been made of a variety of materials including molded opium, aluminum, gold, platinum, silver, and ivory. 

Legend has it that Casanova gave one of his conquests half a squeezed lemon to use as a cervical cap, advising her that the remaining citric acid would serve as a spermicide.

The modern history of the cervical cap is said to have begun in 1938 when Friedrick Adolphe Wilde, a 

German gynecologist, fitted cervical caps made of rubber over the cervixes of his patients for contraceptive purposes. Each cap was custom made from a wax impression of the woman's cervix.

The cap was adopted by many European women and until the 1920's it outsold the diaphragm by four to one. However, for some reason the cap lost its popularity, possibly because the newly introduced diaphragm was easier to insert. 

In the late 1970's, the cap was "rediscovered" by American women, due largely to the efforts of Barbara 

Seaman, cofounder of the National 

Women's Health Network, who discussed the cap in her book WOMEN 

AND THE CRISIS IN SEX HORMONES. 

Since that time there has been increasing interest in the device, and public pressure that it be made available to American women as a contraceptive. 

FDA, which regulates the cervical cap as a medical device, is not yet allowing the cap to be dispensed as a contraceptive except as part of a clinical investigation. The Agency has approved the caps only for the previously mentioned marketing as an aid for artificial insemination and collection of menstrual flow. 

Approval for contraceptive use must wait until studies ascertain whether the cap is safe and effective for this use. The cap is subject to closer scientific scrutiny than previously approved birth control devices because of new legislation. Under the 

Medical Device Amendments of 

1976, cervical caps used as contraceptives are class III devices whose safety and effectiveness must be established before they can be marketed. To date, no safety and effectiveness data have been submitted to the Agency.

Nor does medical literature contain much information on the caps. Several contraceptive studies were published in the 1930's and 1940's, but some of the caps studied were made of different materials than those presently used, and these studies do not lend themselves to statistical evaluation. The most recent study was published in 1953. It reported an efficacy rate similar to that of the diaphragm and no serious adverse effects. 

Before FDA can approve the cap for contraception, the Agency needs to examine scientific data on pregnancy rates, infection rates, and possible cervical changes related to the cap. 

This data may be forthcoming from several studies now underway as a result of FDA's new Investigational

Device Exemption (IDE) requirements. The IDE requirements apply to cervical caps beginning January 19, 1981, and categorize the caps as significant risk devices. This means that physicians or groups dispensing the caps must conduct FDA-approved studies of their safety and efficacy. Dispensers of the caps must also obtain written consent before fitting a patient with the cap. 

FDA has been criticized for not providing swift approval of cervical caps. But the contraceptive device, like all such devices, must be proven under controlled circumstances before it can be allowed on the market. 

The recent experience with the Dalkon Shield, which was marketed prior to the 1976 medical device legislation and thus not subject to its requirements, points up the importance of careful testing. 

Judith Willis is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

FDA Consumer | April 1981 / 21

On Surviving The Sneezin' Season 

"In the spring," wrote Alfred Lord Tennyson, "a young man's fancy lightly turns to thoughts of love." But for millions of Americans, spring fever has quite a different meaning, as Nature's new greenery brings on bouts of sneezing, sniffling, coughing, and wheezing. And spring may not be the only season of discontent, nor outdoor greenery the only cause, for allergy sufferers, as this article explains. 

[ost of us welcome the coming of spring as an end to 

Mthe yearly bouts of runny noses, sore throats, and headaches from winter colds and flu. But millions of 

Americans scarcely have time to wring out their handkerchiefs and take a breath of fresh air before they encounter a second round of misery, for hay fever season is on the way. "Hay fever" is really a misnomer, for the seasonal allergies that afflict more than 15 million Americans do not produce fever and are hardly ever caused by hay. The most common instigator are microscopic grains of pollen spewed by the millions into the spring, summer, and fall air by grasses, trees, and weeds. The usual symptoms are a runny or stuffed-up nose, watery or itchy eyes, violent sneezing (a fit of sneezing, as many as 50 times in a row, can rack the body). Sometimes an itching nose, throat, roof of the mouth, and ear canals round out the misery. 

Although those conditions are enough to spoil anyone's picnic, it's not unusual for seasonal allergy sufferers also to experience fatigue, irritability, loss of appetite, difficulty in concentrating, sore throat, cough, malaise, and even depression. Some hay fever sufferers develop asthma, a serious affliction of the bronchial tubes and lungs that claims between 2,000 and 4,000 lives a year in the United States.

Allergies of one type or another afflict an estimated 35 million Americans, according to the National Institute of 

Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), a part of the 

National Institutes of Health. Simply put, an allergy is an individual's unusual sensitivity to a substance in the environment that does not bother most other people. Allergic individuals can have abnormal reactions not only to pollen but also to foods, drugs, cosmetics, insect venom, animals, mold spores, and even common house dust. 

It is the allergic reaction to certain pollens and mold spores that we think of as hay fever, or seasonal allergies. 

Trees generally produce pollen in the spring, grasses turn it out in the early summer, and most weeds shed it in the late summer and early fall.

Often newspapers and radio and television stations will report a locale's daily pollen count. This is the number of grains of a certain kind of pollen found in the air during the previous 24 hours. Pollen counts can help alert hay fever sufferers to stay indoors to avoid these airborne assaults on high-pollen days. The counts also help allergists (physicians specializing in treating allergies) to diagnose correctly an allergy by correlating the pollen counts with the onset and severity of a patient's symptoms. 

Although pollen counts are useful, allergic persons should be wary of comparing the counts of one locale with those from another. The techniques for collecting and measuring pollens are not standardized, and the vari ety of methods in use can make comparisons meaningless.

Airborne spores from molds are a common cause of allergies because of their many possible hiding and growing places inside and outside the house. These include areas of deep shade or heavy vegetation, damp basements, refrigerator drip trays, garbage cans, air conditioning systems, bathrooms, humidifiers, piles of leaves or logs, even old foam rubber pillows and mattresses.

In warm climates where molds and plants grow all year long, the molds- or pollen-allergic person may have no season of relief. Other such year-round, or perennial, allergies are caused by feathers and saliva, urine, and scales of skin shed from pets. Common house dust can bring on virtually inescapable allergies for persons sensitive to one or more of the components of dust. These include specks of fiber from rugs, drapes, furniture coverings, and mattress stuffings; food particles; pollen; mold spores; plant particles; and even tiny spider-like mites. 

Scientists are not certain why some individuals are sensitive to certain airborne substances and most others are not. It is known that allergic reactions involve the body's immune system. When a virus, bacterium, or other microorganism invades the body, special proteins, called antibodies, are formed in the blood to help protect against future attacks by the same kind of bug. This antibody response helps explain why a person can be immunized against certain diseases. A polio vaccination, for example, consists of an injection of polio viruses that 

22 April 1981 FDA Consumer

have been weakened or killed to render them harmless.

The body recognizes this antigen as something foreign and produces the specific antibodies that will protect against any real attacks by healthy polio viruses in the future. 

An allergic response works in much the same way, but the results are adverse instead of beneficial. Instead of providing protection, the body produces antibodies that render the person sensitive to a particular antigen. In the case of hay fever-type allergies with cold-like symptoms, the major sensitizing antibody is known as Immunoglobulin E (IgE). IgE antibodies are formed during first encounters with an antigen, or allergen, such as ragweed pollen. This first encounter is the sensitization process by which a person becomes allergic to a particular substance. 

From that time on the IgE antibodies are present in the blood, ready to set off an allergic reaction whenever the individual is again exposed to the allergen. When such a subsequent exposure occurs, the IgE antibodies attach themselves to certain cells that are particularly abundant in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, the skin, and the blood. These cells are like landmines, with the antibodies that cover their surfaces acting as detonators. 

When a particular antigen, such as ragweed, contacts an IgE antibody specifically sensitive to it, the landmine "explodes." The explosions release powerful chemicals, such as histamine, that increase the activity of the mucous glands and dilate the small blood vessels. Fluid leaking through the stretched blood vessel walls causes swelling of the tissues. If these "explosions" occur in the nose and eyes, hay fever results; in the chest they produce asthma; in the skin, hives and itching; in the gastrointestinal tract, vomiting and cramps.

These "exploding" cells are present in normal, nonallergic people, too, but the particular antibodies that "detonate" the cells are not. A predisposition to become easily sensitized to an allergen and to produce IgE antibodies can be inherited; thus allergies often run in families. But scientists generally believe that other, nongenetic properties are factors in determining who will sneeze and sniffle with allergies. 

There is no "typical" case of hay fever-type allergy.

Symptoms can show up at any age, although most commonly they appear before the age of 40. The symptoms may be so mild as to be mistaken for a light summer cold. Or they can be so severe that they seriously interrupt work and leisure activities for weeks at a time. The severity may vary from year to year for particular individuals, depending on the amount of allergens inhaled, the weather, and other factors. Sometimes the allergy will disappear but usually, especially if untreated, it persists for years, growing gradually worse until it reaches a plateau. 

Complications can add to the suffering. Blocked sinuses can bring on severe headaches and sinus infections. 

The eustachian tubes, which help the ear drums function normally, can also be affected, causing inflammation of the middle ear and hearing problems. Nasal polypschronically swollen nasal tissue-may produce nasal blockage with loss of smell and taste. Some patients with hay fever-type allergies develop asthma, with its sometimes life-threatening attacks of wheezing and difficult breathing.

Because the symptoms are similar, a mild seasonal allergy may be mistaken for a common cold. But the two, though often of comparable degrees of misery, are not identical conditions. Sneezing, runny nose, and itchy eyes, nose, and throat are more characteristic of hay fever, while sore throat and fever are more often signs of a cold. Allergy symptoms will fluctuate from day to day as the pollen count varies and may also be worse outdoors or in the country or on windy days. Of course, if the condition reappears every year as predictably as the birds and the bees, or if it continues for several weeks, it's a good bet that it's an allergy.

Allergists use a number of tools to help in diagnosis. 

The patient may be instructed to keep a diary of the severity and duration of symptoms, the amount of medication needed to get relief, and other pertinent factors. By comparing the diary with the time and amount of pollination for the suspected substances in the area, the patient's medical history, and the results of "skin tests" or other procedures, the physicians can usually find the probable source of the trouble.

Skin testing consists of pricking the patient's arm or back after a tiny drop of the suspected allergen has been placed on the skin (the puncture test) or injecting it under the skin (the more sensitive intracutaneous test). A positive reaction-in the form of a bump surrounded by redness appears, usually in about 15 to 20 minutes if the patient has specific IgE antibodies to that allergen. Usually the physician will administer more than one allergen at a time but the choice of substances should be based on knowledge of the local environment and the patient's history, not on a predetermined "package" of tests as sometimes supplied by manufacturers.

Very rarely, an extract used in skin testing can cause an adverse reaction in an extremely allergic person. To avoid this physicians use as little of the allergen as possible for the tests. FDA, through its Bureau of Biologics, regulates the extracts used in skin testing, as well as those used in "allergy shots." There are at present, however, no standards of potency to help physicians make a better estimate of the proper amount of allergen to be used to diagnose or treat a particular patient. The bureau's Allergenic Products Branch is supporting and conducting research that should help standardize extracts and assist in the development of guidelines for use of extracts in both skin tests and allergy shots.

Besides skin tests another method has been developed to aid in diagnosing allergies. For example, very young children or patients with very sensitive skin can avoid the multiple punctures or injections through use of the ra dioallergosorbent technique (RAST) test. The RAST test uses a blood sample to determine the amount of specific IgE antibodies circulating in the blood. Although these blood tests are useful in special situations, they are not as sensitive as skin testing and cost four to five times more. 

The 12th century physician Maimonides, when asked to treat the asthmatic son of Saladin, sultan of Egypt, candidly admitted, "I have no magic cure." Eight centuries later, scientists are still seeking a cure for asthma and other allergic diseases, including hay fever. Nor has a means been found to prevent allergies from developing in susceptible individuals. 

24 April 1981 / FDA Consumer

The formidable creature shown above may look like something out of a 1950's monster movie. 

But in fact, this little monster, whose actual size is about 1/100 of an inch, is the North American house dust mite. A common component of house dust (there are probably thousands of them around and on you right now), these mites are a virtually inescapable source of grief for many allergy sufferers. (Electron microscope photo courtesy of Battelle Memorial Institute)

Another Allergy troublemaker is the pollen of the privet shrub. At left, magnified 550 times, three pollen spores are nestled in a privet flower's stamen, waiting to catch a breeze and make life miserable for some poor hay fever sufferer.

FDA Consumer April 1981 / 25

There are, however, a number of ways to ease the misery of allergies. The first and most obvious is for the sufferer to avoid the cause of the affliction. This is most easily done when the allergen is found in a specific item, say a pillow containing feathers, that can be switched for one made of synthetic materials. Sometimes the companionship of a pet must be sacrificed to end allergic symptoms caused by the animal's proximity. 

Because most allergens cannot be avoided, the allergic person may, out of frustration, consider escaping to another locale. But moving is generally not recommended. 

Airborne allergens are widespread-only the west coast of the United States is free of ragweed pollens, for example. And a person with specific sensitivity may in time become allergic to a different substance in a new location.

Allergy sufferers can at least partially avoid troublesome allergens without moving. Thorough housecleaning can reduce dust. Central air conditioning can help reduce the amount of pollen infiltrating the home. (But central heating with poor filtering systems can trap dust and other allergens, circulating them over and over again.) 

Dehumidifiers can help reduce mold growth.

Special air filters are available for room or whole-house use. But beware of exaggerated sales claims for “air purification" devices! Some such products, sold as negative ion generators, have been promoted for treating or even curing allergies, asthma, and other respiratory conditions. 

FDA has seen no scientific evidence that they are effective for such uses and has taken legal action against a number of promoters.

Besides trying to avoid their particular allergens, allergy sufferers should steer clear of insect sprays, fresh paint, tobacco smoke, and other substances that when inhaled can further irritate already inflamed membranes. 

Alcohol, because it dilates blood vessels, can also make allergy symptoms worse. 

When an allergen cannot be avoided, medications may help ease the symptoms. Antihistamines, so named because they inhibit the symptoms produced by histamine, can help dry up a runny nose and relieve itchy or watery eyes. Oral decongestants may help relieve nasal congestion. Many antihistamines are available without a prescription, either as single-ingredient medications or as combinations with decongestants. Because such tablet medications can produce a variety of side effects, such as drowsiness, blurred vision, dry mouth, and rapid heartbeat, label directions should be followed precisely. 

Nose sprays or drops are generally not recommended for relief of nasal congestion because use for more than a few days may cause a "rebound effect" that brings back the symptoms worse than before.

For more severe allergy symptoms, stronger medications are available by prescription. Powerful anti-inflammatory drugs called corticosteroids are of great help to some patients but can produce serious side effects after prolonged use.

For the many allergy sufferers who cannot find satisfactory relief by avoiding the harmful allergens or by use of medications, desensitization therapy-allergy shots"are often helpful. The patient is injected with diluted extracts of the troublesome allergen, beginning with small doses once or twice a week, and building up to higher doses repeated less frequently over time. 

The shots are believed to work by causing the body to produce special "blocking antibodies" called Immunoglobulin G, or IgG. Unlike IgE, IgG antibodies are not attached to "exploding" cells. When IgG antibodies combine with an inhaled allergen they prevent it from reacting with IgE antibodies, so there is no "explosion" and no release of histamine and other symptom-causing chemicals. 

Allergy shots do not help all allergy sufferers. However, clinical studies and other reports indicate some degree of improvement in up to 80 percent of pollen hay fever patients. Some allergy experts believe that desensitization shots not only help relieve the usual symptoms of hay fever but also can prevent asthma from developing. 

There is, however, a lack of scientific information on the effectiveness of allergy shots for this purpose. A NIAID

Task Force on Asthma and Other Allergic Diseases rec ommended in 1979 that long-term studies be done to determine the risk of allergy patients developing asthma and the value of allergy shots in preventing it. 

When the shots are successful, they eventually build up an adequate degree of protection in the body and can be discontinued after several years of good results. Often, however, the protection will "wear off" after a number of years, and the regimen must begin again. This varies from patient to patient, but there is generally no need to continue hay fever-type allergy shots indefinitely.

As with the extracts used in skin testing, on rare occasions patients can experience adverse reactions to the shots. Emergency treatment with adrenalin or antihistamines may then be required. The most severe reaction usually occurs within the first few minutes after the injection. 

That is why physicians ask patients to remain 15 to 30 minutes after getting their shot, as a safety precaution.

While allergy shots can be effective in relieving the symptoms of hay fever-type allergies, they are time-consuming, costly, and carry the risk of adverse reaction.

Current research is aimed at developing extracts that are safer and can provide good results with fewer injections. 

Work is being done to purify extracts that will contain only the part of the allergen responsible for the allergycausing activity. Other researchers are developing chemical modifications of the actual allergens so that the extracts maintain the ability to desensitize allergy sufferers but seem to carry less risk of adverse reactions. Further studies are aimed at better understanding of the role IgE plays in allergic disease; such work may someday turn up a way to prevent allergic reactions from developing, possibly by inhibiting the production of IgE. 

For now, hay fever and other allergy sufferers should discuss with their physicians the best course of treatment, whether it is avoiding the source of the allergy or the proper use of medications or allergy shots. In most instances, proper treatment can reduce an allergy sufferer's misery to just an occasional sneeze or sniffle. 

Bill Rados works in FDA's public affairs office and sneezes occasionally during hay fever season.

A final rule establishing standards of identity for cultured and acidified milks, cultured and acidified buttermilks, yogurts and eggnog was published by

FDA in the January 30 FEDERAL REGISTER. The new standards, first proposed in 1977, are intended to standardize the composition and names of these nonstandardized foods to make informed consumer choices and interstate sale of these products easier. 

The standard becomes effective July 1, 1983, but voluntary compliance may begin March 31, 1981. 

July 1, 1983, also is the effective date for amendments to FDA's standard of identify for canned berries. The amended standard will, among other things, permit the use of safe and suitable calcium salts as firming agents for all berries; permit the use of safe and suitable organic acids for all berries; permit the addition of specified nutritive carbohydrate sweeteners to all berries; and provide for strawberry vari eties of the genus Fragaria. (See January 9 FEDERAL REGISTER.) 

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has asked the Department of Commerce to cooperate in establishing a laboratory accreditation program for processors of personnel dosimeters that measure ionizing radiation received on the job. The need for the program stems from the poor performance of dosimetry processors during recent tests. The request was published in the January 29 FEDERAL REGISTER. 

FDA and the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) 

have signed a Memorandum of Understanding defining their responsibilities in the event of peacetime radiological emergencies. FDA's responsibilities include providing guidance to State and local governments on the use of radioprotective substances (thyroid blocking agents), and monitoring and sampling milk, foods, and animal feeds. CDC has the lead role for planning the Department of Health and Human Serv ices role and coordinating activities in radiation emer gencies. Other CDC responsibilities include epide miological surveillance of populations exposed to radiological accidents and identification of those at high risk of harm from exposure. The memorandum, effective November 26, 1980, was published in the

January 23 FEDERAL REGISTER. 

Anyone planning to ship radioactive materials via the nation's highways had better check the January 

19 FEDERAL REGISTER for Department of Transpor tation (DOT) rules covering the same. Routing and driver training requirements outlined in the final notice provide that carriers must follow highway routes designated by appropriate State agencies and prepare written route plans for submission to DOT. Irradiated reactor fuel must be shipped under a physical security program equivalent to that established by the 

Nuclear Regulatory Commission. 

FDA has proposed to remove from the market 

18 "combination" drugs prescribed for gastrointestinal disorders. The Agency's Bureau of Drugs said manufacturers have not provided adequate evidence that the products meet the effectiveness requirements of the law. The proposal is the first step toward taking the drugs from the market, but manufacturers may seek hearings to present their own views on each of the products. 28 April 1981 FDA Consumer

Investigators' Reports The Powdered Milk Caper 

When the man began counting out cash-$88,000 in hundred dollar bills-for the powdered milk he had bid on, the people at the Port Authority in Duluth began to wonder. 

When he had trouble remembering his name, their wonderment grew. 

And when it took him three times to sign his name as it appeared on the bid sheet, they decided this was more than passing strange. 

So they called FDA's District office in Minneapolis to tell them about the transaction just completed, and at that point a scheme to slip 300,000 pounds of contaminated dry milk into human consumption channels began to fall apart. 

By the time it was over, most of the milk had been seized and destroyed, and the four prime participants imprisoned and fined.

The man with the money was Peter 

Freihammer, an incidental acquaintance of the conspirators, who had been hired to be "A.J. Johnson," to pay for and accept delivery of 6,040 bags of nonfat dry milk (50 pounds to the bag) that the Port Authority had put up for sale.

The bags-plastic inside heavy paper-were wet, dirty, torn and punctured, stained with rat and mouse urine, and contaminated inside and out with rodent excreta (pellets). Each bag was marked REJECT, meaning that the milk powder could be used for animal feed but was unfit for human consumption. 

For his services that January day in 1978 and for arranging shipment of the dry milk powder, Freihammer was to receive a suit of clothes and five buckets of roofing tar. 

As reconstructed by FDA in a letter from FDA's general counsel to the 

U.S. Attorney in Minneapolis, the scheme was largely put together by 

Orlando Weivoda, a food salvage operator in the Minneapolis/St. Paul area, his son Harold Weivoda, and one Allen Eisenschenk, who owned or had access to a tractor trailer rig. 

Working with the Weivoda group were Thomas Novak and Kenneth 

Malecha, officials of a St. Paul distributorship-Best Brands, Inc.-that warehoused flour, flavorings, and other supplies for sale to bakeries in a five-state area.

Each of the Weivoda group put in $32,000 toward the bid purchase of the contaminated dry milk. Freihammer was to make actual payment to the Port Authority and have the milk picked up for shipment. The Weivodas would be buying at 29.2 cents a pound and selling to Best Brands at 

50 cents. Best Brands in turn would sell to unsuspecting bakery customers at the going market price of 65 cents a pound. Everyone could prosper. 

The Weivodas had planned to have the bagged milk loaded on seven piggyback trailers at the Port Authority in Duluth, then have the trailers placed on four railroad flatcars, marked for Portland, Oreg. Once enroute, the trailers were to be diverted to Sioux Falls, S. Dak., and Fargo, N. Dak. There the trailers could be claimed and the milk repackaged and relabeled. 

After getting the message about the strange purchase of dry milk up in 

Duluth, FDA's Minneapolis office followed a trail of leased piggyback trailers, the Johnson/Freihammer alias, diverted railcars, and other evidence. Investigators found three trailers on a lot in Grand Forks. The bagged dry milk was still inside and no owners were in sight. They posted legal notices on the trailers and waited the required time for claimants to come forward. After seizure by the 

U.S. marshal, the condemned dry milk was destroyed. 

So FDA had, within a month, found three of the seven trailers with the reject milk still intact, meaning those diverted to Grand Forks. But four trailers were still out there somewhere. 

That somewhere turned out to be near Alcester, S. Dak., where Allen 

Eisenschenk had hauled them after they were dropped off at Sioux Falls. 

In a farmyard near Alcester, Orlando Weivoda, Eisenschenk, and three relatives were busily repackaging the contaminated dry milk from the reject bags into new bags with the forged label of a respected milk producers' association. Dry milk that was chunked up was sifted through a screen before going into the newly stenciled bags.

Three loads of the resifted milk were sold to unsuspecting firms when 

Orlando Weivoda discovered a notice placed by FDA in a Sioux Falls newspaper, asking assistance in locating four trailer loads of contaminated dry milk. He, Eisenschenk, and Malecha quickly closed down the rebagging operation at the Alcester farm, loaded the sifting screen, metal washtubs, and 

1,084 bags of dry milk (most in their original reject bags) into a Best 

Brands truck and returned to St. 

Paul. There Malecha reloaded everything into a rented trailer and parked it-locked-on a trucking company lot.

By now FDA investigators had reconstructed most of the conspiracy and identified the participants. They confronted Novak and Malecha at 

Best Brands with what was known.

Novak admitted that his company had received the trailerloads of dry milk, and he handed over the key to the last trailer. In it, FDA investigators found both the reject and rebagged milk, sifting screen, and tubs. "There sat the rest of our case, all in a neat little package," said compliance officer Robert Marrs. "We spent 

2 weeks carefully examining the trailer and its contents, taking samples and photos, getting our evidence. There were 660 of the dirty, stained reject bags of dry milk, and 360 new bags of milk that had been sifted and packed. When we had what we needed, the milk was destroyed under court order.'

When the last loads had been accounted for, about 60,000 pounds of

FDA Consumer | April 1981 | 29

the milk had slipped into human consumption channels, mostly through 

Best Brands sales in Iowa City. But some 240,000 pounds had been intercepted, seized, and destroyed, including the three trailer loads that went unclaimed in Grand Forks. 

It took 2 years of FDA hearings and investigations, 1,173 pages of documentary evidence, and appearances before two grand juries before indictments were returned and trials scheduled for the five defendents.

Out of it all came a five-count indictment against Novak, Malecha, Weivoda, Eisenschenk, and Best 

Brands, Inc., a corporation. They were charged with aiding and abetting one another in introducing into interstate commerce the contaminated (adulterated) dry milk by shipping and selling it variously in North and 

South Dakota, Iowa, and Minnesota.

All pleaded guilty to some of the charges. Novak pleaded guilty to four misdemeanor charges and was sentenced to 6 months in prison and a $4,000 fine. Malecha pleaded guilty to one charge and received 3 months in prison and a $1,000 fine. Eisenschenk admitted guilt to four misdemeanor charges, and drew a 60-day sentence and 2 years probation. Weivoda pleaded guilty to one felony charge and received a 6-month prison sentence and a $5,000 fine. The Best 

Brands corporation was fined $10,000. 

-Richard C. Thompson Investigators' Reports presents information on inspections, product seizures, court proceedings, and other administrative and regulatory actions by Federal, State, and local food and drug agencies across the country to provide health and economic protection to consumers of foods, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices.

Visionary Therapy 

A Federal court injunction has stopped a Tulsa, Okla., woman from distributing her "cancer" drug, Liliverum, in interstate commerce. However, the injunction, filed against 

Mildred Trumbull and her firm, M. T. Products, Ltd., does not prohibit manufacture or distribution within that State. 

It was around Easter 1977 that 

FDA's Dallas District first learned about Mildred Trumbull and Liliverum. Investigators went to her home after a consumer called the district office inquiring about the drug. They learned that Trumbull made Liliverum in her kitchen from Easter lillies and water. She claimed she had received a vision from God revealing to her that cancer was caused by a rare cocci germ, unknown to medicine. In her vision she was shown how to prepare a serum from the ovary of the Easter lily (Liliverus longiflora). This was God's "chosen flower" and would cure the dread disease. She gave the drug to cancer victims free of charge. She had no records of distribution, no New Drug 

Application, or proof of safety or efficacy. 

She also was found to be violating

FDA's Good Manufacturing Practices 

(GMP's). Conditions in her kitchen were unsuitable for assuring the drug's sterility. Samples collected and analyzed by FDA contained yeast organisms. This constituted a health hazard because the drug was intended to be injected. The Dallas 

District informed Trumbull that if she wanted to distribute Liliverum, she would have to register as a drug firm, obtain a New Drug Application, and comply with FDA's GMP's.

The district received a letter from her lawyer saying that production of Liliverum would cease until the drug could be tested by a reputable laboratory. 

Two FDA inpections in 1978 confirmed that Mildred Trumbull had stopped making the drug. But in 

1979, a bill was introduced in the Oklahoma State legislature to legalize Liliverum. During a subsequent inspection, Trumbull's lawyer told

FDA that samples of the drug had been sent to the National Cancer Institute, which found the drug safe but ineffective.

In May 1979, Oklahoma passed the 

Liliverum Bill, permitting manufac ture and distribution within the State.

Several months later Trumbull began manufacturing Liliverum-and several other drugs-at a facility in 

Tulsa under the name M. T. Products, Ltd. She also was making interstate shipments. 

State health authorities, also investigating Liliverum, obtained a Temporary Restraining Order after samples of the drug were analyzed and found contaminated. This only prevented distribution of the drug if adulterated, and not for ineffectiveness. The Dallas District then requested an injunction to prevent interstate shipment. This was approved by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma. 

In the Red 

Shortly after an inspection by

FDA's Buffalo District, HNP Prod ucts, Inc., found itself in the red. 

First, the Lewiston, N.Y., cosmetics store defaulted on a bank loan and went out of business. Then, the store's landlord obtained an eviction order and changed the locks on the doors due to nonpayment of rent. 

Finally, a sample of a shampoo product made by the company was collected by district investigators and analyzed. It was found to contain a nonapproved color additive, a type of 

Methyl Red. 

FDA investigators also collected six other samples of herbal rinse conditioners, beauty mask products, and day creams. All had labels indicating they contained nonapproved color additives. Six of the products failed to declare the presence of one or more colors contained in each product, and all seven products falsely claimed ingredients that were not present at all.

The firm had been both a manufacturer and distributer of the various cosmetics, most of which were imported from Canada in unlabeled bulk or packaged containers. 

At the district's request, the New

York State Board of Pharmacy or dered all the cosmetics put under embargo, but the fate of the products 

30 April 1981 / FDA Consumer

was uncertain to FDA because the firm had been evicted. Later investigators received permission from the landlord to enter the building, and the cosmetics were still on the premises. 

Meanwhile, the bank sold the assets (cosmetics) of HNP Products to 

House of Faces, a Toronto, Ontario, cosmetics firm, which sought to export them to Canada. The District alerted the Canadian Health Protection Branch of the Toronto firm's intentions and advised them that some of the cosmetics' color additives and labeling were also illegal in Canada. 

The district then alerted Canadian customs and the first shipment was intercepted from Lewiston, N.Y. The following day, House of Faces voluntarily destroyed all the cosmetics under the supervision of FDA. 

Popping Tops

The sounds in the bonded warehouse at St. Louis's inland port of 

Customs was of a kind to make a person think a celebration was going on inside.

Pressure had built up in a lot of 

330 cases of Macon Lugny Wine from France, forcing some of the corks out and breaking seals. 

The importer, Allstate Distributer, St. Louis, Mo., reported the problem to FDA's St. Louis Station because it had agreed to examine the products and report any damaged bottles to 

FDA to speed up importation. 

The lot, valued at $1,350, was detained until FDA reached agreement with the importer to recondition, reexport, or destroy the products.

The Cost of Cheap Midwest Commodities in Mulberry 

Grove, Ill., is a wholesale and retail food warehouse owned by railroad salvage dealer Frank J. Rench, who buys foods sold at auctions, such as baby cereal, cookies, shortcake biscuits, wafers, and pretzels, and sells them at reduced prices.

During a routine inspection, FDA's Chicago District investigators found the warehouse operating under gross insanitary conditions. Live and dead mice were seen on the premises and some of the food was rodent and insect contaminated. 

Because the firm is a chronic violator (there had been numerous inspections followed by warning letters and/ or seizure of products), the district presented the case to the State U.S. 

Attorney's office for possible prosecution.

After the U.S. attorney turned the case over to a grand jury, the jury returned a seven-count indictment charge of rodent and insect contamination of foods for human use in interstate commerce.

The warehouse and its owner were fined a total of $5,600 in the U.S. 

District Court for the Southern District of Illinois after pleading guilty to all seven counts.

Rabbits Miss Easter 

In a St. Louis warehouse rodents got to some candy rabbits before the 

Easter Bunny could. During an in spection of Grocers Terminal Ware house #1, investigators from FDA's 

St. Louis Station found chocolatecovered marshmallow rabbits with rodent teethmarks and hundreds of rodent pellets on the floor nearby. 

There were also numerous openings beneath doors permitting access for rats and mice.

After analysis by the Kansas City District Laboratory confirmed the contamination, approximately $1,800 worth of the candy rabbits were seized and destroyed. One lot of contaminated rolled oats was destroyed by the firm, which also reconditioned a lot of cookie mix.

Drug Goes Underground 

Last summer FDA began investigating reports of the illegal distribution of hexachloroethane, a veterinary drug that is unapproved and also is a carcinogen. The reports said some stocks were not labeled and were being transported by night to avoid FDA inspections. One firm-in 

Lenexa, Kan.-received the attention of three FDA district offices because it was reportedly manufacturing this illegal drug. 

Hexachloroethane is used to treat cattle, sheep, and goats for liver fluke infection (flat worms infecting the liver). It had been used over 20 years in the United States, but FDA withdrew approval in 1971 when the drug's sponsors failed to submit test data requested by the Agency after questions had been raised about its safety and effectiveness. 

In late summer and fall of 1979, there was a severe outbreak of liver fluke disease. Left untreated, liver fluke infection can severely weaken animals; in some instances, animals may become so emaciated that death results. Farmers faced considerable loss of livestock because, after the withdrawal of approval for hexachloroethane in 1971, there was no other approved drug available to treat the disease. Another drugalbendazole-had been developed but was still under investigation and was not approved for marketing. To deal with the situation, FDA permitted the use of albendazole but only under strict controls and in only 11 States. 

But the liver fluke outbreak induced some manufacturers to market hexachloroethane illegally. FDA, in fact, found that several companies had been marketing the drug all along after approval had been withdrawn. FDA, concerned that residues of the chemical or its metabolites might occur in the meat and milk of treated animals, moved to stop illegal distribution.

The Kansas City District inspected two Kansas firms, including the one in Lenexa, after the Orlando District reported they were distributing a hexachloroethane suspension. Kansas 

City investigators confirmed the report. They checked the shipping records and learned that the drug had been shipped to a number of veterinarians, and requested that other districts collect samples. 

One shipment from the Lenexa firm had gone to a veterinary clinic in Roseburg, Oreg., and an investigator from the Seattle District contacted the veterinarian. He told the investigator he was unaware the drug was not approved and agreed to hold the remaining 87 gallons of the shipment. 

Samples were collected and sent to the Kansas City District, which is continuing its investigation of the two manufacturers. The remaining stocks of the suspension in Roseburg, valued at approximately $935, were seized and destroyed.

Seizures FILED SEIZURE ACTIONS charge violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and are initiated based upon FDA recommendations. A seizure action is commenced by the filing of a complaint in the U.S. district court where the goods are located. A U.S. marshal is then directed by the court to take possession of the goods, removing the product from commerce, until the matter is resolved. 

A total of 18 actions to remove from the consumer market products charged to be violative was reported in February. These actions included 11 seizures of foods: 2 involved charges of poisonous and deleterious substances, and 8 involved charges concerning contamination. Others included 4 of drugs (including 1 of veterinary), and 3 of medical devices.

Charged 11-29-78: while held for sale, the article contained insect filth; 402(a)(3). The article was claimed by DCA Food Industries, New York, N. Y. (as a bona fide holder of a security interest in the article); the claimant also filed an answer to the charge and defended on the basis that FDA had drawn a sample when the article had been imported and that the claimant was not responsible for the condition of the raspberries.

The Government served requests for admissions and written interrogatories on the claimant. Subsequently, the claimant moved to amend its answer and moved to join the article's importer, as additional party claimant. The Government opposed such motions. The court denied the claimant's motion to join an additional party. The claimant moved for post-seizure sampling. With the consent of the 

Government, the court authorized the withdrawal of representative samples of the article. 

A consent decree of condemnation authorized release to the claimant for bringing the article into compliance. However, the postseizure analysis of the post-seizure samples indicated that any salvaging of the article would be uneconomical. Accordingly, the parties moved that the article be destroyed; the court ordered destruction and the article was destroyed. (F.D.C. No. 61971; S. No. 79160-850; 

N.J. No. 15)

Lumpfish roe, colored black, at New York, S. Dist. N.Y.

Charged 7-10-78 and amended on or about 7-16-78: while held for sale, the article contained the nonconforming color additive, Red No. 

2 (also known as amaranth, whose provisional listing as a permissible additive had been terminated on February 12, 1976); 402(c). When the initial seizure of the article was not effected, an inspection warrant was issued for the premises of Iranian Caviar and Sturgeon Corp., New York, N.Y. Upon inspection pursuant to the warrant, the article was discovered and seized. Iranian Caviar and Sturgeon Corp. claimed the article and denied the charges. The defendants conducted postseizure sampling and their private testing laboratory reported that 

Red No. 2 had been found in 11 of the 12 barrels of seized lumpfish roe, and the 1 barrel which did not contain Red No. 2 had not been dyed at all but was clear bright amber in color.

The case came on for trial before the court. The court condemned all of the article with the exception of one barrel of amber-colored 

FDA Consumer April 1981/35

roe which the Government agreed to release. The court ordered the payment by the claimant of the court costs and fees, and the storage and other expenses. The court also authorized, upon the posting of a bond, the release of the 11 barrels to the claimant for salvaging. 

After the claimant failed to meet the conditions for release for salvaging, the Government moved for a supplemental judgment for the necessary additional storage fees and moved that the article be destroyed. 

The court granted the Government's motion and ordered the destruction of the article and the taxing of the additional expenses. 

Ultimately, the article was destroyed and the claimant's corporation was dissolved. (F.D.C. No. 61805; S. No. 78-147-182 et al.; N.J. No. 27)
