NOTICES OF JUDGMENT on Criminal Actions 

New Mexico Mill & Elevator Co., Clovis, Dist. N. Mex. 

Charged 1-5-79: when shipped, three lots of flour, labeled in part 

(counts 1 & 3) "Indian Girl . . . Flour Enriched Bleached... New 

Mexico Mill & Elevator Co. Clovis, New Mexico," and (count 2) "SunLight... Bleached. . . Enriched Flour . . . New Mexico Mill 

36 April 1981/ FDA Consumer

& Elevator Co. Clovis, New Mexico," had been prepared and packed under insanitary conditions; and two of the lots of flour (counts 1 & 3) contained insect filth; 402(a)(3),402(a)(4). Guilty plea; $750 fine on each count. (F.D.C. No. 61702; S. No. 77-32-846 et al; N.J. No. 41)

J. Treffiletti & Sons, a partnership, Carmen D. Treffiletti, partner, Anthony 

J. Treffiletti, partner, and Joseph A. Treffiletti, general manager, Albany, N. Dist. N.Y. 

Charged 2-6-80 by grand jury: process cheese spread (count 1), process white American cheese slices (count 5), licorice candies (count 8), and other foods (other counts) were held under insanitary conditions in a building accessible to rodents and were exposed to contamination by rodents; 402(a)(4). The defendants pleaded not guilty. The defendants filed a number of motions. The court ruled in favor of the 

Government saying: "The defendants are charged in a ten-count indictment with holding food for sale after shipment in interstate commerce that became adulterated within the meaning of Title 21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(4) in violation of Title 21 U.S.C. §§ 331(k) and 333(a). The essence of the charges, all misdemeanors, is that the food was held under unsanitary conditions in a building accessible to rodents whereby it may have become contaminated with filth. "The defendants are the Treffiletti partnership; two of the partners who are brothers, Carmen and Anthony; and their nephew, Joseph, who is an employee in the operation of their food storage warehouse in the City of Albany. A third partner is not charged. 

Attorneys Williams and O'Sullivan originally represented the four defendants, but in open court on May 5, 1980, pursuant to the ruling in Colon v. Fogg, 603 F.2d 403, 407 (2d Cir. 1979), the defendants were advised by the Court of their right to have independent and separate counsel. Joseph Treffiletti stated he would retain his own attorney, Douglas P. Rutnick, 112 State Street, Albany, New York.

The other defendants waived the right to have separate counsel and stated they would continue with their counsel, Attorneys Williams and O'Sullivan. This representation was agreed upon and permitted by the Court. "The original attorneys for the four defendants have filed an unusual array of motions. An Omnibus Motion containing eight separate motions was filed. A substantial separate motion with great detail was filed for a Bill of Particulars. Another separate motion was filed to dismiss the indictment against the defendants on a great number of stated grounds. The motions thus described are voluminous in their wording, repetitions in several instances, and have interspersed throughout the great variety of contentions, numerous references to case law with excerpts therefrom. "To this substantial submission of motion papers in a criminal case involving misdemeanor charges, the Government has filed persuasive and detailed Responses to each of the motions with a List of Exhibits. These responses are keyed in helpful fashion into the numbers and letters set forth in the defense motions. After review of all the papers and the statutory and case law recited, it is my judgment that except for the discovery and pretrial conference motions, there is no merit or substance in the other motions. A reading of the case law cited by the Government in its specific responses convinces me that the case law referred to and cited by the Government is the controlling case law that refutes the contentions of the defendants in their motions. That case law and statutes in the responses of the 

Government that are filed with the Clerk are incorporated herein by reference. It is also my judgment that the statutory interpretations urged by the defendants are not acceptable under settled law. From my review, I am satisfied that in the routine inspections and investigations of a food warehouse, the partnership and the individuals were accorded due process and there was no overreaching or unfairness or violation of their constitutional rights. The statutes upon which the indictments are based are old in the law and not vague and unconstitutional. The Government has provided extensive discovery of many records, documents and administrative regulations that is adequate and more than would be required. "The extensive motions present only several issues worthy of general and brief discussion. A partnership may be charged with Federal statutory violations apart from the participation and knowledge of the partners as individuals. The statute, Title 21 U.S.C. 

§ 331(k), prohibits food being held in unsanitary conditions, where food may become contaminated, and the purpose of the statute is to safeguard the consumer from the time the food is introduced in interstate commerce and delivered to the ultimate consumer. United 

States v. Weisenfeld Warehouse Co., 376 U.S. 86, 91-94 (1964). A 

person in position of sufficient authority can be held responsible for violations, and the statute dispenses with the conventional requirement for criminal conduct awareness of wrongdoing. . . . "The scrutiny of a court in relation to Grand Jury process is not triggered by unsubstantiated and speculative assertions of impropriety. United States v. Rubin, 559 F.2d 975 (5th Cir. 1977); There is no obligation on the part of the Government to reply to such unsupported assertions. In re Millow, 529 F.2d 770 (2d Cir. 1976). There is no obligation to present exculpatory evidence to a Grand Jury. 

United States v. Kennedy, 564 F.2d 1329 (9th Cir. 1977). There is no showing of any substantiated or particularized need or compelling necessity to breach the secrecy of the Grand Jury proceedings. 

Defense access to Grand Jury minutes will be provided at the proper time pursuant to Title 18 U.S.C. § 3500(a) and (b). The ten counts in the indictment are detailed, and aver sufficiently the elements in support of the offenses charged, inform the defendants fairly of the charges, and follow the language of the statute. . . . A hearing is not required before the referral of a matter such as this one to the Department of Justice. Ewing v. Mytinger & Casselberry, 339 U.S. 594 (1950). The Administrative Procedure Act does not apply in this criminal prosecution based upon the return of an indictment by a Grand Jury. The situation is by no means an extraordinary or unique one. 

A routine inspection and investigation took place, and a government agency with the responsibility in that area referred the facts to the United States Attorney for evaluation, with the result the determination was made to present the case to a Grand Jury. "There is no multiplicity inasmuch as the counts charge different offenses. Amer v. United States, 367 F.2d 803, 805 (8th Cir. 1966).

The charges in each count assert only one offense and are not duplicitous. The charges that have to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt involve different food products, labeled differently, manufactured in different cities and shipped to the defendants on different dates. There is not sufficient showing to sever the trial of the partnership from the individual defendants, and the trial of Joseph Treffiletti from the other three defendants. There is not evident any prejudice that will arise during a joint trial that is always favored, when proper, in the interests of justice. "The principles of Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966), are not applicable. It is clear from the affidavits submitted that the business records were voluntarily turned over. See United States v. Ar nold's Pharmacy, 116 F. Supp. 310 (D. N.J. 1953). The procedural steps of Title 21 U.S.C. § 321(y) do not apply in these circumstances concerned with the adulteration of food. The record indicates that the applicable statutory provisions, and the regulations were followed. 

Other statutory provisions referred to by the defendants are not applicable. The subpoena for the production of documents under Title 

21 U.S.C. § 321(y)(5) is unnecessary and unwarranted. "The motions are all denied and dismissed, except the portion of the omnibus motion seeking discovery is granted only to the limited extent furnished, and agreed to be furnished by the Government, and for a pretrial conference, several of which have been held. "The attorneys are now directed to prepare immediately for the trial of this case."

The defendants changed their pleas to guilty as to certain counts, except that all counts against Carmen Treffiletti were Dismissed. The 

FDA Consumer April 1981 / 37

partnership was fined $1,000 on count 1 and fined $500 each on counts 5 and 8. Anthony J. Treffiletti was fined $500 each on count 1 and 

8; and Joseph A. Treffiletti was fined $500 on count 5. (F.D.C. No. 

61710; S. No. 78-107-861 et al.; N.J. No. 42)

NOTICES OF JUDGMENT on Injunction Actions J.W.S. Delavau Co., Inc., Richard M. Leff, president, Paul A. Leff, general manager, Marvin Kaplan, chief chemist, Philadelphia, E. Dist. Pa. 

Charged 3-7-77 in a complaint for injunction: that the defendants, at their Philadelphia plant, manufactured, processed, packed, labeled, held for sale, and distributed in interstate commerce, various drugs which had been manufactured, processed, packed, and held under circumstances that failed to conform with current good manufacturing practice; and that the defendants were well aware that their activities were in violation of the law; 501(a)(2)(B). A consent decree of permanent injunction enjoined the complained of violations, and enjoined further operations at the Philadelphia plant involving interstate drugs, unless and until a number of specified conditions had been met, including the examination of all drugs on hand, an FDA inspection to determine compliance, and payment for FDA inspectional work and for laboratory and analytical work. After the initial FDA inspection, the defendants were billed for the costs incurred by FDA pursuant to the injunction. Additional bills were sent after an additional inspection and after additional FDA costs were incurred in reviewing certain documents submitted by the defendants. When the defendants did not respond, the Government moved to compel payment of costs. Ultimately, the defendants destroyed all drugs on hand and paid the billed costs. (Inj. No. 774; S. No. 77-47-356 et al.; N.J. 

No. 43)

Lee's Farm Service, Inc., and W. Calvin Lee, president, Bronwood, M. 

Dist. Ga. 

Charged 3-1-78 in a complaint for injunction: that the defendants had been engaged, at their Bronwood, Sasser, Reynolds, and Carnegie, Ga., storage facilities, in receiving, storing, and shipping in interstate commerce shelled corn; that such corn contained the added poisonous and deleterious substance aflatoxin, which might render the food injurious to health; that FDA analyses revealed the presence of aflatoxin in excess of 20 ppb; and that the defendants were well aware that the corn they were shipping in interstate commerce contained aflatoxin in excess of 20 ppb; 402(a)(1). A consent decree of permanent injunction perpetually restrained and enjoined the defendants from shipping in interstate commerce the corn on hand and the specified 1977 corn crop, unless and until the corn had been sampled and certified to contain not more than 20 ppb aflatoxin. (Inj. 

828; S. No. 77-100-724; N.J. No. 44) 

Los Angeles Smoking & Curing Co., Louis Vitale, president, and Louis 

Quartararo, plant superintendent, Los Angeles, C. Dist. Calif. 

Charged 6-10-77 in a complaint for injunction: that the defendants manufactured, processed, packed, held for sale, and shipped in interstate commerce hot-process smoked fish (prepared from interstate fish); that the conditions used for the manufacture, processing, packing, and holding of such fish failed to conform with current good manufacturing practice to assure that the fish might not have been rendered injurious to health; that FDA inspections revealed that the production conditions did not conform with current good manufacturing practice regulations so as to produce hot-process smoked fish under sanitary conditions which were adequate to prevent the formation of Clostridium botulinum type E toxin; and that the defendants were well aware that their activities were in violation of the law; 402(a)(4). 

The Government moved for a preliminary injunction. However, before any testimony was taken and without admissions by the defendants, the defendants consented to the entry of a decree of permanent injunction. The decree of permanent injunction enjoined the defendants from the complained of violations with respect to hot-process smoked or smoke-flavored salmon and enjoined further operation with respect to such salmon unless and until a number of specified conditions were met to bring such operations into conformity with current good manufacturing practice. (Inj. No. 793; S. No. 77-10-904 et al.; N.J. No. 45) 

Harold S. Meiser, t/a Meiserville Milling Co., Mt. Pleasant Mills, M. Dist. Pa. 

Charged 12-27-77 in a complaint for injunction: that the defendant, at his feed mill, manufactured, processed, packed, labeled, stored, and distributed medicated feeds and nonmedicated feeds containing interstate components; that the circumstances used for the manufacture, processing, packing, and holding of the medicated feeds failed to conform with current good manufacturing practice-501(a)(2)(B); that the labeling of the medicated feeds failed to bear adequate directions for use and failed to bear adequate warnings against unsafe uses- -502(f)(1), 502(f)(2); that the non-medicated feeds had been prepared, packed, and held under insanitary conditions whereby they might have been rendered injurious to health due to contamination with medicated feeds or medicated feed residues-402(a)(4); that 

FDA inspections revealed a number of specified deviations from current good manufacturing practice; and that the defendant was well aware that his activities were in violation of the law. 

A consent decree of permanent injunction perpetually enjoined and restrained the defendant from the violations complained of, and enjoined continued operation of the feed mill involving any interstate components unless and until a number of specified conditions were met. (Inj. No. 818; S. No. 77-45-365; N.J. No. 46)

NOTICE OF JUDGMENT on Miscellaneous Action 

Federal refusal to compel appearance of FDA expert for use in State lawsuit, Springfield, Dist. Mass. 

Charged 11-18-77 by Susan Giza and Andrew Giza, against the De partment of Health, Education and Welfare, the Public Health Serv ice, FDA, and Ortho Pharmaceutical Corp., Raritan, N.J. in a suit to have FDA furnish information and witnesses: that Ortho Pharmaceutical Corp. had manufactured the oral contraceptive "Modicon," had begun to distribute the drug about January 1975, had subsequently notified physicians and pharmacies that they should no longer prescribe and distribute the drug because it was substandard and had recalled the drug during October 1975; that plaintiff Susan 

Giza began to take the drug in July 1975 until notified in October 1975 that she was pregnant; that the plaintiffs had a son in May 1976 and thereby incurred and would continue to incur very substantial expenses; that the plaintiffs had brought a complaint for damages against Ortho Pharmaceutical Corp.; that plaintiffs had made great efforts to locate an expert witness in Massachusetts with sufficient qualifications willing to testify but had not found such a witness; that plaintiffs had requested documentary evidence from FDA pertaining to Modicon; that FDA had supplied certain of the information requested, but essential information had been deleted; and that FDA had not responded to the plaintiffs' subsequent appeal from the denial of information and the refusal to provide witnesses. The Government opposed the release of further information and documents, opposed the taking of a deposition of FDA's Dr. Marion Finkel, Acting Associate Director for New Drug Evaluation, and moved for a protective order. In ruling for the Government, the court said: "Plaintiffs seek an order to compel the appearance of a Food & Drug Administration (FDA) expert, Dr. Marion Finkel, to give testimony for use in a state action to which neither she nor the United States government are parties. Jurisdiction is alleged to rest upon the 

Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 5 U.S.C. § 552, upon 28 U.S.C. 

§ 1361, and upon F.R.Civ.P. 37. "The underlying state action sounds in products liability, based on the alleged failure of a birth control drug produced by Ortho Pharmaceutical Corporation. Plaintiffs' trial preparation included an 

38 April 1981 FDA Consumer

FOIA request for FDA documents pertaining to 'Modicon,' the drug in question. They also sought to depose certain unnamed FDA experts who would have personal knowledge of 'Modicon's' development. "The adequacy of response to the FOIA request was initially part of the complaint. However, the parties appear to have reached an agreement on production of documents, and that issue will not be addressed further. The more important issue is framed by the attempt to secure a United States government expert to be deposed on behalf of a private litigant in a case pending before a state court. "Plaintiffs' counsel initially sought the testimony of FDA personnel with respect to 'Modicon' by letter of October 21, 1976. 

That request was denied by letter on December 15, 1976. This case was filed on November 18, 1977. Plaintiffs filed a Notice of Taking 

Deposition on May 12, 1978, for the first time specifying Dr. Finkel as the intended deponent. Dr. Finkel failed to appear in Springfield on the specified date, June 14, 1978. Plaintiffs subsequently moved for an order compelling discovery pursuant to Rule 37(d), and the FDA countered with a motion for a Protective Order. The matter was referred to Magistrate Pierce for his recommendation. However, Magistrate Pierce resigned at that point and the record is unclear as to whether he had reached any conclusions. It is clear that no deposition was taken at that time. On May 24, 1979, the Hampden County 

Superior Court [authorized] its subpoena, ordering the deposition of 

Dr. Finkel before a notary in Rockville, Maryland. That subpoena, the subject of an October 16, 1979 conference in this Court, has not yet been obeyed. The state action is being held in abeyance pending determination of Dr. Finkel's availability. "The exact theory under which the plaintiffs are proceeding is unclear at this juncture. At least two distinct issues are raised. If the plaintiffs still seek to take the deposition of Dr. Finkel as an incident to this proceeding, presumably pursuant to Rule 30, their efforts raise questions as to the scope of permissible discovery. If, on the other hand, plaintiffs are now seeking to use the process of this Court to secure the testimony of an expert government witness for use in an unrelated (state) action, more serious issues of witness availability and judicial power are raised. "With respect to plaintiffs first attempt to depose Dr. Finkel incident to this proceeding on June 14, 1978, it is clear that the United States, as a party, is not immune from discovery. . . . Thus, where the FDA is a party, its personnel may be deposed with respect to the pending action. "The touchstone here, of course, is relevancy. F.R.Civ.P. 

26(b)(1). The ultimate question in this proceeding is whether Dr. 

Finkel is available as an expert. What she will say if allowed to speak as an expert is irrelevant to this Court's determination of her availability. "Plaintiffs' complaint indicates that they want to depose FDA personnel because of an inability to secure other experts. Their effort to depose the very person they seek to use as an expert is an abuse of the discovery process. "There does not seem to be any need for a preliminary deposition of Dr. Finkel that would be in addition to the full deposition as an expert that plaintiffs seek. Consequently, the Court would be inclined to issue an order that discovery not be had, pursuant to F.R.Civ.P. 

26(c)(1). This would be an unnecessary step, however, as issues discussed, infra, dispose of the case. "The ultimate result that plaintiffs seek presents the more significant questions as to the power of this Court. Plaintiffs assert that the expert testimony of Dr. Finkel in particular is absolutely necessary to maintenance of their claim in state court. They argue that they are therefore entitled to the aid of this Court in securing Dr. Finkel's deposition. "There is an initial question as to whether the state subpoena may properly be considered by this Court, inasmuch as it issued some two years after the federal action was initiated, and first was raised here in October of 1979. Both sides have addressed the effect of the subpoena, however, and both this action and the state subpoena do frame related issues-is an FDA expert available to testify on behalf of a private litigant (in a state case)? It thus seems proper to consider them together. "Plaintiffs initially urge that mandamus is available to secure the testimony of Dr. Finkel. The jurisdictional statute provides: 'The district courts shall have original jurisdiction of any action in the nature of mandamus to compel an officer or employee of the United States or any agency thereof to perform a duty owed to the plaintiff.' 

28 U.S.C. § 1361. The key term here is duty. Mandamus is not avail able unless the defendant government official has a 'clearly established,' 'plainly defined,' 'preemptory' obligation to act. . . . "The plaintiffs have suggested that 'it is the duty of the Food and Drug Administration to advance the public interest. . . . . . . This may well be true, but it does not suffice to establish a specific duty on the part of the FDA to make its experts available to private litigants. Plaintiffs have not pointed to any statutory, regulatory or judicial rule that requires the FDA to make Dr. Finkel available. The 

Court is thus led to the inevitable conclusion that it lacks mandamus jurisdiction. "Plaintiffs also advance the FOIA, 5 U.S.C. § 552, as a general basis of jurisdiction for their entire complaint. Its provisions are more properly applicable to the now-settled dispute over withheld documents. Moreover, the complaint on its face explains the need for an 

FDA expert by reference to plaintiffs inability to secure any other experts in Massachusetts. They do not complain of any inability to interpret the specific documents provided, such as might require agency (FDA) clarification. Consequently, this Court finds no jurisdiction under FOIA to reach plaintiffs' complaints. "Plaintiffs' final set of arguments supporting Dr. Finkel's availability as an expert are not clearly focused, but appear to center around various theories of discovery and policy. The Court initially notes that both the Federal and the Massachusetts versions of Rule 30 provide that 'any party may take the deposition of any person .,' and that Rule 37 gives this Court sanction power. Those rules recognize that liberal discovery is an invaluable tool. . . . However, where the intended deponent is a government employee, and the examination relates to expertise developed in the course of that employment, significant countervailing policies are involved. "Executive departments are empowered by a 'housekeeping' statute to regulate their internal administration. It provides: 'The head of an Executive department or military department may prescribe regulations for the government of his department, the conduct of its employees, the distribution and performance of its business, and the custody, use, and preservation of its records, papers, and property. 

This section does not authorize withholding information from the public or limiting the availability of records to the public.' 5 U.S.C. § 301. This authority has been exercised to promulgate regulations applicable to the FDA, 21 CFR § 20.1. "The Supreme Court has specifically recognized the authority of agency heads to restrict testimony by their subordinates through this type of regulation. In this case, the Commissioner of Food & Drugs has exercised his discretion to determine that it would not be in the public interest to allow Dr. Finkel to testify as an expert on behalf of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs may not agree with the determination but the Commissioner nevertheless was entitled to act as he did. "The Commissioner's determination reflects the general rule that government experts are not available to private litigants in actions to which the United States is a stranger. 'The policy behind this prohibition is to conserve the time of government employees for the conduct of official business, to minimize governmental involvement in controversial matters unrelated to official business, and to avoid expenditures of government time and money for private purposes.' Pilar v. 

S.S. Hess Petrol, 55 F.R.D. 159, 165 (D. Md. 1972). 

"The limited exceptions to this rule do not help the plaintiffs. 

Where government experts have been made available to private liti- 

FDA Consumer April 1981 / 39

gants, there has been a direct link to other government action. For example, where the Army subjected aircraft parts to destructive testing, rendering them worthless in the process, private litigants were allowed to question the Government experts. . . . Plaintiffs here are clearly frustrated by their inability to locate an expert, but that frustration was not induced by the Government, nor does it outweigh the significant government interests at stake. However, these principles do not illuminate the issue before this Court. "Plaintiffs have elected the state forum, and complied with its procedural rules. That choice does not enhance the remedies available to them. This Court would not order the testimony of Dr. Finkel in an action originally brought here; it is no more within the Court's prerogative to intervene and enforce the process of the state court. "The Court does not find, in this case, the special circumstances that would justify making a government expert available to a private litigant. Issuance of a state subpoena does not alter the conclusion.

Consequently, the Court will not order the deposition of Dr. Marion 

Finkel of the Food & Drug Administration. Plaintiffs' request for an order to that effect is denied. Plaintiffs' request for costs and fees is denied without prejudice."

The plaintiffs appealed. The court of appeals affirmed the district court, saying: "On December 21, 1979, the district court issued an order refusing to compel the FDA to make Dr. Finkel available, and filed a memorandum explaining its decision. First, the district court pointed out that Dr. Finkel's deposition could not appropriately be taken as part of discovery incident to the federal proceeding, because her testimony was part of the relief sought and what she would say was irrelevant to the ultimate question of her availability. See Fed. R. Civ. 

P. 26(b)(1). Next, the court considered whether the Finkel deposition could be ordered as part of the relief sought in the federal proceeding. 

Finding no FOIA or mandamus jurisdiction to grant such relief, the district court turned to the Gizas' unfocused contentions that the district court could compel Dr. Finkel's testimony as a matter of comity, and should do so because they had been unable to locate an expert qualified to testify about Modicon. The district court stated that heads of federal agencies have authority to restrict testimony by their subordinates, and that such had been done in this case pursuant to an FDA regulation. 5 U.S.C. § 301; 21 C.F.R. § 20.1. See United

States ex rel. Touhy v. Regan, 340 U.S. 462 (1951). It saw no basis for overriding the refusal to let Dr. Finkel testify in a case which was purely private litigation and in which the government was not responsible for the Gizas' inability to locate an expert. Nor did the district court see itself as obliged or empowered to compel Dr. Finkel's testimony because the state court had authorized a subpoena for her appearance at a deposition. "With respect to the production of documents, the district court's December 21, 1979 memorandum stated that an agreement had been reached and the dispute had been settled. The order of the same date made no mention of this matter. But in their notice of appeal of 

January 18, 1980, the Gizas not only challenged the order with respect to Dr. Finkel's testimony but also challenged the court's finding that the dispute over documents had been settled, on the ground that five of the documents provided were wholly or partly illegible. "We cannot say the district court erred in denying an order compelling the FDA to make Dr. Finkel available to testify. To the contrary, we have difficulty seeing what authority the district court would have had for compelling her testimony at a deposition. "The district court was plainly correct that the Freedom of Information Act provided no basis for obtaining Dr. Finkel's deposition. 

Under the FOIA, a district court has jurisdiction to order the production of improperly withheld agency records. 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(B). 

To the extent that discovery is allowed in an FOIA action, it is directed at determining whether complete disclosure has been made, e.g., whether a thorough search for documents has taken place, whether withheld items are exempt from disclosure. Gizas imply on appeal 

40 April 1981 / FDA Consumer that under the FOIA Dr. Finkel should have been made available to clarify and amplify certain statements she made in her letter to Ortho's President, a district court simply has no authority under the FOIA to compel an agency to generate explanatory material. "The district court was equally correct that it could not compel 

Dr. Finkel's testimony under 28 U.S.C. § 1361, . . . There was no mandamus jurisdiction because Dr. Finkel owed the Gizas no duty to submit to a deposition. ... "Furthermore, the district court was justifiably unpersuaded that it could and should compel Dr. Finkel's testimony as a matter of comity. In support of their comity argument, the Gizas cited authority for one federal court's enforcement of a subpoena in aid of discovery in a case pending in another federal district court, and for one state court's assisting another state court in securing a deposition. . . . Yet, although comity is an important aspect of the relationship between federal and state courts, the Gizas could muster no authority for a district court's enforcement of a state court subpoena as a matter of comity. The Gizas' comity argument is further weakened by the fact that in the state court proceedings in this case, a subpoena has only been authorized and has apparently not yet issued. "Perhaps aware that general notions of comity provide a shaky basis for arguing that the district court was obliged to compel Dr. 

Finkel's testimony, the Gizas' have elaborated on their comity argument on appeal. Now they contend that under the Full Faith and 

Credit Clause (Article IV, Section 1) of the United States Constitution and 28 U.S.C. § 1738 the district court should have enforced the state court's order for the taking of Dr. Finkel's deposition. It is true that the statutory provision requires a federal court to give full faith and credit to the judicial proceedings of a state. . . . But we are aware of no authority interpreting this statute so as to place an affirmative obligation on, and vest jurisdiction in, a federal court to enforce a state court subpoena, much less to compel deposition testimony for which a subpoena has been authorized but not issued. In our minds, the prerogative of a federal court to enforce state process absent specific authorization remains doubtful. . . . "For the above reasons, we find it impossible to conclude that the district court erred in declining to compel Dr. Finkel's testimony. 

It is unnecessary for us to decide when, if ever, it would be appropriate for a federal district court to compel the testimony of a federal officer who has been instructed by the head of his or her executive department not to testify. "We likewise find it unnecessary to become embroiled in the question whether the FDA has yet to comply with the FOIA because five items it turned over are illegible in whole or in part. This legibility problem appears not to have been submitted to the district court for resolution, but only to have been mentioned in the notice of appeal. 

The Gizas make no argument with respect to this issue in their brief: the FDA represents that it has provided the best copies available, 'but has no objection to doing so again.' In these circumstances, this matter does not warrant appellate intervention." (Misc. No. 472; N.J.No.47)

A silver spoon won't do. 

When someone has a seizure never force anything hard between the teeth. It is physically impossible for a person to swallow his or her tongue during a seizure. Attempts to force the mouth open can often cause damage to the teeth and gums. 

Keep calm. By keeping calm, you can reassure other observers. If possible, look for medical bracelet or neck chain. 

Clear the area. Remove sharp, hard or other hazardous objects. Also remove glasses, loosen tight collars, neckties and/or belt, but do not interfere with movements. 

Turn the person on his/her side.

This keeps the airway clear so that breathing is not obstructed. 

Do not restrain or try to revive. 

You can't stop a seizure once it has started. Place a pillow or a coat folded flat, under the head. Awakening should be voluntary. Don't panic if person seems to stop breathing. 

You may not have to call a doctor. 

You need only to call an ambulance if the seizure lasts longer than ten minutes or if another seizure begins immediately after the first has ended. 

Be reassuring. Some people are embarrassed when consciousness is regained after a seizure. It is very reassuring to see a friendly face. 

Some people are very surprised to hear that you shouldn't place a spoon in the mouth of a person having a seizure. 

There are many myths and superstitions about epilepsy. Get the facts. Contact your local chapter of the Epilepsy

Foundation of America. 

Epilepsy. 

It's not what you think. 

Help light the candle of understanding. 

Epilepsy Foundation of America, 1828 L Street, N.W., Washington, D.C. 20036 (Incorporating the former National Epilepsy League.)

Consumer Forum There's More To Be Said About Never Saying, Please Pass The Meat 

Less Than 2 lbs. to 1

In your recent article on vegetarianism (There's 

Something To Be Said For Never Saying, 'Please 

Pass The Meat,' February 1981), you correctly point out that persons adopting a vegetarian diet must take extra care to meet nutritional requirements. However, many other statements in your story are erroneous or misleading. 

You state that "it's easy to see how the world's food shortages might be greatly lessened if vegetarianism swept the world." It's not so easy for those familiar with the role of ruminant animals in the food chain. Because of the microorganisms that live in the first part of their stomach, ruminant animals possess the ability to utilize cellulose for energy and to synthesize essential nutrients such as proteins and certain vitamins. The nitrogen in the proteins can be derived economically from nonprotein nitrogen compounds such as urea that cannot be utilized by humans.

Approximately two-thirds of the world's agricultural land is permanent pasture, range and meadow; of this, about 60 percent is not suitable for producing cultivated crops that would be consumed directly by humans. This land, however, can produce cellulosic roughages in the form of grass and other vegetation that is digestible by grazing ruminant animals, of which cattle and sheep are the most important. These "walking food factories," traveling without fossil fuel, can harvest and convert the vegetation, which is undigestible for the most part by humans, to high-quality food containing protein, iron, B-vitamins, zinc and other nutrients.

Statistics are also misused to imply that beef cattle are the least efficient converters of feed into meat. In this connection, four points deserve emphasis. 

First, concentrates (including grain) account for only a minor part (17 percent) of the feed used to produce beef cattle. The feeding of concentrates takes place almost exclusively in the finishing stage and amounts to less than two pounds per pound of live-weight of all beef produced. Most of the weight of beef animals results from consumption of roughages produced on lands with few alternative uses, from crop residues and from by-products. 

Second, beef cattle have the flexibility to use varying combinations of concentrates and roughages as costs may dictate. Finishing rations composed largely of concentrates have been the least costly alternative during recent years. 

Third, use of concentrates in the finishing stage increases the efficiency of production by increasing the daily rate of gain and by reducing the nonfeed costs per unit of beef. 

And fourth, the concentrates used in finishing cattle effect a change in meat quality currently preferred by consumers. 66 

You state that "The saturated fats in animal products contribute to high blood cholesterol levels, which is one of the risk factors for heart disease." After having referred several times in the article to the Food and Nutrition Board of the National Academy of Sciences, we wonder why you did not quote from their most recent report, Toward Healthful Diets, in which the FNB says: some organizations have recommended that dietary lipids be reduced from 40 percent to about 30 percent of calories and that the ratio of polyunsaturated to saturated fat (P:S ratio) be changed from the present value in the American diet of 0.4 to 0.5 to a ratio of about 1.0, in order to achieve lower serum cholesterol levels in the population generally. Unfortunately, the benefit of altering the diet to this extent has not been established. As noted, other studies employing diets containing 

35-40 percent of calories from fat and higher P:S ratios have shown equivocal effects on coronary disease and have been accompanied by a somewhat greater incidence of gastrointestinal disease. 

In light of these facts, we believe your article served only to mislead the public about the supposed virtues of vegetarianism. Americans deserve to hear the whole story, especially from the Food and Drug Administration. 

Thomas J. McDermott

Director of Communications National Livestock and Meat Board 

Chicago, Ill.

6.75 lbs. to 1 lb. of Muscle 

With regard to your article ". . .Please Pass the 

Meat", I would draw your attention to a misconception concerning grain conversion to meat by certain animals. 

The number you quote (from Lappe's book,

DIET FOR A SMALL PLANET) for cattle at 16 

pounds of grain for one pound of meat is most misleading. During its lifetime in the feedlot, a steer (which is routinely fed starting at a weight of about 500 pounds and finished at 1,000 pounds) will consume about 7½ pounds of feed (of which 

5½ pounds is grain) for each pound of bodyweight gain. After processing the animal to produce beef for the market, this conversion factor translates to about 12 pounds of grain for each pound of beef.

But, that is only part of the story. Before reaching the feedlot stage, the animal was raised on pasture forages and other roughages not utilized directly by man (non-competitive consumption). In the feedlot, the non-grain portion of the diet is comprised of more non-competitive feedstuffs as well. as by-products from the processing of human foods (items which would be thrown away were they not fed to animals). The animal, through growth and maturation processes, improves its yield of acceptable consumer products. Naturally, the longer the steer is fed in the feedlot, the more grain is consumed, but, on the average, a 1,000 pound animal may have consumed 2,700 pounds of grain. Assuming the animal is roughly 40% muscle tissue, the final ratio is about 6.75 pounds of grain consumed for each pound of muscle produced and marketed.

Perhaps another way of looking at the same subject is to consider that the steer, rather than wasting grain, has used the energy (along with the protein and other nutrients) of this commodity to help convert a large quantity of unusable and/or undesirable (to man) feedstuffs into high quality well accepted protein for humans.

I have addressed protein or meat production since that is the topic in question, but one must consider the multitude of other products (including a portion of human dietary energy needs which can be reasonably and rationally supplied by animal fats) obtained from the animal; clothing, pharmaceuticals, fine chemicals, by-products for animal feeds. The list is on-going and impressive, suggesting that very little indeed of the animal is in fact wasted. 

Howard M. Frederick, Ph.D.

Director, State Feed Control 

American Feed Manufacturers Association 

Arlington, Va. 

And a Further Explanation 

The 16 pounds of grain to 1 pound of meat ratio was presented by Frances Moore Lappe in her book DIET FOR A SMALL PLANET (pp. 8-15, Ballentine Books, 1975). She quotes U.S. Department of Agriculture sources and spells out her calculations in a note at the end of the book. Presented with the controversy, FDA's animal nutritionists said they believe the ratio should be 6 or 7 pounds of grain to a pound of meat for feedlot cattle. The

FDA CONSUMER article also stated that the average livestock ratio, including chickens, was 7 or 8 pounds of grain or soybeans for 1 pound of flesh. 

That was taken from an article in the February 1976 

issue of NUTRITION ACTION. FDA's nutritionists say the grain/soybeans needed for 1 pound of other livestock should be from 2.1 pounds for broilers to nearly 4 pounds for swine. 

Ms. Lappe also argues that land used for cattle and livestock feed could be better utilized if it was planted in human crops. However, the CONSUMER article was not written to suggest ways of solving the world's food shortages but to take a close look at vegetarianism.

As to Mr. McDermott's citation of the Food and 

Nutrition Board's report on cholesterol in diets, that report has had trouble gaining acceptance in the scientific/medical community. For example, SCIENCE, the magazine of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, suggested editorially that the board "shot itself in the foot" with the report.

No such controversy surrounded the board's report on vegetarianism.

Plague ... Still A Potential Peril 

The word "plague" has come to mean a disaster or scourge of any kind. Medically speaking, "plague" has a more specific, but still dreadful, definition-a disease that three times in history ravaged all of the known world and still exists today, even in the United States. 

66 in men and women alike, there appeared at the be- Iginning of the malady certain swellings, either on the groin or under the armpits, whereof some waxed to the bigness of a common apple, others like unto an egg ... and these the vulgar named plague-boils After a while, the fashion of the contagion began to change into blue or black blotches. . . as the plague-boils had been first and yet were a very certain token of coming death, even so were these for everyone to whom they came.' 

only in the United States but throughout the world." 

There has been no major outbreak of plague among humans in the United States since 1924. From 1925 to 

1964, the incidence of the disease in this country was static, averaging less than two cases per year. But the past 16 years have seen a significant upward trend that public health officials view with concern. During the 

1970's, 105 cases were reported, more than any decade since 1900-1909. Last year there were 18 cases; 5 of them were fatal. 

Eighteen cases in 1 year is certainly not cause for alarm. In fact, the annual incidence of plague in this country has rarely exceeded that of botulism caused by contaminated food. Yet the handful of cases does serve as a reminder that, as with the safety precautions adopted by the food industry to protect the public against deadly botulism poisoning, constant surveillance and control are indispensable guardians against widespread eruptions of -Boccaccio, The Decameron, 1353 plague. "Case 12 had travelled to Columbus, Nebraska, on 8/15 and on 8/19 was admitted to a Columbus hospital with fever and right inguinal adenopathy (swelling of the groin). She was treated with ampicillin and left the hospital against medical advice on 8/22. After her discharge it was learned that she might have plague and she was tracked down on Highway 81 by the Nebraska Highway

Patrol and returned to the hospital in Columbus. (Plague) infection was confirmed on 8/28 . . .' 

-U. S. Centers for Disease Control, Plague 

Surveillance, September 15, 1980 Plague the Black Death of the Middle Ages-is not a closed case in the annals of medicine. The dread disease has never been eradicated; it is still smoldering around the globe, even here in the United States. It flares up from time to time to remind us that modern medicine has not completely freed us from the scourges of our ancestors. 

As recently as 1972, the U. S. Centers for Disease

Control stated that plague "must be viewed not as a historical phenomenon but as an ever present threat, not

Plague is the oldest and most dangerous of the major epidemic diseases. From accounts in the Bible, scientists today generally agree that it was plague that the Lord used to punish the Philistines for their victory over the Israelites and their theft of the sacred Ark of the Covenant in the 12th century B.C.

Three times in history plague has exploded across the world as a great pandemic-an epidemic that knows no geographic bounds. These scourges struck in the 6th, 14th, and 19th centuries. The first pandemic began in 

Arabia and reached Egypt in 542 A.D. Called the Plague of Justinian after the Byzantine emperor then on the throne, it killed 100 million people-half the empire's population-in about 50 years. Continuing in minor eruptions, it lasted for more than a century. 

The second and most infamous pandemic erupted about 700 years after the Plague of Justinian ended. Originating in Asia, the plague was transmitted to Europeans in 1347 when a Kipchak (Turkish) army, besieging a Genoese trading post in the Crimea, catapulted the plague-infested corpses of its soldiers into the town. As the afflicted Kipchaks lifted their siege, the Genoese merchants sailed back to Italy, unknowingly carrying a cargo of plague. 

Called the Black Death because it typically inflicted 

4 May 1981 / FDA Consumer

u Salman 81.

JOHANNES NOHL, The Black Death, 1925 JOHANNES NOHL. The Black Death, 1925 

ביעו Medieval physicians consult at bedside of plague victim. klay duuel klop "Knock, Devil, Knock" reads the caption of this medieval woodcut, depicting the arrival of the plague. blood spots beneath the skin, which turned black, the plague found in 14th century Europe a highly susceptible population living in poverty, congestion, and ignorance. 

Within 4 years it blanketed the entire continent with death, killing 25 million persons-one-third of the population a greater toll of life than any war or epidemic. 

It was not until the beginning of the 20th century that disease experts learned that plague is transmitted by rat fleas. During the Black Death, some men of science ascribed the cause of the disease to an ill-fated conjunction of the planets Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. Others blamed it on comets, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes or, simply, the wrath of God.

A handier scapegoat was found by those who attributed the plague to the Jews, most often accusing them of poisoning the wells. Many were put to death; in Basel the 

Jews were penned up in wooden buildings and burned alive.

Other remedies were tried with no greater success in ridding the populace of the plague. In England, great faith was placed in tobacco; even children were encouraged and sometimes forced to smoke to protect themselves against the disease. Other experts of the time held that bad drove out bad, and to inhale foul odors was a useful protection. Thus, fearful citizens were known to spend hours each day crouched over latrines, absorbing the stench. Leeches and purges were two more common treatments, both of which probably hastened-perhaps mercifully-the death of the victims. 

The Black Death didn't die out until the 17th century; part of its grand finale was the Great Plague of London of 1665, which killed 70,000 of the city's 460,000 inhabitants.

The third and most recent plague pandemic began in 

China in 1892 and quickly reached the port city of Hong

Kong. Rat-infested ships spread the disease to all parts of the world, including the United States, and 13 million people died.

Although the World Health Organization (WHO) has declared that the third pandemic is now over, plague remains one of four diseases still quarantinable throughout the world. (The others are cholera, yellow fever, and smallpox.) Because many infectious diseases, including plague, have a natural ebb and flow, public health officials are not being lulled into a false sense of security. 

There were still more than 100,000 cases of plague worldwide in the decade ending in 1974. Epidemics still arise occasionally in India, Burma, China, and Madagascar, and sporadic cases occur in southern Africa, South America, and the western United States, showing that reservoirs of plague continue to smolder around the globe. 

The reservoir in the western United States, created by the third pandemic, is as large as the one in central Asia that spawned the Black Death and much larger than the African focus that gave birth to the Plague of Justinian. 

While some experts believe that plague has been present in the United States since colonial times, the first epidemic did not occur until 1900 in San Francisco. Partly because some local and State officials tried to hush the matter up, the epidemic raged for almost 4 years, striking 

121 people and killing all but three. 

6 May 1981 / FDA Consumer

Other American coastal cities have since experienced 'serious outbreaks of plague. A 1924 epidemic in Los Angeles was the last appearance in this country of classic, urban, rat-borne human plague, although as recently as 

1971 plague-infected rats were found in San Francisco and Tacoma, Wash.

Higher standards of sanitation along with rat control › programs on ships and in cities have reduced the risk of urban plague, but by 1908 plague had begun moving out of the coastal cities and into the interior. It is now firmly entrenched in the wild rodent population throughout vast areas in the western third of the country. Some of the animals are resistant enough to perpetuate the infection—a condition characterized as enzootic; that is, the disease is constantly in the animal population but affects only a small number.

Plague is harbored in more than 220 rodent species worldwide, including at least 50 in the United States. The principal carriers in this country are ground squirrels, prairie dogs, marmots, deer mice, and wood rats. Nonrodents such as rabbits and hares are also occasional carriers of plague.

Since 1949, when human plague was first diagnosed in New Mexico, the southwestern States have displaced California as the primary focus of the disease in the United States. In the past decade, 81 percent of plague cases were acquired in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and 

Utah. Plague-infected rodents have been found in 14 western States, as far east as Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas and northward to Alberta, Canada. Plague probably has not spread any farther east because there are no dense populations of colonizing rodents. 

Humans who encroach upon this vast reservoir of wild rodent plague are at risk of contracting the disease themselves. The spread of housing into previously undeveloped areas in the West adds to this risk; in recent years the majority of human cases has occurred within one mile of the victim's home, indicating that those who live in these areas are at greater risk than occasional visitors, such as hunters and campers (although some cases have occurred among these groups).

Plague is an occasional occupational hazard: sheepherders, ranch hands, and even one telephone lineman have contracted plague while working in rural areas. Two veterinarians, a biologist, and a geologist were exposed during field trips. Last February, a 25-year-old man died of plague in El Paso, Tex.; he was a part-time trapper. 

Plague has become a public health problem in particular for Indians on reservations in the southwest. During the 1970's, 35 percent of the cases of plague in Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah were in Indians. A few years ago a severe outbreak among Navaho Indians followed a dieoff of prairie dogs. Chief victims were children who played with the dead animals and women who skinned the rodents before cooking them.

Human cases of plague, however, such as those that occur sporadically in the West, are not the norm. Plague is and always has been primarily a disease of rodents. 

The cause of the world's most dreaded epidemic disease is a rod-shaped bacterium only 1/10,000th of an inch long. Dubbed by scientists Yersinia pestis, the micro 

During the Black Death, Jews often became the scapegoats in plague-ridden cities and towns. Here, in a German woodcut from the time, Jews are burned en masse.

JOHANNES NOHL, The Black Death, 1925 

scopic bug is so virulent that just one has been shown in laboratory experiments to be a sufficient dose to kill monkeys and guinea pigs. 

Y. pestis flourishes primarily in a rodent-flea-rodent cycle. A flea that has fed on an infected rat ingests many of the plague bacteria. The bugs multiply and eventually block the forestomach of the flea. In order to swallow new blood when it feeds again, the flea must regurgitate. 

In doing so, as many as 100,000 plague bacteria are transmitted into the skin and capillaries of the new host, be it rat or human.

When plague reaches epizootic (an epidemic among animals) proportions in a rodent population, the die-off can leave a large number of fleas not knowing where their next meal is coming from. If a human population is nearby, man is likely to be inducted into the plague cycle.

Plague-infected fleas can reach humans in a number of ways. They can jump directly from wild rodents-the most common pathway to humans in this country. Or they can go from wild rodents to "domestic" ones (urban rats, for example, as during the Black Death) or to pets.

Occasionally, humans contract plague directly from infected animals without the aid of fleas; by skinning them, for instance, or even by eating improperly cooked infected carcasses.

Person-to-person spread of plague, by means of human fleas, also occurs. But this is uncommon in sanitary environments and has never been observed in the United States. A more common pathway of human-to-human transmission of the disease is through pneumonic plague, a form of the disease that undoubtedly played a large role in the spread of Black Death.

Medical reports recognized pneumonic, bubonic, and septicemic plague as three separate forms of the same disease. The classic and most common form is bubonic plague, so named for the bubo, or lump, produced in the 

FDA Consumer | May 1981 | 7

Xenopsylla cheopis, or rat flea, which transmits plague from animal to animal or animal to man groin, armpits or, occasionally, the neck, as the disease attacks the lymph nodes.

Symptoms of bubonic plague normally appear 2 to 6 days after exposure. Onset is usually sudden, with fever, rapid pulse, a white coating on the tongue, and nervous distress ranging from restlessness to fatigue or exhaustion. Speech may be slurred, the patient may stagger and appear apathetic or confused. The intensely painful and tender buboes may not appear until several days after the other symptoms. They may be as small as almonds or as large as oranges. Eventually nearly every organ and body tissue may be involved. 

Untreated bubonic plague is fatal in about 60 percent of the cases. But modern therapy is highly effective if begun promptly; during the 1970's, only 14 percent of bubonic plague patients in the United States died from the disease. 

A second form is septicemic plague, which can kill within hours of onset. During the Black Death, some victims were said to have gone to bed healthy and never woke up. Septicemic plague is similar to bubonic, but the brunt of the infection falls on the bloodstream; within 1 or 2 hours it is swarming with Y. pestis. If untreated, septicemic plague is almost always fatal. Even today, treatment must be started within about 15 hours of the onset of symptoms to have chance of success. 

Equally devastating is the third variant, the one mainly responsible for person-to-person spread of the diseasepneumonic plague. It is possibly the most infectious of all epidemic diseases. Pneumonic plague attacks the lungs; it

Rattus rattus, most common species of plague-carrying rodents is communicable through sputum (spit) and respiratory droplets. As with septicemic plague, untreated victims of pneumonic plague rarely survive more than 3 days. Pneumonic plague is rare in the United States, and it has not been spread from one person to another since 1925. 

Modern medical care has helped to dramatically reduce the fatality of plague. The key is to initiate treatment as quickly as possible when plague is suspected. But plague is such an oddity in most of the world that the early symptoms are often ascribed to meningitis, venereal disease, or influenza. While the diagnosis of plague can be confirmed through laboratory tests, this takes precious time; physicians are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation to begin appropriate treatment when they suspect plague.

The most effective drug in treating plague is streptomycin, usually given orally for up to 14 days. Other antibiotics, such as tetracycline and chloramphenicol, are also effective. 

All plague patients are isolated for at least 48 hours until it can be determined whether the case is pneumonic. 

All persons who had contact with the patient are kept under surveillance to see if they, too, have been infected. 

Contacts of patients with pneumonic plague are quarantined, given antibiotics as a precaution, and watched for 6 to 10 days to see if symptoms appear. Physicians and nurses caring for patients known or suspected to have pneumonic plague must don protective hoods, masks, goggles, overalls, and gloves.

Among those who recover from plague, permanent in- 

8 May 1981 | FDA Consumer

jury is uncommon. But in some cases, especially if treatment was late, permanent damage to the central nervous system can occur. In patients who survive severe septicemic plague, tissue of the lips, nose, fingers, or toes may be destroyed and amputation may be necessary. 

While modern medical skills and tools have made treatment of plague highly successful, prevention of the disease remains more difficult. One approach is to build up resistance of individuals in plague areas by administering vaccine. An FDA advisory panel has concluded, in a report to be published in the FEDERAL REGISTER, that the vaccine produced in the United States is safe and effective. The panel based its conclusion mainly on the favorable experience with the vaccine among U. S. soldiers in 

Vietnam. The GI's, who were routinely inoculated, suffered almost no cases of plague even though the disease was rampant in the country, with about 5,000 cases a year among the Vietnamese population. 

But plague vaccine does cause a large number of adverse reactions, and the protection is temporary. Three initial injections must be given a month or more apart, and then a booster shot is needed every 6 months. (For that reason, the vaccine is of no use as a preventive given in the midst of a plague epidemic.)

Because of those problems, the vaccine is recommended only for those at high risk of the disease; for example, military personnel and others travelling to areas of persistent human plague; and field personnel, epidemiologists, and laboratory workers engaged in certain plague work.

Because of the virulence of the disease, plague vaccine presents a special difficulty for FDA's Bureau of Biologics, charged with assuring the safety and effectiveness of vaccines. In order to test samples for potency, the vaccine must be administered to lab mice, which are then inoculated, or "challenged," as the scientists say, with live plague bacteria. Working with live plague is, of course, extremely hazardous. So the bureau relies on the Naval 

Biological Laboratory in Oakland, Calif., to perform the potency testing for plague vaccine. 

The bureau is working with the Naval Laboratory to develop a radioimmunoassay (RIA) test to replace the hazardous mouse test. The RIA procedure would measure the amount of plague-fighting antibody produced in a sample of blood from a vaccinated animal, with no need to inject the animal with live plague. Such a test would be not only safer, but also faster and cheaper.

More effective than vaccine in reducing the incidence of plague around the world are modern methods of sanitation, surveillance, and control. The danger of classic shipborne plague is virtually nonexistent as a result of international cooperation in applying anti-rodent measures and enforcing quarantines.

Within the United States, the health departments of a number of western States work with the U. S. Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and the U. S. Fish and Wild life Service to routinely check blood samples of coyotes and other wild rodent-eating animals. The presence of plague-fighting antibodies in the blood would indicate that the animal may have been feeding on plague-infected rodents.

When plague does flare up among wild animals, a number of control measures are available. Since rodent eradication is seldom feasible in the wild, getting rid of the rodents' infected fleas is a better bet. Burrows can be dusted with pesticides, usually carbaryl. Or bait stations can be set up so that an animal gets a harmless dusting of insecticide when it enters the "trap" looking for food. (Rolled oats are the favorite bait for most animals but tree squirrels seem to prefer pine cones covered with peanut butter.) The dusting kills the fleas on the animal, as well as those back in its nest.

When plague threatens to spread from animals to people, campers and travelers heading toward plague areas are cautioned to avoid feeding or handling rodents, sleeping on the ground, or camping in areas of high rodent population. Campers are advised that insect repellent (on the wrists and ankles) may be of some help. They also are asked to report any sick animals they see. In very threatening circumstances, campgrounds may be closed and areas quarantined.

Those who live in areas where plague is a threat need to be constantly vigilant. Pets should be kept free of insects. Food sources and harborages for wild rodents should be eliminated from around the home. A study by the New Mexico Health and Environment Department and CDC found that rodent attractions such as gardens, unused outbuildings, wrecked cars, trash piles, and wood piles were associated with an increased risk of human plague. Failure to take steps to control fleas on dogs and cats also appeared to be a possible risk factor. 

Although vigilant surveillance, modern sanitation, and other controls have helped lower the incidence of plague, there is no guarantee that the risk of new epidemics or another pandemic is gone. The apparent success in the battle against plague over the past few decades may not be entirely due to modern scientific achievements. Plague has gone into periods of slumber before, without the benefit of antibiotics, insecticides, or rodenticides.

While modern science may protect us from another deadly scourge on the scale of the Black Death, as long as plague smolders in animal reservoirs around the world, there is always a chance that the dread disease may flare up once again into a major epidemic. Vietnam demonstrates how the ravages of war can spread plague: from 

1963 to 1967 the total number of cases of plague (13,263) in that country almost equalled that of the preceding 57 years.

In 1970 the WHO Expert Committee on Plague warned that "the natural foci scattered over almost the whole world provide plague with ample opportunity to re-emerge. Recent episodes have demonstrated that plague can, at any instant, break out from these foci and cause widespread invasions.” And a noted authority on plague,Dr. K. F. Meyer, wrote in 1965 that "history teaches that plague has often shown a spontaneous decline but has flared up again. . . . The possibility of future pandemics cannot be excluded; therefore, the disease should be given continued attention by those interested in global public health.”

Bill Rados is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

The Story Behind Those High Blood Pressure Readings 

Some 60 million Americans suffer from hypertension-the "silent" disease. One of the commonest diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels, hypertension—or high blood pressure-increases a person's risk of heart attack, stroke, or kidney failure. 

Fortunately, there are many drugs that doctors can use to control both moderate and severe forms of this disease. he scene is a familiar one. The nurse wraps a long fabric "cuff" around a patient's arm just above the elbow, then inflates the cuff until the blood flow through the artery in the arm is shut off. After placing a stethoscope over the artery, the nurse gradually releases the air while keeping an eye on a column of mercury in a gauge attached to the cuff. What is heard through the stethoscope is the sound of the blood as it resumes its flow through the artery. What the nurse is doing is measuring the patient's blood pressure.

Taking blood pressure readings is now an essential part of virtually every medical examination. It is the simplest way of determining whether the patient has hypertension (high blood pressure).

Hypertension is one of the commonest of the diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels. It is often called the "silent" or "invisible" disease because in the majority of cases there are no outward signs or symptoms and the patient is unaware that there is anything wrong. Hypertension significantly increases a person's risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney failure. 

Approximately 35 million Americans-1 of every 6 has hypertension severe enough to require treatment. 

In addition about 25 million are estimated to be borderline cases that should be watched.

Hypertension is something of a medical mystery. Technically, it is defined as a persistently elevated blood pressure, but, except in a relatively small number of cases, the cause or causes of hypertension are still not clear. There is, of course, a normal pressure within the blood vessels. It is the force exerted against the walls of the vessels by the blood flowing through them. This pressure is highest in the arteries and their finer branches called arterioles, drops sharply in the capillaries, and is lower still in the veins returning "used" blood to the heart. Blood pressure can go up when the heart beats faster and it can also rise when smaller blood vessels, such as the arterioles, are constricted. Their resistance to blood flow is increased just as shutting down the nozzle of a garden hose increases water pressure in the hose. Relaxation of the muscles that control this constriction reduces resistence to blood flow and lowers the blood pressure. When the pressure goes up and stays up, hypertension results.

In about 5 percent of hypertensive cases a definite cause can be pinpointed. It may be kidney disease or obstruction to normal kidney blood flow, or excess secretion of aldosterone, a hormone that promotes the retention of salt and water by the kidney. Another cause is pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal glands. Usually benign, this tumor does produce and release into the blood large quantities of the hormones norepinephrine and epinephrine, which raise blood pressure by stimulating the heart and constricting blood vessels. Hypertension with a known cause usually can be cured, often by surgery. Arteriosclerosis, or "hardening of the arteries," also is associated with hypertension. 

As for the remaining 95 percent of the hypertensive population, no one knows for sure what causes their blood pressure to go up and stay up, though there are many theories. One is that hypertension may stem from abnormal irritability of the central nervous system leading to excessive activity of the sympathetic nervous system, which is largely responsible for maintaining normal blood vessel tone.

It has been suggested that there is a hypertensive personality—that people with high blood pressure are more nervous, suppress anger, are oversensitive, and have more frequent and more intense emotional upsets. However, not everyone with these traits has hypertension, nor does everyone with hypertension have these traits. 

High blood pressure runs in families. Harvard and Boston City Hospital researchers have found a familial tendency toward high blood pressure that can be detected in youngsters. 

Women who come from families with a history of hypertension sometimes develop this condition during pregnancy for no apparent reason. The pressure drops after pregnancy, but may go up again later in life. 

Obesity certainly is a factor in high blood pressure because of the added work that excess weight puts on the heart. Blood volume increases with body weight because adipose, or fat tissue, like organ and muscle tissue, must be supplied with blood. It has been estimated that each extra pound of fat requires a mile of capillaries to nourish it. The heart must work harder to push the blood through these added miles of tiny blood vessels.

---

Too much sodium, principally in the form of salt added to food, is also linked to hypertension. A growing body of evidence suggests that people who are genetically prone to hypertension may be increasing their risk of actually developing this disease by eating a diet high in sodium. 

Excess sodium causes the body to retain fluids and apparently affects blood vessel tone. 

Cultural background, too, may play a role in the development of hypertension. For some unknown reason the disease seems to be more prevalent in blacks. Some people say being black is more stressful than being white; others feel that blacks are genetically predisposed or that their hypertension may be related to their concentration in the lower socioeconomic classes where the disease may be more common because of high sodium diets.

Whatever the cause of hypertension, be it one or several of these factors, the good news is that it can be controlled. In mild cases, particularly in young people, hypertension can sometimes be managed without any drugs by simply cutting down on sodium, cutting out the extra pounds, and getting adequate exercise. These measures are desirable even for those who are on antihypertensive drugs. 

There is a large variety of drugs that doctors can use to control hypertension. Because no single drug or specific combination of drugs is going to be right for every patient, doctors try to tailor the treatment to fit the particular needs of the patient.

One way in which this can be done, according to recommendations of the Joint National Committee on the Detection, Evaluation, and 

This drug increases the kidney's excretion of sodium and reduces the amount of fluid retained by the body. 

Diuretics are relatively inexpensive, can be given on a once-a-day or twice-a-day schedule, and have minimal side effects. Because some diuretics increase the excretion of potassium as well as sodium, the patient may also be given supplementary potassium or else a diet high in potassium-containing foods, such as bananas, or an additional drug to raise potassium levels. For some patients a diuretic may be all that is needed to control their high blood pressure.

Step II-If blood pressure remains high, the doctor may next prescribe what are called adrenergic-inhibiting agents. These drugs reduce arterial blood pressure by curbing the activity of the sympathetic nervous system. 

There are several alternative Step II drugs which act on different parts of the system. Any one is generally effective in lowering blood pressure when used with a Step I diuretic. Fatigue or lethargy, depression, and sexual dysfunction may be side effects experienced by patients taking these drugs.

Step III-The third type of drug the doctor may prescribe is called a vasodilator-one that relaxes the smooth muscle controlling the blood vessels. Because they may increase heart rate and cardiac output, vasodilators should be used cautiously in patients with angina pectoris and should be used with a Step II blocking agent and Step I diuretic.

Step IV-If the first three steps don't do the job, there are more potent drugs available similar to those in Step II. 

One of the biggest problems in 

Treatment of High Blood Pressure, is treating hypertension lies in the fact to follow the "Stepped-Care Approach." This means that treatment starts with a small dose of one antihypertensive drug. Then the dose of that drug is increased and other drugs are added as needed until the desired blood pressure is reached. 

This is the way the Stepped-Care 

Approach works:

Step I-The doctor will prescribe a diuretic, popularly called a water pill. that once on these drugs, most patients must take them for the rest of their lives. This isn't always easy, particularly since the patient generally feels fine. Doctors can help, said the Joint National Committee, by making sure the patient understands that hypertension has no symptoms and that it can lead to more serious consequences if it is not controlled.

Simplifying the treatment schedule and providing written instructions on dosage, common side effects, and what can be expected from each type of medication also may help patients stick to their schedule. Patients should be encouraged to report any side effects they experience so that alternative drugs can be prescribed.

Finally, patients should be praised when a blood pressure goal is reached.

As for the patients themselves, the Joint National Committee suggested ways to help themselves keep on the straight and narrow path, including: being involved in decisionmaking about their therapy; relating medication-taking to a daily routine, such as brushing teeth; keeping a record of blood pressure and daily drug dosage; and asking other members of the family to remind them about their medication and to help in special food preparation when necessary. 

Other suggestions include: 

Don't mix drugs. Tell your doctor what other medicines, including over-the-counter drugs, you are taking. Many OTC drugs contain sodium and some contain vasoconstrictors. • Never change, skip, or alter your drugs or drug schedule without consulting your doctor. 

Cut down on your use of salt, both in cooking and at the table. 

Stay away from highly salted foods. 

Use foods labeled as being low in sodium. Some people may be able to use salt substitutes. 

Watch the amount of cholesterol you eat, if you have an elevated cholesterol level, to avoid a risk factor that increases your chance of developing heart disease. • Use alcohol in moderation, if at all. Some antihypertensive drugs have a sedative effect and don't mix well with alcohol. 

Don't smoke. Smokers who have high blood pressure increase their risk of developing heart disease.

MUUTEN LIETURIO The Measure ment of Blood

Pressure Blood pressure is the force exerted against the walls of blood vessels by the blood flowing through them. It is measured with a sphygmomanometer, an instrument usually consisting of an inflatable cloth cuff attached to a mercury meter similar to a thermometer.

Some instruments have a dial attached to the cuff instead of a mercury meter; others record pressure electronically.

To record blood pressure, the doctor wraps the cuff around the patient's arm just above the elbow and inflates the cuff. This drives the mercury up near the top of the column while shutting off the flow of blood in the artery in the arm. Placing a stethoscope on the artery, the doctor slowly releases the air in the cuff while watching the falling mercury column.

At first, blood flows through the artery only when the heart is pushing hardest; when the heart relaxes, flow stops and the vessel collapses shut, making a thudding sound that can be heard through the stethoscope. When that sound is heard, the doctor notes the height of the mercury column. 

This is the pressure produced by the heart's pumping stroke or systole. It is called the systolic pressure.

Air is released from the cuff until the thudding sound is no longer heard. At this point the doctor again notes the height of the mercury column. This is the pressure in the artery when the heart relaxes between beats.

It is called the diastolic pressure. 

Blood pressure readings are expressed in terms of millimeters of mercury, that is, the height of the mercury column observed by the doctor as he listens to the blood flow. 

The first number recorded is the systolic pressure and the second is the diastolic pressure. Normal systolic pressure for an adult between 18 and 45 is around 120 millimeters of mercury
