Tinkering With Nature To Make Drugs 

Recombinant DNA technology-popularly known as "gene splicing"-is one of the most promising means to produce drugs, biologics, and other medically useful products. Some products resulting from the new technology already are on the way, and FDA has developed the science needed to regulate them. by Annabel Hecht

Nott [ot too many years ago headlines warned of impending disaster expected to be spawned in the scientific laboratories of the world: 

"New Strains of Life-or Death" 

"Science That Frightens Scientists" 

"Man-Made Bacteria Could Ravage Earth" 

Scientists themselves, fearful of the consequences of their investigations, called on their colleagues to impose restrictions on certain research. Today many researchers admit their fears were exaggerated and science writers applaud their "tinkering," calling the research the "industry of life." Such fears have been put in the category of "UFO's and witches."

What has emerged from this research is something called recombinant DNA technology-one of the most promising means to produce drugs, biologics, and medically useful proteins. To the nonscientist, the new technology is known as gene splicing or genetic engineering.

The enormous economic and technical advantages of recombinant DNA technology have encouraged several drug companies to investigate this tool to produce new drugs. One company, Eli Lilly & Co., has already started clinical trials of human insulin produced by the new technology. In anticipation of the regulatory issues these products will generate, FDA has taken steps to be ready for them.

DNA, short for deoxyribonucleic acid, is the genetic substance of all living cells. The DNA molecule was first discovered by the German biochemist Friedrich Miescher in 1869, but it was not until 1953 that James Watson and Francis Crick determined the structure of DNA to be composed of two chains of nucleotides, intertwined to form a double helix. (This configuration is sometimes described as being like a spiral staircase or a rope ladder that has been twisted.) Genes that carry hereditary characteristics, such as color of eyes or hair, are simply short lengths of DNA containing specific sequences of nucleotides.

Recombinant DNA, or "rDNA" in scientific short- 

14 May 1981 / FDA Consumer

hand, is a technique by which scientists can break up and rejoin segments of DNA from different organisms to form a new, hybrid molecule. One method of doing this kind of gene-splicing surgery involves use of circular bits of DNA, known as plasmids, that are found within some bacteria. The first step is to remove the plasmid from the bacteria and treat it with special enzymes, called "restriction endonucleases," that cause the plasmid DNA to split apart. These same enzymes are used to isolate a piece of 

DNA containing a specific gene or genes from another organism's DNA. This second piece of DNA is then inserted between the cut ends of the plasmid's DNA, and the recombined molecule is fused enzymatically into a circle again. The hybrid plasmid is returned to a bacterial host. Bacteria that have become hosts to hybrid plasmids then become microscopic factories turning out copies of the recombined plasmids as the bacteria themselves grow and multiply.

Scientists are not playing around with genes just to fool Mother Nature. Using rDNA technology to obtain large quantities of a single gene in pure form, scientists can study the chemical structure and function of normal and mutated genes. This, in turn, will lead to a better understanding of how defects in these genes can alter their functions. With this knowledge, it may one day be possible to correct inherited disorders such as diabetes and hemophilia.

In the more immediate future, gene splicing offers new ways to make drugs and substances for industrial uses. 

Interferon, the antiviral substance that is an active component of human and animal cells, also is being manufactured by the recombinant DNA method and has been used in a recently initiated clinical trial involving interferon therapy of human lymphomas. In addition, scientists in California have induced bacteria to produce somatostatin, a brain hormone that controls growth. In the future it is expected that vaccines and antibodies as well as other drugs will be mass produced by the new technology. 

Indeed, the list of such products that are expected to be regulated by FDA is already substantial. In addition to insulin, growth hormone, and interferon, there are thymosin and other peptide hormones, endorphins, vaccines such as hepatitis B and influenza, and blood products such as urokinase, serum albumin, and clotting factors. The field of veterinary medicine may use gene splicing to produce a bovine growth hormone. In the area of foods, certain enzymes used in food processing, such as rennet, which curdles milk for cheesemaking, may be rDNA products. A specific test for thalassemia, a blood disorder, is among the medical devices that may come from gene splicing.

The potential for rDNA to revolutionize the other segments of economy is "mind boggling," according to the 

FOOD AND DRUG LETTER, an independent bi-weekly publication of the Washington Business Information, Inc. 

The Letter predicts that in the future "microorganisms might be put to work producing any number of chemicals, cleaning up oil spills, extracting oil from the earth, turning corn into alcohol for gasohol, or manufacturing food additives." 

Despite the promise of the new technology, there were times when it appeared recombinant DNA research might come to a screeching halt. The reason lay in the use of 

Escherichia coli (E. coli) as the primary bacteriological factory for reproducing hybrid molecules. E. coli is a harmless bacterium, one most scientists feel comfortable using, but it also is a normal inhabitant of the human intestine. Many people including the pioneer scientists in the field feared that a dangerous recombinant could escape from the laboratory. Once out in the world, it was projected, the hybrid could infect humans and animals by way of their gastrointestinal tract.

These concerns led to a number of scientific conferences in the early 1970's which, in turn, called on the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to develop guidelines for investigators working on recombinant DNA research. 

In 1976 NIH set up an Office of Recombinant DNA Activities and drew up the guidelines specifying conditions and procedures under which recombinant DNA research could be conducted.

Under the guidelines, scientists are prohibited from releasing into the environment organisms with recombinant molecules or transferring a drug-resistant trait to an organism that doesn't have the trait normally. Laboratory design depends on the degree of risk. Very little is required for research with a low risk (the P1 level) besides good microbiological technique, but where the risk is high (P4) laboratories must be super secure with sealed cabinets, glove boxes, and air locks. Bacteria used as hosts for recombined genes must be weakened so they cannot survive outside the laboratory. 

Most industrial research today is being done at the P1 level; P4 containment is not being used at all at the present time.

Initially the guidelines applied only to institutions receiving NIH funds for recombinant DNA research. No mention was made of possible industrial uses of the new technology. However, a subsequent supplement to the guidelines, developed jointly by FDA and NIH, now extends them to industry on a voluntary basis and provides protection for trade secrets.

As it became apparent that new drugs from recombined genes were fast becoming a reality, FDA's Bureau of Biologics established a division of Biochemistry and Biophysics. The division, established in June 1980, has resident know-how in biochemistry, biophysics, and cellular biology and can provide the scientific basis for review of products resulting not only from rDNA technology but also from any other new emerging technologies.

At the present time, the most well known rDNA product is interferon. Interferon is a protein produced by the body's white blood cells in response to some stimulus such as a virus. Its name comes from its ability to interfere with viral infections. Interferon usually makes the headlines because it is being clinically tested as an anticancer substance. Unfortunately, supplies of interferon have been short until now, and treatment for even the common cold requires very high doses. 

There are several types of interferon produced from living cells: • Leucocyte-produced from human white blood cells

DNA 

Discovery of the art of recombinant 

DNA has been described as one of the more striking technological achievements of this century. Like most modern scientific endeavors, it was not something that happened overnight, but was built on a succession of investigations on the nature of the cell that span nearly 40 years.

Some of the high points of recombi nant DNA history include: 

1944-Oswald T. Avery, Colin 

MacCloud, and Maclyn McCarty of the Rockefeller Institute (now Rocke feller University) show that DNA is the hereditary substance of living cells. • 1952-William Hayes and 

Joshua Lederberg, then at the University of Wisconsin, discover that bacterial cells contain circular DNA molecules called plasmids. 

1953-James Watson and Fran cis Crick, at Cambridge University, determine the structure of DNA to be a double helix, i.e., a spiral. 

1962-Werner Arber and Daisy 

Dussoix, University of Basel, Switzerland, learn that bacterial cells contain a substance called a "restriction enzyme" that acts as a chemical scalpel to split DNA molecules. 

1972-Janet Mertz and Ronald

Davis, Stanford Medical School, show that split DNA fragments have "sticky ends," a characteristic that makes genetic engineering possible. 

1973-Annie C. Y. Chang and

Stanley N. Cohen, Stanford University School of Medicine, and Herbert 

Boyer and Robert Helling, University of California Medical School at San 

Franciso, report construction in a test tube of biologically functional DNA molecules that combine genetic information from two diffent sources. 

1977-Keiichi Itakura, Tadaaki 

Hirose, Roberto Crea, and Arthur D. 

Riggs, City of Hope National Medical 

Center, near Los Angeles, and Herbert L. Heyneker, Francisco Bolivar, and Herbert W. Boyer, University of 

California, San Francisco, create a recombinant DNA first-production of somatostatin, a brain hormone that inhibits secretion of insulin, glucagon, and growth hormone. 

1978-Keiichi Itakura and col leagues at City of Hope and David 

Goeddel and colleagues at Genentech, Inc., San Francisco, coax bacteria to make insulin from a chemical synthesis of human insulin. • July 1980-Eli Lilly and Company announces it has begun limited testing in England of biosynthetic human insulin produced in its British plant by recombinant DNA technology. taken from donated blood. • Lymphoblast-produced from small white blood cells which play a part in the body's immune system and which are grown in the laboratory. 

Fibroblast-produced from human connective tissue cells, which are then grown in the laboratory. 

Immune interferon-the most recently discovered form of interferon, immune interferon appears to be made by white blood cells as a function of the body's immune system. 

The interferon that comes from rDNA is somewhat different, because it is generated by bacteria rather than human cells; the final product, however, is similar because the interferon gene in the bacterium originally came from a human cell. Because large quantities of interferon can be produced relatively inexpensively this way, rDNA interferon probably will be the type that will be used for most clinical testing. 

Regardless of the source of interferon, the new FDA

Division of Biochemistry and Biophysics will review each new product using a high technology. Biochemists in the division, who already have developed advanced instruments to analyze the structure of proteins, sugars, and carbohydrates, are putting the finishing touches on a “micro-sequencer" that will give them the most detailed picture possible of the structure of interferon. 

In the early stages of its testing, naturally-derived interferon was only 1 percent pure. Work is underway in the division to develop improved methods of purifying interferon from human lymphoblast and leucocyte cells. A radioimmune assay-that is, a technique using radioactively tagged material is being readied to determine how much of an active interferon is in a given sample. 

Because of interferon's potential as an anticancer agent, FDA scientists are looking at cancer cells to find out how they behave and how interferon affects their growth. 

As for regulating the end result of gene splicing, FDA will look at these products in much the same way as it does those produced by conventional techniques. The 

Agency's authority under the law is to regulate the product itself regardless of how it is manufactured. "There is no magic in recombinant organisms," says Dr. Henry

Miller of FDA's Division of Metabolism and Endocrine 

Drug Products. "Likewise, no magic will be required by the FDA in industry's preclinical and clinical studies. 

General guidelines for approval for marketing drugs derived from recombinant organisms will be similar to those for any drug."

In some respects, however, drugs produced from recombined genes may be regulated differently. For instance, changes in quality control may be necessary to be sure that no mutation has occurred during processing that could result in an altered drug. This may involve use of newer and more sensitive analytical techniques to check both the purity and identity of the product, including isoelectric focusing, mass spectrometry, and high pressure liquid chromatography.

Uncle Sam's Disease Detectives 

It's a zoo of deadly viruses, a maximum security laboratory whose workers wear space suits while they study epidemics, and a Scotland Yard of investigators willing to fly anywhere, any time, to halt the spread of disease. That's the national Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta, an agency of the Public Health Service. 

by William Grigg TSS ello, I'm Dr. Kathryn Shands "Hcalling from the Centers for

Disease Control in Atlanta. We are trying to determine why toxic shock syndrome primarily affects women and usually occurs around the time of the menstrual period. "Since you have had toxic shock, I would like to ask several questions..."

Telephoning into the night-while other Atlantans played tennis, had their cocktails, and began dinner— 

Dr. Shands and her colleagues were seeking clues to a frightening, severe, and sometimes fatal condition that appeared to be rapidly increasing, mostly in young women. 

The calls were part of an investigation involving laboratory analysis, State-Federal cooperation, and other elements of a classic study by the 

U.S. Public Health Service's Centers for Disease Control. So let's look at it:

Alerted by State and private physicians in several locations of an outbreak of toxic shock syndrome,

Shands had flown to the West and back to discuss the cases and get a fix on what they involved-high fever, vomiting, and profuse diarrhea. 

She then devised a questionnaire touching several possible explanations for the disease's increase. Day and night, she and coworkers were on the phone. They found the patients hard to track down but cooperative once they were found.

It is not for nothing that graduates of the Center's Epidemic Investigation Service get lapel pins in the shape of a shoe bottom, with a hole in the sole. "Not home? When could I call? 

Oh, well, do you have the telephone number there?"

Once located, the toxic shock patients proved willing to provide sexual and menstrual information without hesitation, even to male investigators. (But some balked at questions about family income.) The questions went like this: "What contraceptive method, if any, do you use? "How many times a week do you have sexual intercourse? "What athletic activities, if any, do you engage in on a regular basis?" 

The questions threw a wide net. 

Speculation, informed and otherwise, had suggested such causes as colored underwear, pierced ears, celibacy, and swimming in contaminated waters.

But it was the questions on the menstrual products used by the women that paid off. Tampons were named by the patients more often than by the controls. "What brands? "What absorbency? "Have you ever used Rely?"

As the data were analyzed, conferences were held with the Food and 

Drug Administration's Bureau of 

Medical Devices. And CDC announced that although "a causal role has not been shown . . . studies suggest that use of tampons, especially continuous throughout menstruation, is associated with development of 

TSS in some women."

Later, as additional data were developed, the manufacturer pulled Rely, a new tampon named by many of the patients, from the market. 

With FDA concurrence, the manufacturer also developed an unprecedented, nationwide advertising campaign to halt Rely's use. At FDA's urging, other tampon manufacturers then added warnings to their packages telling women to obtain prompt medical care if certain symptoms appear.

The incidence of the disease-and particularly the deaths associated with it began a sharp decline. 

CDC's assault on toxic shock included laboratory analyses that isolated the common germ, Staphylococcus aureus, from the patients' vaginas. And a series of progress reports and alerts to the medical community appeared in CDC'S MORBID 

ITY AND MORTALITY WEEKLY 

REPORT, a little bulletin with a circulation of only about 106,000 but an impact almost without equal among

Government publications. 

In that bulletin are CDC's reports from the battlefields of disease. Some items simply note the case trends in chickenpox, tuberculosis, or rabies, and the occasional U.S. cases of cholera, leprosy, and plague. Behind 1

Why did one commune member (and only one) get lead poisoning? Well, it turned out, the commune's wine had been made in two old bathtubs with lead-based finish. 

Then why did only one chap suffer? 

Answer: He drank most of the wine-in a month, 190 liters!

Did they attend the same classes? 

No. Party and pet together? No. But elaborate questioning finally drew forth a common passion for glazed donuts from a particular bakerywhere the glazer was then discovered to be recovering from the liver disease. 

What common link could there be in a typhoid outbreak spread across seven States? Don't even try to guess. It turned out to be a single restaurant in New York-and the particular powdered mashed potatoes prepared there. 

How did anthrax, an infectious disease of wild and domesticated animals, come to kill an insulation worker in southwest Ohio? The illness stopped when a faulty air conditioning system was repaired.

But CDC maintains more than

There they lay for years. 

In July 1976, CDC again appeared stumped when 189 people at an

Bellevue Stratford Hotel in Philadel phia fell ill. Twenty-nine died. 

Water, ice, room assignments, food, and dust were analyzed. 

Hundreds of hotel workers and conventioneers were interviewed. Specimens from the victims, of course, were studied and restudied. Nothing. 

Months passed. CDC, already somewhat embarrassed by its role in promoting the failed swine flu vaccine that same year, was taking a beating. 

Then, at the end of 1976, the pieces fell in place. The organism was isolated and shown to be an environmental bacterium harbored in the earth-and capable of floating, when disturbed, into air-conditioning systems, where it might become concentrated. 

Just in time to save at least one life in a new outbreak, a drug therapy was identified. 

And tests were made against the serum saved from 1965 and 1969. 

Pontiac's fever and St. Elizabeth's pneumonia proved to be Legionnaires' disease, too. 

A much quicker success came in the recent cases of infant illness resulting from chloride-deficient formula. Dr. Jose Cordero, who had finished Epidemic Intelligence Serv ice training a few days before, got reports of three cases of infant metabolic alkalosis-a rare condition characterized by loss of appetite and "failure to thrive," brought on by a deficiency of chloride. The infants, because they were allergic, had all been fed a soy-based formula-in fact, the same manufacturer's prod- uct. 

That was Friday. Dr. Cordero spent the weekend on the telephone talking with specialists who might be called to treat or confer on such a condition. He turned up about 30 infants with the condition-and most, it turned out, were known to have been fed exclusively the same manufacturer's formula as the first three infants. 

Immediately, Dr. Cordero told

FDA his findings. There were conversations with the manufacturer. 

And by Thursday, less than a week after the first report had reached

then endemic in 14 southern States.

This was CDC's job when it was cre ated to replace a World War II emer gency agency concerned with malaria on the military installation through the South. (Among the wartime unit's projects were pinup girl posters reminding soldiers to take their quinine.) 

From its predecessor, CDC also inherited a nucleus of specialists, a location in Atlanta, and a working re lationship with State health departments that continues to this day. Even as malaria was being eradicated, CDC broadened its efforts to more nearly fulfill its title as the 

Communicable Disease Center, as it was then called. 

CDC's immunization work has helped control polio and monitor the safety of vaccines, and has helped erase smallpox from the world. The last smallpox case was in southern 

Somalia in 1977, following a decade of international cooperation in which 

450 CDC workers participated. 

More than 130,000 cases of smallpox-an old and dreaded plague for which there is no effective treatment had been reported in 1967, as the eradication effort began. 

Actually there may have been that many cases in northern Nigeria alone, with 10 to 15 million cases throughout the world that year, some experts estimate. (In the United 

States, there had been 12 cases with 

2 deaths in New York as recently as 

1947 and an epidemic that killed 163 

people in Detroit in 1924. Histori cally, half the Cherokee tribe in 

Georgia had been killed in an epidemic in 1783, and half the Catawba there in 1759.)

The smallpox program was inaugurated under the auspices of the

World Health Organization in 1967. 

Its aim was not control but eradication-total destruction of the smallpox virus. Some experts scoffed, believing the virus would mutate to survive, as do the influenza viruses, or that enough unvaccinated hosts would always remain to keep the chain of infection going. 

But if birds and animals could be slaughtered or deprived of habitat until they became extinct, why couldn't a virus? That, at least, was the thought of Dr. William Foege, now director of CDC, and other leaders of the smallpox effort. 

Mycology Training Branch chief Leanor D. Haley instructs postdoctoral resi dent Sara T. Beatrice. Mycology deals with fungi-yeasts, molds, smut, and mushrooms among them.

Foege (pronounced FAY-ghee) played a key role in the final victory.

Working in Nigeria when the vaccine was in short supply, he tried out his theory that mass vaccination was not the only answer, but that smallpox could be trapped and starved of hosts by encircling each new case as it occurred, quickly vaccinating all the patient's possible contacts. It worked. 

Health workers believe that the smallpox virus no longer exists "in the wild."

Smallpox remains in the closely secured special laboratories of CDC, however. There workers use sophisticated new techniques they hope will disclose the molecular-level differences that make smallpox virulent and the similar vaccine virus benign. 

Foege is also excited by a recently simplified technique for fusing an antibody-producing cell with a cancer cell whose nature is to continuously grow. The result is a hybridoma-a hybrid cell line, a kind of perpetual factory pouring out the antibody.

CDC's 3,500 workers are often pioneers. Some plan new defenses against toxic spills. Others seek to determine whether long occupational exposures to various substances pose reproductive threats. And still others are engaged in risk assessments in which an individual's habits, heredity, and general health are used to estimate his or her likely lifespanand then the individual is shown how to add 2, 5, 10 years to his life by taking specific remedial actions.

Indeed, Foege and his people seem to have a hard time saying "no" to any puzzle. They recently assessed techniques for avoiding injury in tornadoes and analyzed the influence of weather on death rates. In Atlanta's epidemic murders of Black children,

CDC has assisted in developing questionnaires to determine what children may be more at risk-and how to reduce that risk.

CDC has no plans to go into crime prevention, Foege says, but then he notes that accidents, homicide, and suicide have replaced traditional diseases as third, fourth, and fifth highest causes of deaths before the age of 

65. All three are often alcohol-related, Foege adds. "I personally think a public health approach to crime might be useful.'

New Vaccine Promises Hepatitis B Protection 

Each year thousands of Americans are afflicted with fever, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and jaundice that characterize hepatitis B, formerly known as serum hepatitis. Now, after years of research, it appears that relief is on the way. by Don McLearn

Adev n unusual new vaccine has been developed to combat the debilitating liver disease hepatitis B. The vaccine has had an impressive string of successes in clinical trials using animals and humans, and it has been submitted to FDA for approval.

When it meets Federal standards, it will be the first viral vaccine to be licensed in this country in 10 years and one of the only vaccines ever manufactured directly from human blood. 

Hepatitis B was recognized as early as 1883 when it was described as "an epidemic of icterus" (jaundice) among shipyard workers in Bremen, Germany. Over the years, it's been called serum hepatitis, homologous serum jaundice, long incubation period hepatitis, post-transfusion hepatitis, yellow fever vaccine hepatitis, and post-salvarsan jaundice. Put simply-it's the most serious form of viral hepatitis, accounting for more than half the clinical hepatitis cases and nearly all hepatitis deaths. 

Hepatitis B is of major public health importance here and throughout the world. An estimated 80,000 to 100,000 cases occur in the United 

States each year and 10 times that amount worldwide. Infection may progress to chronic liver disease-including cirrhosis-and there is evidence linking it with hepatic cell carcinoma, a severe, generally fatal liver cancer. 

Infected people, especially those infected early in life, may become chronic carriers capable of transmitting the disease to others. There are an estimated 200,000 hepatitis B carriers in the United States and 200 million worldwide.

Although originally thought to be spread only by blood transfer, the hepatitis B virus is now known to be present in tears, saliva, and semen, which accounts for the fact that it is spread by intimate contact, including sexual activity. Homosexual men and prostitutes incur a high rate of infection. 

Hepatitis B has been reported following illicit drug injections, ear piercing, and tattooing. Drug addicts are frequent victims as are people who improperly handle equipment in blood banks or kidney dialysis units. 

Surgeons, dentists, and others who accidentally come into contact with infectious blood are also at high risk for catching the disease.

The first major advance in hepatitis B vaccine research came in 1965 

when Dr. Baruch S. Blumberg dis covered a virus-like particle, now called the hepatitis B surface antigen, in the blood of an Australian aborigine. Subsequent studies revealed that this antigen, a substance that stimulates antibody production, was part of the exterior of the human hepatitis 

B virus. Understanding the relation ship between this antigen and the virus has paved the way for detecting hepatitis B infection and hepatitis B carriers and for development of the vaccine. 

The virus cannot be grown in the laboratory, so Blumberg suggested that excess antigen in the blood of carriers could be separated from the rest of the virus to produce a vaccine against hepatitis B. 

Spurred by this hypothesis, three

Government agencies-the National Institutes of Health, the Centers for Disease Control, and FDA's Bureau of Biologics-formed a collaborative research effort to transmit the B virus to an animal and, if possible, develop and test an experimental vaccine.

In 1969, the Government researchers found chimpanzees to be susceptible to the virus and this animal model was used in testing experimental vaccines. By the early 1970's, the 

Government scientists had developed an experimental vaccine that was shown to be safe and effective in preventing hepatitis B in the chimpanzees.

That vaccine was, and is, prepared from the surface antigen of the hepatitis B virus. The antigen is a microscopic particle only 22 nanometers wide. (Think of a nanometer as one billionth the size of a yardstick.) The tiny particle is extracted from the blood of human chronic carriers to make the vaccine.

Following publication of these and other studies, Merck, Sharp and 

Dohme, a drug manufacturer, undertook development of a commercial vaccine. The firm's task hasn't been easy. Because the hepatitis B vaccine must continually be purified from the blood of chronic carriers, manufacture of the vaccine is a unique but very time consuming and complex process. The production cycle takes 

65 weeks, a longer production and testing cycle than for any vaccine currently in manufacture.

The process begins with the collection of blood plasma from special 

FDA-licensed blood donor centers in major metropolitan areas across the country. The surface antigen particles are separated from the plasma constituents and purified by a variety of biochemical and biophysical means. 

Any residue of active virus is destroyed when the vaccine is treated with the chemical formalin. Then the vaccine is boosted with aluminum hydroxide to assure maximum antibody response. In addition, under FDA guidelines a variety of tests including a 6-month safety test must be con-

At least three forms of viral hepatitis-each caused by a different virus or viruses-are recognized: 

1. Type A hepatitis, previously called "infectious hepatitis," is spread by fecal contamination of food, clothing, toys, or eating utensils. It is mainly a disease of children and young adults. Type A hepatitis is often so mild and free of jaundice that it is dismissed as a case of "flu" or the "grippe." Type A hepatitis is not transmitted by blood. 

2. Type B hepatitis, previously called "serum hepatitis," is similar to type A in symptoms but can cause chronic hepatitis in 5 to 10 percent of its victims. It is implicated strongly in liver cancer. 

3. Non-A, non-B hepatitis refers to cases of viral hepatitis that cannot be traced to the A or B viruses. Non-A, non-B hepatitis is similar to the B variety in that it can progress to chronic hepatitis and is often spread by blood transfusion. In fact, this type of hepatitis was first recognized when donor blood that had successfully cleared screening tests for hepatitis B was found to produce hepatitis in recipients.

If all goes well, the vaccine could be available for public use in a year. 

There may be an additional benefit from the new vaccine. Research on the hepatitis B virus has pointed out its association with liver cancer common in parts of Africa and Asia.

Hepatitis B occurs more frequently in patients with this cancer than among the general population.

Although the actual relationship between the two is unclear, it has been suggested that a vaccine preventing hepatitis B infection might prevent cases of primary liver cancer as well.

26 May 1981 / FDA Consumer

In late 1979, the National Science 

Foundation undertook a nationwide public opinion survey to find out how the public feels about science and technology. Food additives was one of three areas probed in depth by the pollsters. This article tells the results of that survey. by Roger W. Miller

mericans generally have a high regard for and trust in science; and the majority of them see benefits in food additives. However, they apparently would like to ban saccharin and eat it, too. 

Those are some conclusions that can be drawn from a nationwide survey of public attitudes toward science and technology. The survey covered 

1,635 persons 18 years and older, living in over 100 communities ranging from Orange, Vt., to Los Angeles,

Calif. The survey was undertaken for the National Science Foundation and was conducted in the last 3 months of 1979. 

The surveyors said that "the most advanced probability sampling techniques" were used so that the results, when weighted, could be projected to the entire U.S. population. In addition to food additives, the survey probed specific public attitudes about nuclear energy and space exploration.

The public has a lot of interest in and quite a bit of sophistication about food additives, according to the survey, with nearly 92 percent saying they had heard "about controversies over food colorings or chemicals added to foods." Only 19 percent considered themselves "hardly informed at all" about the controversy. Fifty-nine percent said they could see some benefits from adding chemicals to foods. 

Asked to name the specific benefits, they cited preservation as No.1. 

Pressed for a second benefit, most who responded came up with the additives improving taste, color, or appearance. 

While many saw benefits from add- 

In Science 

We Trust 

Unless It Involves 

Sugarless Soda ing chemicals to foods, even more— 

79 percent saw disadvantages. 

Asked to name the "harmful consequences" of food additives, 49 percent linked the chemicals with cancer. Second among harmful consequences was that additives could cause disease, illnesses, or birth defects. 

Overall, the public thinks that food additives present a health danger but most think that it is not a serious problem. Less than 10 percent said it was no problem at all. 

Generally, Mr. and Mrs. America think that mice are good for studying the effect of food chemicals on humans. Asked a specific question about that, nearly a third said the mice studies provided "very useful" information and over half thought the mouse reactions gave "somewhat useful" information. The citizens also overwhelmingly think that a group of scientists who specialize in food additives is best qualified to decide issues about safety of the chemicals. “A federal regulatory agency or commissioner" was a poor second choice.

The people surveyed showed a lot of interest in science, technology, and FDA-related items. For example, more than 70 percent said they would read articles with headlines about an FDA study on food safety and a study linking a food dye with cancer. Thirty-two such questions were asked about the headlines; the subjects included Howard Cosell and spring fashions. Only two questions sparked more interest than the FDArelated items. Those two concerned location of a nuclear power plant and a cancer research report. 

Attitudes favorable to science and the scientific community were revealed by answers to questions about the value of science. More than 1,300 of the 1,635 respondents said that scientific discoveries were making our lives "healthier, easier and more comfortable." And 1,150 said scientific research produced more benefits than harm, with only 172 saying more harm resulted.

To a question about how they'd like to see their tax monies spent, improving health care was at the top with improving education second. At the bottom of the list were predicting and controlling weather and exploring outer space. Midway choices for spending tax money included preventing and treating drug addiction and developing or improving weapons for national defense. 

A cure for the common cold is possible within the next 25 years, 9 out of 10 people believe. About the same proportion think that there is a likelihood of finding new sources of cheap energy. But people are more pessimistic about crime research, with only 4 out of 10 seeing researchers coming up with new ways to effectively reduce the crime rate. 

The public's apparently contradictory attitude about saccharin was indicated in a hypothetical question about food additives and cancer. The question was: "Suppose a group of scientists report that a certain widely used food additive causes cancer. 

Would you make a special effort to find products without the additive or would you make no special effort to avoid it?" 

Seven out of 10 said they would make a special effort to avoid the additive. Such has not been the case with saccharin.

■FDA has taken no steps to require warnings on fluorescent lamps and is not making any recommendation about plastic shielding for such lamps. A Talk 

Paper, issued February 25 by the Agency, says that an article in the February 1981 issue of READERS DIGEST 

describes work at the Bureau of Radiological Health (BRH) as indicating that ultraviolet radiation from unshielded fluorescent lamps may contribute to skin cancer in humans. The author suggests that FDA “could reasonably require a warning label" on fluorescent lamps and recommend plastic shielding to reduce the "hazard." Based on this article, some media reports have stated that FDA has proposed shielding and that warnings are required.

In a 1980 study, BRH biophysicist Alan Anderson observed that even the low level of radiation from fluorescent lamps was capable of producing mutations in a cell culture test system, not in animals as some reports say. Because the incidence of skin cancer is linked to cumulative exposure to ultraviolet radiation,

BRH scientists propose that it is likely that any source of prolonged exposure to ultraviolet radiation will contribute to the risk, although the largest contribution will undoubtedly be from the sun.

■Certain powdered and effervescent acetaminophen preparations have been exempted from the child proofing regulation of the Poison Prevention Packag ing Act of 1970.

The exemption was granted by the 

Consumer Product Safety Commission, according to a February 23 FEDERAL REGISTER notice, because available information indicates special packaging is not required to protect children under 5 from injury or illness. The effervescent products are difficult to swallow and the effervescence is markedly unpleasant. 

**BiH ALL MEREMMES The Institute of Medicine (IOM) of the National 

Academy of Sciences is conducting an independent assessment of the physiological and behavioral effects of marijuana use, and of Federal research programs in this area. The study is being funded by the National 

Institutes of Health. According to a notice in the February 24 FEDERAL REGISTER, the IOM proposes to review scientific evidence that may suggest hazards to the health and safety of marijuana users. Data suggesting health benefits also will be examined. 

The Civil Aeronautics Board is looking at its regulations regarding smoking on airplanes with a view to either banning smoking entirely or to eliminating all regulation of in-flight smoking. At the present time certain scheduled and chartered air carriers must provide a no-smoking section in each class of service. 

In a February 11 FEDERAL REGISTER notice, the 

Board explained its decision to re-examine the entire range of issues in a review of its smoking rules, including the two alternatives. 

The Government's report on "Health Hazards Associated With Alcohol and Methods to Inform the General Public of these Hazards" is available from the The truth about DMSO is not yet available, says the Harvard Medical School Health Letter. An article in the March issue points out that there is no solid evidence of serious and persistent side effects from the drug, but on the other hand, there is no solid evidence of DMSO's effectiveness for conditions other than interstitial cystitis. Harvard's advice: ". . . avoid the use of various DMSO preparations unless such use is being offered in the context of a carefully controlled study that assures the purity of the preparation and monitoring for any side effects that might develop.” 

■FDA is holding in abeyance a proposed rule that would prohibit or limit the amount of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB's) in sealed electrical transformers or capacitors used or stored in or around food, feed, and food- and feed-packaging materials manufacturing and storage facilities. The proposal was based in part on a limit of 50 parts per million established by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) as a cut-off point for regulating residual amounts of PCB's in retrofilled equipment such as transformers. Because of some questions about the legality of the EPA regulation, FDA has decided to put a hold on its proposed rule while the Agency decides whether to issue a reproposal, withdraw the proposal, or issue a final regulation. 

In the meantime, FDA says anyone who has additional comments may send them to the Dockets Management Branch (HFA-305), 5600 Fishers Lane, Rockville, Md. 20857.

Investigators' Reports DUNGANUI LAI 

· Confucius Say: 

Chuifong Bad

Medicine 

San Francisco District investigators wore out a lot of shoe leather in 1974 tromping the streets of Chinatown.

They were sent out to track the source of a Chinese herbal medication called 

Chuifong Toukuwan after several doctors reported patients taking this product had contracted agranulocytosis, a serious blood condition. About a third of the stores the investigators visited had supplies of Chuifong and other herbal drugs; in many cases they had to ask specifically for the product, which was stored under the counter. The store managers were reluctant to say where they got the product. 

Eventually, they tracked the manu facturer-Nan-Lien Pharmaceutical 

Co., Hong Kong. Meanwhile, the district lab had analyzed the pills collected from hospitalized patients. Although the product reputedly contained only herbs, the tests showed the presence of phenylbutazone, aminopyrine, prednisolone, methyltestosterone, diazepam, chlorozoxozone, and acetaminophen. Only the last is a nonprescription drug. The first three are anti-inflammatory prescription medications, all of which may cause serious adverse effects. Methyltestosterone is a male sex hormone; diazepam is a tranquilizer better known under the brand name Valium. 

That the situation was very hazardous was tragically demonstrated when one of the patients with agranulocytosis died. The other three suffered prolonged hospitalization. 

Chuifong is only one name for the hard, quarter-inch round black and brown pills that come from China.

The drug is usually promoted as a cure for rheumatism and arthritis and sometimes for other complaints, such as anemophobia (fear of high winds). 

It is sold in health food stores, Oriental food stores, novelty shops, and peddled door to door. 

Chuifong was a subtle import, difficult to detect. Sailors landing on California shores brought in handfuls of the tiny pills. Travellers returning from Hong Kong or Taiwan brought boxes of them in suitcases and dufflebags. Packages with modest amounts of the medication entered unobtrusively into U.S. territory by mailplanes and ships. In 1975 FDA issued an import alert about the product.

When stocks of the drug were found, they were detained and either destroyed or returned to their native shores. For many years Chuifong was primarily a name on import lists. If it was coming into America, it was coming quietly and not making any trouble. 

The black and brown pills began to show up in mid-1980 not only on lists of detentions but also in reports from 

FDA districts all over the country. 

The Atlanta District reported the death of a 70-year-old woman in Griffin, Ga. She had been taking Chuifong, her doctor said, for rheumatoid arthritis. The doctor blamed her death on the pills, which his patient had gotten through the mail from Hong 

Kong. He said he believed the pills must contain a corticosteroid, which could have caused the patient's symptoms: gastroenteritis, a perforated stomach, and a perforated duodenum. 

Atlanta investigators recorded the doctor's story, collected samples of the pills, and noted the distributor-Sun

Wuen Trading Co. in Hong Kong. 

Atlanta chemists found indomethacin, a prescription anti-inflammatory drug, in the samples but no corticosteroids or other drugs that could obviously have caused the woman's death.

Investigators from New York Dis trict's White Plains Resident Post also made a visit to a physician whose patient had been self-medicating with 

Chuifong. The doctor said his patient had osteoarthritis and had said the herbal medication made her feel better. However, after about 6 months she began to develop disturbing symptoms: facial rounding, weakness, and mild hirsutism (abnormal growth of hair). When she was withdrawn from the herbal pills, the symptoms disappeared (and the pain from her arthritis returned). The doctor said he thought the pills must contain a corticosteroid but, again, when samples were analyzed by the New York Regional Laboratory this proved not so. 

The samples did contain hydrochlorothiazide, a diuretic drug that should be sold only on a doctor's prescription. The patient told an investigator that her husband had obtained the pills in New York's Chinatown. 

Reports from Atlanta, Dallas, Philadelphia, Los Angeles, and New 

York were compiled at FDA headquarters. Various samples of Chuifong were analyzed and the drugs indomethacin and hydrochlorothiazide identified. Some samples contained chlordiazepoxide (a tranquilizer sold under the brand name Librium), as well as lead and cadmium. Oddly, none of the analyzed samples contained the seven drugs found in the 

1975 survey. The composition of 

Chuifong obviously was variable with time and place. 

The New York District sent two 

Chinese-speaking investigators to check out stores in the Chinatown area in an attempt to get additional samples and to learn where supplies were coming from. The investigators got the samples, but the information was more elusive. Proprietors of the various herbal shops and groceries were not willing, or able, to identify a specific dealer or importer. Investigators reported that rumor had it that the pills were supplied in polyethylene bags with no labeling or markings of any kind. The bags were kept under the counter, the man said, and a customer had to ask the proprietor for the product. He supplied the name of the shop. Investigators collected nine samples, some unlabeled, some labeled as containing only herbs. As with samples analyzed by other districts, however, hydrochlorothiazide and indomethacin were identified. 

Again, it was difficult to trace the source of the drug. 

Although the import alert from 1975 was still in effect, the drug was coming into the country in too many unorthodox ways for this action to be sufficient. So other steps were taken. 

FDA issued a press release warning people of the dangers of Chinese herbal medications sold in brightly-col

Sea Sponges: No Charm 

Against TSS

Even before toxic shock syndrome (TSS) became a household term, some women were using natural sea sponges as an alternative to menstrual tampons. However, after the

U.S. Centers for Disease Control linked TSS with the use of tampons,

FDA district offices began to report an increase in advertising and sale of the sponges, which led the Bureau of 

Medical Devices to request collection of samples and investigation of firms selling the devices. FDA's Kansas

City District was among the districts first to report distribution of menstrual sponges. 

One distributor was the Universal 

Life Church in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. 

A shipment of 4,800 bulk sea sponges, offered for import from 

Greece, aroused the curiosity of a

U.S. customs agent. The importer mentioned casually to the customs agent that the sponges were intended as substitutes for tampons, and the agent informed the Kansas City District. The sponges were subsequently detained at the recommendation of the district. 

It is illegal to sell sea sponges for menstrual use because no studies have been submitted to FDA proving that the sponges, considered class III medical devices, are safe and effective for this use. Safety and efficacy studies for class III devices are required by the Medical Device

Amendments of 1976. Some women's health groups have pointed out that from back and leg pains. If names of manufacturers appeared, they could include Sun Wuen Trading Co. or

Nan-Lien Pharmaceutical Co. in Hong Kong, or Shou Sing Pharma ceutical Co. in Taiwan. 

The Agency also asked the Department of State to request authorities in no safety and efficacy studies on tampons were submitted to FDA either. 

However, because tampons were marketed before the 1976 amendments were enacted, their legal status is different from newer medical devices, such as sea sponges. Along with about 1,800 other types of devices, tampons must first be classified into one of three categories that will determine the degree of control needed to assure safety and efficacy. 

In October 1980, an FDA advisory panel recommended that tampons be put into class III. If FDA accepts the recommendation, safety and efficacy studies would have to be submitted within 30 months.

Tampon manufacturers have been required to submit to FDA a list of ingredients in their products, but the composition of the various types of sea sponges is unknown. Because the sponges are natural, they are exposed to a variety of environmental pollutants and other harmful chemicals during development.

This was demonstrated during 

FDA's inspection of the Emma Gold man Clinic for Women in Iowa City, Iowa. St. Louis Station investigators inspected the clinic after reading in the New York Times that samples of the clinic's sponges had been analyzed and found contaminated. Researchers at the University of Iowa had reported that the sponges contained sand; bacteria, fungi, and other microscopic particles; trace amounts of 11 minerals, including arsenic, iron, sodium, and sulfate; and varying levels of chemicals such as hydrocarbons and nicotine. The investigator learned from clinic representatives that the clinic had issued a press release to television and radio stations reporting the adverse findings. It had also discontinued sale of sea sponges for tampons. 

Ironically, although many women turned to sea sponges because they were afraid of developing TSS, the

Brain Drills Prove Faulty 

Last year a number of neurosurgeons experienced a similar problem with one brand of perforator drills used during cranial surgery to pene trate the skull. The devices-specifi cally, Smith Automatic Perforator

Drills were supposed to automatically disengage as soon as the skull was penetrated. The problem was that in some instances the drills were not disengaging. As a result, one patient suffered brain damage and another received minor injuries. 

One California physician contacted

FDA's Bureau of Medical Devices, and the Boston District was instructed to check out the manufacturer-Codman & Shurtleff, Inc., Randolph,

Mass. The firm had begun a recall of all Smith Automatic perforators marketed since January 1980 because of complaints from doctors and had notified FDA of this. Company officials said they had determined that the failure of those marketed since January 1980 might be attributed to the use of an oil instead of a lapping compound in production. But the 

FDA investigators found that some of the complaints had been about devices manufactured before January. 

And, although in four cases the problem could be tied to the oil, in six instances the problem had been caused by improper assembly, and in one case the user had operated the drill in reverse, which made the drill come apart. There was no literature accompanying the device warning against operating the drill in reverse. 

Three FDA headquarters staff members went to a Maryland hospital to examine two drills and how they were used. The visit revealed other problems. For example, the hospital staff was not aware that a 

30 May 1981 FDA Consumer

water soluble lubricant should be used before sterilization of the devices. The staff also did not know that parts of the drill should not be interchanged with other drills of the same brand and that interchanging parts might cause failure of the de vice to disengage. The labeling con tained no warning about this and the parts were not coded to prevent such interchanges.

At the request of the Bureau of Medical Devices, the firm expanded the recall to include all Smith Automatic Perforator Drills 1/2 and 5/8 inch which Hudson and Jacobs Motor 

Shanks distributed since January 

1971-approximately 8,100 devices.

Under the recall, consignees are returning the drills to the company. 

The drills will be examined and each component will be engraved with matching serial numbers to prevent the interchanging of parts during reassembly. The company is also revising the labeling to include directions and precautionary statements for use, assembly, and disassembly of the device.

The Worst of Times 

A visit by an FDA investigator came at the worst of times for a food manufacturer in Cincinnati, Ohio. 

Grace A. Rush, Inc., which manufactures fruitcakes and other gourmet foods year round, was in the peak production of fruitcakes and brandy sauce intended for the Christmas holidays when FDA's Cincinnati District inspected the company's food plant and found extensive cockroach and fruitfly infestation.

After laboratory testing indicated a sample from one lot of fruitcakes was contaminated, the company voluntarily recalled more than 100 of the cakes already distributed to gourmet shops in Rhode Island and New

York. Additional sample testing of the company's Brandy Sauce Josephine and Brandy Hard Sauce also revealed contamination, and Grace

A. Rush subsequently recalled about 

350 jars of the sauce that had been distributed nationwide.

The recalled products were returned to the company's parent firm in Sun Prairie, Wis., where FDA's 

Minneapolis District investigators witnessed their destruction. In-process and raw materials at the Cincinnati facilities were also destroyed. The estimated value of the raw materials and products recalled and destroyed was $1,500. 

Grace A. Rush, Inc., was allowed to continue production after a followup inspection found the firm operating with adequate sanitary conditions as a result of cleaning the facilities and acquiring the services of a pest control company.

Herbs Need Protection 

The herb group includes food materials that particularly need protection. Unless properly prepared and stored, they may become moldy or otherwise decomposed. And, as a 

Buffalo, N.Y., herbs distributor has found out, failure to protect these articles can result in contamination with excreta from rats, mice, birds, chickens, other animals, and insects. 

Clark's Natural Herbs stored herbs on two floors of a poorly constructed barn located on the owner's property before FDA's Buffalo District inspected the firm. Not only were the herbs stored in such a manner that the owner did not know the identity or quantity of the products on hand, but also the barn afforded easy access for insects, rodents, and other animals.

Investigators found evidence of an active rodent problem in the barn in the form of excreta pellets, urine odor, and bags of herbs and products that had been gnawed. After a laboratory analysis of samples confirmed the rodent contamination, all the herbs in the barn were seized by a 

U.S. marshal.

Under the terms of a consent decree of condemnation, the owner was allowed to recondition the seized herbs and all except two 25-pound boxes of watercress were destroyed under the supervision of an FDA investigator.

After over 9,000 pounds of the firm's products were destroyed, recent shipments of herb crops are now being stored in a rodent free concrete block building. 

Don't Drink the Water

Residents in a small section of 

Glen Burnie, Md., were warned not to use the water in their houses because it contained high levels of caustic soda and hydrofluorosilicic acid.

The warning was broadcast by radio and television in the Baltimore metropolitan area. People in the area specifically affected were visited by county health department employees, who wanted to make sure no one was harmed by the contaminants in the water.

One person who heard the televised warning was an investigator with FDA's Baltimore District, who was home sick. Nonetheless, he called the office to see if they had heard of the problem and were looking into it. 

They hadn't. One of the investigator's coworkers called the Anne

Arundel County Water Works De partment to get details and see if there were any FDA-regulated establishments involved. The department had concluded that a mechanical failure at a well site had caused the problem. A six-block area of Glen

Burnie was affected. The only commercial establishments involved were five restaurants, already being checked by employees from the 

Maryland Health Department. Mean while, the Anne Arundel Health De partment was taking samples of the water to monitor the pH (acidity) levels, which were very high. 

FDA Consumer | May 1981 / 31

County officials later reported to the district that all the affected water lines were flushed, and the pH levels had dropped back to a normal range. 

Dalkon Shields Are Out All women wearing Dalkon Shield 

IUD's should have them removed.

This recommendation was made by the manufacturer of the device, A. 

H. Robins Co., Richmond, Va., in a "dear doctor" letter sent to approximately 200,000 doctors, hospitals, birth control clinics, and Federal, State, and local health agencies.

The safety of the Dalkon Shield has been a subject of controversy since May 1974, when A. H. Robins wrote a letter alerting physicians that there were reports of 36 cases of septic abortion (miscarriage followed by uterine infection) and 4 deaths among women who had become pregnant while wearing the device.

FDA began an investigation and in August held a public hearing on the safety and effectiveness of the Dal kon Shield and other IUD's. By the following year, the Agency had received reports that 245 nonfatal septic abortions and 15 deaths had been related to the Dalkon Shield. A. H. 

Robins stopped manufacturing the device and advised women who were having problems to have the IUD's removed. However, about two million women in the United States had been or were using the shield without problems. Both FDA and the manufacturer advised that if women were not having problems with the device. they need not have it removed. 

In 1980 the Dalkon Shield was again the subject of publicity. During the spring, a number of women brought lawsuits against A. H. 

Robins, claiming they had suffered miscarriages, pelvic infections, and in some cases sterility after having used the Shield. In August, The Washing ton Post reported that all remaining 

Dalkon Shields were being recalled. 

However, when FDA's Baltimore

District checked this story, the firm denied it. 

A month later the firm's president contacted FDA's Bureau of Medical 

Devices to say that a letter was being sent to doctors and other health professionals advising the removal of all Dalkon Shields-even from asymptomatic patients. Baltimore

District investigators again visited the firm and found that this was true. 

The recommendation was based on a 2-year study done at the University of Texas which showed a relationship between duration of IUD use and risk of pelvic inflammatory disease (a group of several pelvic infections that may affect the uterus, the tubes, or the ovaries). There particularly seemed to be a relationship between long-term IUD use and pelvic infection caused by the bacterium Actinomyces israelii. The study showed that this type of infection-pelvic actinomycosis-had been reported in users of a variety of IUD types and noted that the problem could be minimized by replacing inert IUD's at periodic intervals, generally not exceeding 3 years. Because manufacture of the 

Dalkon Shield had stopped 6 years previously, all women now wearing this type of IUD are in the long-term. category and should, therefore, have these IUD's removed.

Dirty Plate Problem 

It took an FDA inspection to convince a culture media manufacturer that the customer is always right. 

Flow Laboratories in Dublin, Va., had received numerous letters concerning its culture media plates. The letters complained that the plates. which are used to grow bacteria, were moldy and that there was a danger that this contamination could cause incorrect diagnosis and delayed treatment. 

FDA's Baltimore District learned of the complaints while reviewing the firm's files during an inspection of the plant. After discovering a high rate of defective products and serious violations of FDA's Good Manufacturing Practice regulations, it became apparent to investigators the firm had not investigated the source of the contamination.

After an FDA laboratory confirmed mold in samples of the firm's products, the district requested a meeting with the manager to discuss the seriousness of the violations. Following the meeting, the firm agreed to cease production and distribution until violations had been corrected and all finished products had been tested with the results evaluated. 

Reinspection of the firm by the district disclosed correction of all

GMP deficiencies and satisfactory retesting of all prior production. 

Shippers of grade A milk need to be on the Interstate Milk Shippers (IMS) list if they are to distribute milk across State lines.

To get on the IMS list, a distributor must score at least 90 out of a possible 100 on a rating, which is conducted every 2 years by a State rating agency. FDA conducts a check rating under the Agency's grade A milk program to assure that the State ratings remain valid within the 2-year period. FDA milk specialists inspect, at random, distributors who are on the IMS list and give ratings similar to those given by the State. 

Green Spring Dairy Co. of Balti more, Md., had been on the IMS list after a rating by the Maryland De partment of Health and Mental Hy giene. However, a specialist from 

FDA's Baltimore District recently checked on Green Spring Dairy. The result was that the firm was withdrawn from the IMS list by the State because of a low score in the FDA inspection.

After a minimum of 15 days the 

State can make a new rating. The 

Maryland health agency did and the company received an acceptable rating putting it back on the IMS list.

Seizures and Postal Service Cases 

FILED SEIZURE ACTIONS charge violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and are initiated based upon FDA recommendations. A seizure action is commenced by the filing of a complaint in the U.S. district court where the goods are located. A U.S. marshal is then directed by the court to take possession of the goods, removing the product from commerce, until the matter is resolved. 

A total of 10 actions to remove from the consumer market products charged to be violative was reported in March. These actions included 9 seizures of foods: 1 involved charges of poisonous and deleterious substances, and 8 involved charges concerning contamination. Others included 1 of veterinary drugs.

Rice (53,840-bag lot of milled long grain U.S. No. 5, and 16,291-bag lot of milled long grain U.S. No. 2), at Gulfport, S. Dist. Miss. 

Charged 8-31-79: while held by Mississippi State Port Authority, Gulfport, Miss., one lot (U.S. No. 5 rice) of the article contained bird filth, and both lots of the article had been held under insanitary conditions; 402(a)(3), 402(a)(4). 

FDA Consumer May 1981 / 35

The lot of No. 5 rice was claimed by Tradigrain, Inc., New Orleans,

La., who denied the charges, but, notwithstanding the denials, the claimant stated a willingness to have the lot reinspected so that it could be determined to be "not adulterated" and could be sold and exported. A consent decree condemned that lot of rice and authorized its release to Tradigrain, Inc., for bringing into compliance. 

Noga, S.A., New York, N. Y., and Agricor, Inc., New York, N.Y., claimed the lot of No. 2 rice and entered into a consent decree of condemnation which authorized release of such rice to them for bringing into compliance.

The claimants undertook to recondition both lots of rice. Bags found to bear visible bird excreta stains were removed. Meanwhile, sampling revealed that the No. 2 rice was insect infested. Orders granting additional time to bring both lots of rice into compliance were granted. 

The claimants of the No. 2 rice moved for complete release to them of 7 of 13 sample lots of the No. 2 rice on the grounds that FDA analysis had not found any insect infestations in the 7 sample lots, and that testing by a firm employed by those claimants found insect infestation in only 1 of the remaining 6 sample lots. The Government opposed such motion. The court upheld the Government saying: "Presently before the Court is a motion filed by the Defendants and Claimants, Noga, S.A. and Agricor, Inc. On August 31, 1979, the Government filed a complaint for forfeiture against, inter alia, 16,291 one-hundred-pound bags of rice. The rice was seized pursuant to a warrant of arrest on September 6, 1979. Subsequently, the parties entered a consent decree regarding the condemnation on September 

8, 1979. "The Claimant's motion seeks the release of 15,485 one-hundredpound bags of rice; claiming that said rice is not adulterated within the meaning of $342(a)(3) of the Food and Drug Act. 21 U.S.C. 

$8301 et seq. An evidentiary hearing was held on February 5, 1980. 

This opinion shall constitute the Court's Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. "On October 14 and 15, 1979, James Blakely, Jr., observed the rice in question. Blakely, of Long Beach, MS., is the resident agent and local investigator for the Food and Drug Administration. Blakely segregated 844 bags of rice since same was covered with bird excreta. 

On the remaining bags of rice, he observed widespread evidence of insect infestation. He divided the remaining 15,485 bags into 13 sublots and extracted random samples from each. The subsequent laboratory analysis indicated live or dead insect infestation in 6 of the 13 sublots. . . . "The rice in question was being stored in warehouses at the State Port at Gulfport, MS. Of the 13 sublots, 2 were stored in warehouse #15, the remaining 11 sublots were stored in warehouse #1. Dupré 

Spiller, the F.D.A. compliance officer, notified the Defendant in mid- 

December, 1979, that the rice was seized and condemned pursuant to 21 U.S.C. §§342(a)(3), (4). . . . 

"Thereafter, the Defendant employed S.G.S. Control Services,

Inc., to sample the remaining sublots of grain. Robert Boecking, the manager of S.G.S.'s agricultural division, testified that random samples were taken and submitted to the United States Department of 

Agriculture for analysis. The F.G.I.S. (Federal Grain Inspection Serv ice) certificates for the rice samples were introduced into evidence. ... Only the first lot was labeled 'sample' grade. The remaining 5 lots were graded. Generally speaking, 'sample' grade denotes rice that fails to meet the criteria for a certain grade, i.e., U.S. No. 1, No. 2, etc. "On cross-examination, Boecking admitted that he had not personally taken the samples, nor had he inspected the warehouses in which the rice was stored. Also, the inspection certificates bear a disclaimer that the '[r]esults. . . apply only to the sample described and NOT to the rice from which the sample may have been taken.` "The rice in question had been denominated 'sample' grade by the federal inspector. Gregory C. Anderson, the F.G.I.S. inspector, testified that rice may receive a sample grade in one of two manners; first, by visual inspection or, second, by lab analysis. Under the first method, if the inspector sees obvious signs of insect infestation he may immediately grade the rice 'sample.' Rice is also graded 'sample' under lab analysis where the rice contains more than two insects per car lot. Rice that receives a 'sample' grading is generally not subject to exportation. In the instant case, Blakely testified that when he conducted his investigation he noticed . . . hundreds of insects; on the bags, the floor, . . . everywhere.' The rice was covered with Visqueen, a clear plastic covering. Blakely observed insects through the

Visqueen. When the covering was removed, the moths flew all over. 

This is the basis for the rice in question being seized. "The Claimants seek the return of the six lots of rice, claiming that the S.G.S. investigation and accompanying F.G.I.S. certificates proved that the rice is not adulterated. However, as Anderson testified, F.G.I.S. standards are different from those established by the 

F.D.A., the former agency having a more limited jurisdiction than the latter. Claimants also rely upon United States vs. Capital City

Foods, Inc., 345 F. Supp. 277 (D.N.D. 1972). However, Capital City involved a criminal prosecution and presented a case where 'miniscule' infestation was present. Such is not the case in this (a)(4) proceeding where widespread infestation was observed. "The Government's seizure of the entire lot of rice is based primarily on 21 U.S.C. §342(a)(4) which provides that food is adulterated (and therefore subject to seizure and condemnation) when it is ... held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become contaminated with filth. . . . Actual contamination need not be proven in order to show adulteration within §342(a)(4) e.g., United States v. 

Wiesenfield Warehouse Co., 376 U.S. 86 (1964). This section deals with the 'reasonable possibility' that the food will or may become contaminated. Berger v. United States 200 F2d. 818, 821 (5th Cir. 1952). "In the present case we have a situation where actual contamination was shown in a significant amount of the rice. Accordingly, the Court agrees with the Government that this shows that the rice was held under such conditions whereby the rice had a 'reasonable possibility' of becoming contaminated. "Therefore, the Court is of the opinion that the claimant's motion is not well taken and is hereby denied. The Court notes the attendant expenses involved in reconditioning the grain. However, the only other alternative is to sanction the release of potentially contaminated grain. "The Court has also considered the testimony of John Shelby Hollingsworth, an employee of Tradigrain Corp. in New Orleans, LA. 

He testified regarding a situation where some of Tradigrain's rice was graded 'sample' and the remainder was released for shipment. This rice, however, was stored in different warehouses and did not have a level of infestation approaching that of the Agricor rice." 

Ultimately all of the rice was salvaged, with most of the rice being reconditioned, and a small number of bags being destroyed. However, a bond forfeiture action was instituted. (See N.J. No. 31 of this issue). (F.D.C. No. 62441; S. No. 79–131-285 et al.; N.J. No. 11)
