DRUGS/Veterinary 

Beuthanasia-D euthanasia injections (Special and Regular), Neopecsul-A antidiarrheal tablets, Neopecsul-A antidiarrheal suspension, and Bucoderm suspension for dermatoses in dogs and cats, at Omaha, Dist. Nebr.

Charged 11-3-77: while held for sale, the articles were new animal drugs and no approved New Animal Drug Application was in effect with respect to the articles' uses or intended uses; 501(a)(5). The articles were claimed by Burns-Biotec Laboratories Division of 

Chromalloy Pharmaceutical, Inc., Oakland, Calif., who denied that the Beuthanasia-D injections were drugs, denied that the court had jurisdiction over the Beuthanasia-D injections and denied the charges. 

The parties served written interrogatories on each other, and litigated the Beuthanasia-D injections. The Government moved for summary judgment. The claimant moved to dismiss the action. The court ruled in favor of the Government on the motions, saying: "Subsequent to some discovery, the United States filed a motion for summary judgment. The claimant resists the summary judgment motion, and seeks an order dismissing plaintiff's complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction or, in the alternative, referring the technical questions arising out of this lawsuit to the FDA, pursuant to the administrative law doctrine of primary jurisdiction. As the claimant's motion goes to the power of this Court to hear the present controversy, it shall be considered first. . . . "The claimant acknowledges that the seized articles Beuthanasia- D Regular and Beuthanasia-D Special, are intended to induce death in animals. Despite this recognition, Burns-Biotec maintains that these articles are not drugs, and that this Court lacks subject matter jurisdiction as a result. "The claimant does not deny that the seized articles are each composed of two active ingredients, pentobarbital sodium and phenytoin sodium. Both of these ingredients are listed in the United States 

Pharmacopeia, and therefore appear to be 'drugs' within the meaning of 21 U.S.C.A. §321(g)(1)(A) (1972). Rather, the claimant principally relies upon two decisions by the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in support of its argument that a listing in the United States Pharmacopeia does not mean that the articles are drugs per se. The cases are 

National Nutritional Foods Ass'n v. Mathews, 557 F.2d 325 (2d Cir. 

1977), and National Nutritional Ass'n v. FDA, 504 F.2d 761 (2d Cir. 

1974), cert. denied 420 U.S. 946 (1975). . . . "These holdings involved an FDA regulation in which certain high dosage levels of vitamins and minerals were to be classified as drugs under the Act. Lower levels of the same vitamins and minerals had been traditionally considered as foods. In its proposed rule, the FDA had referenced 21 U.S.C.A. §321(g)(1)(C) (1972) as the basis for the new classification. In its brief in support of the challenged regulation, the FDA also placed reliance on 21 U.S.C.A. §321(g)(1)(A) (1972).

The Second Circuit held that some reasonable discussion of the applicability of §321(g)(1)(A) was required by the rulemaking procedure if the reclassification from foods to drugs was to be accomplished. 

The Court believes that the present case is distinguishable from the 

Second Circuit precedent, as no reclassification through rulemaking has been attempted by the FDA in the controversy at bar. The Court holds that inclusion of the two active ingredients of the seized articles in the United States Pharmacopeia renders the Beuthanasia-D Reg ular and Beuthanasia-D Special 'drugs' within the meaning of the 

Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. United States v. Articles of Drug Vit-Ra-Tox, 263 F.Supp. 212, 215 (D. Neb. 1967). 

"The claimant further argues that, even if the seized articles are drugs within the meaning of the Act, they are not 'new animal drugs' 

"The claimant has attempted to demonstrate confusion within the FDA by contrasting answers to interrogatories with the agency's compliance policy guide. The Court is persuaded that the alleged confusion as to the status of sodium pentobarbitol alone is not only irrelevant to the consideration of the status of a combination of articles of drug, but is attributable to the FDA's caution in conceding that sodium pentobarbitol is, for all purposes and in all combinations, an 'old' drug.. "Nor is the case of Rutherford v. United States, 582 F.2d 1234 (10th

Cir. 1978), particularly favorable to the claimant's position. In reviewing the FDA's determination that Laetrile, a controversial cancer drug, was a 'new drug' within the meaning of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the Tenth Circuit found that the scope of the statute did not extend to drugs which were to be administered to dying patients. The Rutherford court found that general recognition of a drug as being 'safe' and 'effective' was meaningless in the context of terminally ill human beings. "The Court declines to extend the reasoning in Rutherford to drugs which cause the humane death of animals. Safety and effectiveness are not irrelevant in this context. The JOURNAL OF THE AMERICAN VETERINARY MEDICAL ASSOCIATION has set forth criteria in this re gard which are referred to in the uncontroverted affidavits of three distinguished veterinarians and veterinary educators. Relevant factors include (1) the drug's ability to cause death without pain and discomfort; (2) the time required to produce loss of consciousness; (3) the time required to produce death; (4) reliability of the drug to obtain consistently effective results; (5) safety to the administrator of the dosage; (6) the abuse potential of the drug in proportion to its availability; and (7) the possibility that the drug may become part of a human food supply. "The Court concludes that it has subject matter jurisdiction. "The existence of subject matter jurisdiction in a federal court does not mean the jurisdiction should always be exercised. If the FDA's expertise would facilitate a decision upon the merits in this regard, this Court has the power to decline from ruling in favor of an administrative evaluation and preparation of a record for potential review purposes. "The Court refuses to relinquish its jurisdiction. This lawsuit involves an enforcement action brought by the United States. The statutory scheme under the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act does not provide that a seizure may take place only upon review of an administrative record compiled by the FDA on the 'new animal drug' status of the product. A federal district court is a proper forum for a complete and full hearing. Ewing v. Mytinger & Casselberry, Inc., 339 U.S. 

594, 598 (1950). "To the extent that the case of Rutherford v. United States, 582 

F.2d 1234 (10th Cir. 1978) holds to the contrary, the Court limits its application to situations where the parties seeking review are not manufacturers of a product, and therefore are not able to submit a new drug application. Hanson v. United States, 417 F.Supp. 30, 37 (D. Minn.), aff'd 540 F.2d 947 (8th Cir. 1976) (per curiam). . "After a thorough review of the case law and the exhibits adduced by the parties, the Court holds that summary judgment shall be en- 

LUKLUBI HALI KIMAMBILL 

38 May 1981 / FDA Consumer

tered for the plaintiff. The following analysis demonstrates the propriety of that decision. "In denying the motion to dismiss filed by the claimant, the Court held that the United States Pharmacopeia's recognition of the two active ingredients in the seized articles as drugs was decisive. The 

Court so holds for purposes of this motion as well. "Moreover, the seized Beuthanasia products are also drugs within the meaning of 21 U.S.C.A. 321(g)(1)(C) (1972) because each of them is 'intended to affect the structure or function of the body of man or other animals.' The determinative factor is the product's intended use, that is, the claims made by the manufacturer or other proponent. 

Claimant can hardly claim that euthanasia-the cessation of all bodily functions-does not constitute an effect on the function, if not the structure, of the animal's body. "The burden is upon the proponent of an animal drug to do testing to show that its product is safe and effective. This testing supports its marketing in the absence of general recognition of the drug's safety and effectiveness. Absent such testing, the animal drug cannot be approved. 21 U.S.C.A. §360b (1972). 

"Decisions on safety and effectiveness of drugs are made by the

FDA in the first instance, by reviewing a new animal drug application. 

If a proponent believes that approval of its product was incorrectly denied, it has a statutory right to an opportunity for an administrative hearing. 21 U.S.C.A. §360b(c) (1972). The FDA's decision is subject to review by a United States Court of Appeals, to whom the proponent has a direct statutory appeal. 21 U.S.C.A. $360b(h) (1972). "Absent FDA approval of a properly submitted application, a new animal drug cannot be legally marketed because an unapproved new animal drug is adulterated as a matter of law. 21 U.S.C.A. 

§§360b(a)(1)(A), 351(a)(5) and 331(a) (1972). 

"Proponents of drugs have occasionally taken the position that, despite the fact that their product would not be approved by the FDA if the appropriate application were submitted, the product is so well recognized as safe and effective that no approval is needed. The Supreme Court has already considered and rejected this assertion. 

Speaking of human drugs, it approved the argument that 'the Act is designed so that drugs on the market, unless exempt, will have mustered the requisite scientifically reliable evidence [for approval of a new drug application] of effectiveness long before they are in a position to drop out of active regulation by ceasing to be a "new drug." 

Weinberger v. Hynson, Westcott & Dunning, Inc., 412 U.S. 609, 631 (1973).' This reasoning is equally applicable to new animal drugs which are subject to nearly identical pre-marketing clearance requirements. "Burns-Biotec has not submitted the required tests to the FDA. 

The seized products are therefore 'new animal drugs' unless their composition is 'generally recognized' by qualified experts within the meaning of 21 U.S.C.A. § 321(w) (1972). 

"A product may be shown to be a new animal drug if any of the following is established: (1) a lack of general recognition of safety or effectiveness by qualified experts; (2) a lack of publicly available information regarding the safety or effectiveness of the product; (3) a lack of evidence of the safety and effectiveness of the product equivalent to that required for an approval of a new animal drug application for the product pursuant to 21 U.S.C.A. § 360b (1972). 

"The difference between lack of safety and effectiveness and lack of general recognition' of safety and effectiveness is perhaps best illustrated by the opinion of United States v. Articles of Food and Drug 

.. Coli-trol 80 Medicated, 372 F.Supp. 915 (N.D. Ga. 1974), aff'd 

518 F.2d 743 (5th Cir. 1975); see also Tyler Pharmaceuticals, Inc., v.

United States Department of Health, Education and Welfare, 408 F.2d 

95 (7th Cir. 1971). In Coli-trol the district court found several animal drugs and one food additive to be 'safe' but yet not to be 'generally recognized' as safe. Accordingly, the products in question had to be approved under the FDA's pre-marketing clearance system before they could be legally marketed. The Government need not show that the seized Beuthanasia products are unsafe or ineffective for their intended use, but simply that the products have not been afforded the 'general recognition' among qualified experts which, when demonstrated, exempts a product from the pre-marketing clearance require ments of the Act. United States v. 1,048,000 Capsules . . . Afrodex 

494 F.2d 1158 (5th Cir. 1974). "Unanimity among experts is not necessary for general recognition. 

Where a genuine dispute among appropriately qualified experts is shown, there is a lack of general recognition. United States v. An 

Article of Drug . . . 'Furestrol . . .,' 294 F.Supp, 1307, 1311 (N.D. 

Ga. 1968), aff'd per curiam, 415 F.2d 390 (5th Cir. 1969). The concept of general recognition cannot properly be interpreted as an invitation for courts to resolve swearing contests between 'experts.' United States v. Article of Drug... Coli-trol, supra. Thus, even if it were the case that a significant number of experts considered Beuthanasia products to have been shown to be safe and effective by appropriate evidence, a showing that there was nevertheless a disagreement among experts on those questions would make the products new animal drugs under the Act. "The claimant has submitted no affidavits to controvert those adduced by the plaintiff. Even if Burns-Biotec had submitted the affidavits of qualified experts who testified to the effect that Beuthanasia- D Special and Beuthanasia-D Regular are generally recognized as safe and effective, the showing made by the Government in the sworn statements of Drs. Kitchell, Wass and McDonald that those experts do not recognize the seized articles as safe or effective and do not believe that the articles are so generally recognized is sufficient to prove the lack of general recognition. United States v. An Article of 

Drug... 'Furestrol', supra. Neither Beuthanasia-D Regular nor Beuthanasia-D Special can be considered 'generally recognized as safe among experts' where three highly qualified experts from separate parts of the country conclude that it is not so recognized. Even if there were a genuine and heated dispute concerning the safety and effectiveness of the Beuthanasia products as euthanasia agents, those products must be removed from the market while the dispute is scientifically resolved by the Food and Drug Administration in the context of a new animal drug application. 66 'General recognition' of the safety and effectiveness of a new animal drug requires at least the amount of evidence of safety and effectiveness as is required for approval of a new animal drug application pursuant to §360b. . . . For a new drug application to be approved, the statute requires that there be 'substantial evidence' of its safety and effectiveness for its intended use, including adequate and well-controlled investigations. 21 U.S.C.A. § 360b(d)(1) and (3) (1972). For there to be 'general recognition,' the Supreme Court has held adequate and well-controlled studies must also exist. Weinberger v. Hynson, Westcott & Dunning, Inc., supra, 412 US. at 629-30. "In order to form a basis for general recognition, the scientific evidence must be available to experts generally through publications in the scientific literature. See, e.g., United States v. 41 Cases, More or Less, 420 F.2d 1126, 1130 (5th Cir. 1970), in which the Court, in discussing the 'new animal drug' definition, held that 'the absence of literature establishing safety is proof that a product is not generally recognized.' See also United States v. Article of Drug... 'Furestrol' 

supra, 294 F.Supp. at 1309. Cf. Weinberger v. Bentex Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 412 U.S. 645, 652 (1973), where the Supreme Court makes clear that 'general recognition' requires not only adequate and well-controlled investigations, but also publicly available information dealing with the safety or efficacy of the product. This principle of general recognition stated by the Supreme Court is an affirmance of numerous lower court decisions that the absence or lack of ready availability to qualified experts of a body of published medical and scientific data, including literature describing adequate testing of the drug, establishes that the drug is not generally recognized as safe or effective. See United States v. 41 Cases, More or Less . . ., supra; 

United States v. 1,048,000 Capsules. . . Afrodex. . ., supra. If there is evidence of safety or effectiveness which is not published, that evidence can and should be submitted to the FDA as part of a New Animal Drug Application but cannot support a claim of 'general recognition' of safety or effectiveness. ..." "Finally, the absence of scientific knowledge on the part of an AS SALA 

FDA Consumer May 1981 / 39

expert and his colleagues is sufficient to show a lack of general recognition of safety.' United States v. 41 Cases, supra, 420 F.2d at 1130. "The Government has submitted the sworn statements of experts 

[Dr. Wallace M. Wass, Dr. Leslie E. McDonald, and Dr. Ralph 

Kitchell] qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate safety and effectiveness of animal drugs. These sworn statements establish that the seized drugs are not generally recognized as safe and effective for use in veterinary euthanasia. "Each witness, by virtue of his professional training, as well as his teaching and writing experience, is qualified to perceive the presence or absence of veterinary medical general recognition for an animal euthanasia drug. "Not one of the Government's witnesses is aware of any published scientific data or information which in any respect addresses the combination of sodium pentobarbital and sodium phenytoin, or even the products Beuthanasia-D Regular and Special, much less establishes their safety and efficacy as veterinary euthanasia agents. "Not one Government witness is aware of any adequate and wellcontrolled investigations establishing the safety or efficacy of Beuthanasia-D Regular or Special. Each Government witness has reviewed the only existing information known regarding a Beuthanasia product and drug combination, i.e., the unpublished information supplied during the course of this proceeding in discovery. Each witness, for a variety of reasons, has found that information insufficient to establish the safety or effectiveness of the Beuthanasia products. "No one witness recognizes the drugs Beuthanasia-D Regular and

Beuthanasia-D Special, each of which is the combination of sodium pentobarbital and sodium phenytoin, as safe and effective as a veterinary euthanasia agent. Furthermore, each expert stated that neither the product nor the combination is generally recognized in the expert community as safe or effective for their intended use as veterinary euthanasia agents. "The sworn statements of the experts, as well as the exhibits filed with plaintiff's Motion for Summary Judgment, conclusively establish that neither Beuthanasia-D Special nor Beuthanasia-D Regular are generally recognized as either safe or effective by qualified experts and accordingly are new animal drugs within the meaning of 21 U.S.C.A. §321(w). Each of the three conditions listed by the Court, any one of which would establish a lack of general recognition, has been demonstrated by the evidence presented. A fortiori, these products are new animal drugs subject to the provisions of the Act. See 

Weinberger v. Hynson, Westcott & Dunning, Inc., supra, 412 U.S. at 629-30."

An Introduction by 

 nniversaries are special occasions. They provide an 

Aoppersanity aut opt for ceremony but an flection and rededication.

As I take over the responsibilities and duties of the Commissioner of Food and Drugs, I reflect on the contributions made by the first "commissioner," Dr. Harvey 

Washington Wiley. 

Dr. Wiley is aptly called the "father" of the Food and

Drugs Act of 1906. He fought for a quarter of a century for a safer food and drug supply. As chief of the Bureau. of Chemistry-predecessor of today's Food and Drug

Administration-Dr. Wiley directed the first years of enforcement under the Food and Drugs Act.

FDA's responsibilities today obviously are much broader than those of Dr. Wiley's Bureau of Chemistry. 

FDA today regulates not only foods and drugs, but also medical devices, cosmetics, biological products, veterinary drugs, and products that emit radiation.

Similarly, the size of the industries, the processes used to manufacture products, transportation methods—all are dramatically different today than they were 75 years ago.

But many of the principles for which Dr. Wiley fought remain. He believed that the public was entitled to assurances of safe and accurately labeled foods and drugs.

And he believed that sound science forms the basis for good decisionmaking. As Dr. Wiley's heirs, we must apply those principles to today's world.

The articles in this issue of FDA CONSUMER provide a number of thoughts and perspectives on how FDA has matured over the past three-quarters of a century, and what issues remain for the Agency to address. 

I believe that Dr. Harvey Wiley, could he see his legacy, would be pleased. It remains for us to remember his great tradition and to carry it forward as we go about our work. 

**! UN ENGINEE 

1 by 

Secretary, Department of Health and Human Services he Food and Drug Administration has a solid record of Tachievement helping to assure the safety of our supply of foods, drugs and other health-care products. 

This anniversary year is a time for us to reflect on those accomplishments, and to learn from history as we shape policies for the future.

As secretary, with the advice and guidance of Commissioner Hayes, I hope to build on FDA's record. We can have no higher purpose than to maintain the confidence of the American public in the safety of the products we use. 

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 5

FDA In 1981: 

Some Perspectives 

The Food and Drug Administration in the year 1981, the 75th anniversary year of the Pure Food and Drugs Act, is too diverse to capture in a single snapshot. This article describes what 

FDA is like today from several perspectives. The author is FDA's associate commissioner for public affairs. by  t's 8 a.m. Monday, any Monday. It's 

In Detroit, Christopher Smith, a cup of coffee in hand, opens a file to begin poring over the inspection history of a food company. 

Today, Smith's assignment is to inspect this firm, which processes canned mushrooms. Before Smith goes out on assignment, he will review the history of the firm to see whether there are any specific problems to watch for. Problems were found during the last inspection 18 months before, after which the company notified FDA that they'd been corrected. 

Every Monday morning, across the country, what Chris Smith is doing will be done by hundreds of other 

FDA investigators. Each year they conduct 32,000 inspections of plants where foods, medicines, biological products, devices, cosmetics, or radiation-emitting products are made or stored. 

Their job: to see that quality standards are being followed, that adequate records are kept, that all needed tests are performed, and that the plant is clean and making a product suitable for Americans to use. 

For example, in inspecting a mushroom canner, Smith will check to see that each batch is being processed properly, and that complete distribution records are kept in case a recall is needed. 

Most often, investigators find no violations or only minor ones, testimony to American industry's maintenance of high quality standards in the production of foods, drugs, and other consumer products. 

When more serious problems are found, FDA will ask the company to correct them. Generally the company will agree. If it does not, FDA has a number of legal options available: instituting seizure against the company's products, seeking a court injunction, or seeking to prosecute the offenders. 

Sometimes, FDA will ask the firm to recall a product already on the market. FDA's role is to monitor that recall to see that it's conducted properly. Each year, FDA monitors about 1,000 recalls. 

The kind of work that Chris Smith and other investigators do every day generally goes unnoticed by the public, which tends to think of FDA in terms of highly publicized issues such as saccharin, nitrites, or laetrile. But it is this kind of inspection work that provides the public with the assurance it has come to expect that its foods, drugs, and other consumer products are safe. 

Smith enjoys his inspection work. "It's varied, I get to meet new people every day, and I feel like I'm making a real, measurable contribution to protecting the public," he says. 

Smith's background is typical for an FDA investigator. He holds two degrees in biology. He joined FDA 

in September 1976 during Project Ex tend, a special hiring effort following enactment by Congress of the Medical Device Amendments. 

In September 1980, Smith began a year-long management training program. He was to work in various offices at FDA headquarters to get a clearer picture of FDA's total responsibilities and activities. "FDA is both a large place and a small one," he said after 3 months in the program. "There aren't that many employees (about 7,600 nationwide) but the Agency is doing so many things, so many different tors, Smith, 30, is planning a career of working for the Agency. FDA has a long tradition of encouraging people to join the Agency soon after college and to stay their entire careers, rising up the ladder of responsibility.

Smith is seeking a broad perspective in his year at headquarters. "In the field, I deal mainly with the 

Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and its enforcement sections. I seldom got a chance to see how the food additive sections or the new drug approval section get enforced. That's the kind of exposure I'm going to need if I'm to understand the full range of what FDA is doing." 

It's 8 a.m. Monday. 

From all over the Washington area, some 25 men and women gather in the conference room next to the office of the FDA Commissioner. 

They constitute FDA's Policy 

Board, responsible for Agency activities, and they are there for their weekly staff meeting to tell the Commissioner, and each other, what's happening. 

Going around the table, each reports on past and upcoming activities. 

The chief counsel reports on recent legal decisions. Some are relatively minor, involving, for example, the seizure of a product not fit to have been distributed in interstate commerce. Others are more far-reaching, raising fundamental questions about FDA's legal authority and societal responsibilities.

The executive director of regional operations-who is responsible for the 40 percent of FDA employees who are located in field offices-reports on a chemical spill that happened over the weekend. The Office of Public Affairs also reports on the latest requests for information under the Freedom of Information Act. This law requires 

Federal agencies to disclose most documents in their files. FDA receives 33,000 requests a year, more than any other Federal agency. Most of the requests come from regulated industry, which wants to know what 

FDA is doing and the information that's available about what their competitors are doing.

1970 budget was double the 1964 budget. 

FDA is what is known as a personnel-intensive agency. It spends most of its money on people who inspect plants, who test for product quality, who review data submitted by industry or medical researchers, and who decide what regulatory action to take or regulation to issue. 

And so it goes around the table, with each office (there are eight associate commissioners) and each bureau (there are six) reporting. 

Dr. Judith Jones is one of 6,000 people working in the mammoth 

Parklawn Building in Rockville, Maryland, that serves as headquarters for FDA and two other Public

Health Service agencies. 

Jones is director of the Drug

Experience Division in the Bureau of 

Drugs. Her job is to identify adverse reactions and other new information about marketed drugs. "There was a time when drugs were just approved by FDA and then there was no effort to systematically evaluate what happened after that, she said. "This is a very exciting area," she adds. "We're on the frontiers of medicine in trying to understand what happens in the real world after a drug has been used." 

Jones' staff relies for some of its information on studies conducted by nongovernmental scientists and on reports in the medical literature and from manufacturers. About 2,000 reports a year come directly from physicians and hospitals using a form that appears in most issues of the FDA 

Drug Bulletin, a publication mailed four times a year to a million health professionals. 

What her staff looks for especially, Jones said, are adverse reactions not mentioned in the official "labeling" for the drug-the information supplied to doctors-that probably are associated with the drug. 

For example, last year the staff received a report of an epileptic seizure that could have been associated with birth control pills. They found 18 similar reports in their computer. 

Jones decided this was worth pursuing, so her staff started to call others, including the manufacturers, for more information. "We're hot on the trail of this," 

Jones said last winter. "It seems logical that oral contraceptives might be associated with epileptic seizures, since we know they're associated with strokes. What we need to do now is to figure out what the association is, if one really does exist."

The medical mystery aspect of her work intrigues Jones. "We have to figure out whether an individual report has validity. We have to figure out when a trend is occurring. We never have complete information. 

Usually we have to call around to everyone who might have information and then just piece it together." 

Jones came to FDA in August 1978 after teaching pharmacology and practicing medicine in San Francisco for 5 years. She holds an M.D. degree from Baylor and a Ph.D. in pharmacology from the University of 

California at San Francisco. "I suspected early in the 1970's that I would eventually come to work for FDA," she recollects. "When I was training in clinical pharmacology 

I got interested in the disparity between what was happening in the real world and what was taught in academic institutions. I felt we needed to have a better understanding of the real world of drug utilization. First I wanted some grass roots experience, but then, to get the bigger picture, I had to go to FDA."

The Drug Experience Division is just a small part of the Bureau of

Other parts of the Bureau review applications submitted by manufacturers that want to sell new drugs; review research projects; decide when regulatory action is needed against a company or individual that may be violating the law; set quality standards for manufacture; and test products to be sure they are of high quality and purity. Other FDA bureaus have comparable functions. 

The perspectives of Chris Smith,

Judy Jones, and the Policy Board reflect only a small part of what FDA is like in 1981. Many other perspectives could have been described, such as those of: a microbiologist in an FDA field office testing foods for contaminants; a compliance officer, in headquarters or a field office, deciding whether to take action against a company found negligent in making a product; a consumer affairs officer, one of 55 located in 32 cities, providing consumers with information about 

FDA, and reporting back consumer concerns; a researcher testing safety locks on microwave oven doors to be sure they won't open when the oven is on and expose the consumer to radiation; a physician reviewing studies submitted by a manufacturer who wants to sell a new drug; a scientist in FDA's National 

Center for Toxicological Research, supervising studies to see if small amounts of chemicals fed to animals for long periods will have the same effects as larger doses fed for a short time; an investigator checking blood banks to be sure their products are safe; and ⚫ a veterinarian reviewing data about the use of a drug in one species, to see if it can safely be used in another.

These are the people who, in this anniversary year of 1981, carry out the work of the FDA. 

So, what is FDA like in the 75th anniversary year of the Pure Food and Drugs Act? Inevitably, the answers depend on one's perspective. 

In 1980, Louis Harris & Associates polled four groups: corporate executives, investors and lenders, Congress, and Federal regulators. All rated FDA second only to the Civil

Aeronautics Board in their evalua tions of how well eight agencies were doing "to make our society acceptably safe." FDA was rated "excellent" or "very good" by 56 to 66 percent of the people in these groups. 

From inside, FDA remains a tradition-oriented Agency. New employees learn about Harvey Wiley's crusade for Federal controls over dangerous foods and drugs. Most employees, especially in the field, regard FDA as their career. Around

FDA has grown a large community of company representatives, attorneys, trade associations, and a specialized press. 

Another perspective: in 75 years,

FDA (and its predecessors) have had to adjust to many changes.

In 1906, most food was grown and processed locally. Travel was measured in days, not hours or minutes.

Outright food adulteration and misbranding were significant challenges for the new Government regulators.

Today, food may be grown in one part of the country, processed in another, and eaten thousands of miles away. Deliberate adulteration or misbranding of food no longer is the main issue; FDA is now more concerned with the subtle health hazards posed by long-term exposure to small amounts of chemicals.

In 1906, scientific methodology was primitive at best. Witness Harvey 

Wiley's way to test chemicals: he created a "poison squad" of a dozen young men who reported their symptoms from eating chemically treated foods. Today, scientists test chemicals in controlled circumstances in animals, and can perform large-scale national epidemiology surveys to identify human hazards. Contaminants can be detected in parts per trillion. 

In 1906, drugs were promoted for all manner of ailments and illnesses, but in truth not many were effective, let alone safe. Today, not only drugs and vaccines but medical devices as well routinely help prolong life and alleviate once-deadly sicknesses. Procedures such as x-rays can help physicians diagnose diseases while they are still treatable. More advances have been made in medicine since 1906 than were made in all the past centuries of civilization. 

And, as science and technology have changed since 1906, so too has 

FDA, its activities and concerns.

FDA in 1981 is as different from 

Harvey Wiley's Bureau of Chemistry as the science and technology of 1981 differ from that of 1906. 

FDA is an Agency that must look in three directions at once: past, present, and future. It is reviewing thousands of products, some that have been on the market since as long ago as 1906, to see if they are still considered safe by modern standards. At the same time the Agency must prepare for evaluating new 

10 June 1981 FDA Consumer

୦୦ technologies that hold promise of improving public health and well being.

Despite its long history and sense of tradition, FDA is only just now getting accustomed to being in the limelight. For most of its history, it was a relatively small, even obscure Agency. During the 1970's, issues such as Red No. 2, saccharin, laetrile, and nitrite pushed it onto the front page. A new consumer movement has made people more concerned with safety in the marketplace. To FDA's traditional scientific and regulatory roles has been added that of public communicator and educator. 

But over these 75 years of history, some things remain the same. FDA still must draw a difficult and delicate balance between competing factors: between approving new products promptly and protecting the public from hazard; between giving people maximum freedom of choice while protecting those who can't protect themselves; between regulations that are unnecessary (and, today, inflationary) and those that make a real contribution to public health. 

That is the balancing act that

FDAers have always faced and it remains the challenge as FDA enters the last 20 years of the 20th century.

The Long Struggle For 

The 1906 Law Many forces combined to create the need for the 1906 Food and Drugs 

Act. James Harvey Young traces the history of the law and the conditions that led to its enactment. The author is professor of history at Emory University and is the author of many books and articles on food and drug regulatory history. by James Harvey Young n June 30, 1906, a broiling day 

Oin Washington, President Theodore Roosevelt went to the Capitol to sign into law nearly a hundred bills hurried through the Congress as its session came to an end. Among them was one passed the day before by both Senate and House in a form agreed to in conference committee, the Food and Drugs Act. Although a latecomer to the cause of a pure food law, Teddy Roosevelt had used his weight decisively in 1906 to ensure that this time Congress would not adjourn, as so often before, leaving such legislation languishing. 

The 1906 law's relevant background in America starts with colonial food statutes concerned with bread and meat. The first national law came in 1848 during the Mexican 

War. It banned the importation of adulterated drugs, a chronic public health problem that finally got 

Congressional attention. 

The first prolonged and impassioned controversy in the Congress involving a pure food issue took place in 1886, pitting the reigning champion, butter, against a challenger, oleomargarine. Butter won, and oleomargarine was taxed and placed under other restraints that persisted on the Federal level until 

1950. The debate in 1886 between the defenders of a natural food and those of its alleged artificial substitute centered not only on matters of vested interest, but also pondered concerns about the public health, issues of governmental authority, and the myths in which were enshrined the meaning of the American experience. Such themes re-echoed in 

Congressional chambers as Senate and House later debated broader bills to control food and drugs in interstate commerce. The first broad bill had been introduced in 1879, although a decade passed before Congress displayed serious interest. 

One way to structure the intricate pure food story is to consider seven "C's." These are change, complexity, competition, crusading, coalescence, compromise, and catastrophe. 

Change means the turbulent readjustments in the American way of life that occurred as society industrialized and urbanized. Accompanying, indeed fostering, such modifications came a revolution in science and technology, with its planned and also unforeseen consequences. Discoveries in chemistry, for example, led to new synthetic medicines and altered radically both the growing and the processing of food. Transportation developments brought processed food to an increasingly national market, making the growth of giant cities possible. The residents of those cities lost the ability villagers had possessed of being first-hand judges of the food they ate.

Some of the food that city dwellers took from cans and jars deviated greatly from village garden produce. 

Chemicals could be used to heighten color, modify flavor, soften texture, deter spoilage, and even transform ingredients like apple scraps, glucose, coal-tar dye, and timothy seeds into a concoction labeled strawberry jam. 

Adulteration might be an age-old problem, but, in the words of a Senate report in 1890, "it has only been since the great opportunity for fraud provided by modern science . . . that the sophistication of articles of commerce has reached its present height.' 

The second "C" stands for com- 

plexity. All of man's concerns grow more complex, and a particular kind of complexity became wedded to the question of how the Federal Government might confront deceptions and hazards in the food and drug supply. 

A few products, like oleomargarine and tea, were controlled by individual laws. Mainstream legislation proposed in the Congress, however, was complex, omnibus bills encompassing food and drink and drugs. All food and drink and most drugs entered the body through the mouth, and all were subject to similar adulterations. 

So it was natural to face the problem all at once. British precedent pointed in this direction, a factor of consequence in the campaign for an American law. Not only did drafters of both State and Federal bills turn for guidance to British experience; 

American businessmen and farmers engaged in exporting food frequently felt the bite of, and hence became keenly aware of, British law. Broad omnibus bills meant that many interest groups would be subject to the law's provisions, with producing and processing units located in every congressional district. Such a circumstance made inevitable a long and 

At the turn of the century, false hopes were sold with vigor similar to today.

tortuous legislative process. 

Competition in the marketplace, the third "C," lay behind the earliest omnibus bills. By a sort of Gresham's law, adulterated foods that could be sold more cheaply threatened to drive out sounder fare. Alarmed, the more reputable wing of the food industry appealed to the Congress for help and gave counsel to that body.

In 1879 a trade press editor persuaded his brother-in-law, a wholesale grocer, to put up a prize for the best draft statute submitted to the 

National Board of Trade. The prize was won by an English food analyst who adapted the 1875 British law to 

American circumstances. The Board of Trade prize committee revamped the analyst's proposal, and in 1881 a 

Connecticut congressman introduced the committee draft as a bill. 

Throughout the succeeding quarter of a century, the pain of what they deemed unfair competition kept business groups reviving their appeals to the Congress for the protection that would be afforded by a national law. 

As the 1890 Senate Report put it, faith in commercial integrity, the "very foundation of trade," was being undermined. The proliferation of State laws containing contradictory provisions made action on the national level the only sensible solution. "As it is now, a maker of jam complained, "we have to manufacture differently for each state." A national statute might set a standard 

States would follow. 22 Farmers in agrarian States, as their campaign against oleomargarine demonstrated, also felt aggrieved by what they thought was unfair competition. 

Shady processors adulterated fertilizers, deodorized rotten eggs, revived rancid butter, substituted glucose for honey. Farmers began to learn about such deceptions from a new breed of agriculture chemists, often trained in Germany, located in State officialdom and helped by Federal funds. 

These chemists could apply their scientific skills to expose the work of chemists employed by industry to depreciate food products, as the Senate 

Report put it, in "a greed for gain." 

Exposure bulletins agitated farmers, who increased their demand for a protective national law.

Those threatened by the new competition could bring omnibus bills before the Congress but could not secure their passage. At the height of the Populist movement in 1892, agrarian pressure got one bill through the Senate, but divided business interests and constitutional scruples blocked it in the House. During the remaining years of the 19th century, no broad pure food bill made it through either chamber of Congress. 

Competitors spoke with conflicting voices, all heard in Washington. The broad public was not yet very much aroused.

When the first omnibus bills began to appear, George T. Angell represented the prime example of crusading, the fourth "C." A lawyer whose claim to public recognition lay in his fight against cruelty to animals, Angell advocated rigorous regulation of all food processors, charging that dire hazards to health plagued every marketplace. Angell thought businesssponsored bills were too unmindful of the consumer, whereas businessmen thought Angell a devilish alarmist. Later, such committed champions of the consumer as the National Consumer League and the General Federation of Women's Clubs joined the crusade for a tough law, and so, too, with the new century, did muckraking journalists. 

Harvey W. Wiley came to be the leader of the "pure food crusade." A chemist and physician, State chemist of Indiana and professor at Purdue 

University, Wiley went to Washington in 1883 as chief chemist of the 

Department of Agriculture. He made the study of food adulteration his bureau's principal business, at first merely outraged by what he deemed essentially harmless fraud. In time, sensing real threats to health, Wiley could express himself in writing, conversation, and oratory with vividness, clarity, homely wit, and moral passion. He toured the country making speeches, every rostrum a pulpit for the gospel of pure food. 

Besides crusading for a law, Wiley played other indispensable roles. He sought to organize his allies and recruits into a coalition which might be powerful enough to move Congress to action. Coalescence is the fifth "C." Wiley forged bonds among agricultural chemists, State food and drug officials, women's club members, the medical profession, sympathetic journalists, the reform wing of business, and favorably disposed members of Congress. This was a mighty effort requiring the utmost in patience and diplomacy.

Could all factions favoring a law in principle, especially elements from the complex business community, be brought to agreement in support of a specific bill? Compromise, the sixth "C," seemed to offer a route to success. In three National Pure Food and Drug Congresses held between 1898 and 1900, Wiley sought to work out agreements in the private sector that might smooth passage of a law. 

The magnitude of the task is suggested by a look at some of the groups represented: trade associations, for example, of millers and brewers, marketers of butter and makers of candy, fishermen and beekeepers, wholesale and retail grocers, wholesale druggists, and proprietary medicine manufacturers. Also present were representatives from State and Federal agencies, farm organizations, professional societies of chemists and pharmacists, even the National Peace Conference and the

Women's Christian Temperance 

Union. Delegates labored diligently and made much progress, but not enough. Some differences seemed too wide to bridge, like those be- 

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 15

tween dairy and margarine interests, between makers of alum and creamof-tartar baking powders, and between straight whiskey distillers and blenders. As the new century dawned, efforts at compromise continued, but in the halls and committee rooms of Congress.

In some ways the constantly revised version of the battered basic bill became more rigorous because crusading accelerated. Increasing criticism by the revitalized American Medical Association and by journalists of patent medicine abuses, for example, brought controls aimed at nostrums into the bill-at the cost of drug trade support. And Dr. Wiley's sober scientific effort, begun in 1902, to test his hypothesis that chemical preservatives in processed foods posed threats to health, reported flamboyantly in the press as "Poison 

Squad" experiments, made a growing audience aware of adulteration and of the pending bill.

Twice an omnibus bill passed the 

House of Representatives under the aegis of its managers, Congressmen from western States in which agricultural interests were dominant. But business lobbies, especially whiskey rectifiers and proprietary drug manufacturers, despite all the power of

Wiley's coalition, kept the pure food bill from becoming law. The opposition was more silent than outspoken, making its weight felt through parlia mentary obstructionism. Southern conservatives did openly challenge the constitutionality of such legislation. "The Federal Government," opined a Georgia Congressman, "was not created for the purpose of cutting your toe nails or corns." 

In the end it took the seventh "C," catastrophe, to fuel the final compromise and get the law enacted. The catastrophe concerned meat. Meat had been separated from other food for special legislative treatment in 

1890 and 1891. Federal inspection had been started not to safeguard the 

American diet but to reassure European nations that had banned importation of American pork on the exaggerated charge that it had caused epidemics of trichinosis. A newspaper scare closer to home arose during the Spanish-American War, when packers were blamed with shipping "embalmed beef" that sickened the troops. Investigation traced some of the trouble to the rapid growth of bacteria in meat exposed to the hot 

Cuban sun. 

Then, in 1906, Upton Sinclair pub lished his socialist novel, THE JUN- 

GLE, aimed, as he later said, at people's hearts but hitting their stomachs instead. His few pages describing filthy conditions in Chicago's packing plants, widely reported and confirmed by governmental inquiry, cut meat sales in half, angered President 

Roosevelt, and pushed a meat inspection bill aimed at protecting the domestic market through the Congress.

The President, in December 1905, had at long last sent a terse message to the Congress urging it to enact a pure food bill. The Senate had responded. Amidst the meat crisis, when the House leadership seemed again determined to give the food measure the silent treatment, Roosevelt called the speaker in and insisted that the bill be brought to the floor. 

Wiley energized his coalition to a last burst of pressure. Committees engaged in a final flurry of compromise. And the bill became law.

The 1906 law forbade interstate and foreign commerce in adulterated and misbranded food and drugs. Offending products could be seized and condemned; offending persons could be fined and jailed. Drugs had either to abide by standards of purity and quality set forth in the UNITED

STATES PHARMACOPEIA and the NATIONAL FORMULARY, Works pre pared by committees of physicians and pharmacists, or meet individual standards chosen by their manufacturers and stated on their labels. An effort failed to place in the law food standards as defined by the agricultural chemists, but the law prohibited the adulteration of food by the removal of valuable constituents, the substitution of ingredients so as to reduce quality, the addition of deleterious ingredients, and the use of spoiled animal and vegetable products. Making false or misleading label statements regarding a food or a drug constituted misbranding. The presence and quantity of alcohol or certain narcotic drugs had to be stated on proprietary labels.

The law sought to protect the consumer from being deceived or harmed, mainly by following a favorite assumption that the average man was prudent enough to plot his own course and would avoid risks if labeling made him aware of them. In this spirit, some ardent pure food advocates predicted that the law would usher in the millenium. Defeated business interests, on the other hand, congratulated themselves that the bill's strictures, largely through their own lobbying, had not turned out to be tougher than they were. Anxiously these interests waited to observe the temper of enforcement. Dr.

Wiley believed that, for a pioneering statute, the measure had turned out rather well. He felt optimistic that 

Congress would readily remedy weaknesses in the law which he immediately recognized and which he knew would be further revealed by enforcement efforts. Although some fuzziness existed in the administrative provisions, the law gave Wiley's Bureau of Chemistry the task of spotting violations and preparing cases for the courts. Both a crusader and a compromiser in the long struggle to secure the law, Wiley determined, now that Congress had put power into his hands, to wear his crusading armor and enforce the measure to the hilt. The new battles, he would quickly learn, would be the most rugged he had ever fought. 

16 June 1981 FDA Consumer

State Officials: A Force Then And Now 

Dr. Harvey Wiley is rightfully recognized as the "Father of the Food and Drug Law" for his zealous efforts in the struggle that led to passage of the 1906 Pure Food and Drugs 

Act. That law was the first Federal statute to provide protection to consumers from dangerous, adulterated, and misbranded foods and drugs.

While Dr. Wiley, as Chief Chemist at the U.S. Department of Agricul ture, led the fight for passage of the law, he was not alone: other food and drug officials from across the country had been working for years at the State level in support of Dr. Wiley's cause.

In fact, fully 10 years before the 

1906 law was signed by President 

Theodore Roosevelt, several of these officials banded together to form what was to become the Association of 

Food and Drug Officials-an interna tional, nonprofit group still active today in promoting consumer protection in the fields of food, drugs, and other consumer products.

In the late 19th century, many kinds of food were being adulterated with a variety of preservatives and other chemicals, such as coal-tar dye, borax, and salicylic acid. The fraudulent practices increased producers' profits but at the cost of serious harm to the public. The purity of drugs was also a major health issue: the promotion of fraudulent and adulterated remedies was widespread.

As a result, many States began to pass consumer protection laws, often with the support of manufacturers seeking relief from unfair competition with adulterated products. While the laws were well-intended, they often were inconsistent and seriously deficient because of a lack of control over out-of-state manufacturers. The manufacturers, in turn, were subjected to widely varying State requirements, posing great difficulty for interstate commerce.

Such problems pointed to the need for a Federal food and drug law to impose uniform safety requirements to protect the citizens of all States. 

With that goal in mind, Joseph 

Blackburn, the Food and Dairy Commissioner of Ohio, met with his counterpart from Michigan, Elliot Grosvenor, to discuss plans for a national organization of workers in the field of food adulteration from the various 

States. The first meeting of the Na tional Association of State Dairy and 

Food Departments was held August 

25, 1897, in Detroit, with representatives from 10 States. 

The objectives set forth by the charter members were much the same as today: to promote uniform legislation to protect the public and prevent deception in the manufacture and sale of dairy, food, and other products intended for human consumption. 

The fledgling association soon joined forces with the crusading Dr.

Wiley in numerous efforts to promote better consumer protection laws, particularly a series of pure food congresses. It was during the landmark 

Pure Food Congress of 1898, in fact, that support for a Federal statute became truly evident nationwide and ultimately sparked the political support necessary to pass the law 8 years later. 

Wiley was often the keynote speaker at the association's meetings; so zealous was he in his presentations that his boss, Agriculture Secretary Wilson, occasionally felt obliged to "request equal time" to present the official department position-frequently very different from that of his chief chemist.

In the 85 years since its birth, the 

Association of Food and Drug Offi cals (AFDO)-as the organization eventually came to be known-has continued to work for uniform consumer protection regulation. The association has been at the forefront in support of such legislation as the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 

1938 and subsequent amendments.

The group has also developed the 

Uniform Food, Drug, and Cosmetic

Act, the Uniform Consumer Product Safety Act, the Uniform Hazardous Substances Labeling Act, and the Uniform Poison Prevention Packag ing Act. These "model bills" have been adopted as law in many States and AFDO advocates their adoption nationwide. 

As a tribute to its early ally, the association annually presents to one of its members the Wiley Award for outstanding work in protecting the public and furthering the principles of the association.

Although some of the problems that caused State food and dairy commissioners to band together 85 years ago have been corrected, many remain. 

The association continues to strive for the goals of consumer protection set forth years ago by men and women like Blackburn, Grosvenor, and Wiley. -Whitney Almguist 

Executive Assistant,

AFDO

Taste Of Raspberries, Taste Of Death: 

The 1937 Elixir Sulfanilamide Incident 

By the 1930's it was widely recognized that the Food and Drugs Act of 

1906 was obsolete, but bitter disagreement arose as to what should replace it. By 1937 most of the arguments had been resolved but Congressional action was stalled. Then came a shocking development-the deaths of more than 100 people after using a drug that was clearly unsafe. The incident hastened final enactment in 1938 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the statute that today remains the basis for FDA regulation of these products. Carol Ballentine describes this episode in food and drug law history. The author is a staff writer in FDA's Office of Public Affairs. by Carol Ballentine 

Nobody but Almighty God and but veband through these past few days. I have been familiar with death in the years since I received my M.D. from Tu lane University School of Medicine with the rest of my class of 1911. 

Covington County has been my home. I have practiced here for years. Any doctor who has practiced more than a quarter of a century has seen his share of death. "But to realize that six human beings, all of them my patients, one of them my best friend, are dead because they took medicine that I prescribed for them innocently, and to realize that that medicine which I had used for years in such cases suddenly had become a deadly poison in its newest and most modern form, as recommended by a great and reputable pharmaceutical firm in Tennessee: well, that realization has given

4728 me such days and nights of mental and spiritual agony as I did not believe a human being could undergo and survive. I have known hours when death for me would be a welcome relief from this agony." (Letter by Dr. A. S. Calhoun, October 22, 1937) 

The medicine that killed Dr. Calhoun's patients was Elixir Sulfanilamide. During September and October 1937 this drug was responsible for the deaths of more than 100 people in 15 States, as far east as Virginia and as far west as California.

The drug and the deaths led to the passage of the 1938 Food, Drug, and

Cosmetic Act, which increased 

FDA's authority to regulate drugs.

Sulfanilamide, a drug used to treat streptococcal infections, had been shown to have dramatic curative effects and had been used safely for some time in tablet and powder form. In June 1937, however, a salesman for the S.E. Massengill Co., in 

Bristol, Tenn., reported a demand in the southern States for the drug in liquid form. The company's chief chemist and pharmacist, Harold Cole 

Watkins, experimented and found that sulfanilamide would dissolve in diethylene glycol. The company control lab tested the mixture for flavor, appearance, and fragrance and found it satisfactory. Immediately, the company compounded a quantity of the elixir and sent shipments-633 of them all over the country.

The new formulation had not been tested for toxicity. At the time the food and drugs law did not require that safety studies be done on new drugs. Selling toxic drugs was, undoubtedly, bad for business and could damage a firm's reputation, but it was not illegal. 

Because no pharmacological studies had been done on the new sulfanilamide preparation, Watkins failed to note one characteristic of the solution. Diethylene glycol, a chemical normally used as an antifreeze, is a deadly poison.

In October 1957 the "new sulfanilamide" was first an nounced. Here is the paragraph describing it, appearing in the manufacturer's house organ for that month.

Public Enemy The Elixir Roundup 

Something over a month ago a manufac turer of medicines in Bristol, Tenn., shipped hither and yon over the Nation 200 gallons of a sticky, sweet liquid known as an elixir of alfanilamide About the same time 40 gallons of the same mixture were released in Kansas City. Within a few days there came evidence in the agonized death of men and women that the stuff was deadly poison. 

No sooner was the fact assured than officers of the United States Food and Drug

Administration, aided in every possible way by state health departments, physicians and druggists, began an intenstve effort to round up the deadly mixture. 

It is now possible to report that all but a very few ounces of this so-called elixir have been located and withdrawn. The small amounts still unaccounted for were sold to Itinerants or others who cannot be located. 

The death toll from this stuff standa now at 73, and fearful though that is the circumstances considered, it is amall by compar ison with what might have been if the officials and practitioners concerned had been somewhat less swift and tenacious in their search for the poison. It was an excellent job on all counts, and particularly for the speed with which it was done. 

The history of this elixir of sulfanilamide falls into a pattern unfortunately familiar to the American people. It may be that no other folk on earth are as lax and easy going as we in the matter of prevention and none so solicitous and thorough in our attempts to remedy damage after it has been done. We are capable of infinite courage and pains to patch up the wounds of the injured, to bury the dead, and to try to solace the bereft. Our heroism and sacrifice to rescos victims of physical catastrophe like flood er storm are boundless, and we dig deep into our pockets for whatever money is needed-after the harm has come to pass Only gradually do we learn the profundity of wisdom contained in the old saw that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. 

It remains to be seen whether Congress now can fit. after this harrowing exempli fleation of the need, to equip the Inspecters of the drug administration with regulations that will enable them to prevent the nocemity of ever again having to go on a frenaled bant for deadly poison that has been ufactured, distributed broadcast and onld freely under the assumption that it medicine for human ailments. ter it would have been for and in this widespread trig ded it, as could ecally have hardly heed to say. Manufaemista, drug houses, retail eng phyaletans and all and sundry should anly accept but insist on adequate safeards for the future.

FDA Consumer / June 1981 | 19

A child victim of the "Elixir of Sulfanilamide" disaster of 1937. Her mother's letter to President Roosevelt helped to secure safety clearance of new drugs in the 

1938 law. in early September. On October 11, the American Medical Association (AMA) received reports from physicians in Tulsa, Okla., that an unfamiliar sulfanilamide compound was responsible for a number of deaths.

The AMA asked for samples of the drug and then wired the Massengill 

Co., requesting the composition of the compound. The AMA laboratory isolated diethylene glycol as the toxic ingredient and immediately issued a warning, through newspapers and radio, that Elixir Sulfanilamide was toxic and deadly. 

A New York physician learned of the deaths on the 14th and promptly notified Food and Drug Administra tion headquarters. An inspector from the Agency's Kansas City Station confirmed that eight children and one adult had died and that all had taken a product labeled "Elixir Sulfanila mide, the S.E. Massengill Co., Manufacturing Pharmacists, Bristol,

Tenn.-Va." 

Inspectors were immediately dispatched to the firm's headquarters in 

Bristol and to branch offices in Kansas City, New York, and San Francisco. They found that the firm had already learned of the poisonous effects of the liquid sulfanilamide and had sent telegrams to more than · 1,000 salesmen, druggists, and doctors. However, the telegrams merely requested the return of the product and failed to indicate the urgency of the situation or say that the drug was lethal. At FDA's insistence, the firm sent out a second wave of messages, worded more strongly: "Imperative you take up immediately all elixir sulfanilamide dispensed. Product may be dangerous to life. Return all stocks, our expense.' 

FDA then set out to make sure all of the drug was retrieved. Practically the entire field force of 239 FDA inspectors and chemists was assigned to the task. State and local health officials joined the search. Newspapers and radio stations continued to issue warnings.

The staff began by checking the company's shipping records and the distribution lists in the four distributing houses and in a number of wholesale and retail drugstores. Thousands of order slips were examined one by one. In one establishment alone, 20,000 sales slips were checked. 

FDA employees tracked down the firm's 200 salesmen and questioned them about the dispersion of shipments and physician samples. Finding the salesmen was the first problem.

In one typical case, a salesman was reported to be in a hotel in Washington, D.C. He was not there but forwarding addresses had been left for him in Jackson, Mich., and in Baltimore. These turned out to be for another man with the same name. Four days of searching finally found the man in University Park, Md. Once the salesmen were found, there was still the problem of getting the distribution information. One man in

Texas, for instance, revealed the necessary information only after being jailed by State authorities.

In many cases, locating the purchasers of the elixir required some real detective work. In some drugstores, the elixir had been sold without prescriptions to purchasers whose names the druggist didn't know. In other cases, doctors had incomplete records or none at all-of the names and addresses of patients for whom they had prescribed. In East 

St. Louis, Ill., for instance, 49 prescriptions were filled and the only identification on some were such notations as "Betty Jane, 9 months old," or "Mrs. Jackson (no address).'

Even when the purchaser was finally located, the inspectors frequently needed to do some ingenious questioning to determine what happened to the purchased elixir. One 

East St. Louis woman told an inspector she had destroyed the drug. The inspector persisted in his questions however. What did she mean "destroy"? Had she poured it down the sink? Had she buried it? No, the woman said, she had thrown the bottle out the window into an alley. The inspector found the bottle still unbroken, still containing enough elixir to kill any child intrigued enough to swallow its sweet, raspberry-flavored, aromatic contents. 39 Many doctors and pharmacists did everything in their power to recover the elixir. One physician postponed his wedding to help an FDA chemist search for a 3-year-old boy whose family had moved into mountain country after obtaining a prescription. 

Other physicians apparently were reluctant to admit that they had prescribed the drug, perhaps fearing they would be held accountable for its consequences. One inspector, checking out a Georgia drugstore, was told that a shipment of 1 gallon 

20 June 1981 FDA Consumer

of elixir had been returned to the manufacturer after only 6 ounces had been dispensed. The patient who had taken the 6 ounces had suffered no ill effects, the druggist reported, and the inspector confirmed that this was true. But the inspector assigned to 

Bristol reported that 12 ounces was actually missing from the returned gallon, so the inspector in Georgia did some more questioning around town and tuned his ears to the local gossip. He learned that two other people had also bought the elixir. 

Both had died. 

Similarly, a South Carolina doctor told an inspector that he had dispensed the medicine to only five people and none had died. But when the inspector began asking questions around town, someone told him of the death of a lumber mill employee. 

The inspector recognized the symptoms as those characteristic of Elixir Sulfanilamide poisoning. Through the mill superintendent, he located the employee's sister. Yes, she said, her brother had gone to the doctor and had been given some red medicine before he died. She told the inspector that, in accordance with custom, all medicines and sickroom utensils had been placed on the grave, about 

1½ miles back in the fields. Accompanied by family and friends, the dead man's sister and the inspector walked to the wooded knoll. On the single mound of fresh earth were several bottles, dishes, spoons, and a 4ounce bottle containing about 1 

ounce of Elixir of Sulfanilamide. It bore the weathered but legible prescription label of the doctor. In fact, the inspector learned, four of the doctor's patients had died after taking the elixir.

Victims of Elixir Sulfanilamide poi soning-many of them children being treated for sore throats-were ill about 7 to 21 days. All exhibited similar symptoms, characteristic of kidney failure: stoppage of urine, severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, stupor, and convulsions. They suffered intense and unrelenting pain.

At the time there was no known antidote or treatment for diethylene glycol poisoning. 

In a letter to President Franklin D. 

Roosevelt, a woman described the death of her child: "The first time I ever had occasion to call in a doctor for [Joan] and she was given Elixir of Sulfanilamide. All that is left to us is the caring for her little grave. Even the memory of her is mixed with sorrow for we can see her little body tossing to and fro and hear that little voice screaming with pain and it seems as though it would drive me insane. . . . It is my plea that you will take steps to prevent such sales of drugs that will take little lives and leave such suffering behind and such a bleak outlook on the future as I have tonight." 

A few simple tests on experimental animals would have demonstrated the lethal properties of the elixir. Even a review of the current existing scientific literature would have shown that other studies such as those reported in several medical journals—had indicated that diethylene glycol was toxic and could cause kidney damage or failure. But in 1937 the law did not prohibit the sale of dangerous, untested, or poisonous drugs. Dr. Samuel Evans Massengill, the firm's owner, said: "My chemists and I deeply regret the fatal results, but there was no error in the manufacture of the product. We have been supplying a legitimate professional demand and not once could have foreseen the unlooked-for results. I do not feel that there was any responsibility on our part." The firm's chemist apparently did not share this feeling; Harold Watkins committed suicide after learning of the effects of his latest concoction. 

Through the dogged persistence of 

Federal, State, and local health agencies and the efforts of the AMA and the news media, most of the elixir was recovered. Of 240 gallons manufactured and distributed, 234 gallons and 1 pint was retrieved; the remainder was consumed and caused the deaths of the victims. 

Twenty-five seizures were made under Federal law. The charge was misbranding. "Elixir," FDA said, implied the product was an alcoholic solution whereas it was, in fact, a diethylene glycol solution and contained no alcohol. If the product had been called a "solution" instead of an "elixir," no charge of violating the law could have been made. FDA would have had no legal authority to ensure the recovery of the drug and many more people probably would have died.

FDA Commissioner Walter Camp- 

bell, who was then pressing for better 

Federal regulation of drugs, pointed out how the inadequacy of the law had contributed to the disaster. "It is unfortunate that under the terms of our present inadequate Federal law, the Food and Drug Administration is obliged to proceed against this product on a technical and trivial charge of misbranding. . . . [The Elixir

Sulfanilamide incident] emphasizes how essential it is to public welfare that the distribution of highly potent drugs should be controlled by an adequate Federal Food and Drug law.

We should not lose sight of the fact that we had many deaths and cases of blindness resulting from the use of another new drug, dinitrophenol, which was recklessly placed upon the market some years ago. 

Deaths and blindness from this [drug] are continuing today. We also should remember the deaths resulting from damage to the liver that have occurred from cinchophen poisoning, a drug often recommended in such painful conditions as rheumatism. We also have unfortunate poisoning, acute and chronic, resulting from thyroid and radium preparations improperly administered to the public. "These unfortunate occurrences may be expected to continue because new and relatively untried drug preparations are being manufactured almost daily at the whim of the individual manufacturer, and the damage to public health cannot accurately be estimated. The only remedy for such a situation is the enactment by Congress of an adequate and comprehensive national Food and Drugs Act which will require that all medicines placed upon the market shall be safe to use under the directions for use. 22 

As it turned out, the Elixir experience did more than hasten enactment of the 1938 Federal Food, Drug, and

Cosmetic Act. The New Drug sec tion, added to prevent such tragedies, gave the United States a new system of drug control which provided superior protection while stimulating medical research and progress. And 25 years later, it saved the

Nation from an even greater drug tragedy a thalidomide disaster-like that in Germany and England. Here again, history repeated itself. A pending bill, the Drug Admendments of 1962, was finally enacted.

About Fairness In Applying The Law 

FDA is a pioneer in the establishment of fair administrative procedures to enforce the law. Peter Barton Hutt traces briefly the approach FDA and its predecessor agencies have used since 1906 to assure fairness and openness. The author, former general counsel of FDA, is with the Washington, D.C. law firm of Covington & Burling. 

by Peter Barton Hutt aws regulating the marketing of Lav are foods and drugs are fundamentally different from many other laws enacted by Congress and the States. 

Food and drug laws are not intended to be enforced directly by the local, State, or Federal policemen and FBI agents who are charged with enforcement of most civil and criminal laws, or by private lawsuit. Instead, they require the designation of a specialized regulatory agency to which 

Congress delegates administrative authority to interpret and apply the congressional policy expressed in the statute.

The Food and Drug Administra tion (and its predecessor administrative agencies extending back even prior to 1906) was designated initially to implement the Food and Drugs 

Act of 1906 and then the Federal

Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 

1938, together with numerous amendments and related public health statutes that Congress has enacted over the years. 

In enforcing these statutes, FDA has found it essential to establish uniform administrative practices, now incorporated into written procedures, to guide its work. Those practices and procedures have had many purposes, but none more important than to assure the public that FDA will exercise its vast powers with fairness and openness. As Supreme Court 

Justice Felix Frankfurter pointed out many years ago, "The history of liberty has largely been the history of observance of procedural safeguards." 

Thus, these FDA practices and procedures have helped to (1) establish orderly mechanisms for FDA to carry out its daily business, (2) assure fairness and completeness in the 

Agency's handling of proceedings to establish regulations and adjudicate disputed regulatory action, (3) help structure FDA's choices among alternative courses of action, (4) establish specific enforcement methods where regulatory action is required, (5) promote consistent action by the Agency in like circumstances, (6) open up the

Agency to public scrutiny, (7) define and assure rights of all members of the public-from individual consumers to professional groups and the regulated industry-to participate in Agency decisional processes, and (8) protect the opportunity of individuals and groups to question any 

FDA action, or failure to act, both at the Agency level and ultimately in the courts.

From its inception, FDA has been a pioneer in the development of fair administrative practices and procedures. As the complexity of the specific statutes governing regulation of food and drugs and of general administrative law requirements has increased, the volume and complexity of FDA's procedural regulations have, of course, kept pace.

The Food and Drugs Act of 1906 

required the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Agriculture, and the Secretary of Commerce and 

Labor to make uniform rules and regulations for carrying out the provisions of that act. After meetings to obtain the views of the regulated industry and the public, final regulations were adopted. Those regulations were issued less than 4 months after enactment of the 1906 act and were regarded as sufficiently important to be published as an official 

Senate document. 

In those days there was far less opportunity for public participation in the development of regulations than today. There was no requirement that a proposal first be published for public comment. Regulations were simply published in final form and subsequent revisions were adopted in the same manner.

These first regulations needed only 20 pages to include all of the procedural and substantive requirements of the Agency. Subsequent changes were made through the issuance of 

Food Inspection Decisions (FID's) and Service and Regulatory Announcements (SRA's). 

Although FDA periodically issued a number of important decisions affecting enforcement of the 1906 act through FID's and SRA's, the basic administrative procedures of the 

Agency remained virtually unchanged for 30 years. Enforcement of the 

1906 act was relatively stable and simple. 

The Federal Food, Drug, and Cos metic Act of 1938 reflected a much greater emphasis than the 1906 act on the importance of administrative procedures. Congress included two provisions in the 1938 act authorizing 

FDA to issue implementing regulations. In one section, for certain types of regulations and proceedings that were regarded by Congress as particularly important or potentially controversial (for example, food standards, special dietary food regulations, and new drug proceedings),

Congress provided the safeguard of a formal administrative hearing before FDA could take final action. In another section, FDA was given general authority to promulgate regulations for the efficient enforcement of the 1938 act without the requirement of a formal hearing.

As it did under the 1906 act, FDA dures after enactment of the 1938 quickly adopted administrative proceact, largely to establish rules for the formal administrative hearings required by the new law. These procedures were published in the FED- 

ERAL REGISTER, which had been created by Congress in 1935 as the official Federal Government publication for all notices and regulations. er of the House of Representatives. Other notices expressing FDA's فت معهم معهد Faira of the United States and ег
