views about enforcement of the 1938 act were initially issued as informal 

Trade Correspondence from 1938 

through 1946. After the Administrative Procedure Act was passed by 

Congress in 1946, however, all statements of policy or interpretation issued by FDA were published in the 

FEDERAL REGISTER and informal pronouncements were discontinued.

The Administrative Procedure Act also required that all FDA regulations first be published as proposals, for public comment, before they are promulgated in final form. 

Until the 1970's, the only administrative procedures of major importance published by FDA were those that governed formal administrative hearings. The 1938 act, like the 1906 act, was enforced primarily through action brought directly in the courts.

FDA frequently instituted legal action to seize products or to enjoin or punish companies and individuals for violations of the law. Thus there was relatively little need for elaborate administrative procedures or lengthy substantive regulations to guide the 

Agency's activities. 

Beginning in the 1970's, however, FDA has placed greater reliance on regulations and other administrative action to implement the law, instead of direct court enforcement. This change in enforcement policy was reinforced by four decisions by the 

Supreme Court in 1973, holding that 

Congress intended that FDA possess the full range of administrative powers customarily exercised by any regulatory agency and thus is authorized to interpret and implement the law through administrative action.

These Supreme Court decisions placed heavy obligations on FDA to assure the development of comprehensive and fair administrative procedures. Since then a wide range of procedural regulations has been issued by the Agency. Indeed, in part because of the importance of and strong public interest in the products regulated by FDA, the Agency has led the way in issuing comprehensive regulations describing the procedures governing all of its activities. No other Federal agency has thus far made a comparable effort.

These procedural regulations can be found in Title 21 of the CODE OF FEDERAL REGULATIONS, which con tains several separate volumes. They cover such matters as the right of the public to meet with FDA and to obtain action by or information from 

FDA. Procedural regulations govern all of the various types of hearings held by FDA, including hearings before advisory committees, regulatory hearings, informal legislative-type meetings, and formal trial-type administrative hearings. Specific procedures have also been developed for handling important Agency projects like the review of the safety and effectiveness of all over-the-counter drugs and the review of the safety of ingredients that have been generally recognized as safe for use in food.

Thousands of notices and regulations have also been promulgated by FDA to interpret and apply the requirements of the 1938 act. From the original 20-page regulations issued in 1906, they have now grown to more than 3,000 pages of much smaller type. 

Although the present FDA regulations are lengthy and complex, they reflect the extraordinary breadth of laws whose implementation is entrusted to FDA and the complexity of the issues those laws present. They also represent the major safeguard for assuring that those laws are indeed interpreted and applied fairly and efficiently by FDA. 

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 25

FDA And The Congress 

Congress enacts the laws that FDA enforces, appropriates the money to carry out enforcement, and then oversees how well the Agency is performing. In this memoir, Donald Kennedy relates his perception of the role Congress plays with respect to FDA. The author was  from April 1977 to June 

1979, and is now president of Stanford University. by Donald Kennedy memento of Government my

The mice that attracts most attenservice tion from visitors to my office at 

Stanford is a chart prepared for me by the Office of Legislative Affairs when I left FDA in 1979. It consists of two horizontal rows of outline boxes, each with labels; it looks vaguely like an organization chart, except that in the top row the boxes contain the names of various House and Senate committees and subcommittees, and in the bottom row they identify senior officials of FDA. Connecting the two rows is an indescribably complex welter of colored lines, each representing an appearance by 

FDA before a Congressional hearing.

For the period 1977-79--the portions of the 95th and 96th Congresses during which I was at FDA-43 colored lines leave the box labeled Commissioner and lead to the various 

Congressional boxes. The experiences they represent include some of the more painful ones I had in Government. 

Surprisingly, they also include some of the most stimulating, thoughtful, and encouraging. Some have argued that the burden of responding to Congressional oversight is so crushing that it detracts from executive performance and deflects useful energies from more important matters. I do not agree. Accountability to Congress is, or can be, an important and positive aspect of agency management. Moreover, by no means all of the lines on my chart represented hearings aimed at the oversight of agency performance.

Some were more general inquiries into some emerging problem of broad significance, like regulatory reform. Others related to the development of new legislation. 

In this last area, I think our recent experience yields several lessons about the importance of interplay between the executive and legislative branches. From a purely descriptive standpoint, our efforts at legislation could fairly be called a failure. We produced, during 1977 and the early part of 1978, a comprehensive revision of the sections of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act dealing with drug regulation, and President Carter submitted it to the Congress with strong bipartisan support. But despite the labor invested in its preparation, and despite extraordinary efforts with members and staffs of the relevant 

House and Senate subcommittees, the legislation did not pass either house of Congress-though it did serve as the basis for an array of amendments that passed the Senate in the following year.

Nevertheless, I consider these efforts at statutory reform to have been successful. Deep and thorough consideration was given to the Agency's recommendations by the appropriate committees. Through it, the Congress recalibrated its understanding of 

FDA's problems, and reacquainted 

26 June 1981 FDA Consumer

itself with the views of the Agency and its various constituencies. As a result of the debate, I found understanding and receptivity increased markedly where it counted most. On several points, a consensus developed that allowed the Agency to make administrative changes short of modifying the legislation, and these changes improved the Agency's performance.

We can thus hope that the debate, and the resolutions to which it has already led, will improve the climate for later change. 

What about oversight? It is something about which every agency complains, and sometimes it does indeed seem as if one's Congressional overseers are more intent on making the six o'clock news than on making the agency better. But, on the whole, I found that Congressional oversight of 

FDA produced more good effects than bad. On some occasions it exposed authentic defects in our programs, which we were later able to rectify. On others it allowed the 

Commissioner and his staff to perceive inadequacies and correct them in the course of preparation for hearings. 

Of course, not all subcommittees and not all chairmen were equally adept overseers. During most of my time at FDA, the chairman of our 

House oversight committee was Representative John Moss (D-Calif.). He was much feared for his frosty demeanor and his testy assaults on agency heads, but-unlike many members-he understood the importance of oversight and was deeply dedicated to its principles. His resignation brought a mixture of joy and relief to many people who had testified before him, but I cannot doubt that on balance his scrutiny of FDA made it stronger and better than it would otherwise have been.

There are serious defects in the general practice of oversight, but they are not irremediable. The first is that too many members of Congress prefer the making of laws to the measurement of performance. Prestige, prized on Capitol Hill as much as it is elsewhere, depends more upon getting one's name on a bill than on being a good overseer. As a consequence, many members fail to learn the craft because they never practice it in a serious or sustained way. And part of the reason it is hard to be a good Congressional overseer is that unbiased information about agency performance is hard to come by. Large investigative staffs attached to committees are often pursuing an agenda of their own, and find it hard to be objective. The 

General Accounting Office was in my experience quite disappointing in its capacity to provide objective analyses. 

All too often, they supplied what they thought the customer wanted, or failed to bring adequate background to the task. 

FDA's operations, like those of an increasing number of Government agencies, involve complex scientific and technical issues. To exercise its oversight responsibilities properly, the Congress badly needs information from technologically sophisticated people who are willing to "speak truth to power." Perhaps the still-de veloping Office of Technology As sessment can fulfill this role; until it is filled, good Congressional oversight will continue to depend on the individual dedication of exceptional members. 

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 27

FDA's Changing Role In Food Safety 

Over the years, FDA's role in regulating the safety of the American food supply has changed, and inevitably more changes will take place in the future. Louis Rothschild Jr. analyzes the current issues facing FDA in the food area, and offers some suggestions on what the future might hold. 

The author is editor and publisher of 

FOOD CHEMICAL NEWS, a newsletter he founded when Congress enacted the 1958 Food Additive Amendments. 

by Louis Rothschild Jr.

Fo Good ood safety regulation is at a crossroads as FDA celebrates the 75th anniversary of the Food and Drugs 

Act. New tools, new priorities, and perhaps new organization will be needed to deal with the food safety challenges facing government. 

The needed redirection of food regulation has become apparent coincidentally with the shift in White 

House and Senate power from the

Democrats to the Republicans and with the continued bipartisan emergence of so-called regulatory reformers. However, these developments did not cause the long-term needs in food safety regulation, which will certainly outlast swings in the political pendulum.

Nor did the need for new approaches result from a failure on the part of FDA. On the contrary, the

Agency has worked itself into its current position by capably handling the perceived top priority in the food safety spectrum-food additives. 

Food additives came into the spotlight with Representative James Delaney's (D-N.Y.) hearings during the 

1950's and culminated in the enactment of the Food Additives Amendments in 1958. 

FDA has considered and cleared a multitude of additives since 1958, and has engaged in an ambitious review of substances with "generally recognized as safe" status.

The net result has been that only two major food ingredients have been found potentially hazardouscyclamate and saccharin. In the case of saccharin, Congress-apparently supported by the public-has blocked implementation of the Delaney Anticancer Clause of the Food Additive 

Amendments. It is clear that if cyclamate had been the only non-nutritive sweetener on the market, Congressional and public pressures would not have allowed a ban of that substance either. 

If only a few important additives have been found suspect, and the grounds for banning have been open to tumultuous controversy, it is apparent that FDA has managed the food additive situation well.

Even the controversial saccharin issue can be resolved if Congress relaxes the Delaney Clause to allow some exercise of judgment regarding the risk of an additive causing cancer. One of the solutions pushed by members of Congress involves use of risk-benefit analysis as an alternative to outright ban of a substance. 

Ironically, the probable results of a risk-benefit provision would run directly counter to the current political tides. While politicans talk of reducing the powers of agencies, an approach of this type would give FDA authority it has never before had and which it has never sought. With the use of risk-benefit criteria, the 

Agency would be able to pick and choose among competing food additives on the basis of assessments which would have to be in part subjective because of a lack of tools for making definitive judgments. Despite the current drive against Government regulations, implementation of a benefit-risk law would require massive new rules, adding hundreds of pages to the CODE OF FEDERAL REGULA- 

TIONS. 

However, Congress may enact legislation as a signal that the Government has done its job of protecting the public against food additives and should now stay within certain bounds.

FDA has long planned a cyclic review of all approved food and color additives. In all probability, this plan will be killed in the name of regulatory reform on grounds that it is too complicated, too expensive, and unnecessary.

This will mean, as was stated at a recent meeting by former FDA Chief 

Counsel William W. Goodrich, that it will be a "selective" review. This would differ little from what FDA is doing now and has been doing. 

With or without a Delaney Clause change, carcinogenic impurities and intermediates in food and color additives at insignificant levels will cease to be a major problem. A court decision involving acrylonitrile bottles has bolstered FDA's ongoing plans to exempt minor "constituents," and the de minimis principle enunciated by the court may ultimately reduce the burden of regulating thousands of minor packaging material components. 

These developments will not mean that FDA will cease to regulate additives. They will mean that the regulation of additives will become a routine part of the Agency's operations. 

As a result, a new set of food safety priorities will come to the fore. 

Administrators and scientists believe the most serious food safety hazards involve microbiological con-

Tea tasting is one of FDA's oldest functions, but it is done today much the same way it was in the 1920's. It all boils down to one person using his own taste buds to check tea against the standard. 

Bureau of Chemistry inspector John Earnshaw looks over incoming material in a spinach cannery, about 

1915. Note the badge. tamination, an area which again must receive top priority, as it did in the 1960's.

The additive versus microbiological struggle was clearly seen in the sodium nitrite situation. Even if nitrite had turned out to be a carcinogen, the Government would have been reluctant to ban the substance and abandon its protection against deadly botulism. FDA is constantly on guard against botulism, even though there have been few deaths from it attributed to commercial food products in this country. 

More expensive in dollar costs are the effects of salmonellosis. This "food poisoning" disease, although usually not fatal, causes undetermined numbers of cases with untold economic losses. While Salmonellae are the most prevalent food borne pathogens, new varieties of microorganisms which can cause illness are being found all the time. 

Although most attention has been focused on substances "added" to food, one of the most threatening health situations has involved contamination of products with aflatoxin, a toxin caused by mold which is many times more carcinogenic than any of the food additives whose safety has been questioned. Because of the life-threatening nature of aflatoxin, its presence jeopardizes large amounts of this country's grain supply. As FDA prepared to celebrate its 75th anniversary, southeastern

States were worried about corn crops, and in other areas aflatoxin threatened use of cottonseed meal for animal feed.

Regulation of industrial contaminants is another important area of food safety regulation. More food has been removed from the marketplace because of contamination with polychlorinated biphenyls than has 11 

30/ June 1981 FDA Consumer

ever been threatened by substances subject to regulation under the Food 

Additive Amendments. 

New organizational changes may be needed to cope with these newly emerged priorities, because they cut across all of the jurisdictional lines placed on food regulation. The U.S. 

Department of Agriculture (USDA), which regulates meat and poultry, and the U.S. Department of Commerce, which regulates fishery products, face the same problems posed by microbiological, natural, and industrial contaminants.

As a result of overlapping jurisdiction, duplication of effort and continuing controversies mar food safety regulation efforts. For example, FDA and USDA have been attempting to reconcile different approaches to measuring pesticide residues in food samples differences which spring from conflicting provisions in the laws which they must administer. 

Each agency has an independent "emergency" system to deal with contamination incidents. Both are plagued by problems of Salmonellae.

While USDA works to prevent aflatoxin contamination in peanuts, FDA worries about aflatoxin in corn. The 

Commerce Department fishery program is strictly voluntary and is attracting little interest.

It has been suggested periodically that FDA again be made an operating agency of USDA. However, USDA appears to be reverting to its traditional focus on bolstering "agribusiness" rather than consumer protection, a move which makes that department less than ideal for regulating food. On the other hand, it seems unlikely that the immediate future holds any promise for switching meat, poultry, and fish inspection from USDA and Commerce to FDA. 

FDA does not have the freedom within the Department of Health and 

Human Services that it once had. 

Under the former Department of 

Health, Education and Welfare, it played a nearly autonomous role.

Under the Carter Administration, the 

HHS Secretary's office formalized its structure to scrutinize virtually every 

FDA action in an apparent attempt to make FDA just another Public

Health Service agency within the De partment. It is not clear whether subsequent administrations will continue this kind of control over FDA. 

Periodic suggestions for an independent food regulatory agency might ultimately be adopted, allowing a unified approach to the regulation of all food products, and permitting more expanded budgets for the work of fighting food contamination. 

FDA now must split its resourceshort budget between food and such high-visibility areas as drugs and medical devices.

The growing limitation of FDA enforcement work in the food area has meant a general decline in regulatory actions involving foods. In a prior budget crunch, FDA sharply reduced its inspections dealing with food sanitation-the prosaic and tedious work of combatting such things as rodent and insect infestation. The House 

Appropriations Committee then gave the Agency marching orders to beef up its food sanitation program. However, the level of inspection and the number of regulatory actions again have fallen.

It has become clear that insanitation is not just a matter of aesthetics (as it has been called), but is a matter of protecting consumers from microbiological contamination of food. 

USDA has traditionally been wedded to the idea of having continuous inspection of meat and poultry plants.

The department now has reservations about the effectiveness of this system. which is so expensive that USDA uses much more money to police meat and poultry than FDA has to police the rest of the food industry. 

A better way must be found for doing things, and the food regulatory agencies ultimately must jointly develop it. FDA attempted a Coopera tive Quality Assurance Program which flopped. USDA is now trying a voluntary "quality control" program among meat and poultry plants, which may have only a limited chance of success. An FDA effort to gain legislation to authorize it to mandate industry quality assurance programs failed to gain Congressional approval. Congress may want to take a second look.

In attempting to combat contamination problems, FDA has moved in the right direction with its Good

Manufacturing Practice regulations for the food industry. Progress has been made with the use of hazard analysis and critical control point inspections, which focus on potential trouble spots.

The priorities of the 1980's and thereafter will require that the elements of a food protection policy be formalized and applied to all food products. This may need Congressional direction. FDA (or a newly unified agency) will almost certainly gain the right to inspect some food industry records. A new national food protection policy will also have to include Federal preemption, ending the hodge-podge of varying State requirements for foods which has been so costly without adding measurable safety protection. 

Steps such as these will enable

FDA to continue the key role it has played in food protection since 1906, and to build consumer confidence in the safety of the U.S. food supply.

The Story Of The Laws Behind The Labels 

The history of the Food and Drug 

Administration is also the history of consumer protection as applied to food, drugs, cosmetics, and other products now regulated by the Agency. That history began long before the initials f, d, and a became household words, as this article points out. Wallace F. Janssen began writing about FDA as a trade journal editor in 1931. He joined the Agency in 1951 as assistant to the commissioner for public information and continued to be its information chief until 1966. He now serves as FDA's historian. by Wallace F. Janssen

FDA Historian 

Tow old is the FDA?

HOW 

There are two answers to this frequent question: as a law enforcement organization its 75th anniversary year is 1981, but as a scientific institution it dates from 1862 when 

Charles M. Wetherill, first chemist of the new Department of Agriculture, set up a laboratory and began at once to analyze samples of food, soils, fertilizers, and other agricultural substances. The first reported project-a chemical study of grape juice for winemaking-dealt with, among other topics, the question whether adding sugar to increase the alcohol content would constitute "adulteration." It was concluded that the practice was legitimate. (Forty-six years later the first Notice of Judgment under the new 1906 Food and 

Drugs Act reported a court ruling to the contrary. Cider made harder by adding sugar was found adulterated.)

Being engaged primarily in agricultural research and development, the early FDA scientists inevitably became involved in matters of food safety. The 1862 report referred also to problems of food preservation and uses of chemical preservatives. The report of 1873 contains analyses of cereals, wine, and opium. In 1874 the adulteration of milk with water and chemicals was discussed, along with experiments on the effects of arsenic and copper pesticides on plants and the possibility of harm to humans. 

Federal concern for drugs started with the establishment of U.S. Customs laboratories to administer the 

Import Drugs Act of 1848. The 

United States had become the world's dumping ground for counterfeit, contaminated, diluted, and decomposed drug materials-a dangerous situation. American troops in 

Mexico had suffered from spurious medication for malaria. Pharmacists and the new American Medical Association joined forces to secure the legislation. The mission of the new 

Customs laboratories was to enforce the purity and potency standards of the U.S. Pharmacopeia, established by trade and professional leaders in 

1820. But support dwindled and the program gradually faded away. No organizational connection has been found with the agency now known as the FDA.

The United States was very slow to recognize the need for a national food and drug law. Frederick

Accum's "Treatise on Adulterations of Food and Methods of Detecting 

Them" had been published in London and Philadelphia in 1820, and

Great Britain's first national food law was passed in 1860. In the United 

States a variety of State laws dated from colonial times. Enacted mainly to serve the needs of trade, these laws set standards of weight and measure, and provided for inspections of exports like salt meats, fish, and flour, to promote foreign sales. 

But there were also local bread inspection laws to insure consumer protection as well as fair competition between bakers.

After the War of Independence the States continued to pass laws that varied greatly, reflecting their special interests. Not until interstate commerce began its great expansion after the Civil War did the need for Federal rulemaking become widely real ized. The Pure Food Movement-a grass roots phenomenon that germinated in the 1870's-was the original and principal source of political support for the Food and Drugs Act of 1906. It was originally a trade movement. Long before Upton Sinclair's

THE JUNGLE exposed insanitation in the Chicago stockyards; even before 

Harvey Wiley's arrival in Washington to head the Division of Chemistry, food industry members had begun to advocate a Federal law against adulteration. Trade interest arose from two causes: first, competition from a new breed of food products-glucose as a replacement of sugar, "lard" made from cottonseed oil, and oleomargarine, a threat to butter; and second, intolerable variations in the laws of the States. "As it is now," to quote one food packer, "we have to manufacture differently for every state." 

In 1879 Peter Collier, the fifth head of the Division of Chemistry, urged Federal legislation to make food adulteration a crime.

Dr. Wiley Comes to Washington In 1883 Dr. Harvey W. Wiley, 

State chemist of Indiana and professor of chemistry at the new Purdue

University, was appointed to succeed Collier.

Conditions in the U.S. food and drug industries a century ago can hardly be imagined today. Use of chemical preservatives and toxic colors was virtually uncontrolled. 

Changes from an agricultural to an industrial economy had made it necessary to provide the rapidly increasing city population with food from distant areas. But sanitation was primitive in the light of modern standards. Ice was still the principal means of refrigeration. The great pioneers of bacteriology were just starting

J. F. McPhee's 1906 cartoon reflected the public's expectations concerning the "Wiley Act." The new law, it was hoped, would put a stop to food adulteration and quack remedies-the two major evils and targets of a 20-year crusade for Federal regulation of foods and drugs. 

(WILEY PAPERS, Library of Congress) A center spread in COLLIER'S for December 1, 1905, told a pathetic story of the harm done by narcotic "tonics" sold to trusting women. Labels, generally, said nothing about the ingredients in the patent curealls. 

The medicine men competed with the circuses, the minstrel shows, and "wild west" performers to entertain the public and sell their products. Hamlin's 

Wizard Oil had one of the most popular and spectacular of the big touring medicine shows. For minor aches and pains, this liniment continued to be sold for many years after the shows had ceased.

their string of victories over infectious diseases. Milk was still unpasteurized. Cows were not tested for tuberculosis.

In the same era, thousands of socalled "patent" medicines such as "Kick-a-poo Indian Sagwa" and "Warner's Safe Cure for Diabetes" reflected both the limited medical capability of the period and public acceptance of the doctrine that the buyer could and should look out for himself. Medicines containing such drugs as opium, morphine, heroin, and cocaine were sold without restriction. Labeling gave no hint of their presence. Otherwise harmless preparations were labeled for the cure of every disease and symptom. 

Labels did not list ingredients and warnings against misuse were unheard of. What information the public received came frequently from bitter experience.

While such practices were by no means universal, and many firms were producing reliable and wholesome products, Dr. Wiley's chemists had no difficulty getting material for their investigations and reports. 

Wiley took their findings to the public, becoming a popular speaker at women's clubs, civic and business organizations. Crusading writers joined in the campaign. National magazines, such as COLLIER'S WEEKLY, the LA- DIES HOME JOURNAL, and GOOD HOUSEKEEPING, aroused public opin ion with their cartoons, articles, and editorials. 

In 1903, Wiley captured the attention of the country by establishing a volunteer "poison squad" of young men who agreed to eat only foods treated with measured amounts of chemical preservatives, with the object of demonstrating whether these ingredients were injurious to health. 

Strenuous opposition to Wiley's campaign for a Federal food and drug law came from whiskey distillers and the patent medicine firms, who were then the largest advertisers in the country. Many of these men thought they would be put out of business by Federal regulation. In any case, it was argued, the Federal Government had no business policing what people ate, drank, or used for medicine. On the other side were strong agricultural organizations, many food packers, State food and drug officials, and the health professions. But the tide was turned, according to historians and Dr. Wiley himself, when the voteless but militant club women of the country rallied to the pure food cause.

Final action followed a sensational portrayal of insanitary conditions in the Chicago meatpacking industry. A single chapter in Upton Sinclair's novel, THE JUNGLE, precipitated leg islation expanding Federal meat regulation to provide continuous inspection of all red meats for interstate distribution, a far more rigorous type of control than that provided by the pure food bill. Both measures became law the same day, June 30, 1906. 

Administration of the new law was assigned to the Bureau of Chemistry.

The young men and women recruited by Wiley and his successors quickly developed an efficient organization.

They continued the development of scientific methods of analysis-the foundation of food and drug protection. They worked out the legal procedures and the techniques of inspection, and applied them in hundreds of hard-fought court cases. And they won scores of judicial decisions which strengthened the law and also uncovered its weaknesses. Many found such satisfaction that they made FDA their life work. 

The Bureau of Chemistry enforced the 1906 law until 1927 when it was reorganized. Law enforcement functions were separated from agricultural research in order to emphasize and secure better funding for the lat

In 1902 Dr. Wiley started research with human volunteers to determine the effects of food preservatives on digestion and health. Overnight the press made the "Poison Squad" a national sensation. Even the minstrel shows had songs about the squadofficially designated the "Hygienic 

Table." Chemicals fed to the young men included borax; salicylic, sulphurous, and benzoic acids; and formaldehyde. The experiments went on for 5 years. Wiley and the public became convinced that chemical preservatives should be used in food only when necessary; that the burden of proving safety should fall on the producer; and that none should be used without informing the consumer on the label-basic principles of today's law and regulations.

Administration was formed, to be renamed in 1931 as the Food and Drug

Administration. In 1940, to prevent recurring conflicts between producer interests and consumer interests, FDA was transferred from the U.S. 

Department of Agriculture to the 

Federal Security Agency which, in 1953, became the Department of 

Health, Education, and Welfare now the Department of Health and

1938 The Federal Food, Drug, and

Cosmetic Act 

The six-page Wiley law prohibited the manufacture and interstate shipment of "adulterated" and "misbranded" foods and drugs. It enabled the Government to go to court against illegal products but lacked affirmative requirements to guide compliance. Labels were not even required to state the weight or measure only that a contents statement, if used, must be truthful. By 

1913, food manufacturers, alarmed by a growing variety of State weight and measure laws, sought uniformity through the Gould Amendment to the Federal law-requiring net contents to be declared, with tolerances for reasonable variations. 

False therapeutic claims for patent medicines had escaped control in 

1912 when Congress enacted an amendment outlawing such claims but requiring the Government to prove them fraudulent; i.e., that the promoter intended to swindle his victims. A defendant had only to show that he personally believed in his fake remedy to escape prosecutiona major weakness in the law for 26 years.

Food adulteration continued to flourish because judges could find no specific authority in the law for the standards of purity and content which FDA had set up. Such products as "fruit" jams made with water, glucose, grass seed, and artificial color undercut the market for honest products. 

Economic hardships of the 1930's magnified the many shortcomings of the 1906 act and brought a new consciousness of consumer needs. The book YOUR MONEY'S WORTH, by 

Stuart Chase and F. J. Schlink, signaled the start of a new consumer movement. 

Most important, the 1906 law became obsolete because of the technological changes which were revolutionizing the production and marketing of foods, drugs, and related products. 

In 1933, a few days after the inau guration of Franklin D. Roosevelt as 

President of the United States, the

Chief of the Food and Drug Admin istration, Walter Campbell, seized an opportunity to discuss the food and drug situation with Rexford Tugwell, a member of the President's "brain trust," who had been named Assist ant Secretary of Agriculture. The same afternoon Campbell was again called to Tugwell's office. "Mr. 

Campbell," said Tugwell, "since I saw you this morning I have talked with the President. I repeated our conversation to him, and he has authorized a revision of the Food and 

Drugs Act." 

The "Tugwell bill," introduced in

Congress a few weeks later, was a legislative disaster. The opposition of industry and advertising interests to this New Deal legislation was total and overwhelming. When the smoke cleared away the Senate sponsor, Royal S. Copeland, M.D., of New 

York, aided by FDA officials, consumer-minded Congressmen, attorneys, and staff members, began the laborious process of fashioning a bill that could be enacted, yet not surrender essential consumer protection. A bitter 5-year legislative battle began.

Again, organized club women provided most of the public support.

In 1907 Walter G. Campbell (left) was one of the first 28 food and drug inspectors (over 2,000 took the civil service examination). Selected by Dr.

Campbell remained in charge of enforcement for 37 years, becoming the first "Commissioner of

Three of Dr. Wiley's most effective supporters: Mrs. Walter McNab 

Miller, president of the General

Federation of Women's Clubs; Dr. 

Edward F. Ladd, of North Dakota, a leader among the State food and drug officials; and Miss Alice Lakey, of the

Historians and Dr. Wiley himself credit the club women of the country for turning the tide of public opinion in favor of the "pure food" bill. 

Trade leaders made positive as well as negative contributions. Again public opinion was aroused by a shocking disclosure-the deaths of more than 

100 people from a poisonous "elixir of sulfanilamide." On June 25, 1938, President Roosevelt signed the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

Many compromises had to be made to secure passage, but still the new law was a major improvement. 

The following is a list of a few of some 40 substantive changes which altered the law to fit the new conditions. • Drug manufacturers were required to provide scientific proof that new products could be safely used before putting them on the market. 

Cosmetics and therapeutic devices were regulated, for the first time. • Proof of fraud was no longer required to stop false claims for drugs. 

Addition of poisonous substances to foods was prohibited except where unavoidable or required in production. Safe tolerances were authorized for residues of such substances, for example pesticides. • Specific authority was provided for factory inspections. 

Food standards were required to be set up when needed "to promote honesty and fair dealing in the interest of consumers." • Federal court injunctions against violations were added to the previous legal remedies of product seizures and criminal prosecutions.

The Preventive Amendments The new law, and World War II, greatly expanded FDA's workload.

Wartime demands had stimulated the development of new "wonder drugs," especially the antibiotics, which were made subject to FDA testing beginning with penicillin in 1945. Fortunately there was a law requiring premarket clearance of new drugs, but consumers continued to be guinea pigs for a host of new chemical compounds of unknown safety. The law prohibited poisonous substances but required no showing that food ingredients were safe. It provided for exemptions and safe tolerances for unavoidable or necessary poisons such as pesticides, but when FDA attempted to set a pesticide tolerance an adverse court decision showed that the lengthy procedure required by law was unworkable. FDA could stop the use of known poisons, and did so in numerous cases, but the vast research effort needed to assure that all food chemicals were safe was clearly beyond all foreseeable resources. 

In 1949, FDA Commissioner Paul

B. Dunbar took the problem to a friend in Congress, Rep. Frank B. 

Keefe of Wisconsin. Mr. Keefe introduced a resolution to investigate chemicals in food, and later, cosmetics. The hearings, chaired by Rep. 

James T. Delaney of New York, went on for 2 years. From the committee's work came three amendments that fundamentally changed the character of the U.S. food and drug law: the Pesticide Amendment (1954), the Food Additives Amend ment (1958), and the Color Additive

Amendments (1960). 

With these laws on the books, it could be said for the first time that no substance can legally be introduced into the U.S. food supply unless there has been a prior determination that it is safe. By requiring the manufacturers to do the research, a problem of unmanageable size was made manageable. Preventing violations through premarket clearance gave consumers immeasurably better protection than merely prosecuting the few violations which could be proved by investigating after injuries were reported.

Very significant was a proviso in the food and color additive laws that no additive could be deemed safe (or given FDA approval) if found to 

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 39

cause cancer in man or experimental animals. Known as the "Delaney 

Clause," the section was initially opposed by FDA and by scientists who agreed that an additive used at very low levels need not necessarily be banned because it may cause cancer at high levels. Proponents justified the clause on the basis that cancer experts have not been able to determine a safe level for any carcinogen.

This was the underlying basis in 1959 for a nationwide FDA recall of cranberries contaminated by the weedkiller aminotriazole. Notwithstanding publicity critical of FDA, this action had beneficial results, particularly in convincing farmers that pesticides must be used with care. Other important and controversial FDA actions stemming from the Delaney Clause will be mentioned later. 

1962 Drug Amendments 

The trend toward preventive lawmaking continued. A drug tragedy in 

Europe, the births of thousands of deformed infants whose mothers had taken the new sedative thalidomide, focused public attention on pending

U.S. legislation to further strengthen the Federal Food, Drug, and Cos metic Act. The Drug Amendments of 

1962, passed unanimously by the

Congress, tightened control over prescription drugs, new drugs, and investigational drugs. It was recognized that no drug is truly safe unless it is also effective, and effectiveness was required to be established prior to marketing-a milestone advance in medical history. Drug firms were required to send adverse reaction reports to FDA, and drug advertising in medical journals was required to provide complete information to the doctor-the risks as well as the benefits. In the years since 1962 literally thousands of prescription drug items have been taken off the U.S. market because they lacked evidence of safety and/or effectiveness, or they have had their labeling changed to reflect the known medical facts. 

Preventing harm again was the goal of amendments passed in 1976, to insure safety and effectiveness of medical devices. Federal authority to regulate therapeutic devices was first provided in the FDC Act of 1938. As a result, hundreds of quack machines and gadgets were taken off the mar ket. The growth of medical technol ogy, however, soon made the 1938 act obsolete in regard to legitimate devices. Spectacular growth also occurred in the related field of medical diagnostic aids. Anticipating the need for better regulation in both areas, an FDA Bureau of Medical Devices and Diagnostic Products was officially created in February 1974.

Years of study and many drafts of proposed laws developed by FDA and Congressional staff workers and industry experts culminated in the

Medical Device Amendments of 

1976, signed by President Gerald 

Ford on May 28. To avoid excess regulation the new law provides for classification of devices for controls appropriate for each class. Critically important devices, such as heart pacemakers or surgical implants, must be proved safe and effective before they can be marketed.

Preventing harm is again the purpose of the newest amendment of the basic Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the Infant Formula Act of 1980, drafted by Congress to insure minimum amounts of essential nutrients in commercially prepared baby foods, and to establish safety and quality standards for such foods. The 

Congressional action followed reports during 1979 that over 100 infants had been made seriously ill because of the lack of chlorides in two soy-based formulas. The new law authorizes 

FDA to adjust nutritional standards for such foods to conform with the best available scientific knowledge.

Manufacturers are required to periodically test their products and report promptly to FDA when they do not meet the official specifications.

Major Trends and Developments 

At the start of the 1950's, the resources of FDA were seriously deficient. Appropriations and staff, never adequate, remained at approximately the levels prevailing in 1938 when

Congress passed the present basic 

Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic 

Act, greatly increasing the Agency's responsibilities. In 1954, Commissioner Charles W. Crawford won approval by Nelson Rockefeller, undersecretary of the department, for the appointment of a representative Citizens Advisory Committee on the 

FDA, to study the adequacy of enforcement. The committee, adopting recommendations drafted by a distinguished industry lawyer, Charles 

Wesley Dunn, recommended a threeto fourfold increase in funds, to be accomplished in 5 to 10 years. The budget makers and the Congress were impressed by the committee's report, and a spectacular increase in

FDA appropriations has since occurred from a $5 million budget in 1955 to over $320 million in 1980, with a staff increase from less than 

1,000 to over 7,000. 

Equally striking in the last quarter century has been the increase in 

FDA's scientific capability to detect and measure substances in foods, drugs, and cosmetics. FDA scientists, always outstanding for their skill in analytical chemistry, developed a new arsenal of spectrographic and chromatographic techniques, whereby contaminants can be measured in parts per billion or even per trillion. 

Today automated instruments can even print out the results of sample analyses in minutes, a procedure which once would have required weeks of laboratory benchwork. The increase in sensitivity of methods, by roughly one million times, revolu-

Programs Transferred

From its beginning, FDA's mission has been consumer protection. As a consequence the Agency has initiated several major consumer protection programs now administered by other agencies, and today includes consumer programs transferred to FDA from other agencies. 

The Caustic Poison Act, lobbied through Congress in 1927 by Dr. 

Chevalier Jackson and the American 

Medical Association, required labels to warn parents and protect children from accidental injury and death caused by lye and 10 other caustic chemicals. In 1960 thousands of other chemical products for home use came under FDA control when the Haz ardous Substances Labeling Act was passed with strong industry support. 

To administer this law and subsequent amendments which expanded it, FDA developed an effective consumer safety program. With the pas sage of the Consumer Product Safety 

Act, in 1972, the FDA Bureau of

Product Safety became the operating organization of a new independent

Consumer Product Safety Commis sion.

A great chapter in FDA history came to an end in 1968 when the 

FDA Bureau of Drug Abuse Control was merged with Federal narcotic law enforcement in the Department of 

Justice. On its own initiative FDA had pioneered in the 1940's the Federal effort to curb abuse of nonnarcotic drugs, by prosecuting dealers who sold barbiturates and amphetamines without prescriptions. The advent of the dangerous hallucinogenic drug LSD in the 1960's magnified the problem. Working with inadequate law, unarmed, and with little experience in criminal investigation, FDA inspectors went undercover as drug peddlers and secured the conviction of hundreds of racketeers and pushers. When stronger drug abuse control amendments were passed in 

1965, a new FDA Bureau of Drug 

Abuse Control was established, with a nationwide field service and over 

300 trained agents. Anticipating ultimate consolidation with the Federal

Bureau of Narcotics, FDA Commis sioner George Larrick planned the new bureau as a separate establishment. With the transfer, FDA lost many experienced employees, and criminal investigation became a relatively minor field of activity.

the Public Health Service became concerned with workers who contracted cancer from luminous paint they applied to watch dials. Overdosage with diagnostic x-rays increased greatly, becoming a major public health problem. Following World 

War II both PHS and FDA were involved in monitoring contamination of food, milk, and public water supplies due to radioactive fallout from open testing of atomic weapons.

Meanwhile, electronic technology developed a host of new products-television, microwave ovens, lasers, etc., which could emit harmful radiation. In 1968 a comprehensive Radia tion Health and Safety Act was passed, and in 1971 the product-related activities of the PHS Bureau of 

Radiological Health were transferred to FDA, while its environmental activities were shifted to a new Envi ronmental Protection Administration. 

One more important health program was assigned to FDA in July 

1972, from the National Institutes of 

Health-the regulation of biological drugs. This, the oldest continuing

Federal drug control program, was begun in 1902 to insure the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, serums, antitoxins, etc., by setting standards and licensing both the producers and their products. The transfer immediately strengthened control by applying provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as well as the licensing controls previously in effect. More effective regulation of blood banks has been a major accomplishment of FDA's new Bureau of Biologics. 

From its beginning, the law defined food and drugs as products "for man and other animals." But livestock feed and veterinary drugs were left largely to State regulation until 

World War I made it important to increase food production. One way was to crack down on quack veterinary medicines, especially the numerous "cures" for hog cholera. For years the Bureau of Chemistry and FDA waged war against such products, saving farmers uncounted millions in livestock losses as well as the cost of worthless drugs. Today the law for animal products closely parallels the regulation of products for humans, and FDA's Bureau of Veterinary 

Medicine is as much involved with the health of human consumers of animal products as it is with the animals which produce them.

The Trend Toward Prevention 

There are many ways to write

FDA's history. It can be a story of the laws which Congress enacted, a story of famous cases to enforce those laws, a story of the organization and the people who built it, or a story about the changing technology and the scientific controversies, some settled, others still unsolved. And it can be all of these, but not in a few pages.

If there is one dominating theme it is the change from a law that was primarily a criminal statute, protecting consumers through the deterrent effect of court proceedings to a law that is now dominantly preventive through informative regulations and premarket controls. 

The premarket approval laws made important changes in FDA's methods of control. They specifically required the Agency to issue regulations explaining the requirements and proce dures. The 1962 Drug Amendments called for Current Good Manufacturing Practice Regulations to set standards for plant facilities, maintenance, laboratory controls, etc., to prevent errors or accidents which could harm consumers. The idea was too good to be restricted to drugs, and in 1969 the first GMP's for food establishments were issued. All such regulations are based on actual industry practices. Today FDA inspectors especially look for GMP violations, as well as product violations. 

The American public has little knowledge of the routine work of FDA, important as it is to every consumer. Much better known are its efforts to deal with newsmaking scientific problems. A succession of these, beginning with the cranberry recall of 

1959, has greatly affected the

Agency's work as well as its public image.

Those who read the papers or watch TV know FDA in terms of such topics as cyclamate in soft drinks, the food color Red No. 2, saccharin, nitrite, and caffeine. 

Chemicals and cancer are the great public health concerns of today.

Much more is known about such matters than just 20 years ago, yet uncertainty about the risk of borderline carcinogens continues to hamper decisions. Generally a great deal of money is involved-both for the users and the regulators who must seek scientifically valid answers. At the same time an inflexible law (the 

Delaney Clause) leaves little room for the exercise of judgment. 

Fortunately, the regular business of consumer protection goes on as usual. Millions of times a day people in factories, warehouses, drugstores, and hospitals do things to comply with the food and drug law-yet never give it a thought! Consumer protection happens because so many people do things the right way.

Drug Regulation Today: 

How Much Is Appropriate? 

One of the critical issues that FDA, the medical community, the drug industry, and the public will face in the 1980's is how much drug regulation is appropriate. Samuel M. Gilston examines this issue from his perspective as a long-time observer of the FDA drug regulatory system. The author is executive editor of WASHINGTON DRUG LETTER. 

By Samuel M. Gilston 

Tnited States drug regulation is based on what appears to be a simple premise: a new drug must be proven safe and effective and have the approval of FDA before it can be marketed. Furthermore, a drug must be properly labeled and manufactured with careful quality controls.

But the legal, scientific, and medical debates that have surrounded

Federal drug law since it began belie the seeming simplicity of this concept. 

As FDA marks its 75th anniversary, observers in and out of Government continue to question the

Agency's role in reviewing and approving drugs, and the need for stringent safety and efficacy requirements. 

Should there be less drug regulation? Should there be more? How much is enough? Are Federal rules hampering the availability of helpful drug therapies, increasing drug costs, and discouraging industry's investment in research and development? 

Or are Americans suffering illness and death because of unsafe or ineffective medicines allowed onto the market by overly weak regulation? 

After 75 years, these questions are still being hotly debated in the 

Agency, Congress, and the courts. 

FDA remains in the midst of legal battles over its authority to require premarket review for new drugs and generic copies of older products, to mandate patient package inserts that inform consumers about prescription drugs they are using, and to set standards for Good Manufacturing 

Practices in the compounding of drugs. 

One misconception often held by those who weigh the need for FDA regulation is the belief that the 

Agency and the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act are the only forces controlling the behavior of drug manufacturers. This is simply not so. 

In considering the current state of drug regulation, it is important to recognize other major factors that exert controls on drug marketing. 

These include (1) the drug industry's voluntary self-regulation, (2) legal and competitive forces in the marketplace, (3) the intervening role of trained physicians, (4) the technology of drug research and production, and (5) the ever-changing political and social definition of safety.

American drug laws and FDA regulations owe their existence, in large measure, to a fundamental belief that the drug companies could not be trusted to assure the safety and efficacy of their products. Unfortunately, there have been enough bad examples in the past and presentof dangerous and ineffective drugs on the market to perpetuate this mistrust. 

However, only the extremely nearsighted would disregard the conscientious and voluntary efforts by the majority of drug firms to meet and exceed the requirements of the law. 

Without this self-motivated compliance on the part of industry, FDA never would have enough staff or resources to enforce its requirements. 

Drug companies are motivated, quite understandably, by the desire to make profits from developing new products and improving old ones.

This business "fact of life" has important benefits for the American economy, providing jobs, tax revenues, and exports to help our balance of trade. The public also benefits from the availability of new or better treatments. 

Unless the American free-enterprise system undergoes a radical upheaval, drug regulation in the United

States must take into account the mechanism of the marketplace and medical practice-with all of their faults and benefits-in every regulatory decision. 

Although much can be said for the preventive powers of the "flashing blue light" of a police car, this narrow view disregards several significant business and legal factors that impose restraints on drug marketing.

In what is a very competitive industry, bad publicity about a drug can be extremely damaging to a com pany's sales and image. Competitors are not above spreading the word about the dangers of products for which they have a substitute.

In many cases, news of a previously undiscovered serious side effect has led to a precipitous drop in a product's sales. This response from physicians who prescribe drugs and consumers may come even before 

FDA takes any action against the product. 

Adverse reactions to drugs occasionally are found in products carefully tested by respected firms before marketing and approved by FDA. 

Nonetheless, the nature and severity of such unexpected effects may not be discernible until the drug is used by a much larger number of people than can ever be included in premarket testing. 

The competitive marketplace also spurs companies to improve existing products and find new ones that can capture a share of another drug's market. This aspect of the business has been criticized for producing duplicative treatments for the same condition. However, continued improvement, no matter how minor, keeps pressure on firms to maintain and upgrade the quality of their drug products. 

In addition to bad publicity and competition, there is the long-standing but increasingly more pervasive threat of product liability suits. A

Serial No. 12890, 0.678-415 company can face serious financial losses if it is found liable for marketing an unsafe product. Even if the firm never actually loses a suit, it often must bear heavy litigation expenses. 

In recent years, courts have applied a stricter liability to manufacturers of all types of products. While drug firms may not be losing more suits than before, this increased vulnerability has encouraged litigation.

Recent court decisions also have rendered drug firms vulnerable to class action suits, in which groups of people claiming to have been injured by a product can join together to sue not only for physical injuries, but also when alleged antitrust or pricefixing practices have cost patients money. 

Another court ruling, involving women who developed cancer because their mothers had taken a drug called DES (diethylstilbestrol) during pregnancy, has raised the possibility of shared liability. Under the interpretation of the law by the California court that decided the case-a ruling which the U.S. Supreme Court left standing-liability may be shared by a number of manufacturers for injuries resulting from products made by several firms and used years ago, but whose specific manufacturer cannot be identified.

Thus, a combination of forcesregulatory, economic, and legalwork together to assure the safety and efficacy of the American drug supply. None of these elements alone, however, should be considered sufficient to provide the margin of control that the American public expects and demands. 

FDA enforcement of U.S. drug law primarily involves two areas: premarket evaluation and approval of new drugs, and postmarket monitoring of drug labeling, advertising, and quality control. 

For many years, the Agency's job almost entirely consisted of inspections aimed at uncovering adulterated or unpure products and exposing fraudulent labeling. As law and technology have evolved, that work has become much more sophisticated, and on-the-spot visual observations need to be backed up by laboratory tests and investigations to uncover hazards. 

Today, FDA is seen by many as the gatekeeper of "technology transfer" the process by which the latest and sometimes most unconventional scientific discoveries and knowledge enter the marketplace. In some cases, this involves allowing the marketing of new drugs that operate in the body in new ways. It can mean deciding what to do about alreadymarketed products revealed as being linked to a previously unsuspected hazard. 99 

FDA clearly is more comfortable with its older role as "policeman."

Inspections of drug plants and investigations into product labeling remain a major part of FDA's work, even though the deficiencies uncovered often are technical in nature, involving quality control, illegal marketing of unapproved drugs, and unsupported medical claims. 

Here, the "flashing blue light" of the Agency investigator is an important element in the daily operations of drug companies. Company quality control officials admit privately that they can much more easily gain funds, staff, and corporate support for their departments when FDA is perceived as active and aggressive in its inspection programs and its enforcement of quality control and labeling rules. 

Still, questions have been raised about the effectiveness of so-called "without cause" inspections that periodically are made of drug plants. 

Such programs require a large staff in an agency that is severely short of personnel in other areas. Moreover, the chances of an inspector finding a violation of the law that could lead to legal action is much less in these type inspections than when one is made 

48/ June 1981 / FDA Consumer

based on reported injuries or laboratory test results.

The single area of FDA drug regulation of which the public is most aware-and where the concept of "technology transfer" has its greatest impact—is the premarket approval of drugs. 

The notion of "wonder" drugs always has had popular appeal. People want to be able to believe in cures for painful or chronic conditions whether the malady is dandruff or heart disease.

As part of the new drug approval process, FDA reviews laboratory, animal, and human research data compiled by drug companies to prove the safety and efficacy of the products they want to market. These studies are supposed to be well-controlled and performed by qualified experts. 

Few responsible leaders in either industry or government doubt the need for careful research that resolves as many unknowns about a chemical as possible before it is allowed to be generally available to the public. Nor can assumptions of safety be accepted in lieu of proper testing. 

At the heart of FDA's legal fight over the controversial drug laetrile, which is claimed to be a cancer cure, was the belief that even the most in- • nocuous product can be found to contain hidden hazards. Although terminally-ill cancer patients may have less concern than the normal population about the safety of a drug that might save their lives, a legitimate drug deserves to have the imprimatur of sound research, while false cures that prey on people's hopes and innocence need to be exposed. 

Therefore, the question of how much regulation is appropriate for new drugs must center on how the system can be made most efficient. 

Until recently, there was a large gap between the testing and review stages of drug development. Drug companies would design and implement a drug protocol or testing plan with very little comment or review by 

FDA except in regard to the protection of patients. 

At the end of the testing period, the data would be bundled up and presented to the Agency in the form of a New Drug Application (NDA). 

At that point, Agency scientists would begin to examine these data to determine if the testing proved the product's safety and efficacy or if deficiencies would prevent its approval. 

Invariably, FDA reviewers found it easy to find faults and second-guess company scientists. And drug testing is a complex process filled with many variables that may be judged differently by equally qualified experts.

Sometimes it has been suspected that NDA submissions were intentionally deficient, because drug sponsors expected the Agency to ask for additional specific tests. Also, recent reports suggest that successful navigation through the NDA process may depend on the simple axiom: "practice makes perfect." Firms that have prepared and submitted many applications over the years do better at getting them approved than companies that submit only a few. 

In either case, some tests may have to be redone or new ones designed and conducted. The result? A "custom-building" of the materials in an NDA until FDA staffers are satisfied. This still happens today to many drugs. 

In the last few years, however, there has been an attempt to involve 

FDA and its advisory committees of outside experts in the process of designing and evaluating drug studies earlier in the game, especially for drugs considered important breakthroughs. These outside advisors also serve as a buffer between industry and FDA, offering a "second opinion" on safety and efficacy judgments. Guidelines for testing many classes of drugs also have been developed, and industry has become more familiar with what Agency officials expect. 

Together, these factors have improved somewhat the speed and efficiency of the premarket approval process. Clearly, much more remains to be done, especially in altering attitudes held by industry and Government scientists. Closer cooperation between FDA and industry in drug testing and review, with proper safeguards, should not be viewed as a conflict of interest. It should be accepted as a natural part of the development of new medicines that benefit society. 

Preliminary review of drug testing plans should be made optional for all drugs, not just breakthrough products. Reserving early review privileges for only breakthrough drugs discriminates against most new products and perpetuates the "wonder drug" myth. 

Although many individual drugs have represented significant advances in medical treatment, it is the total armamentarium of American drug therapy that places our health system among the best in the world. The constant upgrading of that drug supply is only possible when all drugs can move through the NDA process in a considered but efficient manner. 

In addition to earlier review of drug testing, it may be necessary to clarify and expand some current research guidelines, and-where none exist-develop them. Many observers in industry as well as in FDA believe drugs would be approved faster by the Agency if FDA had the power to remove the drugs from the market quickly if they turned out to be dangerous. The current procedures, which are cumbersome and can take years, can only be changed by convincing Congress to amend the Fed eral Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act. 

The FDA staff assigned to NDA 

review should be enlarged, by somehow attracting more scientists and physicians with outstanding credentials and experience in drug testing to work at the Agency. 

In the immediate future, FDA can

Whatever changes are made in

FDA drug regulation either legislative or administrative-should not be implemented precipitously. Stability and consistency in Agency personnel and policies are the keys to successful regulation for both FDA and industry. Simple familiarity with the drug law and Agency requirements is a major factor in making the system work well. Sudden shifts and disruptions can take years to overcome.

Many of the changes that are needed in FDA regulatory procedures may require amendment of the 

FDC Act. Drug regulation legislation has been closely examined by Congress in the past, but not enacted.

With the election of a Republican majority in the Senate for the first time in 25 years, drug legislation is likely to resurface again, but its course may be significantly different than envisioned by Democratic legislators.

The basic goal of drug legislation changes appears to have gained bipartisan support. These revisions would allow FDA to speed up the approval process for important breakthrough drugs, while also giving the Agency the legal tools to get dangerous drugs off the market faster than it can now. 

New legislation, of course, can have many pitfalls. Opening the law

As FDA begins on its way toward the 100th anniversary of the Pure 

Food and Drugs Act, it does so with a wealth of experience upon which to build. While the Agency faces more subtle and technologically sophisticated challenges than it encountered in the past, its basic goal of consumer protection remains unchanged and still worthy of public support and recognition. 

50/ June 1981 / FDA Consumer

Drugs Of The Future 

Many scientists believe that during the 

1980's there will be another golden age of drug development, perhaps comparable to that which took place in the years after World War II. Paul de Haen projects where some of the new drugs may come from, and what diseases they may cure or alleviate. 

The author is a pharmaceutical consultant in New York. by Paul de Haen 

The last 75 years comprise the most productive period of new drug introduction since the beginning of time. 

Up to the middle of the last century, extracts of plants delivered most drugs and only since 1880 have drugs been made by chemical synthesis. Aspirin and several other analgesics are among them. 

Sleep-producing drugs came with the turn of the century but have largely been replaced. In the twenties, insulin arrived from Canada and drugs aiding the kidneys arrived from

Germany. The major new discoveries started in the thirties with the rediscovery of sulfanilamide, originally made at the end of the last century, but not then recognized as a useful drug for the treatment of infections. 

Then came drugs for the treatment of kidney and heart diseases, which account for the largest number of prescriptions today. Then followed antibiotics, antihistamines to relieve allergic disorders and the common cold, drugs for the treatment of duodenal ulcers and arthritis, hormones for a variety of diseases and birth control, and tranquilizers to assuage the troubled mind. Many other diseases, including certain forms of cancer, can now be successfully treated with drugs. Surprisingly, 70 percent of all prescriptions filled in drug stores require only 120 single drugs and 65 combination products.

A great deal of the recent research with new drugs is based on advances in our knowledge of body functions, both normal and diseased. Here the guidelines for new drug development are set. There is much more emphasis on preventing a disease than on treating its symptoms. The funds spent by 

Government, universities, and the pharmaceutical industry on basic and drug research amount to billions of dollars annually.

What are the primary areas in which research today hopes to produce drugs in the next 5 to 10 years that will benefit the young, the middle-aged, and the expanding number of older people? 

The prostaglandins are hormonelike substances found in almost every type of human tissue. They were discovered 50 years ago, but scientists lacked the knowledge to interpret their many physiological functions. In the thirties, Dr. von Euler in Sweden and Dr. Goldblatt in England discovered independently that injections of these agents dramatically reduced blood pressure. Research resumed after the war with the financial aid of the Upjohn Company. This firm today sells two derivatives that induce labor. 

Prostaglandins regulate cellular metabolism. Many are now made synthetically for the following therapeutic uses: to lower or increase blood pressure, increase gastric secretion, shrink swollen nasal passages, produce rapid relief from asthma, and prevent the development of blood clots associated with heart attacks and strokes. The present research effort involving prostaglandins is tremendous: in 1979, 6,000 papers were published in the scientific literature. We shall see application of some of this work in the not too distant future. The prostaglandins are basically natural substances which the chemist has changed into derivatives exerting a specific action. 

Vaccines have protected millions of people from bacterial diseases, such as smallpox, measles and typhoid fever. Promising work continues in many areas, but it takes time and effort to produce an effective and safe vaccine. Protection against pneumonia and meningococcal infections has been developed. Prevention of hepatitis and gastric enteritis is approaching. 

There is a good chance that by the end of this decade we shall have a vaccine that protects against gonorrhea. 

Interferon, the name for a group of antiviral proteins existing in the body, was discovered in 1958, but the difficulty in producing it in sufficiently pure form and adequate quantities has been tremendous. It is only in the last few years that progress has been made by several manufacturers, and that we can look forward to treatment of various viral diseases, especially influenza, hepatitis B, herpes, and cancer.

But much work remains to be done. 

In cardiology there is hope that we shall be able to synthesize drugs related to bodily agents in order to attack the cause of hypertension and not merely lower blood pressure. In the case of arteriosclerosis, elevated plasma cholesterol has been identified as a leading risk factor. There is a good chance that drugs can be developed that will increase the high density lipoproteins that remove cholesterol from cells. Other efforts are to find a substance to inhibit a key enzyme required for cholesterol synthesis. 

In immunology we can look forward to better destruction of cancer cells with less harm done to the rest of the body. New approaches are being developed for the treatment of psoriasis and arthritis. More potent nonaddicting analgesics are being prepared. Promising work is being done in targeting administration of drugs more precisely to a diseased organ.

The new laboratory technique known as recombinant DNA will aid in the production of biological substances, such as insulin. The next 10 years in drug development will be dominated by the biological sciences; biochemists and medicinal chemists will change the natural compounds into usable drugs.
