A New Era For FDA: 

The Medical Device Amendments Of 1976 

Congress gave FDA a major new responsibility in 1976 when it enacted the Medical Device Amendments to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. 

Paul G. Rogers and Stephan E. Law ton describe how that law came about, and what principles it established for future health regulation. 

Mr. Rogers, a Florida Congressman from 1955 to 1979, was principal author of the legislation, having chaired the Subcommittee on Health and Environment from 1971 to 1978. He now is a partner in the Washington, D.C. law firm of Hogan and Hartson. Mr. 

Lawton, as chief counsel to the subcommittee, was the staff member principally responsible for developing the legislation. He is now with the Washington law firm of Pierson, Ball and Dowd. by Paul G. Rogers and

Stephan E. Lawton he Medical Device Amendments 

The 1976 represent one of the most specific and detailed health laws ever enacted by Congress. At first blush, the length of the medical device law-over 200 pages—seems to signal heavy regulation. To the contrary, the law demands that public protection be accomplished with the least degree of regulation necessary to provide safe and effective devices. 

Moreover, the legislation encourages indeed, mandates-cooperative efforts by industry, consumers, and Government to accomplish this purpose.

The amendments were a forerunner of the current call from the 

White House, Congress, industrybut mainly from the public itself-for as little regulation as possible and for a more cooperative approach between Government and industry in achieving the law's requirements. 

Why any law at all? There were several reasons. Prior to the amendments, the authority for device regulation by FDA was surprisingly sparse. Legal action could be taken only after a medical device had been offered for introduction into interstate commerce and then only when the device was "adulterated" or "misbranded." This authority resulted in the control of relatively simple devices which were grossly hazardous or the subject of unwarranted and fraudulent claims; it was insufficient, however, to assure, before marketing, the safety and effectiveness of more complicated (and lifesaving) devices being developed so rapidly as a result of the post-World 

War II revolution in biomedical tech nology. 

In addition, marketplace experience demonstrated some unfortunate consequences of insufficient premarket testing. Marketing of the Dalkon 

Shield, an intrauterine device, without proper testing reportedly resulted in a removal rate for medical reasons of 26.4 percent, an infection rate of 5 percent, 25 miscarriages, and 16 deaths. Substantial defects in cardiac pacemakers necessitated over 30 recalls, involving 23,000 units.

In the absence of specific legislative authority, FDA was required to attempt to regulate as drugs some products generally regarded as devices. Two court decisions in the late 

1960's upheld FDA's authority to regulate certain medical devices as drugs. While, of course, helpful to

FDA in fulfilling its mission of protecting the public, the potential of regulating all devices as drugs presented the threat of regulatory overkill. 

The kind of cooperation ultimately called for in the bill was employed during its drafting. Representatives of FDA, industry, and consumers met with the staff of the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment of the U.S. House of Representatives over a 3-month period to produce a bill that would serve as the focal point during the legislative process.

A 1970 study by the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare 

(HEW) formed the basis of the policy to be drafted. The report recommended that medical devices be classified into three distinct regulatory categories (those subject to "performance review," those which should be subject to "safety and performance standards," and those for which neither type of regulation was necessary). Devices would be regulated according to their classification. 

In addition, the study recommended that FDA be provided with statutory authority to require defect notification, adherence to good manufacturing practices, factory inspection, reports and recordkeeping, and registration of all device manufacturers.

Three instructions were issued to the drafting team:

First, the legislation was to be extremely specific and establish very

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 53

OU This display case, produced by FDA after enactment of the 1976 Medical

Device Amendments, illustrates the wide variety of products that fall under the law. Among the products are: a silicone breast implant (upper left), surgeon's gloves (lower left), an insulin syringe (upper right), and intrauterine devices (lower right). Also shown are other implants, a catheter, a sling, a total hip replacement, a thermometer, a pacemaker, a hearing aid, and a contact lens. clearly the authority and limitations of FDA concerning device regulation. This development was to some extent due to the propensity of FDA in the past to engage in "creative lawyering" in drafting regulations and in seeking court decisions to expand its authority. Also, there was the certain knowledge that the lawaffecting, as it did, thousands of medical devices-would receive close judicial scrutiny, and precision was necessary to avoid years of litigation over its meaning.

Second, the draft legislation was to be flexible and demand only the least regulation necessary with safety and effectiveness as the bottom line. This resulted from a general desire to avoid unnecessary controls, as well as a belief that innovation would suffer at the hands of over-regulation. 

Third, members of the public and representatives of the device field were to be assured of participation in the regulation of medical devices. 

This would contribute to better understanding by all parties and facilitate cooperative implementation of the new law.

The drafters adopted the HEW study's recommendations, albeit in somewhat modified form. They added authority for "down classification" of devices and mandated extensive use of advisory committees (with industry and consumer representatives) to provide advice on all important FDA decisions. The draft bill also authorized a product development protocol whereby devices could undergo testing under an FDA-sanctioned plan and receive quick approval if test results met expectations. It authorized FDA to order the repair, replacement, or refund of the purchase price of defective devices; it provided authority for the Agency to ban unsafe and fraudulent devices. 

The Subcommittee on Health and the Environment spent 4 days in hearings and 8 days in executive sessions to fully consider and develop the legislation. During subcommittee consideration, members of the subcommittee placed their imprints on the bill. One amendment required special treatment of "implantable" devices. A second concern involved treatment of articles which would fit the new law's definition of "device" but which were then being regulated as "drugs." A relatively simple solution was reached: so-called "transitional" provisions provided that articles which are devices under the new law's definition, but which were regulated as "drugs" prior to enactment of the new law, were placed into comparable regulatory status as devices. 

Also adopted was an amendment which facilitated the authority of States which had already imposed significant regulatory controls on medical devices to continue to do so-despite a general Federal preemption provision. Under this provision, much of California's Sherman Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Law, which in some instances includes more stringent requirements than the

Federal law, has been authorized by 

FDA to remain in force. 

Throughout the executive sessions, many subcommittee members expressed concern that implementation of the bill's provisions, though neces sary, could result in the demise of smaller manufacturers, which had been responsible for development of many innovative devices. It was read ily recognized that the degree or intensity of regulation should not be based on company size. Thus, the subcommittee adopted an amendment which required the establishment of an identifiable office to provide technical and other nonfinancial assistance to small manufacturers of medical devices to assist them in complying with the provisions of the new law. This office is now in exist. ence at FDA.

The legislation was agreed to unan imously by the subcommittee. The full committee gave rather quick ap proval and only token opposition developed on the House floor. The

House-Senate conference on the bill took only 2 days and the Medical 

Device Amendments were signed by

President Ford in May 1976. 

The cooperative spirit exhibited during preparation of the bill obviously facilitated its passage. To date, implementation of the law has reflected the industry-consumer-Go ernment cooperation intended by the Congress. We believe that this coop erative development and implement tion of regulatory laws-as well as the concept that only the least nece sary regulation to achieve public pr tection should be authorized-will b mandated by the Congress in future health legislation.

Challenge For The 80's: 

Controlling Animal Drugs 

The issues facing FDA's Bureau of Veterinary Medicine (BVM) involve fundamental concepts in public health protection and must often be confronted on the frontiers of scientific understanding: the benefit vs. the risk of cancer-causing drugs given to livestock to make them grow faster and cheaper; and the potentially disastrous consequences to human health of bacteria grown resistant to antibiotics because of the regular use of these drugs in animal feed. These were among the issues Dr. Lester Crawford grappled with while director of BVM from 1978 to 1980. Now back at the Col lege of Veterinary Medicine of the 

University of Georgia, Dr. Crawford here reflects on these and other issues facing BVM in the 1980's. 

by Lester M. Crawford uring its 14 years, FDA's Bureau of Veterinary Medicine (BVM) 

has forged a comprehensive program designed to protect the public health with minimal burden on industry. In its attempts to steer clear of technology-forcing issues, however, the bureau has sometimes been criticized. 

And in sharing authority over animal drugs with another part of FDA (the 

Bureau of Foods), as well as with the

U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Environmental Protection Agen cy, management problems have understandably arisen. But, all in all, BVM has exerted notable leadership in livestock agriculture regulation and has emerged as a world leader in that area. 

The burden of that recently recognized leadership is twofold: (1) the bureau must intensify efforts to reduce to simplest terms the priority issues in the animal drug and animal feed arena; and (2) the bureau must insist on continued efficiency in all its operations, especially lines of management responsibility. Implicit in these undertakings must be the equanimity to identify and accept those areas best left unregulated. 

Most of the cares that infested the 

1960's and 1970's for BVM devolved from the stipulation-stated in the 

Delaney Clause of the Federal Food, 

Drug, and Cosmetic Act-that no cancer-causing substances may be added to food. As it applies to animal drugs and medicated feed, the clause is modified to state that no cancer-causing agents may be administered to livestock if residues of those substances can be detected in human food derived from the animals.

Recent developments in cancer research, as well as the ability to detect ever smaller amounts of potentially carcinogenic compounds through improvements in analytical methodology, tend to render obsolescent the absolutism of Delaney. Fine tuning, if not repeal, is in order. Congress is the proper forum for these considerations. 

FDA's attempt to realistically address the issue of residues of cancercausing additives in livestock products-the so-called Sensitivity-of 

Method (SOM) proposed regu lation from the beginning has been beset with difficulties. The proposal has become a focus for debate among the affected parties-animal drug manufacturers, livestock producers, and Government regulators. FDA's intent in the proposal is to assure that any residues escaping detection by an approved analytical method would pose "no significant risk" of cancer to humans. But the untempered furor over this attempt to deal with the absolutism of Delaney-and the ensuing litigation-is proof that 

FDA needs Congressional direction. 

It is my personal opinion that Congress should codify the level of risk or move towards repeal or substitution of the Delaney Clause. And, I believe the administration should proffer a recommended course of ac tion, vis-a-vis Delaney, at the earliest instance. Appropriate action on De laney will perhaps ameliorate such is sues as SOM, cyclic review of animal drugs to see that they meet current definitions of safety, and a plethora of New Animal Drug applications that are either in jeopardy or have been pending approval for too long. 

But not all of BVM's dilemmas derive from Delaney. The low-level penicillin-tetracycline issue has gone on too long. The bureau's concern is that continuous, low-level use of these antibiotics in animal feed may contribute to antibiotic resistance among bacteria infecting humans, possibly rendering ineffective the invaluable therapeutic agents traditionally used to combat human diseases. 

The legal maneuvering over this issue over the past several years has sapped governmental resources and confused the public. The National 

Academy of Sciences found these low-level uses in animals could not be shown to be safe (or unsafe); therefore, the law requires restrictions. The Congress, however, has forebade the proposed restrictions. 

Congress must be encouraged to allow BVM to proceed or to specifically exempt these uses of penicillin and tetracycline from the purview of FDA. 

Perhaps the most formidable prospective problem is the definition of authority in animal drug regulation. 

All too often, BVM has been held hostage by other government units with overlapping responsibility. The only justification for this kind of duplication is the concept of checks an balances. That concept, however, is not applicable to units operating within the same branch of government, i.e., the executive. 

As the leadership of BVM braces 474 YDS 12 12 2 

56/ June 1981/ FDA Consumer

for the future and surveys those problems that have persisted, there should be an urgency for a housecleaning of issues and an urgency to look at those areas that need not be regulated. In that regard, in thinking of my 2-year tenure at BVM, I wished I had remembered Eric Severeid's law more often ("There are no problems, only solutions").

Although there clearly are problems that need resolution, the real challenge for the 1980's resides in separating those regulatory issues. that can best be resolved by the Government from those that might be better resolved by a deregulated in dustry. The Second Generation of 

Medicated Feeds regulation provides a case in point. Practice had shown the enormous volume of paperwork involved in BVM's regulation of medicated feeds was largely counter productive. The revised regulations are intended to concentrate FDA's efforts on those areas of serious public health concern, while lessening regulatory controls where risk to humans is minimal.

There are other areas within 

BVM's purview that should likewise be considered for refocusing, such as animal nutrition regulation, surveillance of nonfood animal drug usage, surveillance of animal vaccine production, and cooperative programs with USDA for development of essential drugs of limited commercial importance.

The major issues for the next decade will include approval and regulation of alternatives to animal drugs as we presently know them; the establishment of risk levels for multiple carcinogen exposure; the safety of genetic manipulation in animal husbandry; and the role of BVM in societal debates such as the ethics of animal testing, the humaneness of intensive rearing of livestock, and the use of antibiotics in animal feed.

Current Issues In Biologics Regulation 

Federal regulation of biologics (substances, such as vaccines, serums, and toxoids, prepared from living organisms) predates that of food and drugs, but the issues facing biologics regulation still are controversial. Dr. June 

Osborn describes some of the progress that's been made in biologics development over the past decades, and sets forth the issues that are still being discussed. The author is a professor of medical microbiology and pediatrics and associate dean of the Graduate School at the University of Wisconsin at Madison. by June Osborn iologics regulation presents spe- 'cial challenges that distinguish it from other areas of FDA concern. In no other area of medical science do the brilliant advances of molecular biology, biochemistry, microbiology, and immunology focus so directly on avenues of potential promise to be explored; nor is there a realm of biomedicine in which greater potential controversy exists. The very successes of biologics have created an environment in the United States in which the population feels safe from epidemic threat but, by the same token, has forgotten the earlier times in which dread epidemic diseases made the slight risks in preventive immunization programs seem trivial. 

The colorful history of our arrival at this juncture is punctuated by misadventures which have served as intermittent reminders of the need for careful regulation. Even before the 

58/ June 1981 / FDA Consumer

Food and Drugs Act of 1906, an accident with tetanus vaccine spurred 

Congress to enact a Virus-Toxin Law in 1902 which gave the U.S. Public 

Health Service regulatory power over biologic products. Subsequently, laboratories for biologics control evolved, as did their statutory authority. But it was not until 1955 when a failure to achieve full inactivation of one lot of polio virus resulted in an epidemic of paralytic disease in vaccine recipients that a separate Division of Biologic Standards (DBS) was established within the National Institutes of Health. 

In 1972 the DBS mandate was transferred to the Food and Drug

Administration and the present Bu reau of Biologics was created. Thus, while governmental regulation of biologic products predates most other 

FDA activities, it is a relatively new mandate for the Agency itself.

The creation of the Bureau of Biologics in the early 1970's was followed quickly by the organization of an orderly and intensive efficacy review of all licensed biologic products.

Because of the exceptionally broad range of expertise involved in biologics and the underlying scientific base, review panels were drawn from all reaches of the academic community; and because of the intense public interest in vaccines and in blood products, consumer and industrial participation was included as well. The reports generated by these exhaustive reviews are in process of publication in the FEDERAL REGISTER and their recommendations provide a state-ofthe-art assessment of currently licensed biologic products. 

The first years of FDA control were also distinguished by the establishment of standards for blood and blood products. This important area of medicine, which had advanced in parallel with the creation of vaccines and the development of modern immunology, had not been uniformly subject to Federal regulation. But by 

1974 the Bureau of Biologics had developed enforceable standards for blood banks and for the plasmapheresis industry, thereby assuring greater donor protection.

The scientific future of biologic products is every bit as promising as in the past: recombinant DNA research holds the promise that gene products such as interferon will soon become available as potential therapeutic agents. Viruses which have proved refractory to adaptation to tissue culture technology can now be replicated by other means through use of the tools of molecular biology.

The creation of new approaches such as hybridoma techniques for efficient production of large quantities of specific antibodies reopens the realm of passive immunization for the control of infectious diseases. One of the major accomplishments in the blood field has been the evolution of highly sensitive procedures for detecting hepatitis viruses and the subsequent development of experimental vaccines. 

With this exciting promise it is urgent that the special threats to biologics development and regulatory control be recognized and addressed, for it is conceivable that misapplied and restrictive control could thwart the promise that these scientific advances hold. 

Litigation and the threat of punishing damages in the courts have added to a growing disinclination on the part of the pharmaceutical industry to continue their investment in biologics research and manufacture. Human subjects' participating in developmental research is increasingly circumscribed, and the difficulties of organizing and conducting adequate trials of experimental biologic products are especially affected by these trends. Finally, animal research as an alternative approach is hampered on the one hand by cost and scarcity of primates and other key species, and on the other by resurgent antivivisec tionism. 

These threats to continued progress in biologics make it all the more important that public involvement in issues of vaccine use be maintained and increased, so that discussion of benefit-risk considerations can proceed intelligently. An awareness must be maintained through public education of the successes in preventive medicine we currently enjoy: the absence of epidemic disease must not be allowed to weaken public health programs through inattention. Most important, consumer involvement in future biologics developments must be sufficiently sophisticated to facilitate the making of difficult regulatory decisions which are sure to attend continued progress.

WA FS FILE The 'C' In The FDC Act 

The 1938 law had three product categories in its title: food, drugs, and cosmetics. Although there has been a major focus on food and drug regulation, there has been considerably less on cosmetics. Stephen H. McNamara writes that cosmetics generally pose fewer risks than other FDA-regulated products, and that present laws and regulatory programs provide ample public protection. The author is senior vice president and general counsel of the Cosmetic, Toiletry and Fragrance 

Association. by Stephen H. McNamara

YALL 

egulation of cosmetics became an 

Regulation of cosmetics beca, wit 

FDA responsibility in 1938, with passage of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Subsequently, the

Color Additive Amendments of 1960, the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act of 1966, and succeeding FDA regulations all expanded on those basic requirements.

The FDC Act provides that a cosmetic shall be deemed to be adulterated if it bears or contains "any poisonous or deleterious substance which may render it injurious to users" under expected conditions of use. (This provision does not apply to coal-tar hair dyes that bear a statutory caution concerning safe use.) 

In addition, the Color Additive 

Amendments of 1960 provide that a color additive (other than a coal-tar hair dye) may not be used in a cosmetic product unless it has been approved for cosmetic use by FDA. 

FDA regulations supplement these statutory provisions by requiring that each cosmetic ingredient and finished product "shall be adequately substan tiated for safety prior to marketing." 

Pursuant to the FDC Act, the Fair

Packaging and Labeling Act of 1966, and FDA regulations, the labeling of a cosmetic product is required to include the following information: (1) a statement of identity; (2) the net quantity of contents; (3) the name and place of business of the manufac turer, packer, or distributor; (4) a listing of the ingredients contained in the product; and for certain products (5) cautionary statements or warnings concerning safe use. 

Cosmetics bear more informative labeling for consumers than any other article regulated by FDA. For

Panel reports assessing the safety of cosmetic ingredients are published by the CIR, following peer review, in a scientific journal.

The cosmetic industry believes that existing laws and FDA regulatory programs governing cosmetics, coupled with the industry's commitment to self-regulation and product safety (as reflected in programs such as 

CIR), provide an ample measure of public protection. Cosmetics generally present a very low level of risk, especially when compared with other products regulated by FDA.

Furthermore, this innovative industry, built on a highly competitive market subject to sudden changes, needs to be free to introduce new products without unnecessary regulatory delays. The cosmetic industry looks forward to an era of continued growth founded on the production of safe and informatively labeled products that respond to consumer needs and desires.

Getting A Grasp On Man-Made Radiation 

Man has been exposed to radiation ever since creation, but it's only relatively recently that we have been able to create radiation. And with that ability came the need to regulate.

Mark Barnett describes the current 

FDA programs in this important area.

The author is assistant director for educational and communications projects in FDA's Bureau of Radiological 

Health. 

by Mark Barnett

The human species has been ex- The posed to natural background radiation from cosmic rays and terrestrial sources since its beginnings on Earth. But it wasn't until the turn of the century-coincidentally, about the same time the Food and Drugs

Act was passed that people were exposed to man-made radiation. Almost immediately after radioactive materials and x-rays were discovered, they began to be used widely in medicine and industry, largely without knowledge of or regard for their hazards, and without Governmental control. 

By the 1920's, the unfortunate effect of this early, promiscuous application of the new radiation sources was taking its toll: cancers and other ill effects began to show up among the first medical and industrial workers exposed to radiation on the job.

By this time, it was generally known that high and repeated doses of radiation could lead to long-term harm, but the idea that smaller amounts of radiation could be hazardous was still unappreciated. 

The attitude that radiation was harmful in large amounts but "safe" at lower levels largely prevailed until the late 1940's, when the development of atomic weapons signaled the dawn of the nuclear era. The wartime bombings of Japan, and the concern over nuclear testing fallout in the postwar years, focused public and scientific concern on the possibility of delayed effects from small amounts of radiation. (Long-term risks were not totally unknown in those days-the genetic effects of radiation were discovered in 1927, and in 1940 two Public Health Service sci entists, in a remarkably farsighted article, warned that "genetic effects may have no threshold.") 

During the atomic testing era of the 1950's and early '60's, the Public

Health Service played an active role in monitoring and assessing the effects of radioactive fallout. By 1958, widespread concern about low-level radiation effects led to a consolidation of protective activities, and this in turn resulted in the establishment of the Division of Radiological 

Health; the division later became the 

Bureau of Radiological Health, which in 1971 was transferred to FDA. 

Although measuring fallout levels and assessing their health impact was the primary job of the division in the 

1950's and early '60's, it was also recognized that roughly 90 percent of the population's exposure to manmade radiation comes from medical sources, primarily diagnostic x-rays. 

For this reason, the Public Health

Service in those days worked closely with State and local radiation control agencies (as it still does) in checking on the safety of x-ray equipment.

In 1968, the Radiation Control for 

Health and Safety Act was passed, a major milestone in the development of radiation protection activities at the Federal level. The act set two precedents. First, it expanded the 

Bureau's mandate beyond x-rays and radioactive materials to cover a broad spectrum of radiation, including microwave, sound, and light. This meant that products such as microwave ovens, sunlamps, and ultrasound devices would come under control. And it authorized the establishment of manufacturer performance standards for these products, assuring a basic degree of safety when they leave the factory.

In the 1970's, the Bureau began to explore several new directions in the medical radiation area. First, it embarked on an educational program to provide quality assurance tools and techniques to medical facilities to help improve the diagnostic quality of x-rays and minimize unnecessary exposure. At the same time, the Bureau began to focus on an even more basic issue: what are the medical indications for various kinds of x-ray examinations? To answer this kind of question, criteria to help decide when to order x-rays are being developed by expert panels of physicians convened by the Bureau, and through

Bureau-sponsored research grants at medical centers across the United States. Finally, the Bureau has embarked on a nationwide program to educate consumers about how to help minimize unnecessary medical radiation exposure to themselves and their families.

This new emphasis on the consumer-on informing people about the benefits and possible risks of various radiation sources in their daily lives, from sunlamps to x-rays-will be even more important in the future, as technology provides us with more and more radiation-emitting products. Beyond assuring that these products are as safe as current techniques can make them, it will be 

FDA's job to help consumers understand benefits and risks, and make intelligent decisions about their own radiation exposure. 

62 June 1981 FDA Consumer

Federal involvement in health hazards of radioactivity began circa 1913, with reports of cancer contracted by luminous watch dial painters who moistened brushes with their lips. The National Consumers League led a fight for regulation.

Regulation: Looking To The Future 

What broad factors are going to influence regulation in the remaining decades of this century and beyond?

Richard M. Cooper describes some of these influences and how he expects they will affect FDA and its sister agencies. The author, former general counsel of FDA, is an attorney with the Washington, D. C. law firm of 

Williams and Connolly. 

by Richard M. Cooper 

If you can look into the seeds of time, And say which grain will grow, and which will not, Speak then to me. -Banquo to the Three Witches 

Macbeth, I, iii.

Aber n awesome request and, as Macbeth and Cassandra learned to their sorrow, one not likely to profit the asker or the asked. But political prophecy being a popular national pastime, FDA CONSUMER may be forgiven for having asked and I may be forgiven for responding as best I can. 

Start with the economy, the machinery that produces goods and services. The market is primary. 

Without it, there would be no regulation and no need for it; it is the object on which regulation acts. It is also primary in that it provides the things people most want-food, clothing, housing, medical care, transportation, and so on. Regulation cannot provide these things-though it can bring about the provision of other, "secondary" things (some also highly desired), such as a greater degree of workplace safety, a more honest securities market, a cleaner environment and greater purity in foods and drugs. 

The regulatory process as a whole applies a variety of standards to the economic processes by which goods and services are produced and distributed. Thereby, it affects not only the processes, but also the mix of goods and services offered in the marketplace. As a result of regulation, some goods and services are not offered at all, some are offered at higher prices (and thus are available to fewer people), a few are offered at lower prices (and thus are available to more people), and some are offered that otherwise wouldn't be. 

For a number of reasons having little to do with regulation, we live in a time of unacceptably high inflation, which is likely to continue for the rest of the century. Inflation means that consumers find it more expensive to buy desired goods and services. The result is a general dissatisfaction with the limits of what money will buy. That dissatisfaction has political consequences, one of which is a search for ways to improve the power of consumers to buy the primary goods and services offered by the economy. Popular discontent with prices puts pressure on politicians to make trade-offs between primary goods and services and the secondary ones brought about by regulation. The purpose of these efforts is to make primary goods and services easier to buy by reducing the regulatory demand that productive resources be diverted toward secondary objectives. 

I think it fair to interpret the Presidential and Congressional elections of 1980, together with the emergence of an intellectually respectable set of antiregulatory public policy recommendations, as warranting some loosening of regulatory controls on the economy. This is a democracy in which voters and responsible ideas have their chance. If they call for more primary goods and less regulation, then the political process will and should respond. Moreover, distrust of regulation is not a monopoly of conservatives. It was William O. 

Douglas who said, "[A]s I read the

Constitution, one of its essential purposes was to take the government off the backs of people and keep it off." 

I suggest one set of exceptions to this general view. Certain fundamental rights, mainly those protected by the Constitution, but a few others as well, are so important-essential to even a rudimentary notion of justice that reasonable regulations to assure them ought to be removed from the vicissitudes of politics. I refer here principally to regulation of 

State electoral laws to assure the right to vote, the core regulations that seek to assure equal employment opportunity, regulations to assure equal access to the benefits of government programs, and regulations to require some degree of fairness in broadcasting concerning politics and public issues. There is room for debate about the merits and public acceptability of regulations providing for affirmative action, busing, bi-lingual education or inclusion of women in military programs, but I see no mandate for changing our society's commitment to implement nondiscrimination.

The efforts to reduce regulation will be pursued in two general ways-across-the-board and sectorby-sector. The across-the-board efforts, commonly known as "regulatory reform," are attempts to change the mix of primary and secondary goods and services without facing up to the detailed consequences of such a change. The mechanisms proposed in such efforts-amendments to the

Administrative Procedures Act, re quirements for impact statements of various sorts, sunset, legislative veto, regulatory budget-are intended to stem the flow of new regulations by making it harder to regulate or by forcing reconsideration of the need for regulatory programs. These efforts may have some marginal effect, but-as the lack of passionate public controversy about them reflectsthey don't get to the heart of the 

64/ June 1981 FDA Consumer

ol matter; they will not bring about a substantial shift of resources back from secondary goods and services to primary; and some, such as moratoria on regulation, may even hinder efforts to reduce regulation (and delay innovation where new product approvals must take the form of regulations-for example, food additives and antibiotics). The recent experience with the delayed extension of 

FDA's provisional list for color additives is instructive.

Substantial shifts will occur only when the substance of regulatory standards (whether legislatively or administratively imposed) is addressed sector by sector, statute by statute. Then the tough political fights will be fought, the interests of different segments of society will clash, and we will see how the political process responds to the contending forces.

The overall political interest in reducing inflation will clash on many fronts with other social goals. Sometimes one interest will prevail, sometimes another; most often, the result will be ad hoc compromises. 

The biggest blow to the anti-inflation forces will come in the field of energy. Decontrol of oil prices means the inflation numbers will be significantly worse. The overriding interests here are national security and the need to cushion the economy against interruptions of foreign oil supply by stimulating increased domestic energy production and raising the cost of energy consumption to induce conservation.

Other types of economic regulation have for many years served little purpose other than protection of inefficiency or prevention of competition.

Such regulation of airlines (excluding airline safety) is already on its way out. Substantial deregulation of banking, communications, and trucking has taken place, and more should come. Further deregulation of sur- 

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 65

face transportation is in order. 

In the fields of health and safety regulation, a variety of discrete battles will be fought. The heavy hitters in the inflation field are the Occupa tional Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and they are likely to receive the brunt of the anti-inflation attack. 

As the proportion of unionized workers in the labor force declines, and as the political power of the unions declines with it (particularly relative to the power of corporations acting through their political action committees), OSHA is likely to see its authority cut by the Congress. In administering the Occupational 

Safety and Health Act, the new administration probably will be more willing to be satisfied with individual protective equipment (as an alternative to engineering controls) than was the Carter OSHA. Moreover, the Su preme Court's decision in the benzene case last July probably marks the beginning of an era of stricter judicial review of health and safety regulation. The strictness will be focused initially and most intensively on 

OSHA, but will spread to other agencies as well. If President Reagan makes an appointment or two to the

Supreme Court, this trend is likely to be imposed even more forcefully. 

The future of EPA is more difficult to predict. Certainly major industrial interests will press hard for a softening of environmental standards through both administrative and legislative action. And some relaxation will occur to facilitate a productionoriented approach to the energy problem (particularly with respect to mining and burning coal and production of synthetic fuels), and to help the beleaguered auto industry. And as real food prices soar in coming years, pesticides are likely to be regulated more leniently. 

There are powerful countervailing forces, however. Concern for the environment is a product of the affluence of the upper middle class, a politically influential and growing segment of society. Much of the likely environmental degradation as a result of energy development (and the MX missile system) will occur in the West, the heartland of the rejuvenated Republican Party. Whether the West will peacefully acquiesce in such degradation on a large scale remains to be seen. In general, we can expect to see hand-to-hand combat over standards for air, water, pesticides, and chemicals generally, waste disposal, and so on: and the probable outcome is some softening of existing standards and a slow-down in the rate at which new standards are imposed.

In the field of food and drug regulation, major change is unlikely. 

Congress may relax the requirement that the effectiveness of new drugs be proven with scientific vigor. The 

Carter Administration (with the support of Senator Kennedy) proposed some relaxation for "breakthrough" drugs. So the issue is now drawn as one of degree rather than principle.

In the new political climate created by the 1980 elections, the relaxation is likely to be greater. Some "proof" of effectiveness will continue to be required, however, because even the 

Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Asso ciation doesn't want to legalize laetrile. 

Food safety is a minefield for legis lators. The Delaney Clause is a pop ular whipping boy, but its repeal would have little effect if the general safety clause were left intact. Will 

Congressmen vote to repeal the provisions that food and color additives be shown to be safe? In practice, the issue may be defused if FDA makes aggressive use of the discretion given it by the D.C. Circuit in the acrylonitrile case in 1979. That decision (whose general approach was subsequently fortified by the Supreme 

Court's benzene decision) allows

FDA to disregard de minimis migration of carcinogenic food packaging materials into food. The principle is obviously extendable.

Some critics of current food safety regulation will be dissatisfied even with that degree of loosening up and will press for broad risk-benefit standards. Indeed, pressures for riskbenefit decisionmaking are building across the field of health and safety regulation. The idea has undoubted intuitive appeal: the costs of regulation are too high, and it is only rational for regulators to take costs into account and to impose a regulation only when its benefits (in reducing risk) outweigh its costs. 

What are seriously underestimated in most discussions of risk-benefit decisionmaking, however, are the costs of the technique itself-the vesting of broad and virtually unreviewable discretion in regulatory officials, the imposition of large transaction costs in connection with each risk-benefit decision, and the great unpredictability of risk-benefit decisions in view of the uncertainties in the analysis of individual risks and benefits and the additional uncertainty as to how the various quantifiable and nonquantifiable factors will be valued. In some settings, risk-benefit decisionmaking is the only sensible approach, but enthusiasts ought to review closely the history of the technique as applied to pesticides. My own view is that over the next few years new requirements for risk-benefit analysis will be enacted by Congress and imposed by the courts in a variety of areas of health and safety regulation, but over the longer term disenchantment with the application of the technique will grow; and, perhaps under the stimulus of the doctrine of unconstitutional delegation, we will eventually see a movement back toward more detailed congressional specification of 

HAL I EL E F 1 

: en: ALI # 3883 

66/ June 1981 FDA Consumer

regulatory decisionmaking rules. 

In the field of health and safety regulation, such specification has commonly taken the form of a riskbased standard (for example, that food additives be shown to be safe).

Thus far efforts to define standards like "safe" or "reasonable risk" in quantitive terms have not succeeded. 

After several years of trying, FDA still has not adopted a sensitivity-ofthe-method regulation. But progress is being made, and we can expect to see over the next couple of decades increased analytical sophistication and increased ability to design studies to yield the kind of data needed for quantitive estimations of risk. The difficulty is that the actual generation of the data is prohibitively expensive. 

A breakthrough in the science of toxicology (particularly cancer testing) through increased reliability of shortterm assays, for example, could open the way for greatly expanded use of quantitive risk estimation, and thus for more tightly drawn statutory standards for regulation. 

Labeling strategies are also a currently popular approach to dealing with health and safety risks. In some circumstances, they are the optimal approach, but in others they are likely to be ineffective; and they almost always raise questions of social justice (as to the people who can't use them effectively). We can expect to see increased use of labeling as an alternative to other regulatory techniques (bans, stricter standards); the test will come when, in the case of some labeling approaches, it is determined after several years of experience that the labels have not significantly reduced the health or safety problem that created the need for regulatory action in the first place. 

A fair test of the Reagan Administration's philosophical commitment to labeling strategies will be its handling of FDA's patient package insert (PPI) program. Perhaps FDA has not yet found the optimal way to provide information to consumers of prescription drugs. But an administration committed to shifting decisionmaking from the Government to the people cannot jettison or pare down the PPI program without inviting the comment that it has no consistent philosophy at all. Similarly, an administration committed to reducing inflation and assisting State governments ought to maintain the informational activities grouped under FDA's therapeutic equivalence program. 

The regulatory reform discussions during the Carter Administration led to a broad consensus supporting a number of "innovative" regulatory techniques. These have achieved the status of "simply good government, and their use is likely to expand. The techniques include: use of performance standards rather than detailed specification of means of compliance, use of economic incentives rather than "command and control" regulation, modifying general requirements to suit the circumstances of different groups within the regulated sector (for example, less onerous requirements for small businesses), and in- 12 creased opportunities for effective public participation in the development of regulations. In gross, these techniques may not do much to reduce inflation, but at the margin they should make regulation more intelligent, more responsive to the complexities of the world, and somewhat less irritating to those regulated. 

One type of regulatory innovation that may yield significant economic savings is the substitution of economic incentives for traditional regulatory requirements. EPA has pioneered in this area by developing the "bubble concept," under which the various emissions from a plant are subject to a single overall limit, but the firm operating the plant decides how to allocate the permitted quantity of pollution among the various sources of emissions. This flexibility should enable firms to minimize the costs of compliance. Last October EPA again broke new ground by proposing that certain uses of chlorofluorocarbons be regulated through the sale of permits, which could be resold in the open market. EPA's assumption is that the permits would end up allowing the economically 

FDA Consumer / June 1981 / 67

HALTα ? AHV712 7 24217 most valuable uses, and that as their prices rose firms would seek alternatives to chlorofluorocarbons. In these ways, the approach may be more efficient than a system of bans-withexceptions. Coordination of regulatory activities carried out by agencies was begun during the Carter years. The

Regulatory Analysis Review Group (RARG) in the Executive Office of the President tried to harmonize major regulations with overall economic policy. The Regulatory Council was a creature of the agencies themselves, designed to provide a measure of voluntary coordination to stave off further intervention by the White

House. Other interagency coopera tive efforts also sprang up (for exam ple, the Interagency Regulatory Liai son Group, consisting of EPA, OSHA, FDA, the Consumer Product 

Safety Commission, and the Depart ment of Agriculture's Food Safety and Quality Service (FSQS)); ad hoc cooperative efforts among FDA,

FSQS, and the Federal Trade Com mission. On the whole, these efforts had some impact, did some good. 

But it cannot be said that the regula tory activities of Executive Branch agencies (let alone the independent commissions) are coordinated to any substantial extent. 

Sooner or later some President will undertake to bring about substantial coordination. And he (or she) will find that the way to do it will be to vest the responsibility not in a staff office like RARG or in the Regulatory Council, but in a line institution: 

the Office of Management and 

Budget (OMB). Then we should see regulatory coordination (and control) assume an importance within OMB akin to its responsibilities for the budget, general management, and legislative coordination. Regulatory coordination would become an everyday part of the workings of the Government and a channel for Presidential power. This is the direction the current administration is taking, but it remains to be seen whether the impetus will extend beyond the review of a small number of highly visible regulations. 

Finally, I foresee private and quasi-private institutions playing increasingly important roles in the reg ulatory process. The National Acad emy of Sciences continues to provide a forum for scientists in the private sector to articulate the state of scientific knowledge and advise on issues of public policy. Advisory commit tees to agencies-consisting of private individuals serving temporarily as special government employeesplay a similar role. Some industries are establishing more or less independent organizations to develop data for use in the regulatory process. 

Perhaps the most interesting recent venture to enter the regulatory field is the Health Effects Institute, an in dependent, nonprofit corporation created and funded jointly by EPA and the manufacturers of automobiles and truck engines. The purpose of the institute is to conduct (through contracts and grants) scientific research on the health effects of motor vehicle emissions. The institute will have its own scientific committees which with the concurrence of a board of directors will set research priorities, design protocols, and conduct peer review. The institute will simply produce research, with the expectation that the research will become the agreed-upon basis for debates about regulatory policy. EPA, the industry, public interest groups, and other interested parties will, of course, remain free to criticize the research, to argue about the significance of the results, and to debate about what should be done. But, if all goes well, the quality of discussion will be greatly improved by the generation of the basic data under the nonadversarial auspices of an independent institution able to draw on the best available scientific knowledge and talent.

The Health Effects Institute may become a model for similar government-industry cooperative efforts in other regulated areas. If so, the result is likely to be better and more broadly accepted regulations. 

I have dealt here only with what has traditionally been regarded as "regulation" commands and controls issuing from "regulatory" agencies. Many other kinds of governmental action, however, effectively regulate behavior, even though they are not cast as "regulations"-tax provisions, grants and subsidies, tariffs and trigger prices, procurement policies, and so on. In terms of economic impact and the "hassle factor," these areas offer far more significant opportunities for reducing costs to taxpayers and consumers and for reform generally than does traditional regulation. 

Finally, any prediction about the future of regulation must allow for the unpredictable-the surprises in store for us in the toxicology and analytical chemistry labs, in the conduct of hazard-producing activities, in the experience of people as they encounter toxic substances and hazardous conditions in their daily lives. The capacity of fortuitous events to alter the agenda for governmental action is astonishing-as history from Elixir

Sulfanilamide to thalidomide to 

Three Mile Island and the 1979 infant formula recall testifies.

The Notebook 

FDA is feeling the effects of inflation in more ways than one. Effective April 13, the fees FDA charges manufacturers for the certification of antibiotic drugs for human and animal use have gone up. Ac cording to a March 13 FEDERAL REGISTER notice, the certification program had an operating deficit of $617,000 in fiscal year 1980, while the anticipated deficit for 1981 was expected to be $600,000. 

July 1 is the date by which manufacturers of canned peas and canned dry peas must comply with FDA's amended standards of identity, quality, and fill of container. The new regulation, issued June 27, 1980, provides for specified nutritive carbohydrate sweeteners, garnishes of other vegetables, continues to permit artificial color to be used but requires declaration as part of the name of the food, and establishes a limit for blond and yellow peas. Confirmation of the effective date was published in the April 10 FEDERAL 

REGISTER. 

A new product may be in the making. T. H. 

Richards Processing Co., Sacramento, Calif., has been given a temporary permit to market test tomato juice from concentrate. The permit, announced by FDA in the March 17 FEDERAL REGISTER, allows marketing of the juice in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oregon, and Washington.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) issued a notice in the March 26 FEDERAL REGISTER 

that it intends to keep in its regulations the treatment of cardiac dysfunction by iodine 131 as an accepted therapeutic procedure. FDA in 1976 reclassified this procedure as lacking substantial evidence of effectiveness; however, NRC's Advisory Committee on the

Medical Use of Isotopes, the American College of 

Cardiology, and several physicians have recommended the treatment should remain in the NRC regulations. 

The FEDERAL REGISTER notice indicated that FDA's action should not be taken as a definite conclusion that the treatment is ineffective. 

■FDA is proposing to amend the biologics regulations to increase the permissible level of aluminum in licensed products in order to make the biologics standards consistent with those of the World Health Organization (WHO). Aluminum in the form of aluminum hydroxide, aluminum phosphate, or alum is commonly used as an adjuvant in such products as diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and pertussis vaccine to increase their immunogenicity. The notice appeared in the April 28 FEDERAL REGISTER. 

Under new regulations issued March 11 by the 

Nuclear Regulatory Commission, NRC-licensed hospi tals and medical research institutions will have greater leeway in disposing of liquid scintillation media and animal carcasses containing tracer levels of hydrogen-3 (tritium) or carbon-14. In the past, these items were sent to a radioactive waste burial ground or were incinerated or buried onsite with special NRC authorization. The new regulations permit disposal of specified concentrations of these materials without regard to their radioactivity. ■In the color additive department, FDA has proposed to permanently list caramel as a color additive for general use in cosmetics and has issued a final rule putting D&C Orange No. 10 and D&C Orange No. 

11 on the permanent list for use in externally applied drugs and cosmetics. Both actions were detailed in the 

March 27 FEDERAL REGISTER, which also contained a list of 23 colors whose provisional listing has been extended to allow for completion of scientific investigations. 

Anyone who wants to comment on proposed changes in FDA's soda water standard and in the sta-

The Federal Trade Commission has terminated its rulemaking on advertising of OTC drugs and will prosecute unfair and deceptive drug ads on an individual case basis, according to an April 29 announcement. The proposed rule would have prohibited any claim in OTC drug ads that FDA does not allow in labels. However, as FDA completes its analysis of additional categories of drugs, the

FDA has begun a teletypewriter. (TTY) service to make it easier for consumers with speech or hearing handicaps to communicate with the Agency. The service enables handicapped consumers to contact FDA by means of a special telephone-typewriter machine. By dialing (301) 443-1818, a hearing-impaired or deaf person or one who cannot speak can type a message over the phone; the message is printed on the FDA 

TTY in FDA headquarters in Rockville, Md. FDA staff can, in turn, type a response over the phone to the caller. The TTY is in operation from 8 a.m. to

■Generic drug prescriptions have nearly doubled since 1966, a report in DRUG TOPICS magazine indi cates. In 1966, generics accounted for only 6.4 percent of all prescriptions, but in 1980 generics got 12.4 percent of the market. The 1980 total was 174,762,000 new and refilled generic prescriptions dispensed. That was up 5.9 percent from 1979. Leo McIntyre, drug and cosmetic industry specialist with the U.S. Department of Commerce, predicts that generic drug sales will comprise 25 percent of the prescription market by

CHOCOLATE Has A Rich History And Certain Standards 

Chocoholics are found in all corners of the globe today. But the sweet stuff is relatively new to most of mankind, having come out of the New World.

Today it is grown in a number of countries and processed into a number of products. In the United States, standards are set for chocolate and chocolate products by the Food and

Drug Administration. 

by Harold Hopkins old, silver, and precious stones were not the only loot that found its way into the insatiate Spanish maw as the Americas were opened to European exploitation early in the 16th century. One unforgettable treasure was a little brown bean that some natives of the warmer regions of the New World set great store by. From the bean they made a bitterish but flavorful drink known in the Nahuatl tongue of the Aztecs of

Mexico as cacahuatl, and also as xocoatl-whence the cacao or cocoa and the chocolate of today. 

This delightful plunder, upon its introduction to the court of his Catholic majesty, Charles V, so entranced the Spanish nobility that they kept its joys and even its existence a secret from outsiders for nearly a hundred years. Even when at last the beans were spilled and the rest of Europe found out, chocolate remained for many years a prerogative of the wealthy and influential. 

They were only doing what comes naturally. Those who had chocolate and those who did not were as fixed in the hierarchy of the Aztecs as among the royalty of Europe. Accounts of the possessive ways of both 

Aztecs and Spaniards over this delicacy become a little more believable when you look at how chocolate today can affect the behavior of your kids and mine, my spouse and yours, and even thee and me. People who in the past have heaped praise upon chocolate in song and story were not much different from today's devotees who call themselves chocolate freaks or "chocoholics." When dyed-in-thebean chocolate lovers hear reports that their favorite food is going to get scarcer and more expensive, they simply dig deeper and make plans for one final chocolate fling, and, of course, another and another until the nightmare abates.

The story of how we got that way about chocolate starts with how we got it away from the Indians. It was on Good Friday in the year 1519 that a fleet of 11 Spanish ships appeared off what is now Vera Cruz in Mexico, and the conquistador Hernando 

Cortes set 500 men and 16 horses ashore. The natives who watched the preparations for his march into the heart of the Aztec empire were not a little agitated at seeing the helmeted, mail-clad Europeans, with their weapons that belched fire and thunder, and the strange accompanying creatures who appeared to be half man and half beast, and stood 9 feet tall.

The news traveled swiftly to Tenochtitlan, or Mexica, the Aztec capital, where the emperor, Montezuma 

II, was both amazed and practically hypnotized with dread. He could not rid himself of the lingering notion that the white conquistador embodied the God of the Air, Quetzalcoatl, returned to earth to claim his throne in fulfillment of Aztec legend. Montezuma's Hamlet-like indecision was to lead to his downfall and disgrace and to the almost incredible conquest of his powerful empire by a handful of Spanish adventurers.

Burning his ships to prevent any retreat, Cortes began his march toward the emperor's capital-today's 

Mexico City-as Montezuma dawdled uncertainly. Instead of leading his vast army in a decisive campaign to overwhelm the few hundred invaders, the emperor dispatched messengers to Cortes with baskets of Aztec gold and silver ornaments, precious stones, and other valuables. Appeasement of the gods with such gifts, and even human sacrifice, was common in the Aztec culture and 

Montezuma was nursing the hope that the celestial invader could be bought off and would go away.

Cortes simply accepted the emperor's bribes, demanded more, and continued his march. 

That the emperor's ransom included cocoa beans there can scarcely be any doubt. With the beans, taken from the seed pods of a native tropical plant, the Aztecs made a drink that the nobles and merchants of the society's upper class considered too good for the common herd, and kept it all for themselves. The Aztecsand the Mayas and Toltecs before them deemed their drink fit for their gods, and valued chocolate so highly that they used the cacao beans as currency. Caches of the beans were among the gorgeous artifacts recovered from the gravesites of these civilizations and on view today in the 

Museum of Anthropology in Mexico 

City. (continued next page)

6 July-August 1981 / FDA Consumer

Although these early Americans customarily added flavor to their chocolate with the beans of an orchid the Spanish called vanilla, and with other spices and herbs, it had somehow never occurred to them to sweeten the pot nor to heat water for brewing it. The chocolate of the Aztecs, therefore, was a cold and somewhat bitter tasting drink that they nevertheless enjoyed, in their ignorance of what sugar and hot water could do for it. One reason they did, perhaps, was revealed by Montezuma himself, who became a pathetic captive of the Spaniards in his own palace. To them he confided that he drank chocolate by the potful because it enhanced his sexual powers.

Cortes, who forwarded a supply of cacao beans to his king, Charles V, had a more discreet way of putting it. 

In his letter to Charles, he called chocolate "the divine drink that builds up resistance and fights fatigue." 

The Spanish had their first chance at chocolate a generation earlier, when Columbus returned a few cacao beans to the court of Ferdinand and 

Isabella-but the courtiers didn't know what to do with them. Now, thanks to Montezuma, they did. The 

Spanish at first didn't much care for the "divine" drink because of its bitter taste, but they soon discovered that a little sugar and some hot water made a world of difference. 

In 1606 chocolate crossed into Italy, and subsequently turned up in 

France, no doubt to the clink of gold in the coffers of Spanish traders. It caught on quickly, and spread throughout Europe, where it became fashionable to serve the drink to royal guests. By the early 18th cen tury, chocolate houses, for the privileged, of course, were springing up all over the continent. 

In 1720 the Swedish naturalist Carolus Linnaeus, the father of plant and animal taxonomy, known more for creating order out of things than for flights of poetic fancy, named the chocolate plant Theobroma cacaoor "food of the gods, cacao," an indication he agreed with the Aztecs' opinion of their drink. By 1765 chocolate completed the circle from the 

Old World back to the New: in that year a chocolate processing house opened in Dorchester, Mass.

During the three centuries that followed the Spanish discovery there was little change in the way of preparing chocolate. The beans were gathered and fermented, roasted to develop flavor, then cracked and shelled, and the resulting kernels or nibs ground and formed into cakes. 

For preparation of the drink, the cakes were broken up and mixed with other flavoring and sweetening into a pot of hot water. 

In 1828 C. J. van Houten of the 

Netherlands produced powdered chocolate, or "cocoa," by using pressure to remove some of the cacao fat, or butter, from chocolate liquor the product resulting from grinding the roasted nibs—and pulverizing the residue. He also found a way to treat chocolate with alkali to reduce its acidity, a practice that thus came to be called "dutching," and is still used to make some cacao products. In 1847, a British firm, Fry & 

Sons, combined cocoa butter with chocolate liquor and sugar to form solid "eating" chocolate. In 1876

Daniel Peter of Switzerland added dried milk to chocolate to make milk chocolate. In the years since, many other refinements have been made in the flavoring and production of solid chocolate and chocolate coatings for foods. 

Chocolate manufacturers guard the secrets of their formulas and processing methods jealously, but FDA publishes and imposes standards of identity which require that specific commercial products contain minimum amounts of cacao along with other ingredients. The Agency also has published special Good Manufacturing Practices regulations for cacao products (and confections) to assure that they will be safe to eat and free from filth and adulteration. 

Generally, the term "chocolate" is applied in the trade and elsewhere to cacao products with a high content of cacao fat (or butter) as compared to cocoa content, but there is no sharp difference in grade of quality from one chocolate or cocoa product to the next.

The first stage of processing pro duces the cacao nibs or kernels. 

These are removed from the shell when the beans are cracked, following drying and roasting. At this point the nibs may also be treated with alkali to reduce acidity, a method used for some manufacturing formulations. 

The next stage produces chocolate liquor, a basic cacao product defined in FDA standards. By the use of pressure, chocolate liquor may be further broken down into cocoa of various grades (based on fat content) and cacao butter. Any or all of these three products may be ingredients in finished products offered to the consumer, some to be consumed directly, others to be used as ingredients for cooking or mixing in the home kitchen. 

Chocolate liquor is a soft solid or semi-plastic food prepared by fine grinding of the roasted nibs. To this ground mixture may be added cacao butter or cocoa, or both, to adjust the consistency or texture. FDA requires that chocolate liquor contain no less than 50 percent and no more than 58 percent cacao butter (fat), essentially the same ratio as the unground nibs. Chocolate liquor, under the FDA definition or standard, may also contain any of several optional ingredients, including ground spices, vanilla beans, or other flavoring; butter or milkfat; malt; ground coffee; nutmeats; or salt. "Chocolate liquor" is not a household word but the same product is also known and labeled as "chocolate," "baking chocolate,' "bitter chocolate," "chocolate coating," or "bitter chocolate coating." 99 Cacao fat or cacao butter is a whitish or yellowish semi-liquid product obtained from chocolate liquor by the use of high pressure. There are no FDA standards of identity for cacao butter. It is not normally an end product for the consumer. Cacao but- 

FDA Consumer | July-August 1981 | 7

ter is used in a large number of drug and cosmetic products, mainly because it has a low melting point and because it keeps well without becoming rancid. It may be mixed with other foods, or remixed with other cacao products to achieve blends or consistencies desired for a specific product. The industries that use it, and FDA as well, may assay samples of imported cacao butter to determine whether it has been adulterated by less expensive fats or oils. 

Cocoa is produced by pulverizing the "presscake" that's left from chocolate liquor after cacao fat has been expressed from it in varying amounts. 

Breakfast or high-fat cocoa must retain a minimum of 22 percent cacao fat, under FDA standards; mediumfat cocoa (also known simply as cocoa) must contain between 10 and 22 percent cacao fat; low-fat cocoa has less than 10 percent cacao fat. These grades of cocoa may be spiced, flavored, or otherwise seasoned with salt for use in recipes. 

Other standardized cacao products: 

Sweet chocolate, a standardized product that must have a minimum of 15 percent chocolate liquor. It contains sugar, spices, flavorings, and other foods or seasonings, plus certain permitted functional additives such as lecithin, monoglycerides and diglycerides, sorbitan monostearate, and polysorbate 60. It contains less than 12 percent milk solids. Semisweet chocolate, bittersweet chocolate, and semisweet or bittersweet chocolate coatings are similar to sweet chocolate but must contain at least 35 percent chocolate liquor. 

Milk chocolate, a standardized product somewhat like sweet chocolate. It must have a minimum of 10 percent chocolate liquor, 3.6 percent milkfat, and not less than 12 percent milk solids. Buttermilk chocolate and skim milk chocolate are similar to milk chocolate. Other standardized items are mixed dairy product chocolates and mixes of sweet cocoa, sweet chocolate, and milk chocolate coatings that contain vegetable fat other than cacao fat.

The consumer who keeps in mind the names of and requirements for standardized cacao products can shop with reasonable expectation that he'll get at least a minimum amount of chocolate, cocoa, or cacao butter for his money, but the amount of cocoa or chocolate used in nonstandardized foods is known only to their manu facturers. Label ingredient lists are some help, since they show the order of predominance of ingredients, but they don't say how much sugar, lowfat milk, flour, animal and vegetable fat, or some other ingredient was put in ahead of the "cocoa" away down the list. These nonstandard foods that use some cocoa or chocolate far outnumber standardized cacao products. 

Among foods that contain some cocoa or chocolate are instant coffee mixes, lowfat milk, cookies including those with "chips," other baked goods, puddings, brownie and cake mixes, syrups and toppings, "breakfast" bars and "instant" breakfasts, "liquid" diets, dry cereals, baby foods, powdered or liquid drink mixes that may go by the name of "chocolate flavor" or "real chocolate flavor," and ice cream.

Cacao trees grow 20 to 30 feet tall and form part of the lower canopy of equatorial forests, but cultivated trees may be smaller. The plant species originated in tropical America, but cacao culture has spread around the world in areas within 20 degrees of the equator. Today West Africa is the chief cacao producing region. Cacao trees are evergreen and never stop blooming. Two crops of seed pods a year are harvested over periods of several months for various localities. The cacao beans are 

8 July-August 1981 | FDA Consumer

embedded in the fleshy parts of freshly picked pods, from which they are removed and dried, then stored and fermented. A cacao bean is comparable in size to a kidney bean.

They come 20 to 40 in a pod and it takes about 400 beans to make a pound of chocolate liquor. 

In processing, the beans are roasted to develop flavor and to remove most of the moisture. Roasting loosens the nib for easier separation from the shell when it is cracked. 

The nibs must, by FDA requirements, contain no more than 1.75 percent shell materials. 

Nibs contain 50 to 55 percent cacao butter or fat, 9 to 14 percent protein, 20 to 25 percent starch, and 10 to 15 percent of other carbohydrates, along with minerals. The beans, after fermentation, are shipped unroasted to processors in this country or elsewhere in jute or sisal bags of 140 pounds (64 kilograms). In recent years there has been a trend toward partial processing in some producing countries. Imports of chocolate liquor have quadrupled in the past 6 years.

Cacao butter imports have doubled. 

Gill and Duffus, N.Y., a large commodities dealer which gathers extensive statistics in the cacao products trade, in a February 1981 report forecast a world cacao production of 

1,622,000 metric tons of beans (after drying to remove moisture) for the 

1980-81 (October 1 to September 30) 

crop year, and predicted that there will be 155,000 metric tons of beans ground in the United States in calendar year 1981. This does not include processed or semi-processed products offered for import.

U.S. Department of Commerce figures indicate about 1.9 billion pounds of chocolate was consumed in this country in 1979. Consumption of finished chocolate (including all ingredients) was about 9 pounds per person, actual chocolate content being about a third of this amount, according to a spokesman for the 

Chocolate Manufacturers Association of the U.S.A. 

The largest U.S. ports of entry are 

Norfolk, Va., for cacao beans and 

Philadelphia for semi-processed forms of cacao. Most of the cacao products coming through these ports go to Pennsylvania, the nation's big gest chocolate processing State. 

Pennsylvania is the home of Hershey

Co. and plants of M & M Mars and 

Peter Paul Cadbury are located there. 

In the past few years the Ivory 

Coast in West Africa has taken over the number one spot in cacao production with 390,000 metric tons forecast in its February report by Gill and Duffus for the 1980-81 crop year. Ghana, also in West Africa, drops from first to third place with 270,000 metric tons, and Brazil is in second place and moving up fast with 

367,000 metric tons; Nigeria is fourth with 149,000 metric tons.

The shift toward more processing in producing countries is most apparent in Brazil and the Ivory Coast.

This trend could have a significant effect on the reasons for and possibly the rate of FDA detentions of cacao products made at the wharf when products fail to meet the Agency's requirements of fitness for human consumption. Insect contamination is the primary reason for detaining cacao beans. Occasional detentions are made for mold or other contaminations. The Agency reports that the reconditioning of cacao beans presents no current major problem, since insects are easily killed by fumigation and removed by blowing. 

When beans get moldy, growth does not usually extend through the shell into the nib. 

In fiscal year 1980, FDA detained 

102 lots of cacao beans offered for import, totaling 23.2 million pounds and valued at $41 million by their countries of origin. Of these detentions only about a dozen were made for reasons other than insect filth. 

Chocolate has the reputation of being an energy food, perhaps for good reason, since there are 2,291 calories to a pound of the stuff. Soldiers ripping open their K rations during World War II looked just as eagerly for the energy-giving bar of chocolate as for the other food and cigarettes. Some of them passed on the chocolate to children overseas, and possibly created in these young minds the belief that chocolate was invented in a plane, tank, or a foxhole. 

These days the words "chocolate" and "cocoa" often lie buried (if present at all) in long ingredient lists swirling with sugar, emulsifiers, carob beans, and other listless consolations.

The labels on candy bars and confection boxes show fewer pounds and ounces and more dollars and cents, and it will pay the consumer who wants his money's worth to look past the dark brown colors of products and the packages they come in and examine the labels beyond. The neighborhood soda fountain these days may be pushing such flavors as bubble gum and peachy keen instead of the honest brown blob you have come to adore. But don't despair. If you put some money where your sweet tooth is, there's still plenty of chocolate around.

Harold Hopkins is editorial director of FDA CONSUMER.
