On Being 

Too Rich, Too Thin, Too Cholesterol Laden 

SEP WATO 

by Roger W. Miller

It was a socialite from another era It was a socialite from another could never be too rich or too thin."

Judging from the number of weightloss diet articles that appear in women's magazines, women today are still trying to become too thin (if not too rich).

While the weight reduction articles may offer some good advice, it certainly is possible to be too thin. And shunning fat in the diet is neither quite possible nor a good idea.

For fat, despite its bad press, is essential in the diet. Fat is the source of some vital fatty acids, such as linoleic acid, which are necessary for proper growth and healthy skin. Fats and oils in the diet are also carriers, into the body, of some vitamins, including A, D, E, and K. Fat, along with carbohydrates and protein, provides calories, and calories are food energy. Fat is the most concentrated form of food energy, providing 9 calories per gram (28.3 grams = one ounce), compared with 4 calories per gram for carbohydrates and protein. 

Further, shunning fat leads to a sad diet indeed, for fats contribute to the enjoyment of foods because they add flavor and improve texture. A limited amount of fat on the body can also serve some useful purposes, such as cushioning body organs.

Not only is a fat-less diet apt to be dangerous and dull, but it is also impossible to achieve. Mother Naturewise in the ways of knowing what we need-incorporated fat into most of what we classify as edible, including wheat, corn, avocado, soybeans, and coconut, not to mention, fish, chicken, and beef.

Today people might be advised to stick to a diet that is lower in fats, not to become snobbishly skinny, but to avoid obesity and the problems associated with it, such as high blood pressure and heart disease. A low-fat diet may also be medically prescribed for individuals with high blood cholesterol levels and attendant heart disease.

Cholesterol, like fat, has a definite role to play in that grandest of mechanisms, the human body. Cholesterol is an important constituent of cells and body fluids. Chemically, it is related to fats and, like other fat, those pearls of cholesterol can get deposited in unwanted places in the body.

The link between high blood cholesterol levels and heart disease goes like this: cholesterol is carried in the bloodstream by lipoproteins which are fat and protein complexes. Some of the cholesterol in the blood may be deposited in fatty streaks along the inner linings of arteries. These fatty deposits may build up to form fibrous plaque. The result is that the artery wall thickens, thereby becomli. וון. 1. ווי 11. ህ. 

10 / July-August 1981 | FDA Consumer

ing less flexible and less able to adjust to the flow of blood. As the plaque builds up, the channel through which the blood flows narrows, increasing the pressure required for normal blood flow. Eventually, the artery may be stopped up completely. If it is an artery feeding the brain, a stroke may result. If the clogged up artery connects to the heart, a heart attack may occur. In other areas, the narrowed or clogged artery may result in injury or death to the tissue normally supplied with blood by that artery. 

A high blood cholesterol level is 

I one of the factors that can increase the risk of having a heart attack. 

I Other factors include high blood pressure and cigarette smoking. To reduce the overall risk, most doctors will suggest several steps to take: • If you smoke, stop. • If you don't exercise, start. 

Watch your fat intake. 

Dr. Donald Berwick, author of

CHOLESTEROL, CHILDREN AND HEART DISEASE, wrote in the Harvard Medical School Health Letter, that "without a doubt" cholesterol is associated with heart disease. Further, Berwick links fat consumption and cholesterol, saying: "The major determinant of cholesterol levels in otherwise normal people is the total amount of fat eaten. Therefore, the most powerful way to reduce cholesterol levels is to reduce the amount of fat in the diet." 

How much fat do we eat? The 

American Diet is around 40 percent fat. The Dietary Guidelines for 

Americans issued by the Department of Health and Human Services and the U.S. Department of Agriculture advise that reduction in our current intake of total fat, saturated fat, and cholesterol is sensible. This suggestion is especially appropriate for peoole who have high blood pressure or who smoke.

Calcium 

More Than Just The Strong Stuff Of Bones 

Everyone knows that calcium is an important part of our bones and teeth. But this mineral also plays an important role in other vital functions of the body such as clotting of blood, contraction and relaxation of the beating heart, and transmission of nerve impulses.

There is more calcium in the hute calcium the man body than any other mineral. This should not be surprising because calcium, along with its metabolic twin, phosphorus, form the "strong stuff" of bones and teeth.

But that is only part of the story. 

Calcium also is needed for some other very important tasks.

For instance, calcium plays a role in the clotting of blood. It is important in the contraction and relaxation of the beating heart. Calcium is a vital link in nerve transmission and aids the passage of fluid through cell walls. Calcium is also an essential element in enzyme regulation and in the stimulation of insulin secretion in adults. 

Most of the calcium in the body- 99 percent of it-is in the bones and teeth where it is combined with phosphorus in tiny crystals to give strength and hardness. Bone is not solid and changeless, as many people think, but is made up of cells and fiber as well as mineral crystals. There are continuing exchanges of minerals and other nutrients between bone tissues and body fluids all during life.

When the amount of calcium in the diet exceeds body needs, some of the surplus is stored inside the ends of the bones. This calcium store is available when day-to-day intake doesn't cover body needs. Thus, the skeleton is more than framework to support the body; it is a storehouse for calcium that can be released when needed. 

The remaining 1 percent of the body's total calcium is present in solution in the blood and body fluids.

This small amount is vitally important for the clotting of blood, for normal nerve transmission, for normal rhythm of the heart, blood, muscles, and other vital functions. 

Phosphorus is the second most prevalent mineral in the body. About 

80 percent of the body's phosphorus is located in bone; about 20 percent 

14 July-August 1981 / FDA Consumer

is in body cells in combination with intracellular fats, proteins, and carbohydrates; and a tiny portion exists in a delicate balance with calcium in the body fluids and blood.

Keeping the calcium level normal in the blood is principally achieved through the action of two hormones, parathormone and calcitonin. The parathyroid glands, located on the thyroid, secrete parathormone. If the calcium level in the blood falls below normal, this hormone stimulates the release of calcium from bone and also stimulates the kidneys to absorb calcium that is being filtered through them on the way to excretion. At the same time, excretion of phosphorus mgs 

Pregnant Women 

Lactating Women 

Child over 4

Adults 1,300 1,300 

1,000 1,000 800 600 

Children Under 4 is increased to maintain the proper calcium-phosphorus ratio. If the calcium level rises above normal, a thyroid hormone, calcitonin, goes to work stopping the release of calcium from bone. Circulating levels of these two hormones are adjusted automatically to maintain normal calcium levels in the blood. Many other hormones such as cortisol and insulin and those that affect growth can also influence calcium metabolism.

People of all ages need calcium and phosphorus in their daily diets. 

During growth periods, the demand is particularly heavy for these nutrients in bone building. Thus children, particularly adolescents, and

The Recommended 

Daily Allowances 

For Calcium

Set By FDA. 

Infant Up To 12 Months pregnant women have special need for these nutrients. Nursing mothers also need extra amounts because of the calcium secreted in breast milk. 

Adults need to replace the amounts that are continuously lost in the urine. and feces, and to a smaller extent through the skin. Special conditions such as healing of bone fracture may, of course, increase the adult need. 

Surprisingly, the body does not absorb all the calcium it takes in. The amount absorbed depends on how great the body need is for calcium, as well as the nutritional status of vitamin D and other dietary constituents that ease or slow absorption. The highest absorption occurs in infants and children whose bodies are rapidly building and strengthening bone. 

Because their needs are greater, pregnant and nursing women absorb a higher percentage of calcium than the average adult.

The body's need for calcium does not diminish with age, and adults who think drinking milk is kid's stuff may be in for trouble unless their diet includes other sources of calcium. According to Nutrition and 

Health, a newsletter of Columbia

University's Institute of Human Nu trition, there is evidence that osteoporosis, a disease in older people associated with gradual decrease of calcium in bones, may in part be caused by a faulty calcium and phosphorus balance that begins about age 30 in many women and 40 in many men. 

This disease is the major cause of serious fractures in older people, such as fractures of the hip from simple falls. Getting enough calcium regularly in the diet during earlier years may be important in helping to prevent the development of osteoporosis later in life. Also later in life it may be difficult to replenish bone calcium.

How much calcium is needed to meet the body's needs? The recommended daily allowances (US 

RDA's) set by FDA call for 1,000 milligrams (mg) for children over 4 years of age and adults; 1,300 mg for pregnant and lactating women; 800 mg for children under 4; and 600 mg for infants up to 12 months of age. 

The US RDA's for phosphorus are the same as for calcium. Phosphorus is found in most foods, thus getting adequate supplies of this mineral presents no problems. 

FDA Consumer | July-August 1981 | 15

Calcium is one of the nutrients it may be difficult to get enough of unless you make an effort to include some foods that are good sources. 

Milk and milk products, such as cheese, yogurt, and ice cream, are good sources of calcium. So are canned fish with edible bones such as sardines and salmon. Green leafy vegetables (except spinach, beet greens, and chard) are also good sources of calcium.

Helping in the absorption of calcium are hydrochloric acid from the stomach, carbohydrates such as the lactose in milk and, most particularly, vitamin D which also plays a role in the movement of calcium and phosphorus from bone to blood. 

Lack of vitamin D, "the sunshine vitamin," disturbs the proper deposition of calcium and phosphorus in bone causing the condition called rickets. Long before vitamin D's role in bone formation became known, taking cod-liver oil and exposing the body to sunshine were known to treat rickets. It was not until the 

1920's that vitamin D was discovered and its role in bone formation became known. Vitamin D's most unique feature-that it can be formed in the body by the action of the ultraviolet rays of the sun-was discovered later. 

Before anyone knew about vitamin 

D's role in bone formation, the bowed legs, knock-knees, and other symptoms of rickets were a common sight among children, especially in northern climes where winters are long and sunlight seldom. Today in this country deficiency of this vitamin is seldom seen, because of our general awareness of the need for this vitamin in infant's and children's diets, and the fortification of some foods with vitamin D. 

Vitamin D is a fat soluble vitamin; therefore, surplus amounts in the diet are stored in the body. The FDA has established 400 International Units 

(IU) as the US RDA for vitamin D for infants, children under 4 years of age, children over 4 years of age and adults, and for pregnant and lactating women. Vitamin D is a potentially toxic substance, particularly in young children. In view of the potential toxicity and because there is lack of evi- 

16 / July-August 1981 / FDA Consumer

dence that amounts above the recommended allowance are beneficial, the 

National Academy of Sciences has stated that intakes should closely approximate the recommended allowance for both children and adults.

It's important to good health to get enough calcium in the diet. This should not be difficult to do if you remember to include regularly in your diet some dairy products and other foods on the chart which are good sources of calcium.

NCTR 

Testing The Chemicals That Man Hath Wrought 

The National Center for Toxicological Research, located between Little Rock and Pine Bluff, Ark., was once devoted to germ warfare production and has been since described as a facility that voluntarily was transformed from science enlisted to dealing out death to science employed for the provision of life. This is the first of a series of articles on the development and scientific pursuits at this research center. by Chris Lecos t a remote, isolated area of central Arkansas, surrounded by forests of oak, sweetgum, and pine trees, a fair distance from the refined environs of a university campus and the hassle of modern, urban life, the conversations are about science and research, monkeys and man, and the terribly difficult problems of scientists and federal regulators in trying to keep up with the thousands of chemicals that are inundating the human marketplace.

The speakers are all scientists with the National Center for Toxicological Research (NCTR), a federally supported research complex that 9 years ago was nothing but a shell, a gutted hangover from this country's now abandoned germ warfare production days. Their new offices and labs are in old, yellow-tiled buildings, and their talk is in this vein:

Hunched over his desk, puffing thoughtfully on a cigarette, pharmacologist Herbert J. Schumacher speaks of the complexities of searching for "standards of scientific measurements" for testing chemicals that are potential causes of cancer, mutations, and birth defects in human beings. "We are measured by the standard of the science we produce," he says with a certain finality. 

At a nearby laboratory, Dr. William Slikker-who is using rhesus monkeys and their offspring to study how natural and synthetic estrogens pass from the mother to its fetus-talks of "basic mechanisms" and "metabolic conversions" and how primates are ideal animal models for this kind of research, because the general metabolism of estrogens is very similar between man and monkey. "There's a reason our body goes through all these metabolic conversions," he continues. "There are reasons for all these things, and although we may not understand them all, you have to look at the endogenous system and say, 'It's doing this for a reason. Let's find out why and then we'll know why this other synthetic agent is going to behave in the same way.'

• Meanwhile, Dr. Carole A. Kimmel and her two associates have just embarked on a major research project after four arduous years of planning and preliminary experimentation. It involves five other labs around the country to test the "sensitivity" of methods for testing compounds that are known to cause behavior and learning disorders in children. Some day, they point out, enough may be known to predict not only which chemicals will cause malformations but also which will induce a behavior or learning defect in a child. But, for the present, the immediate goal is to develop a reliable, consistent, acceptable way to test the compounds. "This is not a study to answer questions about the the compounds," Dr. 

Kimmel stresses. "What we're seeking is information about the methods and their ability to pick up behavior and learning defects. We want to know if our tests (with animals) are sensitive enough to pick them up." • And, in the confines of his own office, NCTR Director Ronald W. Hart paces the floor and waves his hands for emphasis as he flows from "predictive testing methodology" to somatic and germinal cell research, to "biological markers in vivo," to the growing need for finding faster, cheaper, more predictable-but still reliable-methods for testing a host of potentially toxic chemicals. 

Methodology. The word keeps popping up over and over again, from one scientist to another, and it is a key to understanding what is taking place at this research facility that was created to conduct long-term research on chemicals for the Food and Drug Administration and the

Environmental Protection Agency. The two agencies jointly fund its operations, although FDA oversees its administration and activities.

NCTR is not a place that produces earthshaking discoveries and headlined "cures." Its cadre of scientists, technicians, and other personnel are engaged in a form of patient, plodding, step-by-step science that does not provide overnight solutions and panaceas but which strengthens the ability of agencies like FDA and EPA to regulate and evaluate the safety and hazards of a wide array of direct and indirect food and color additives, drugs, cosmetic chemicals, pesticides, airborne contaminants, plastics, synthetic fibers, industrial compounds, and many others.

In many of its experiments-there are more than 100 ongoing research projects at the present time—NCTR's scientists are not primarily trying to find out if a chemical is toxic. Often, that is known before an experiment even begins. More often, their goal is to find the best method for testing compounds, understanding how one chemical interacts with others, how the body handles or metabolizes them, what their effects are on genes, what dangers they pose to future generations, how economically imporcant substances may ultimately be made safe or detoxified. Obviously, research that probes the ability of chemicals to cause cancer, or mutations, or deformed or stunted development of a fetus can only be done with animals, but it is from such research that agencies like FDA and EPA try to establish sound guidelines for regulating chemicals that may be a hazard to humans as well as to predict more reliably the degree of risk to people exposed to toxic substances.

Concern over the effects of chemical uses is, of course, not new. The 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act was passed by Congress to deal with flagrant abuses of food and drug adulteration, the kind that could lead to death or severe injury. When the world entered the modern day chemical era during and after World War II, more federal legislation was required to keep pace with public health and safety needs. There are more than two dozen federal statutes that, in effect, provide an umbrella of "cradle-tograve" regulation of chemicals and their effects on air, water, food, the workplace, consumer products, and other common uses. 

For scientists, in general, and regulatory agencies, in particular, the task of research and regulation is a staggering one. As NCTR's Director Hart noted: “We can, perhaps, analyze 40 or 50 compounds a year, yet we have something like 500 to 1,000 to analyze, and hundreds more are coming on the line every year. The thing is, how do you keep up? We're getting further and further behind, that's what's happening!" There are an estimated 

70,000 chemicals in commercial production. According to a 1979 report of the Federal Regulatory Council, some 7,000 compounds have been tested for carcinogenic effects and only about 500 of those have been found capable of causing the disease. "It's a question of improving our capability, for we don't know the best ways to test for many of these toxic effects, and at NCTR we are trying to develop ways to make our ignorance less," added Dr. Rosa Gryder, associate director for research operations and planning at 

FDA's headquarters in Rockville, Md. One of her principal tasks is to serve as a liaison between the remotely located NCTR facility in rural Arkansas and the various agencies and bureaus it serves. 

By improving capability for testing a wide array of diverse compounds, scientists and regulatory agencies also are strengthening their ability to predict a chemical's toxic potential. "Everyone agrees we need to understand the mechanisms-the how and why a cancer is produced," Dr. Gryder continued. "When you understand the how and why, then you can predict better. When you understand what the variables are-why you get a cancer in a mouse and not in a rat from the same chemical, or why you get a cancer in the liver of a rat and not in its kidney—when you understand those mechanisms, then we'll be able to make better predictions, which is the ultimate aim of all this testing." Such science also produces sensible and realistic regulation. "We cannot outlaw the use of everything," Dr. Gryder said. "Because some of the compounds we regulate are animal carcinogens (cancer-causing), or mutagens (dam-

aging to genes), or teratogens (causing birth defects), we cannot say in every case that you cannot use that chemical, we have to set so-called 'safe conditions for use,' which means we need dose response information from animals, from which we can estimate safe levels for human exposure. 99 Since its inception, FDA and EPA have invested some $200 million to develop NCTR into a center of interdisciplinary science. Its scientific pursuits are carried out through its divisions of carcinogenesis, mutagenesis, teratogenesis, biometry, chemistry, chemical toxicology, and microbiology, immunology, pathology, animal husbandry, and diet preparation. And critical to its operations is its ever-expanding computer and data information systems, installed at a cost of around $9 million. "We have to be one of the most highly automated toxicology labs in the country," noted Edward B. Fernstrom, a systems analyst for NCTR. "I have not talked to anyone who had this much of an investment in the control and collection of information. In the final analysis, all you've got is the data."

When one tours NCTR's laboratories, watches experiments through closed circuit television monitors, listens to the clickety-clack and purring of its computers, sees employees don sterilized garb to breed and feed thousands of mice and rats that are raised and kept in a socalled "specific pathogen free” environment to protect the animals from outside contamination, and hears scientists talk of the "state-of-the-art" in their work with other highly complicated, sensitive, and expensive equipment, it is easy to forget that 9 years ago this complex was nothing but an assemblage of buildings that had to be decontaminated and then certified as safe and renovated before a single experiment could be launched. "When we first came here, there were areas we couldn't even get into," recalled Stephen A. Douglas, NCTR's chief of planning and evaluation. "In terms of lab facilities, there was virtually nothing-maybe six substandard animal rooms and some labs good for production and control of microbiological materials, but they didn't lend themselves to toxicological research. They were all gutted and scrapped." 

To see it from the outside, NCTR does not look like a research center. It looks like something the Army built. 

Three tall water towers, a seven-story structure (that once housed stainless steel fermentation tanks three stories high) and a seemingly endless stretch of overhead piping dominate the 100 acres over which its more than 30, low-lying buildings are spread. The production of bacteriological warfare materials was halted on former President Nixon's orders 12 years ago. On January 27, 1971,

Nixon ordered the establishment of a National Center for 

Toxicological Research.

The Army's Pine Bluff Arsenal, which encompasses 

15,500 acres of Arkansas countryside, is still NCTR's principal neighbor. NCTR itself occupies a land area of 

496 acres with title to the land vested in the old Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (now HHS).

Douglas said it took about 8 months to remove and destroy the deadly materials kept there and to decontaminate the complex. HEW finally was able to take title in 

May 1972.

Through fiscal 1980, nearly $31 million has been spent for renovation, reconstruction, and new equipment. Even today, NCTR does not look like a science research center simply because its new labs, animal breeding and holding rooms, modern computer facilities, offices, and other work areas are hidden from view by the basically unchanged exteriors of these sturdy 30-year-old structures. 

Yet today, it is the workplace for a commuting population of 625 people-about 340 of them civil service, the rest employed on a contract basis-who come there daily via large busses, vans, cars, and motorcycles. 

NCTR currently has 72 rooms suitable for housing laboratory animals, including 51 experimental holding rooms for ongoing research, 17 for breeding and 4 for quarantining animals (mainly mice and rats). The animals are acquired from outside sources and checked to see if they have any viruses, parasites, or other microbial contaminants that could jeopardize the success of an experiment. 

Twenty-one of the 72 rooms are in a 35,000-square-foot building called the "A" Barrier. It has a pathogen-free environment, which simply means it is there to safeguard its animal populations from microbiological, viral, and other contamination. Capable of housing up to 85,000 mice, it was built at a cost of $3 million and was one of the first major renovation projects at NCTR. It was com pleted in April 1974. (See FDA CONSUMER, July-August 

1979).

Air, water, light, temperature, humidity, and other environmental factors are controlled. Anything entering the barrier-human or animal-is sterilized by steam, heat, gas, or by passing through a decontamination solution. 

Personnel entering must brush their teeth, gargle, shower, and then wear sterilized work clothes (including a surgeon's mask) before proceeding to any animal room. 

Its filtering system is capable of capturing virtually all bacterial and viral contaminants in the air as well as dust particles and airborne chemicals. Personnel move from the cleanest areas to progressively less clean ones. There is no retracing of steps. 

Joseph A. Tortorich, acting director of the division of microbiology, heads a staff whose principal task is to monitor the people, animals, and environments at NCTR. Employees are given periodic physicals and tested prior to entry into the barrier rooms. Periodic checks also are made on the breeding colonies and animals slated for experiments to be sure that any contaminants they carry are well within acceptable “tolerance" limits.

Such surveillance of microbial intrusions is mandatory, he said, to assure the credibility of the research going on at NCTR. "I don't think anyone should interpret any results until you are sure that you did not have any inter- 

FDA Consumer | July-August 1981 | 23

Temperature, humidity, and air pressure are rigidly controlled and monitored by instrumentation that is linked to a mini-computer system and monitors a wide variety of functions-environmental and equipment-at NCTR's laboratories, and animal breeding and holding rooms. The control panel shown here is one of the Center's animal breeding facilities.

Such signs as this in various areas are grim reminders that cancer-causing and other toxic substances are in common use at NCTR. This door opens into a necropsy lab, where animals coming from experimental treatment are sacrificed and tissues prepared for microscopic examination. To prevent exposure by inhalation, lab personnel operate in well-ventilated rooms that suck the air away from the technicians' work spaces.

ference from any microbial agent”—that is, interference from viruses that "could cause false tumors traceable to the virus and not the chemical being tested," he said.

Besides the workers and the animals, NCTR also keeps close microbial tabs on feed, water, cages, and bedding. "We don't care that much about you, we care about the animals," he jested. “Anybody that goes into the barrier-offhand, about a hundred people-are subjected to our checks." 

Dr. William F. McCallum, chief of the animal husbandry division, said NCTR currently is holding between 

10,000 and 21,000 experimental mice and around 9,000 rats. "That has been the average daily inventory for experimental animals in recent months," he pointed out. 

Care of the animals on experiment—including checking their weights, food consumption, and growth, and cleaning of cages, removal of animals for pathologic examination, oral injections, etc.-is part of his staff's responsibility. 

The preparation of the feed, usually a cereal chow in mash or pellet form, is the responsibility of Bobby J. 

Gough, chief of diet preparation. A microbiologist and chemist, Gough said that all feeds obtained are checked for their nutritional and contamination levels. 

Gough noted that the sharp increase in research activity at NCTR is reflected in the center's outlay for feed alone. For example, NCTR spent $22,400 for 66 tons of feed in 1977; then $32,040 for 89 tons the following year; then $42,560 for 112 tons in 1979; and $78,000 for 195 tons last year. This year NCTR will spend $130,000 for about 300 tons of feed. The cost of feed has gone up $60 a ton in that 5-year period.

Feed and cages in which animals are kept during experiments are major expense items for any research center that has so many experiments underway at the same time. John Hunziker, a 59-year-old equipment development expert, recently designed a new rat feeder that he estimates will cut NCTR's costs for such hardware from $188,000 to $36,000 in the first year. He developed and tested his new feeder last year after scientists there complained about the performance of the standard feeders that were being used and obtained from outside commercial sources. A patent is being sought. 

Their complaints focused on excess feed waste from spillage and contamination of feed with urine and feces because they either were consuming the feed after it spilled on the floor of the cage, or they were crawling into the feeder compartment, sometimes getting trapped inside, and contaminating it there. The standard feeders also posed a logistics problem: when the feed was consumed, the feeders had to be washed and returned to the diet preparation branch for refilling, then returned in sterile containers to the labs.

What Hunziker designed was a detachable feeder box made of stainless steel that hangs on the inside of the shoebox-shaped, plastic cages. It can hold more feed (from 600 to 700 grams, enough to feed three rats for a week), and only the box has to be removed when more feed is needed. When he tested his new feeder with 300 rats over 9 weeks last fall, Hunziker said the average spillage was only .8 of 1 percent. No urine was observed in the feeders, and there were only isolated cases of feces deposits. Yet the rats were able to reach virtually all the feed, further assuring consumption and reducing waste. 

Animals eating from the new feeder have exhibited no difference in growth rate or weight gain over animals feeding on pellets. "Most scientists are willing to put up with below 10 percent spillage," he said.

Like most government bodies, NCTR this year has had to trim its budget and cut back on some of its planned research; yet, Dr. Hart noted, “We are doing more now than ever in our history." Its revised budget for fiscal 

1981 called for an outlay of $21,021,000 with FDA providing $16,021,000 and EPA the balance. An emerging influence in NCTR's research activities has been the National Toxicology Program that was established in November 1978, and for which $7 million-or about onethird of the budget-is committed.

One of the objectives of the National Toxicology Pro gram, one in which other research agencies of government also participate, is to provide validated and reliable short-term tests of a carefully selected list of compounds that generally have wide uses and public health implications. NCTR's toxicological evaluations of various compounds gentian violet, sulfamethazine, caffeine, saccharin, nitrites are just a few examples-also include research into postnatal effects after chemical exposure of the pregnant mother as well as research into genetic hazards from exposure and the ability of chemicals to induce chromosomal and genetic damage.

The pattern of research at NCTR, and the directions it may be heading, closely fit the experience and strategies of the center's director. Hart, 39, who was sworn in as director in January 1980, was a professor of radiology at 

Ohio State University's College of Medicine and director of its Chemical and Biomedical Environmental Research 

Group positions that put him in charge of some 80 scientists and technicians. 

Although over the years NCTR's principal focus was on long-term, low-dose testing of single chemicals, Hart now envisions a gradual shift to shorter term studies and the development of toxicological methodology that will allow FDA, EPA, and other agencies to predict effects in animal systems and how different chemicals interact and affect the genetic makeup of animals. "Out of this, FDA and EPA will be able to formulate cost effective guidelines and faster means of getting better, higher quality data," he noted.

Chris Lecos is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

The Overselling Of Aloe Vera by Annabel Hecht

VERA ALOE 

Aloe vera is a common houseplant that has a long and exotic history. In recent years, the plant and its juices have become big business in the do-ityourself health field, as promoters around the country are selling aloe vera products with implied claims that they can cure or alleviate a variety of human complaints.

s any avid crossword puzzle fan knows, "aloe" is a four-letter word meaning "medical plant." Scientifically and commonly known as aloe vera, that medical plant has a centuries-old reputation as an aid to beauty and a handy first-aid treatment for cuts and burns. 

Aloe vera has been used for many years as an ingredient in cosmetics such as face and hand creams, lotions, and skin moisturizers. Advertisements for these products often base their appeal on the suggestion that they contain the "ancient secret of natural beauty" or "nature's own precious ingredient," a suggestion as deceptive as it is mysterious. 

Use of aloe vera is not limited to cosmetics, however. Recently the plant and its juices have become very big business in the do-it-yourself field, and FDA is concerned about the widespread distribution of aloe vera products promoted for self treatment of human complaints. Exaggerated and unsubstantiated claims are being made that these products can cure or alleviate a variety of unrelated conditions including colitis, bursitis, asthma, glaucoma, hemorrhoids, boils, arthritis, colon problems, acne, anemia, poison ivy, tuberculosis, cancer, diabetes, depression, multiple sclerosis, stretch marks, varicose veins, and even blindness.

Such unproven health claims usually are not made on the product label, but appear in literature (often distributed in shopping centers), in newspaper articles, or are passed by word of mouth. 

Some aloe vera products are being distributed through a pyramid-type operation in which dealers can move up through the hierarchy as new dealers are brought into the organization. Meetings held to solicit new distributors bring forth some of the more extravagant claims for aloe vera. The claims come, not from the leaders of the organization, but from supposedly "satisfied customers" in the audience. These people tell stories of how they were spared the agonies of crippling arthritis or debilitating emphysema, thanks to aloe vera. Chronic ear infections have cleared up, jaundice in infants disappeared, and a diabetic's need for insulin was cut in half following use of the plant's juice, according to these "testimonials."

Similar representations are made in aloe vera literature alongside of carefully worded statements indicating the manufacturer can make no health claims for the product. 

Aloe vera products are sold in health food stores where clerks are yet another source of information

FDA Consumer | July-August 1981 | 27

ATATATATATATATATATA about what the products are alleged to do. Consumers report they have been told aloe vera takes care of what is wrong with you or that it will detoxify the body and cleanse it. 

Drinking it will beautify the skin, one woman was told.

A radio talk show host in Kansas 

City not only sells DMSO but also recommends aloe vera to treat skin irritation resulting from the controversial solvent. 

In some cases aloe vera is sold as a food supplement, allegedly with FDA approval. In truth, FDA only approves certain species of Aloe as a natural flavoring substance in food. 

Not content with 20th century testimonials, aloe vera manufacturers take full advantage of the plant's long history to embellish their literature. After all, who would not be impressed by a substance that was mentioned in the Bible, was used by 

Cleopatra to enhance her legendary beauty, or was the object of conquest by Alexander the Great? (Alexander was advised to seize the island of Socotra to assure a ready supply of the plant to heal his warriors' wounds.) 

Is aloe vera truly a rare and mystical plant, as many of the promoters claim or are the products containing aloe vera simply a quack's delight? 

Actually, aloe vera is one of hundreds of species of Aloe, a perennial succulent of the lily family. Although its lance-like spiny leaves give it the appearance of cactus, aloe is not of that family, nor is it related to the American aloe, or century plant.

It originated centuries ago in southern Africa and later found its way to the Mediterranean. Spanish visitors to the New World are credited with bringing it to the West Indies, once one of the primary sources of the juice used in drugs. 

Today several species of aloe grow wild in many areas of the United 

States, particularly in the Southwest.

Aloe vera is a popular house plant whose leaves are still occasionally used by housewives to sooth minor cuts and burns. Despite a 1964 crop research report of the U.S. Department of Agriculture indicating that aloe vera would never be commercially profitable, the plant is now being cultivated in the Southwest to supply the growing market for aloe vera products.

The genus Aloe belongs to the lily family (Liliaceae), which includes a large number of ornamental genera such as lilies, tulips, and hyacinths, as well as onions and asparagus. Of the hundreds of species of Aloe, only a handful have any commercial use.

The Aloe gel most often used in cosmetics is taken from the species known botanically as A. barbadensis 

Miller (sometimes also known as A. vera Tournefort ex Linne, or as A. vulgaris Lamark). This gel is a waterthin, almost colorless liquid extracted from the peeled, spineless leaves of the plant.

Aloe also provides a drug. The 

U.S. PHARMACOPEIA, the nation's official drug compendium, recognizes the pharmaceutical substance known as Aloe as the dried latex from the leaves of either A. barbadensis Miller (the same as above), which is known to commerce as Curacao Aloe, or of A. ferox Miller, or hybrids of it with two other species 

(A. africana Miller or A. spicata 

Baker), known to commerce as Cape Aloe.

The drug aloe is a powerful cathartic used both in laxatives for humans and for horses. Aloe also is an ingredient in compound benzoin tincture. 

The AMERICAN DRUG INDEX indi cates its use as "topical protectant. 99 

Aloe approved by FDA as a natural flavoring substance in food comes from Aloe perryi Baker, A. barbadensis Miller, A. ferox Miller, and hybrids of this species with A. africana Miller and A. spicata Baker.

While physicians of antiquity are said to have used aloe vera to treat a variety of conditions, including headache, skin inflammations, constipation, and menstrual problems, modern medical references to the socalled medicine plant did not appear until the 1930's and 40's. A number of researchers reported on their use of the leaves and gel to treat radiation burns and skin ulcers. Some experiments with animals also were done about the same time. In 1957 another researcher reported on the use of an ointment made from powdered aloes in a lanolin base to treat ulcers on amputation stumps and other skin conditions. 

Since then few references to the external use of aloes have appeared in the medical literature. Claims that 

28 July-August 1981 | FDA Consumer

AAAAAAAAAA ATATATATATATATATATA aloes are antibacterial and anti-inflammatory have not been demonstrated in tests with humans. And there is no scientific evidence to support allegations that aloe vera is effective as a treatment for cancer, diabetes, tuberculosis, or any other serious disease. In fact, the National 

Cancer Institute has tested aloe emodin, a common ingredient found in aloe vera latex and found it not worth further study as a cancer cure.

In light of the many unproven claims being made for aloe vera products, consumers are asking why

FDA doesn't do something about them. To take such products off the market, the Agency would have to prove they are adulterated or misbranded. As has been noted already, the manufacturers are careful to make no health claims on the product labels and to include disclaimers in their literature. The products also are often sold as food supplements or cosmetics. The complexities of the marketing schemes for aloe vera products coupled with the fact that health claims are made in the form of testimonials also make it difficult to relate such claims to a specific product. 

FDA is reviewing aloe, aloin (a derivative), and aloe vera gel as active ingredients in over-the-counter drugs as part of its massive review of the safety and effectiveness and appropriate labeling of all OTC drugs. Two expert advisory panels have found here is not enough scientific evidence to show that aloe vera is useful 

For the treatment of minor burns, cuts, and abrasions or for the treatnent of minor vaginal irritations. 

Both panels have recommended that urther tests be made before aloe era is declared safe and effective for ts intended use.

Yet another expert panel has studied the pharmaceutical aloe and recommended that it be allowed in laxatives, but cautioned that it be used sparingly and not by children under 6 years of age. 

FDA has not yet decided whether to accept the panels' recommendations. Until a decision is made and final monographs setting forth the acceptable ingredients and labeling for these classes of OTC drugs are published, drug products containing aloe vera can continue to be sold.

It is interesting to note that, despite the laxative panel's recommendation, a number of medical sources, including the American Medical Association and the American Pharmaceutical Association, say that aloe vera should not be used in laxatives because it is unpredictable and sometimes violent. It can cause intestinal gripping, cramping, and colic and can affect smooth muscles such as the uterus, making it a dangerous drink for a pregnant woman. Veterinary use of aloe as a purgative for horses is no longer recommended for the same reason. 

Aloe vera in cosmetics comes under a different set of rules. FDA does not have the authority to require that manufacturers test cosmetic products for safety before they go on the market. However, the

Agency can take action against a product that proves to be adulterated or misbranded. So far, no problems have been encountered with cosmetics containing aloe vera. 

Exaggerated medical claims notwithstanding, consumers have asked whether there is any real harm in taking aloe vera as a tonic, one of the suggested uses for the plant. A 

1974 study did show that oral doses were not toxic to rats. However, no scientific studies have been done to determine whether drinking aloe vera might be harmful to humans. This is something that should be kept in mind by anyone planning on quaffing a daily dose. In addition, there is the possibility that continued use of an aloe vera tonic could make a person sensitive to the plant. In that case, later applications of creams or lotions containing aloe vera might result in an allergic reaction.

Far more serious, however, is the harm that comes when proper medical treatment of serious illness is neglected or abandoned in favor of products that have no proven value. 

Victims of arthritis and other diseases for which there is no known cure often are easily persuaded to try almost anything in the hope of relief.

They, in particular, should be skeptical of any product that is promoted as a cure-all based on testimonials rather than solid scientific evidence. 

Annabel Hecht is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

Drugs That Take The Joy Out Of Sex 

Reports of sexual side effects are included in the professional labeling of a number of drugs. It is not clear, however, just why drugs might have these effects and what reports of such effects mean for the individuals taking them. by Judith Willis 

That alcohol increases desire but decreases sexual ability is an old adage. Now it is becoming apparent that alcohol is not the only drug that may affect libidinal energies. 

Indeed, the list of drugs which have been reported to affect sexual ability or desire-has now become so long that those on medication who experience sexual problems they didn't have before taking that particular drug would be well advised to discuss with the physician whether the difficulties could be drug related. 

On the other hand, just because a drug has been reported to be associated with sexual problems does not mean that it is likely to cause them in any one individual. And, even if it does, all such effects are entirely reversible upon discontinuance of the drug.

A person prescribed a certain medication should not be alarmed that his or her sex life will be affected.

The chance of this happening is, with most drugs, quite low. 

In fact, with most drugs, the relationship between their action and any effect they might have on sexual function is not clear, and the connection is made mostly through individual case histories, rather than through controlled studies. Therefore, it is not really known how many instances of sexual dysfunction reported by those on medication could be related to the illness itself, advancing age, or psychological factors, rather than the chemical action of the drugs.

Nevertheless, reports of effect on sexual function are included in the professional labeling of the following types of drugs: high blood pressure medications, tranquilizers, antipsychotics, antidepressants including both the tricyclics and the MAO inhibitors, amphetamines and other drugs used for weight loss, cholesterol-reducers, and lipid-lowerers. 

Even Antabuse, a drug used to withdraw people from alcohol, has been reported to be associated with impotence during the first week or month. 

With some other drugs, notably anticholinergics such as decongestants, belladona derivatives, and antihistamines, the data are even more sketchy and, thus, sexual dysfunction is not included as an adverse effect in the labeling. However, there have been scattered reports that these drugs, some of which are combined in over-the-counter cold and allergy preparations, might be related to sexual problems because of their drying effect. 

The sexual difficulties reported with drugs include erectile and ejaculatory problems in men, increase or decrease in libido (sex drive) in both men and women, and orgasmic problems in women. 

Although there is not enough information for experts to determine why drugs might have these effects, one possible explanation is that many such drugs interfere with certain actions of the autonomic nervous system in order to have therapeutic effect. Theoretically, this interference could also block the stimulus necessary for normal sexual response. 

For example, MAO inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, amphetamines, and the drugs reserpine and propranolol, all in one way or another block or inhibit the adrenergic system, a part of the autonomic nervous system. It is this blocking action that enables them to have their therapeutic effect. However, because adrenergic impulses are necessary for ejaculatory response, it is possible that this action also might be related to sexual difficulties. Similarly, positive cholinergic impulses are necessary to erection. When these are blocked or interfered with by such drugs as atropine, some decongestants, and some antiarrhythmics, it is theoretically possible, although not clinically proven, that erectile problems could result. The phenothiazines (major tranquilizers such as Compazine, Mellaril, Stelazine, and Thorazine) have a complex effect on the autonomic nervous system and are said to inhibit ejaculation without interfering with erection. 

An additional possible, although unproven explanation for the sexual effects of some drugs is that they alter sexual function through their mood-altering effects. For example, rauwolfia derivatives such as reserpine (used to treat high blood pressure) sometimes cause depression, and depression is often connected with sexual problems. Similarly, because the tricyclics elevate mood in depressed persons, there have been reports of increases in sex drive, as well as decreases, with this drug. The benzodiazepine tranquilizers (Valium, Librium, Serax) have also been reported to be related to both in 

FDA Consumer | July-August 1981 / 31

Drugs Labeled Regarding Sexual Side Effects crease and decrease in libido.

The major tranquilizer, Haldol, has been associated with both increased sex drive and impotence, and there have been reports of increased libido with the antischizophrenic medication Lidone.

The effect of drugs on sexual function is by no means limited to men, although there is more information on males presumably because they are easier to study for sexual dysfunction. Further, it can be assumed, until proven otherwise, that almost any drug found to change the libido in man also may be related to similar changes in woman. 

However, the whys and wherefores, the cause-and-effect explanations of these changes are, at this time, elusive and merely conjectural. 

The reported incidences of sexual disturbances with most drugs is very low and should not be considered a commonplace reaction of any drug. 

Therefore, patients prescribed a certain drug should not refuse to take it because it has listed among its side effects possible sexual problems. 

Drug effect on sexual function is a very individual matter, and the chances of any particular drug affecting a person's sex life adversely are very small. But if problems do develop, the informed consumer will discuss them with the physician and perhaps ask if the dosage can be adjusted or if there is another drug with similar action which may not have this effect. 

Judith Willis is a member of FDA's public affairs staff and editor of the

Investigators' Reports Psychiatrist Set Down By FDA 

Dr. Nathan Kline, prominent New

York psychiatrist, became a topic of interest in FDA's Bureau of Drugs in August of 1977. That was when Kline first reported his experiments on humans with Beta-endorphin, a drug not yet approved by FDA. Kline, director of one of the

Rockland Research Institutes (part of the 

New York State Department of Mental 

Hygiene), later told an ATLANTIC

MONTHLY magazine interviewer: "Scien tists all have an adolescent sporting sense. After all, we all want to be first and besides it is fun to pioneer such things. So, in 1977 we decided to jump the others in human experiments.

We were not members of the group we had heard they call the 'Endorphin

Club.' But we thought we were in a race with them, nevertheless, and we were determined to win it." Kline went on to say, "We have gotten around the FDA's catch-22 that you cannot give a substance to humans until you have proved it safe in humans.. At the time, Kline had IND's (Investigational New Drug exemptions) for four drugs. As an IND investigator, he was supposed to be compiling data to prove that the drugs were safe and effective so that they could be legally marketed. But some FDA officials were concluding uneasily that Kline was using the investigational drugs to treat patients and was not doing the careful monitoring and recordkeeping required for drugs under investigation. 

The previous June (1977) Kline had reported to FDA that one of his patients taking the IND drug clozapine, a promising antipsychotic, had had an adverse reaction a lowering of the white blood cell count. Reports had been received from Europe that other patients taking clozapine had had similar reactions, developing a condition called agranulocytosis. FDA had warned all clozapine investigators-including Kline-to limit the number of patients on this drug. When 

Kline made his report, investigator Frank

C. L. Sikorsky-from FDA's New York 

District-was assigned to get the patient's medical records. The investigator was told that the records had been misplaced told that the records had been misplaced because of a recent change in locations. 

When FDA subsequently learned that 

Kline was still treating over 300 patients with clozapine, after receiving FDA's warning, Kline's IND for the drug was terminated. That was in February 1978. 

Then FDA learned about Kline's work with Beta-endorphin, a drug for which he did not have an IND. Sikorsky and FDA medical officer Dr. Michael 

Hensley went to Kline's offices in April 1978, this time to investigate all of Kline's IND's, as well as his data on the endorphin study. The records, for the most part, could not be found; those that were found were considered deficient by the investigators. When it was noted that 

Kline was still dispensing clozapine to patients, FDA had the psychiatrist's supplies of the drug seized. 

A Bureau of Drugs hearing on Kline's methods for investigating new drugs was held in early 1979. This hearing led eventually to a hearing before FDA's deputy associate commissioner for health affairs, to determine whether Kline would be disqualified as an IND investigator. 

During the hearings, Bureau of Drugs officials argued that the psychiatrist appeared to be using investigational drugs, for which an exemption had been made, as therapeutic agents, rather than con- 

FDA Consumer / July-August 1981 / 33

ducting clinical investigations of their safety and effectiveness. He was not following the patients' progress closely enough, the officials said, and he was not keeping FDA informed of the progress of the studies. These drugs were not approved, not fully tested, they might have dangerous side effects, and should be closely monitored. 

Kline's attitude worried FDA, said medical officer Hensley of FDA's Division of Scientific Investigation. Hensley referred to the ATLANTIC MONTHLY in terview and an article that had appeared in the WASHINGTON POST in January 

1978. In the Post article, Kline had said, "The FDA is very careful not to interfere with medical practice... the big question is going to be to determine whether the FDA, and indeed the medical profession, should have any say in how normal people decide to augment their brain functions. The pharmaceutical industry is stupid in only treating pathology, why not drugs for normal people? I just got off on a sideline with Beta-endorphin, why not a memory drug, why not sold over the counter?" That kind of comment, Hensley said, suggested a very casual attitude toward the use of investigational drugs, as well as FDA regulations. 

He added that he felt there was significant threat to public safety by research conducted in such a manner. 

Kline's lawyer said that the psychiatrist was, in fact, using the drugs as therapeutic agents. In the case of clozapine, he said, "These were patients who had not, as I understand it, been responsive to other therapy that was available. So, he was treating patients but he was also compiling data for investigational purposes." The lawyer said that Kline was a pioneer in the field, having been involved Investigators' Reports presents information on inspections, product seizures, court proceedings, and other administrative and regulatory actions by Federal, State, and local food and drug agencies across the country to provide health and economic protection to consumers of foods, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices.

Flaky Forks 

Cribmates Inc. marketed some 

53,800 potentially toxic infant training utensil sets between July 1978 and November 1980. But because of a concerned mother, the firm is now asking for them all back. 

The Hollis, N.Y., firm voluntarily recalled the sets after being advised 

Er by FDA's New York District that the levels of cadmium found in the spoons and forks exposed infants to an unnecessary and hazardous situation.

The problem was brought to the attention of the Agency's Buffalo 

District office by a mother who called to complain of finding metallic flakes in a portion of baby food she was feeding her child. After looking at the evidence, an FDA investigator noticed that a spoon, which was used to feed the child, appeared to have lost some of its plating. He theorized that the spoon had peeled because the child was teething on it. 

The Buffalo District decided to send an investigator out to locate the local distributor and collect samples. 

Meanwhile, the spoon would be tested for toxicity. Utensils are covered under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act if they contain a toxic metal that can leach into foods. 

Local distributions were traced to 

G & G Sales Inc., Depew, N.Y. 

While at the firm, an FDA investiga- 

Etor noticed metallic flakes inside the utensil set packages plus evidence that some of the metal was flaking or peeling off their surfaces. Sample sets were collected for analysis by the 

Buffalo laboratory.

The laboratory analyses revealed that the utensil sets far exceeded FDA's current guideline of 0.5 parts per million for cadmium. The metallic pieces obtained from the spoons showed they contained 3.9 percent cadmium (equal to 39,000 parts per million) and those from the forks contained 5.7 percent cadmium (equal to 57,000 parts per million). 

Further investigations by New York 

District investigators at Cribmates 

Inc., determined that the firm had imported the sets from Soung Fea 

Enterprises Co. Ltd., Taipei, Tai wan. 

Since the recall, Cribmates has distributed only stainless steel sets. 

Business Too Slow 

Although Chemvet Laboratories of 

Olathe, Kans., ceased manufacturing and marketing veterinary drugs early in 1980, the firm seemed reluctant to dispose of its inventory of drugs and drug ingredients. Officials had promised FDA's Kansas City District that they would voluntarily destroy those stocks, but instead they moved everything into an auto body shop for storage. 

FDA had been following the inaction of the firm and its failure to dispose of the inventory properly. Investigators checked the building where the drugs and equipment were stored and found no controls or security whatever. Chemvet officials again would not say how they intended to resolve this, so FDA asked for seizure of the drugs and ingredients as being held in storage in viola tion of Good Manufacturing Practice regulations.

The U.S. marshal for the District of Kansas carried out the seizure, and the drugs, valued at $30,000, were ordered destroyed after the owners made no effort to claim them. 

Kidney Machines Damaged 

Three artificial kidney (dialysis) machines at Jackson Memorial Hospital in Miami were severely damaged when the machines were flushed with a formaldehyde disinfectant that was found to contain carbon tetrachloride, an organic solvent that dissolved several delicate parts of the machines. 

Hospital officials called FDA's 

Miami Resident Post, and the FDA investigator traced the problem to the Egyptian Chemical Company in that city. The company supplies formaldehyde to funeral homes as embalming fluid and to hospitals for use as a fixative for tissue and as fectant for dialysis machines. disin- 

Egyptian Chemical receives the formaldehyde in 65-gallon drums, then repacks it into 1and 5-gallon containers for distribution to its customers. The repacking-done in an area where other chemicals are used and stored-allowed the solvent to contaminate the formaldehyde. The repacking was done in violation of 

FDA good manufacturing practices, and the repacked product was legally misbranded, since the labeling did not show the presence of the tetrachloride.

Collected samples were sent to 

FDA laboratories in Atlanta, where chemists found trichlorethane and trichlorethylene in the formaldehyde. 

Egyptian Chemical voluntarily recalled all formaldehyde distributed in 

1and 5-gallon containers to the hospitals, and changed its way of handling the solution.

An infectious strain of bacteria resulted in the recall of nearly $300,000 worth of antiseptic products by a 

New Jersey firm. Pseudomonas capacia was discovered in the special water supply at Sherwood Pharmaceutical Co., Mahwah, N.J., a manufacturer of products used as antiseptics in a variety of hospital and laboratory-testing and sample-collection procedures.

At FDA's request, made in view of the contamination of previously distributed antiseptic products, the firm initiated a nationwide recall.

The recall was classified by FDA as class II, which is defined as a situation in which the use of a product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences.

The recalled products included all lots of Providone Iodine 10% solution, foil packets, swabsticks, swabaids, spray, and whirlpool disinfectant produced from May through November 1980. 

Lingering Litigation

Many "days in court" turn into years, as FDA knows only too well.

In one contest between the Agency and an Arizona veterinary drug manufacturer, litigation has lasted more than 3 years and is still not over.

Western Serum Company is a manufacturer of small volume parenteral veterinary drugs in Tempe. FDA's 

Los Angeles District inspected the firm a number of times over a 4-year period and found continuing viola tions of Good Manufacturing Practice regulations, as well as manufacture by the company of unapproved new animal drugs. The firm was warned, both orally and in writing, against violating the law. The district initiated seizures of violative products on several occasions and sent the firm a regulatory letter. Company officials promised corrections but did not make them. 

Therefore, in 1977, the district compliance staff wrote up a request for injunction. The request cited the 

GMP violations, including failure to test all raw materials, incomplete testing of finished products, incorrect labeling, errors in recordkeeping, inadequate stability studies, and ques tionable sterilization procedures. The firm was also charged with manufacturing and distributing 11 drugs that had not been approved by FDA as safe and effective. 

The complaint for injunction was filed in December 1977 in the U.S. 

District Court for the District of Arizona. The case spent the next few years in various legal stages. The pretrial hearing, originally set for July 

1979, was postponed four times, and eventually moved to June 1980.

The Government moved for summary judgment on the new animal drug and GMP issues. The firm's lawyer opposed the motion and requested that the case be dismissed.

He argued that the court had no jurisdiction to act in the matter and that FDA should first have held an administrative proceeding on the "new animal drug status" of the products before going to court.

The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss and approved the injunction. Western Serum Company is now appealing the new animal drug decision, as well as the denial of its motion to dismiss. The appeal process can also tack on months or years to the case, but during this time the firm will not be allowed to market the 11 drugs. 

Mixed Chemicals Don't Mix Looking back, it may have been a mistake to put that drum of liquid boiler-cleaner so close to those cartons of cocoa blocks on that trailer in 

Philadelphia. By the time they got to 

Connecticut, the drum had burst and much of the cocoa had been drenched with phosphates, carbonates, and sodium hydroxide. 

Trucking company personnel at 

South Windsor, Conn., separated 263 cartons that seemed to be undamaged from the original shipment of 

353 cartons and sent them on to 

Deran Confections of Charlestown,

Mass., the consignee. Deran accepted 208 cartons and returned 55, which the trucking company put with those it had earlier segregated. 

The incident had been reported to 

State of Connecticut officials, and a 

State inspector and an FDA investigator from the Hartford Resident 

Post checked the cartons. Most had visible damage from the soaking they had received; many were still wet and soggy. The entire lot (145 cartons) was put under embargo. Two cartons examined at FDA's Boston

District laboratory showed stains and other physical evidence of damage, and carbonate and phosphate crystals were found on cocoa blocks inside.

The cocoa stayed under State embargo for several weeks. Then the manager of North Penn Transfer, the trucking firm, agreed that the 145 cartons, valued at $56,628, should be destroyed. This was done under State of Connecticut supervision by burying them in a landfill.

Seizures and Postal Service Cases FILED SEIZURE ACTIONS charge violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and are initiated based upon FDA 

recommendations. A seizure action is commenced by the filing of a complaint in the U.S. district court where the goods are located. A U.S. marshal is then directed by the court to take possession of the goods, removing the product from commerce, until the matter is resolved. 

A total of 26 actions to remove from the consumer market products charged to be violative was reported in April. These actions included 12 seizures of foods: 10 involved charges concerning contamination, 1 involved charges concerning color additives, and 1 involved charges concerning food additives. 

Others included 13 of drugs and 1 of medical devices.

False Representation Orders Issued by Judicial Officer Under 39 U.S.C. 3005

Charged 3-1-78: when shipped by Gold Kist, Inc., Atlanta. Ga., the article (which consisted of five lots in five bins) contained the added poisonous and deleterious substance aflatoxin, which might render the article injurious to health; 402(a)(1). The article was claimed by the shipper, who denied the charge. The Government served requests for admissions, for the production of documents, and for answers to written interrogatories. The claimant served written interrogatories on the Government. The claimant also moved to add the two smallest lots of corn (the 12,000 bushel lot and the 13,000 bushel lot) to the next larger lots of corn (the 30,000 bushel lot and 41,000 bushel lot). 

The Government opposed such commingling. FOOD/Economic and Labeling Violations 

Cottonseed and sesame oil blends, at San Francisco, N. Dist. Calif. 

Charged 7-29-80: while held by Sin Ma Import Co., San Francisco, Calif., who was mixing and repacking cottonseed oil and sesame oil and was labeling the blends as (bottles) “Lucky Brand Superior Sesame Oil . . . Packed for: Lucky Foods Co., San Francisco, Ca." and as (cans) "Longevity . . . Sesame Oil Product of Japan," the articles had had the valuable constituent sesame oil, in part, omitted or abstracted-402(b)(1); cottonseed oil had been substituted in part for sesame oil-402(b)(2); the label statements representing that the articles were sesame oil were false and misleading since the articles contained both cottonseed oil and sesame oil—403(a)(1); and the vignette of an elderly person and the word "Longevity" on the label of the article in cans falsely and misleadingly claimed that the article would prolong life—403(a)(1); the label of the article in cans lacked the name and place of business of the manufacturer, packer, or distributor, and the label of the article in bottles lacked the place of business of the manufacturer, packer, or distributors, since the name "Lucky Foods Co." was not currently listed in a city directory or telephone book and the label lacked the street address-403(e)(1); and one lot of the article in ½-gallon bottles was in violation of the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act, since the quantity of contents statement was expressed as "Net Contents: ½ Gallon" instead of "Net 64 fl. oz. (2 qts)"-15 U.S.C. 1453(a)(3)(A)(i). The dealer and the Government stipulated that the articles would be forfeited, that the dealer waived all claim to the articles, and that the Government would dismiss the action. The court approved the stipulation, ordered the articles forfeited, and dismissed the action. (F.D.C. No. 63129; S. No. 

80-219-493 et al.; N.J. No. 20)
