At a fish-packing plant, Investigator 

Ellison walks down the painted stripe of a storeroom with a flashlight (upper photo), looking for signs of rodent or insect infestation. In the lower picture, Ellison takes the temperature of batter used on fish pieces.

The temperature should be in the low 

50's F. to keep toxicity problems to a minimum. grees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit).

The samples are shipped via commercial courier to FDA's microbiology laboratory in Minneapolis (see "Microbe Sleuthing in Minneapolis,"

FDA CONSUMER, Dec. '79-Jan. 

'80). At Minneapolis, the samples undergo five microbiological determinations. Swartzentruber tries to work his surveys in with the routine inspections of investigators so as to minimize the disruption for a firm. 

In his inspection, Ellison would look for the presence or evidence of flies, rodents, or birds in the plant; the handling of ice; the strength of hand-sanitizing solutions; and evidence of sores, tape, or other such abnormalities on the hands of employees. Inspecting a crab plant is different than inspecting most food plants because the meat is handled directly by workers and because the product must be kept cool. Crabs are bottom dwellers and are usually cooked while still alive. Eating bad crab meat may not result in a oneway trip in a long limousine, but it may make one wish he or she were on that trip. 

Not being able to inspect the crab plant hardly caused Ellison to miss a stride. In no time at all, he had decided to drive to the other side of town and inspect another seafood plant. "We spend half our time on seafood and half on vegetables," Ellison explained. He uses "we" frequently, although he works alone virtually all of the time. Asked about that first person plural, he explained that he means "FDA and me.'

While food takes up most of his time, Ellison has other, typical FDA 

investigator duties. The 10 counties he covers also contain one major medical device plant that makes emergency oxygen units, a small drug plant that produces a bulking agent for laxatives, a couple of research farms, a couple of experimental laboratories, and medicated feed manufacturers who produce chicken fodder for the Eastern Shore's sizeable broiler and fryer industry. In addition, Ellison "and FDA" inspect blood banks and audit State contract inspection programs of food warehouses and feedmills.

In a typical week, Ellison likes to start off with a major inspection of vegetable processing or a seafood firm and work in other projects along the way. For example, the week that started out with elusive crabs was rounded out with more thrusts at crab packing plants and inspections of an oxygen repacker and a commercial ice firm in the resort town of 

Ocean City, Md. 

Guidance for the resident post inspectors comes from the monthly work plan sent down by the district office. In Ellison's case, the plan comes 103 miles from Baltimore.

However, the work plans aren't always that easy to follow, what with interruptions by shortages of crabs, recalls, and other emergencies. 

Ellison's resident post and his duties are typical of resident posts around the country, and yet his work is different. It's typical in that he has the responsibility for seeing that the 

Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and other laws entrusted to the Agency are enforced among the 252,700 people in his area. It's different in that most investigators spend much more of their time on drug matters and other concerns. 

Ellison's new concern that day was a seafood plant, and it was not yet eight in the morning when he drove into the parking lot of the plant. 

Donning his white coveralls and a white hard hat, he armed himself with a flashlight, a thermometer, and a notebook. The notebook is his diary, in which he would record his observations as he tours the plant. The diary also keeps track of the day's other activities.

Inside he waited briefly for a plant official to greet him, and then moved to a conference room off the plant cafeteria where he made out a "standard notice of inspection" that he signed and gave to the official. 

The notice spells out the purpose of the inspection and the laws that are involved. 

The plant manager joined Ellison in the conference room and together the two of them started out to tour the plant. Two assembly lines were working that day. The fish had come from Iceland in frozen blocks, the blocks were sawed up to the desired shape and size and moved along conveyor belts, the pieces were breaded or dipped in batter, baked and refrozen, or simply refrozen, and then packed in individual containers. The frozen-baked-frozen cycle keeps germ contamination possibilities to a minimum. Likewise, water used in batter is kept near freezing so that the batter stays close to 50 degrees to avoid the threat of toxicity. 

Ellison first did a quick run through the plant so he would know where to concentrate on return. The run-through included storage areas, loading docks, the freezer room (where it's five below zero), the powerhouse (where electric capacitors are clearly labeled as containing PCB's), and the carton storage area.

Ellison was constantly on the lookout for signs of dirt and insects. In this plant, the search was made easier in the storage areas by white painted stripes about 18 inches wide along the edges of the rooms. The white stripe enabled Ellison, flashlight in hand, to detect evidence of rodents and insects. The stripe also serves as a border for the storage areas, telling employees to keep 

241 September 1981 | FDA Consumer

products away from the walls so that they can be inspected and turned over easier. 

Rodents like to run along walls and insects gather in corners or seek dust to settle in. Ellison looked for rodent droppings or insect carcasses. 

Should he find signs of rodent infestation, he would go back to his vehicle for his black light that enables him to spot urine stains. But in this case, he found none. The plant manager explained that the firm has a pest control contractor who comes in every weekend.

In the production area, Ellison periodically tested the handwashing solution used by the workers. For this, he took a strip of paper out of a plastic vial. The strip was dipped into the solution. Ellison watched the dipped portion of the strip change color and then compared the color with coded colors on the label of the vial. On the first such experiment, the dipped color turned out to be a dark purple, indicating between 100 and 200 parts per million chlorine, an acceptable solution. 

As the workers went off for a 10 a.m. break, the FDA man watched while tables where fish were handled were sanitized. He waited for the workers to come back on the job to see if they made use of the hand sanitation solution before resuming their tasks. 

Ellison used his thermometer to test the temperature of the batter at several points along the assembly lines. His observations also included checking around equipment to see if any past accumulations indicated that the night cleanup crew at the plant was doing less than its job. 

He watched as workers "stripped down" bags of batter mix, bread crumbs, and the like. Stripping down means taking off the outer layer of the bag so that no shipping dust gets in the product when it is dumped. 

The stripping might also reveal hidden insects. 

Ellison's inspection also included a visit to the plant's records room where computers provide a processing and shipping history of each item turned out by the plant. This would be helpful should a product have to be tracked down in a recall.

The investigator declined an offer for lunch in the plant cafeteria and chose instead a nearby highway restaurant that he had learned about in his travels about the area. 

After lunch, Ellison made a final run through the plant and then met with the plant manager to go over his findings. "We didn't find anything out of line and so we don't want to spend any more time here than we have to," he told the plant official. However, he did collect information from the plant manager about his standing in the company, whom he reports to, etc. It was information that could come in handy for the Agency some day should an emergency involving the plant arise. Had Ellison found problems at the plant, he would have written up an FD-483 “observations of insanitary practices," which he would give to and discuss with management. 

The inspection over, Ellison drove to a nearby pay phone to contact 

Swartzentruber back at the Salisbury office. The two arranged to rendezvous later to make a try at another crab packing plant.

By this time the day had darkened, the sun having lost a battle to the clouds. A breeze blew off the bay and a mist began to develop. Somewhere in the Chesapeake Bay a blue crab was about to make a fatal mistake by grabbing for the piece of eel on a waterman's trotline or making the no-return trip down the funnel of a crab pot. That crab would end up with its shell pried open by the deft actions of a picker, its meat plucked by swift fingers. Mike Ellison might be there observing as the crab met its fate. And Ammon Swartzentruber might select a bit of the victim's meat for a plane ride to Minneapolis.

There, a microbiologist would examine it under a microscope, looking for taint.

But most likely the treasured meat from the blue fellow would go the commercial route, selling for as much as twice the value of porterhouse steak. And well worth it, the ultimate consumer might tell you.

Such is the stuff that resident in spection posts deal with. 

Roger W. Miller is editor of FDA CONSUMER.

The Notebook 

The Notebook: a potpourri of items of interest to consumers, gathered from FDA press releases, FEDERAL REGISTER notices, and other news sources. Publication dates of Federal RegistER items, designated FR, are included to aid readers who want further information.

FDA has eliminated the requirement that drug manufacturers must submit supplements to their New 

Drug Applications (NDA's) whenever there is a change in distributors. Such information will be provided in periodic reports. The change was effective 

June 19. (FR June 19). 

The first drug to treat internal fungus diseases, such as valley fever and histoplasmosis, without serious side effects has won FDA approval. The drug, ketoconazole, will be marketed under the trade name

Nizoral. 

FDA has warned consumers in Miami, Fla., and surrounding counties not to drink a vitamin/mineral product called "Nervo Forza" because it contains strychnine sulfate in harmful amounts that are potentially life threatening to small children who might drink an entire bottle. The product was sold primarily in pharmacies and food stores in South Florida serving Spanish-speaking people. 

Florida pet owners have been warned not to use a product called Flee for controlling fleas and ticks on their pets. The product was voluntarily recalled by the manufacturer because of reports that it may paralyze or kill the animals. 

New drug approval was ranked first among FDA programs that should be given top priority by six groups of health professionals, consumers, trade organizations, State officials, and FDA representatives who took part in the Agency's annual priority setting exercise. Research on the biological effects of chemical substances made the "top five" list of all six groups, while food contamination and food additives were given priority ratings by five of the six groups.

Consumers were the only ones to put patient package inserts among their top choices.

30 September 1981 / FDA Consumer

Investigators' Reports Deep Trouble 

Around the Great Lakes, fishing is not only a sport but an important business. It's definitely a multimillion dollar business. It's also a business that has had its share of trouble. 

Many of the lakes' fish species began to decline in numbers in the first half of this century. Overfishing was one of the major reasons, although not the only one. Overfishing led to extinction of Atlantic salmon in Lake 

Ontario early in the century, and of the blue pike in Lake Erie in the early 

1960's. In Lake Superior, the herring industry folded because of overexploitation of spawning stocks (the catch declined from 6.3 million pounds in 

1945 to a mere 53,444 pounds in 

1978). A combination of overfishing and parasitic predation by the sea lamprey caused drastic reduction in lake trout populations in all the lakes: for example, in Lake Superior the population was reduced 80 to 90 percent from 1945 to 1961; in Lake Ontario that species was wiped out altogether in the 1950's and only recently has been restocked. 

Under the auspices of the Great

Lakes Fishery Commission, the Department of Interior's Fish and Wild life Service joined with the States,

Canadian Provinces, and the Cana dian government to deal with the problem. Millions of dollars were spent on programs to control overfishing and the sea lamprey population.

A vast restocking program was begun in the 1960's to reintroduce certain species, such as the lake trout and salmon, into the lakes. The programs seemed to be succeeding. Sports fishing took on new life, and the commercial fishing industry expanded. In 

1967, Michigan had its first commercial salmon sale and the first year shipped out some 780,000 pounds of salmon and 68,000 pounds of salmon eggs (for caviar). Then a new problem, born of the industrial age, appeared: chemical contaminants. 

Pesticide monitoring was in its infancy. It had been less than 10 years since Rachel Carson's SILENT SPRING 

had awakened public consciousness to the threat of environmental contami nants. The National Pesticide Moni toring Program, initiated by the U.S. 

Department of Agriculture in 1964, had led to expanded surveillance by that agency and by FDA of pesticide contamination of foods, in excess of pesticide tolerances set by FDA since 1953. The same program required the 

Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to monitor contaminant trends affecting fish and wildlife. FWS began monitoring Great Lakes fish in 1967; by the time the first year's results were in, that agency and the Michigan Department of Agriculture had made the same chilling discovery. The fish in the lakes-including the newly stocked and marketed salmon-were contaminated, primarily with high levels of

DDT and dieldrin. The State immedi ately recalled and embargoed the products, and the Michigan salmon industry ground to a halt for over a decade. 

Organochlorine pesticides such as dieldrin, DDT, and their metabolites appeared to be the major problems at first. But in early 1969 FDA found residues of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB's), which are industrial chemicals, in food for the first time. This new contaminant, regulatory agencies soon found, was highly toxic and possibly carcinogenic. Although residues of it were originally found in milk, they soon began to show up in other foods, including fish. 

Monitoring of Great Lakes fish was intensified in the early half of the 

1970's. One Federal-State program, for instance, combined the resources of the Fish and Wildlife Service and 

FDA's Detroit District with the Michi gan departments of Natural Resources and of Agriculture in 1972 in the

Great Lakes Environmental Contami nants Survey (GLECS). In 1975, based on the findings under this program, the Detroit District initiated seizure of several shipments of fish. 

District officials warned that chubs, coho salmon, and lake trout might not be allowed in interstate commerce because contaminant levels were too high, and commerical fishermen began to feel they were up against unfair odds. DDT and dieldrin had been banned in 1972 and 1974 respectively, but no regulatory action had been taken on PCB's. At a national conference on PCB's, sponsored by the En- 

FDA Consumer / September 1981 / 31

vironmental Protection Agency (EPA) 

in 1975, the Great Lakes fishing industry was well represented and vocal. "The PCB problem has been handled backwards," said the wife of one commercial fisherman. "My husband and his brothers were stopped from fishing carp on Green Bay, while nothing has been done to stop the sources of PCB's." Another wife told the conference, "We are fourth-generation commercial fishermen. On the last part of July of this year, the 

FDA shut down our business when fish tested from our nets measured 54 ppm [parts per million] of PCB's. 

Overnight we've lost a business it's taken years to build." A representative of the National Fisheries Institute (a trade association comprising 550 companies) added, "This is somewhat of an old refrain. In the last several years we've talked about things like DDT in our waters. After that it was mercury, and today it's PCB."

Many of the Great Lakes fish hadand some still have-PCB residues very close to the 5 ppm tolerance established by FDA. The agency's proposal to reduce the tolerance to 1 or 2 ppm could curtail the entire lakes fishing industry, said Nathaniel Reed, former assistant secretary for Fish and 

Wildlife and Parks. (In fact, FDA did publish a proposal in 1979 to lower the tolerance for PCB's in fish and shellfish to 2 ppm. However, several parties-including the National Fisheries Institute-objected and requested a hearing. This hearing is currently in progress; meanwhile the 5 ppm level is being enforced by food and drug officials.) Reed detailed the Federal-State programs designed to prevent extinction of the lake trout by controlling the sea lamprey population and restocking. "After 17 years and 33 million dollars, the sea lamprey no longer represents a major threat to the fisheries of the upper Great Lakes," Reed said. "The dissolution of the lamprey threat has allowed a successful State and Federal restocking program involving more than 150 million [fish]. . . . All our efforts are for naught if these fish cannot be harvested-and we now face this stark possibility. . . . If we stop [these] current programs, it is almost certain that the sea lamprey would reestablish itself and the salmonid populations and fisheries dependent upon them would collapse, thus 

32 September 1981 | FDA Consumer wiping out the past Federal investment of many years and millions of dollars and a Great Lakes economy worth several hundred million dollars... 

And yet if we cannot eat these fish, I cannot justify spending millions of dollars contributed by the American taxpayer. 

Reed also pointed out a second threat posed by PCB's, as well as by other organochlorine chemicals: The contaminants appeared to be impairing the ability of the fish to reproduce. "Nothing short of immediate drastic action will enable us to raise anything better than lakes full of eunuchized fish," Reed declared. 

Drastic action of sorts came in 

1976. The Toxic Substances Control 

Act was passed by Congress banning the production and distribution of 

PCB's in the United States. The Fish and Wildlife Service reported decreasing levels of DDT and PCB's in fish in 1977, although dieldrin levels were still high. The first significant decline in dieldrin was reported by that agency in 1981, findings which talleyed with analyses by the Michigan 

Department of Natural Resources. 

That year marked the first commercial sale of salmon from Lake Michigan since pesticides had been found in the lake's fish. One firm has since processed 1 million pounds of salmon and 

100,000 pounds of salmon eggs, all with contaminant levels below the tolerances. This year, the State's Department of Natural Resources collected 

49 salmon samples, all of which were below FDA tolerances.

Federal-State efforts seem to have been as effective in reducing chemical residues in the Great Lakes fish as they were in reducing other problems, such as overfishing and predation.

But the Fish and Wildlife Service re ports that pesticides, industrial chemicals, and metals, if not excessive, are now common in these fish. Although the GLECS program folded in 1978, FDA and the States continue to sample fish intended for food; and the 

States and FWS monitor the effects of the contaminants on the fish. FWS reports that the impaired reproductive ability of these fish-which has been linked to chemical contaminants-remains a serious problem: Certain species, such as the cisco and chub, which are native inhabitants of lakes Superior, Michigan, and Huron, seem to be disappearing; and no lake-produced juvenile or adult trout have been found in Lake Michigan for almost 25 years-despite annual plantings of an average of 2 million trout each year since 1965. The agency expanded its surveillance program in 1978 to include cooperation with EPA and not only to study the major contaminants (such as DDT, PCB's, dieldrin, and mercury) but also to identify and quantify lesser or previously undetected contaminants. One such contaminant was found in 1979 when polychlorinated dibenzofurans (PCDF's), by-products of PCB's, were detected in fish from U.S. waters for the first time. There are 135 possible PCDF compounds, some up to 

500 times more toxic than the most potent PCB's. Detection of PCDF's has become possible only recently through use of sophisticated new techniques of negative-ion high resolution mass spectrometry. 

The Great Lakes fishing industry may have weathered a host of storms so far this century, but its waters are still troubled. Federal and State agencies alike will be keeping a close watch. -Carol Ballentine

■Investigators' Reports presents infor mation on inspections, product seizures, court proceedings, and other administrative and regulatory actions by Federal, State, and local food and drug agencies across the country to provide health and economic protec tion to consumers of foods, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices.

Metallic Mix 

Whether it's in greenbacks or bread, $29,000 is a lot of dough. In greenbacks, that was the value of a variety of bread products recalled by 

Pennington Brothers, Inc., a bakery 

■in Washington Court House, Ohio. 

In bread, it was 4 days' production for sale to approximately 2,500 retail grocery stores, restaurants, and school food services in southern Ohio and northern Kentucky. The prod- ■ucts included hot dog and hamburger buns, sandwich rolls, and white and rye sliced breads.

The products were recalled after students at Covington, Ky., schools complained that they had found pieces of wire-up to an inch longin buns served in the school cafeteria. An investigator from FDA's Columbus (Ohio) Resident Inspection 

Post went to the bakery and soon found the problem. One of the initial steps in baking bread is to sift the flour to break up the lumps. Wire mesh sifters with decreasing mesh sizes are used. The investigator found that the final wire mesh sifter had disintegrated and the pieces were being mixed into the dough. Over 

350,000 pounds of flour (used to make 90 varieties of bread and sandwich rolls) were suspected of being contaminated. 

Pennington Brothers destroyed all possibly contaminated breads at a county landfill. The company also installed an $11,000 metal detection system to prevent contamination of its products by metals should a similar mishap occur again. 

Sharp Cheese

A recent case that was handled by 

FDA's Chicago District involved a shipment of cheese that was literally too sharp. That is, it contained splinters, among other contaminants. 

The cheese, approximately 16,500 pounds of romano and parmesan, was seized by a U.S. marshal at the distributor's warehouse in Monroe, Wis., after the Chicago District laboratory found wood splinters ranging from 0.2 to 13.5 millimeters in length in samples taken from the shipment. 

Analyses of the samples also turned up rodent, cat, rabbit, and other animal hairs, feather barbules, and metal fragments. 

The district recommended seizure because of evidence that the cheese had been prepared and held by the manufacturer under insanitary conditions.

The evidence was collected during a routine inspection of the manufacturer, Forreston Cheese Co., Forreston, Ill. During the inspection, investigators noticed that the firm was using wooden cheese racks that were splintering and piercing the cheese.

Shortly after the inspection, Forreston shipped the cheese to the Wisconsin firm for distribution. The cheese was valued at $25,000.

Hyper Help-Less 

Maurer's Medical and Research 

Association in Canton, Ohio, probably didn't expect an FDA response to the "Hyper Help" advertisement it placed in the COLUMBUS DISPATCH 

and other Ohio newspapers. 

The ad said that one drop of "Hyper Help" in fruit juice twice a week would change a crying, disagreeable child into a truly sweet boy or girl. "Hyper Help" was described as a special vitamin that relieved tension through action on the thyroid gland. 

An investigation by FDA's Cincin nati District found that Maurer's Association was actually Gary Maurer, a Canton bricklayer, who was bottling "Hyper Help" in his home, using well water as an ingredient. He had no quality or manufacturing controls, except that the water had been tested for purity.

Labeling on the "Hyper Help" 

vials advised parents of hyperactive children to discontinue amphetamines, special diets, and other treatments they might be using, and replace them with "Hyper Help" in fruit juice. FDA laboratory analysis showed that "Hyper Help" was a dilute form of Lugois solution, which is a prescription iodine preparation used for treatment of goiter. 

Maurer's had obtained the iodine from a pharmacist, then added the well water to it. 

In a letter sent to Maurer's Association, FDA pointed out that the claims made for "Hyper Help" would make it a daytime sedative, not a vitamin. Such sedatives cannot be sold without a doctor's prescription. The letter also noted that, as a prescription sedative, "Hyper Help" would have to be tested for safety and effectiveness by the manufacturer and the data sent to FDA. The letter suggested that Maurer's discontinue marketing this mislabeled, untested product. 

Recent checks by FDA indicate that "Hyper Help" is no longer being advertised or sold.

Fire, Fire 

It was getting to be a habit for 

FDA's resident post investigator in

Lafayette, La. He was called to the scene of two fires in nearby Alexandria on the same day. 

On February 13, the Louisiana

State Health Department requested help from the Lafayette resident to supervise clean-up and reconditioning operations at the Venture Marketing 

Corp., a beer distributor warehouse, resulting from a fire that occurred on 

January 30. The beer was housed in two adjoining buildings, both severely damaged by fire. The roof of one building collapsed on several trucks and beer that was stored there, and beer stored in the other building was damaged by fire, smoke, and water. Over 70,000 cases of beer were condemned by the State and subsequently destroyed. 

Also on February 13, the same

Federal/State inspection team worked together at the Cotton Brothers Holsum Bakery. Fire in the production area destroyed about $15,000 in raw materials, finished products, and packaging materials. Afterward, the bakery was able to continue operations on a limited basis. 

No Slight Difference 

The labels on the three boxes said 

V-100 N Isophane Insulin, but inside each box was a vial with a label read ing V-100 R Insulin Injection. To a diabetic the difference is more than a couple of letters in the alphabet. 

FDA Consumer / September 1981 / 33

Insulin is sold over the counter (without prescription) and is self-administered. But the N isophane version is a long-acting insulin taken once a day, while the 100-R is "regular" insulin, taken three or four times a day and more quickly absorbed. 

Each person with diabetes knows the kind of insulin he or she should be taking, and getting the wrong one could lead to diabetic shock or other complications. Many diabetics have vision problems, however, and could not be expected to check the label on the vial against the label on its box, especially if it is something as familiar to them as their daily insulin. 

The vials of regular insulin in the isophane boxes were discovered at the Public Health Service Hospital in 

San Francisco. Hospital staff quickly notified the manufacturer, E. R. 

Squibb in New Brunswick, N.J. A

Class I recall-meaning a "probable health hazard"-was initiated by 

Squibb and monitored by FDA's 

Newark District. Squibb sent recall letters to all its wholesale and other consignees, which included hospitals, nursing homes, prisons, mental institutions, and retail pharmacies, asking that they check all Squibb insulin received since November 1980, and return any with package or label mixups. The company also issued a press release.

The recall was completed in mid- March, 1981, about a month after it began. No other boxes were found with wrong vials and no injuries from the mishap were reported.

With the price of peanut butter soaring, peanut butter and jelly sandwich devotees may be ecstatic to hear that imports of peanuts have also increased. But the rise in imports means a lot more work for investigators from the U.S. Department of 

Agriculture and FDA. 

In February, USDA told FDA's 

Norfolk Resident Post that its inspectors had been finding a large number 

ASK POR THE NEW KIND PEANUTS 

of beetle-type insects in peanuts offered for import through the Port of 

Norfolk, Va. The inspectors had not found any prohibited insects-such as the Kaphra beetle-but said the infestation appeared to be extensive.

About 15 million pounds of the inshell nuts were being held in warehouses and trucks near the port. Norfolk investigators made a spot check, emptying and sifting through whole bags of peanuts, and found about 70 percent of the lots were infested with both live and dead insects. The bugs in one bag numbered 53. 

Baltimore District staff people met with Norfolk Customs officials and customhouse brokers and asked that these two groups tell the importers that the problem was serious and that the nuts required reconditioning before marketing. Reconditioning consists of killing the insects by fumigation (either with methyl bromide or another approved chemical) and then separating the insects from the nuts. This can be done by aspiration (using suction to pull off bugs and other lightweight debris), or a mechanized screening process in which the peanuts are agitated over screens to separate the insects from the nuts. 

About 90 percent of the importers agreed to recondition the nuts. The peanuts of those importers who did not recondition them voluntarily were detained and reconditioned under FDA supervision or returned to the country of origin. Baltimore 

District Compliance Officer Marvin 

Blumberg estimates that between 

January and June about 100 million pounds of peanuts have come through the Port of Norfolk and have been reconditioned. "If it weren't for the importers' cooperation," he says. "we'd be spending all our time looking at peanuts."

Seizures and Postal Service Cases FILED SEIZURE ACTIONS charge violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and are initiated based upon FDA 

recommendations. A seizure action is commenced by the filing of a complaint in the U.S. district court where the goods are located. A U.S. marshal is then directed by the court to take possession of the goods, removing the product from commerce, until the matter is resolved. 

A total of 28 actions to remove from the consumer market products charged to be violative was reported in May. These actions included 9 seizures of foods: 6 involved charges concerning contamination, 2 involved charges concerning economic and labeling violations, and 1 involved charges concerning food additives. Others included 18 of drugs (including 2 of veterinary), and 1 of medical devices.

Pecan pies, frozen, Field's World Best, at Dallas, N. Dist. Tex.

Charged 11-14-79: when shipped by Field's Inc., Pauls Valley, Okla.. 

the article had been prepared and packed under insanitary conditions: 

402(a)(4). The article was claimed by the shipper, who denied the charge. The parties served interrogatories on each other. Upon motion of the claimant, an agreed order was filed authorizing the claimant to conduct postseizure test of a number of randomly selected pies. 

The claimant also requested the production for copying of various documents produced as a consequence of FDA's inspection of claimant's plant and sampling of claimant's product. 

The case came on for trial before the court without a jury. The court found for the Government, saying in part:

Findings of Fact "1. The United States of America pursuant to provisions of the 

Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act seeks seizure and condemnation of certain articles of food consisting of pecan pies manufactured 

[on Sept. 24-27, 1979] by Field's, Inc.. (Fields). Pauls Valley, Okla homa. * 

"8. During the [FDA] inspections [of Field's plant on Sept. 27-28 

and Oct. 1-2, '79] there existed and was observed by the FDA inspectors insect and significant rodent activity in, on, and around the bags and boxes of raw materials stored in the raw materials storage room. The rodent activity was evidenced by numerous rodent pellets. extensive rodent urine stains, rodent gnawed areas on the bags and boxes, often gnawed through to the product contained therein, rodent nests, live rodents, and dead rodents. Insects existed in and on some of the bags and boxes of raw materials. "9. The raw materials storage room housed raw materials-such as 

38 September 1981 FDA Consumer

tapioca starch, flour, pecans, and sugar-which were used as ingredients in the seized pecan pies. “10. During the inspections there existed and was observed by the 

FDA investigators similar insect and rodent activity in the production room (adjacent to the raw materials storage room), where the seized pecan pies were prepared. "11. The rodent activity described in Findings of Fact Nos. 8 and 

10 was of long duration and existed during the period of time the seized pies were prepared. "12. The doors between the raw materials storage room and the production room were installed in a manner which permitted rodent traffic between the two rooms. Openings existed in the walls and entranceways of the plant which permitted access by rodents from the outside to the interior of the plant. "15. Testing of random samples from the seized pecan pies demonstrated minimal evidence of rodent or other foreign matters. "16. The raw materials storage room and the production room of 

Field's plant were in an insanitary condition when the seized pies were prepared due to the existence of the rodent activity described in Find ings of Fact Nos. 8 and 10. *** Conclusions of Law "1. This court has jurisdiction of this action under 21 U.S.C. §334 and 28 U.S.C. §1345. * * * 

"4. The [Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic] Act provides that a food shall be deemed adulterated if it is prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become contaminated with filth, 21 U.S.C. §342(a)(4). Since the seized pecan pies were prepared under insanitary conditions whereby they may have become contaminated with filth, the pies are adulterated under [21 

U.S.C.] $342(a)(4). "5. Fields argues that tests performed on the pecan pies show the presence of only very small amounts of foreign matter and thus they were not adulterated under §342(a)(4). The Court does not find this argument to be either persuasive or relevant. Section 342(a)(4) focuses solely upon the conditions under which the food was prepared. It is not necessary to prove that the food itself consists of, or contains, filth. Moreover, §342(a)(4) does not incorporate a "tolerance" permitting some minimal level of filth in food. "6. Because of the magnitude of the insanitary conditions existing during the FDA inspections and the close proximity of such inspections to the dates of preparation of the seized pecan pies, it is a reasonable inference, as found in Finding of Fact No. 11, that similar insanitary conditions existed when the seized pecan pies were prepared. . . .' 

Accordingly, the court ordered the article destroyed. (F.D.C. No. 

62680; S. No. 80-116–524; N.J. No. 15)

The article was claimed by the manufacturer and its president James Barnes. Subsequently, the manufacturer and its president consented to a decree of condemnation authorizing release of the articles to the manufacturer and its president for bringing the articles into compliance by: (1) labeling the articles "For Research 

40 September 1981 FDA Consumer

Use Only. Not for Use in Clinical Diagnostic Procedures"; (2) notifying the consignee, return receipt requested, that FDA had raised questions about the article's manufacturing procedures; (3) furnishing 

FDA with a list of consignees; (4) refraining from any representations, oral or written, that the articles were suitable for clinical diagnostic purposes; (5) obtaining consignees assurances that the relabeled products were not to be used for clinical diagnostic purposes; (6) destroying a 41-case lot of serum which FDA inspection indicated had been stored at 4° C instead of -20° C as directed by its labeling; and (7) retaining such letters, return receipts, and assurances in the company files. 

In addition B&B Research Laboratories, Inc., and James Barnes were enjoined from the interstate shipment of devices for clinical invitro use produced at their plant, unless and until a number of specified conditions had been met. (F.D.C. No. 62998; S. No. 80-103-697; N.J.

NOTICES OF JUDGMENT on Criminal Actions New England Grocer Supply Co., Julian J. Leavitt, president, Joel A. 

Leavitt, vice president, Julian Schultz, vice president & general manager, James J. Kaminski, sanitation officer & supervisor, and Ronald 

B. Cain, director of warehousing, Northboro, Dist. Mass. 

Charged 7-6-76: unbleached enriched flour (count 1), sugar (count 

2), bleached enriched flour (count 3), presifted bleached enriched flour (count 4), potato chips (count 5), canned tomato puree (count 6), and salt (count 7) were held under insanitary conditions in a building accessible to rodents and exposed to contamination by rodents; and the unbleached enriched flour and the sugar were contaminated with rodent filth; 402(a)(3), 402(a)(4).

The defendants moved to suppress evidence and moved to suppress all oral and written statements of the defendants. In partially granting and partially denying those motions, the court said: "On January 6, 1975, F.D.A. Investigator Bruce G. Sturgeon ('Sturgeon') began a comprehensive inspection of New England (Grocer Supply Co.] He displayed his credentials (January 6, 1975) and issued a Notice of Inspection to David Ginsberg ('Ginsberg'), Vice President of Purchasing. F.D.A. Investigator Richard H. Penta ('Penta') 

displayed his credentials and issued another Notice of Inspection to Kaminski, Sanitation Supervisor, on January 8, 1975. At the conclusion of the inspection, a list of observations was issued to Schultz, Executive Vice President and General Manager, and a receipt for samples was issued to Kaminski. "During this inspection, the Investigators were accompanied at all times by Kaminski and/or Roger Lafortune (‘Lafortune'), Sanitation Supervisor. Kaminski furnished information on warehouse operation, inventory control, sanitation procedures, quality control, the names of some of the corporate officers, and distribution. Lafortune supplemented information on sanitation practices and quality control. 

Schultz provided further information on the corporate structure, significance of trade names, and annual volume of sales. Kaminski refused to allow photographs in the warehouse, and none were taken. 

Photographs of labeling were allowed. "A discussion with management followed the inspection, and was attended by Schultz; Ralph Dudley ('Dudley'), Director of Warehousing and Transportation; Cain, Warehouse Manager; Kaminski and Lafortune. "On February 6, 1975, an ‘Information Letter' was issued to Julian, stating that the January, 1975, inspection revealed evidence of rodent infestation which included rodent excreta pellets, fluorescent stains and gnawed holes in and on food products, as well as the presence of live and dead mice throughout the warehouse. A response indicating the cause of this problem and the steps taken toward correction was requested. "A follow-up inspection of New England commenced on June 4, 1975. Credentials were displayed by F.D.A. Investigator Robert L. 

Hart ('Hart'), and a Notice of Inspection was issued to Peter De- 

Gannaro ('DeGannaro'), Assistant Treasurer. DeGannaro was the only corporate officer present at the warehouse at the onset of the inspection. Credentials were subsequently displayed to Kaminski, who also received receipts for samples issued on June 5, 6, and 10, 1975. 

Schultz was issued a Notice of Inspection on June 13, 1975. "Hart was accompanied during much of the inspection by Kaminski, FDA Consumer / September 1981 | 41

who provided relevant information, and Terry O'Toole ('O'Toole'),

Sanitation Officer, was present for brief periods of time. Kaminski provided all shipping records to cover the samples that were collected. 

On June 13, 1975, a List of Observations was issued to Schultz. This list was discussed with Schultz, Kaminski and Cain; all commented on the observations. Schultz provided information regarding corporate structure and individual responsibility regarding sanitation. Cain provided some technical information regarding the layout of the warehouse... "The F.D.A. is not required under $374 to set forth in its notice the reason underlying the inspection or what it expects to find; it is simply and unequivocally authorized to enter and inspect certain specified premises at reasonable times, Daley v. Weinberger, 400 F.Supp. 

1288 (D.C. N.Y. 1975), aff'd. 536 F.2d 519; and if this Chapter is to be effectively enforced to protect an urgent federal interest, unannounced inspections are unquestionably of the utmost importance. 

U.S. v. Del Campo Baking Mfg. Co., 345 F.Supp. 1371 (D.C. Del. 

1972). 

"In U.S. v. Acri Wholesale Grocery Co., 409 F.Supp. 529 (D.C. 

Iowa 1976), the court held that the owners of the warehouse were neither in custody nor deprived of their freedom at any time during the inspection of the warehouse by the F.D.A. Investigators, and since the Government's intent in inspecting the warehouse did not shift from mere inspection to criminal investigation, the owners of the warehouse were not required to be given Miranda warnings. The 

Government contends that no Miranda warning was necessary or required in the instant matter. . . . 

"The CODE OF FEDERAL REGULATIONS ('C.F.R.'), Title 21, Chapter 

1, Section 2.121(p)(i), with respect to the delegation of authority to 

F.D.A. investigators, provides: 'To conduct examinations, inspections, and investigations; to collect and obtain samples; to have access to and to copy and verify records; and to supervise compliance operations, for the enforcement of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic 

Act, ...' "Clearly, the F.D.A. Investigators have authority under the direction of the Commissioner and pursuant to a general delegation of authority, C.F.R. §2.121(a), wherein the Deputy Commissioner and the Associate Commissioner are authorized to perform all the functions of the . In a notice in the 

FEDERAL REGISTER, published on November 16, 1972, 37 C.F.R., Page No. 24377, with respect to the office of the Assistant Secretary for Health, there is outlined a 'Statement of Organization, Functions and Delegations of Authority, which includes the operation of the 

Food and Drug Enforcement Administration, wherein the Assistant

Secretary of HEW is assigned the duty of directing the activities of the F.D.A. "Although the Government properly contends that no search warrant is necessary, there are a number of important questions to be answered with respect to the instant matter: "1. Whether the Investigators should have given the Miranda warning after the first inspection when they realized that there was a possibility of criminal prosecution? Pursuant to the decided cases on this issue, the answer is 'no,' so long as the investigation was not a criminal investigation. "2. Were the acts of the Investigators reasonable in returning 16 times to inspect the premises without at any time indicating to the owners that criminal prosecution was contemplated? The inspections of January were not unreasonable in light of the size of the establishment. However, it was unreasonable and unfair that the Investigators did not indicate at some point to the owners that criminal prosecution was contemplated, for it appears to this Court that the Investigators, at some point during their investigation, turned their attention from supervision to prosecution under the very Act which gave them the authority to enter the premises for administrative purposes. In the opinion of this Court, they had exceeded the reasonable limits permitted under this Act at that stage. "3. Were the inspections, in fact, reasonable inspections unde! $374 of the Act? 'Yes, to the extent that the Investigators were acting under the authority of $374, at least during the initial inves tigations in January of 1975. "4. Should the defendants have been given the opportunity to be represented by counsel when the hearing was held on September 17. 

1975, notwithstanding that the Government still claims that it was in the process of making an administrative investigation? The defendants should have been given the opportunity to be represented by counsel on that date. "5. Does an administrative investigation authorize the Government. under the guise of such investigation, to obtain incriminating evidence against the parties who are the subject of the investigation? If the administrative investigation is solely for the purpose of obtaining crim inal evidence, the answer is obviously 'no.' The Government, in thi case, claims otherwise, and there is no evidence to indicate that the did so during the initial investigations in January. "6. Were the people who were interviewed agents, managers or merely employees of the defendant corporation? In the opinion of this Court, all were either agents or officers of the corporation. "7. Should the court look at the facts of the individual cases to determine whether the investigation was, in fact, focused on the defendants, and should they (F.D.A. Investigators), at some time, have given a Miranda warning when a determination was made that criminal liability and action was involved? In United States v. Thriftimarı, 429 

F.2d 1006 (9th Cir. 1970), cert. denied 91 S.Ct. 188, 400 U.S. 926. the court held that the Miranda warning was not required because it was a 'routine' inspection. Obviously, the defendants did not know that they were the targets of a criminal prosecution, as it is unlikely that they would have attended the meeting of September 17, 1975 At least, they probably would have been represented by counsel. "8. Was the Government's conduct purposeful or oppressive"?

Although the Government's conduct was not purposeful or oppres sive, it was, in fact, unfair. . "This situation is analogous to an I.R.S. situation which permits administrative investigations. See United States v. Bembridge, 458 

F.2d 1262 (1st Cir. 1972), and United States v. Leahey, 434 F.2d7 

(1st Cir. 1970). . 

"This Court concludes that in reviewing this entire matter, it should be considered in the context of the holding in Schneckloth v. Busta monte, 412 U.S. 218, 93 S.Ct. 2041 (1973) in that, in making a determination with respect to these motions, the Court must look to 'the totality of the circumstances' and must consider the actions of the Government during the period in which the investigations were conducted. "Although it cannot be said that the investigators in this instance acted fraudulently or were deceptive, certainly their conduct satisfies this Court that during the course of the investigation they should have. at some stage of the investigation, stated to the defendants the prob ability of criminal prosecution. Although the statute gives them the right to enter without a warrant to examine the premises in an administrative investigation, that authority should not be an 'open se same' to subvert the constitutional rights of defendants. "Pursuant to §374(a), the standard of reasonableness is defined. 

in relation to the F.D.A. inspections, in Durovic v. Palmer, 342 F.2d 

634 (7th Cir. 1965), in which the court indicated that the inspectors had conducted themselves with a view to carrying out their statutory duties and, therefore, the examination of the administrative invest gation was not unreasonable. "The evidence indicates that when the Investigators spoke to Cur tin, they gave her the distinct impression that they were there to s that corrective measures were taken. 

42 September 1981 FDA Consumer

"The record also indicates that even after the complaints had been issued, the investigators returned to the plant (see Tr. p. 380), another indication that the actions of the investigators did not comport with fairness. "The Court cannot conceive that each of the cases cited were decided on the basis that this statute provides an open season for the 

F.D.A. Investigators. The statute does not permit the Investigators to go beyond the bounds of propriety and fairness in preparing a prosecution against an individual without at some point during the procedure informing him of the fact that they were proceeding on a criminal basis. "Even in Camara, supra, cited by both the Government and the defendants, the court held, at page 537: ‘. . . that an administrative search is neither personal in nature nor aimed at the discovery of evidence of crime . . .,' and thus involves a 'relatively limited invasion of the citizen's privacy.' This Court is satisfied that Camara does not authorize Government investigators to wander into one's business and make an extensive investigation (in the instant matter, 16 visits) without indicating at some time that criminal proceedings are contemplated. "The evidence indicated that after the third or fourth inspection the investigators had received sufficient information to proceed criminally, if they thought it was necessary. However, they proceeded to obtain additional evidence. The Investigators knew that there was a probability of criminal prosecution with respect to these defendants arising out of the inspections. “In Barlow's Inc. v. Usery, 424 F.Supp. 437 (1976) the court held that the inspection provisions of OSHA, which authorize warrantless inspections of business establishments, are unconstitutional as being violative of the Fourth Amendment. The defendants distinguished the 

Biswell case, which involved firearms, from F.D.A. cases. The Court does not agree with that distinction, as the basic regulations and laws are similar. The Court does agree, however, that as in Camara and 

See, supra, some degree of fairness with respect to the inspection should be shown. See also: Air Pollution Variance Board of Colorado v. Western Alfalfa, 416 U.S. 861 (1974). 

"Although the Government contends that it was a general inspection, the defendants argue that the second inspection constituted a general search in violation of the Fourth Amendment rights of the defendants, and cite in support of this contention Coolidge v. New 

Hampshire, 403 U.S. 443 (1974) and Warden v. Hayden, 387 U.S. 

294 (1967). The Court does not agree that these cases are even remotely similar to the instant matter, nor did either of those cases involve statutes specifically authorizing administrative inspections. "The Supreme Court, in fact, has recognized the importance of informing potential defendants concerning the distinction between civil and criminal liability for the purpose of determining whether 

Fifth Amendment violations have occurred. U.S. v. Kordel, 397 U.S. 

1, 905 S.Ct. 763 (1970). The purpose of this legislation was not intended to circumvent the Constitution of the United States; rather, it was intended to enable the F.D.A. (Government) to maintain periodic supervision and control over the quality of food sold by distributors and over the health conditions that exist at storage warehouses. "The case most similar to the instant matter is United States v. 

Litvin, 353 F.Supp. 1333 (D.C. D.C. 1973), in which a motion to suppress was denied. "The defendants argue that the Investigators were not duly designated by the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare; the Court is satisfied that there is no substance to this contention, as they were fully authorized, not only by the Act, but by the Rules promulgated with respect thereto. "On the basis of the foregoing, and after reviewing the evidence and considering the arguments of counsel and the briefs filed, this 

Court concludes as follows: 

"1. That permission was granted to the F.D.A. Investigators to enter the premises of the defendants; there is no evidence that the defendants were coerced in any way. "2. That consent was given voluntarily. "3. That all inspections during the month of January were within the purview of and in conformity with 28 U.S.C. §374. “4. That beginning with June of 1975, the investigation was a criminal investigation and did not conform with 28 U.S.C. $374; the 

Miranda warning should have been given to each of the defendants because of the shift in the investigation. "5. That at no time were any of the defendants given Miranda rights or warnings. "Therefore, based on the foregoing, this Court orders: "1. That both motions are denied with respect to all evidence obtained and all seizures made during the month of January, 1975. "2. That with respect to all evidence and seizures made during June of 1975, both motions are granted."

Upon the various adverse rulings, the defendants appealed and the Government moved for a hearing de novo. The U.S. District Court heard the appeal, ruled that Miranda warnings were not required, ruled that a rehearing de novo was not needed, and asserted that the Court of Appeals lacked jurisdiction to hear appeals made from decisions of United States magistrates. The District Court said: "This is an appeal by the United States from a ruling of the Magistrate which ordered the suppression of certain evidence seized during an inspection of defendant's premises made in June of 1975. A sevencount Information charges one corporate and six individual defendants with allowing food being held for sale to become adulterated in vio lation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 21 U.S.C.A. 

§301, et seq. The offenses allegedly occurred between October, 1974, and May, 1975. The Information alleges that two Federal [Food and] Drug Administration (FDA) inspections of defendant corpora tion's warehouse revealed rodent infestation in violation of 21 U.S.C.A.

§331(k). 

"On February 10 and 17, 1977, all defendants waived their right to jury trial in the District Court and elected to be tried by the United 

States Magistrate pursuant to 18 U.S.C.A. §3401. The defendants thereafter moved to suppress (1) all written and oral statements and (2) all evidence obtained as a result of the two inspections, the first of which occurred in January, 1975 and the second the following June. 

After a hearing on the motions, the Magistrate issued a Memorandum and Order on September 1, 1977, in which he denied the motions to suppress in regard to the January, 1975, inspection but granted the motions as to the June, 1975, inspection. The basis of the Magistrate's order was his ruling that Miranda warnings should have been given each of the defendants during the second warehouse investigation, since a possibility then existed of eventual criminal prosecution. "Pursuant to Rule 5 of the Rules of Procedure for the Trial of Minor

Offenses Before United States Magistrates, the Government subsequently moved for a rehearing de novo before this Court on the granting of the motions to suppress the results of the June 1975 inspection. The Government argues that the rehearing de novo is warranted because the June investigation, conducted under 21 U.S.C.A. $374, was noncustodial. Defendants thereafter moved to dismiss the Motion for a Rehearing de novo on the grounds that: (1) Magistrate's Rule 5 contains provisions which create substantive rights and is beyond the power of the Supreme Court to promulgate; (2) the rule as constituted denies defendants due process. Both parties have submitted memoranda in support of their motions. "It is undisputed that under Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966), warnings of certain constitutional rights must be given during custodial interrogations. It is also well-settled that warrantless searches are not permissible during certain regulatory investigations. United 

FDA Consumer / September 1981 | 43

States v. Biswell, 406 U.S. 311 (1972); see also Colonnade Catering

Corp. v. United States, 397 U.S. 72 (1970). The Supreme Court stated in the Biswell case, supra, that: 'In the context of a regulatory inspection system of business premises that is carefully limited in time. place, and scope, the legality of the search depends not on consent but on the authority of a valid statute.' 406 U.S. at 315. The statute giving authority to inspect in this case is 21 U.S.C.A. $374. In cases concerning FDA inspections, courts have consistently held that Miranda warnings need not be given by investigators conducting such inspections pursuant to the statute. "Moreover, last term the Supreme Court reemphasized that Miranda warnings are necessary only in purely custodial settings. 'Miranda warnings are required only where there has been such a restriction on a person's freedom as to render him "in custody"." Oregon v. Matheson, 429 U.S. 492, 97 S. Ct. 711 (1977). The Magistrate's 

September 1 order required Miranda warnings during the June, 1975 inspection, under the rule of United States v. Leahey, 434 F.2d 7 (1st

Cir. 1970). The case relied on by the Magistrate involved investigations conducted by Internal Revenue Service agents. It was decided prior to the Supreme Court's recent decision in Beckwith v. United States, 425 U.S. 341 (1976), where a taxpayer not in custody was interviewed by I.R.S. agents. "Under the standard enunciated in Beckwith, Miranda warnings were not required during the June investigation of defendant's warehouse. "Since our reading of the prevailing law regarding administrative searches establishes that Miranda warnings were not required during the June, 1975 inspection, the real issue before us is the scope of our review of the Magistrate's legal ruling to suppress. It has been held that '[t]he scope of appeal is the same as on an appeal from a judgment of a district court to a court of appeals. United States v. 

Barbaro, 369 F. Supp. 1302 (D. Mass. 1974); see also DeCosta v. 

Columbia Broadcasting System, 520 F.2d 499 (1st Cir. 1975) (Aldrich,

J. concurring). As such, we reverse the Magistrate's order on the ground the June, 1975 inspection was in conformity with 21 U.S.C.A. §374 and was noncustodial. We need not grant a rehearing de novo to consider the factual questions involved in the case. Thus, we need not reach the constitutional claims raised by defendants regarding Rule 5, supra. We do, however, flatly reject their suggestion that the proper route for the Government's appeal is the Court of Appeals rather than the District Court. To the contrary, the Court of Appeals lacks jurisdiction to hear direct appeals made from decisions of United 

States magistrates. United States v. Haley, 541 F.2d 678 (8th Cir. 1974). "Accordingly, an Order will be entered reversing the Magistrate's ruling."

The defendants made a number of motions, including the following: (1) Motion of defendants to dismiss information; (2) Motion of defendants for severance and separate trials; (3) (Defendant Kaminski's) motion to produce; (4) (Defendant Cain's) motion to produce; (5) defendant's motion for the court to view premises; (6) "In camera" 

inspection of Jenks Act material; (7) Defendants' Julian Leavitt, Joel 

Leavitt, James Kaminski, Ronald Cain, and Julian Schultz supplemental motion to suppress evidence. The motions were heard by the 

U.S. magistrate, who said:

Defendants' Contentions 

"The defendants contend: "1. That the information should be dismissed because it fails to allege that the individual defendants hold a 'position of responsibility in the business of the defendant, New England. "2. That Counts 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 of the information should be dismissed on the grounds of duplicity.

Government's Contentions "The Government contends: 

"1. That the allegation [that] the information is insufficient, because it fails to state the 'position of responsibility' of each individual defendant, is without foundation. "2. That each count of the information tracks the language of the statute and charges each defendant with causing 'specified articles of food to become adulterated,' in violation of Title 28, U.S.C. $342: 

Title 21, U.S.C. §301(k); and Title 21 U.S.C. $331(k). . . . 

Intent-Knowledge "Title 21, U.S.C. §301 et seq., requires neither intent nor knowledge for misdemeanor violation, Roseman v. U.S., 364 F.2d 18 (9th 

Cir. 1966), cert. denied 87 S.Ct. 879, 386 U.S. 918; see also United

States v. Park, 421 U.S. 658, 95 S.Ct. 1903 (Maryland 1975); and it prohibits any act which may result in adulteration of the product. 

Food is adulterated if it has been held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become contaminated with filth. U.S. v. H.B. 

Gregory Co., 502 F.2d 700 (7th Cir. 1974), cert. denied 95 S.Ct. 2629. 

42 U.S. 1007. In U.S. v. H.B. Gregory Co., supra, the Circuit Court also held that in light of the testimony of the FDA Inspector and the admission of the warehouse company's president regarding his area of responsibility and actions in the operation of a bakery supply warehouse business, the District Court did not err in convicting the individual defendant of violations of this Chapter, notwithstanding his claim that proof of scienter should have been required. "Under Section 342(a)(4), it is not necessary that the food actually become contaminated, for this subsection is designed to prevent adulteration in its incipiency by condemning insanitary conditions which may result in contamination. Berger v. U.S., 20 F.2d 818 (8th Cir. 1952).

Information-Language of Statute-Multiplicitous "Rule 7 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure provides that the information shall be a plain and concise statement of the essential facts constituting the offense charged. The allegations in this complaint are separate and distinct acts. "If, in fact, the Information tracks the language of a statute, it complies with Rule 7 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure with respect to a concise and definite statement of the essential facts constituting the offense charged. United States v. Bernstein, 553 F.2d 775. 

(2nd Cir. 1976). U.S. v. Mamber, 127 F.Supp. 924 (D. Mass. 1955) 

is clearly distinguishable from the instant matter inasmuch as the nine counts in Mamber were under one statute and referred to a single utterance. "The Information is sufficient if it apprises the accused, pursuant to Rule 7, of the charges against him so that he can prepare for trial. prevent surprise, and be protected against double jeopardy. U.S. v. 

Leach, 427 F.2d 1107 (1st Cir. 1970); U.S. v. Schembari, 484 F.2d 

931 (4th Cir. 1973). "If each count of the Information constitutes the holding for sale of certain units of food, the Act itself contemplates that each article of food, generally, must be in compliance with the law; therefore, the adulteration of different articles constitutes a separate offense for each article. . . . "In this section there are seven distinct acts of adulteration, and there are seven distinct and different articles of food. Therefore, with respect to the question of multiplicity, this Court is satisfied that the complaint tracks the statute and is not multiplicitous. 

Position of Responsibility 

"With respect to the position of responsibility, it was held in United States v. Park, supra, that in order to make an individual liable under 

Title 21, U.S.C. $331(k), the Government must establish his authority or position of responsibility either to prevent the violation of to promptly correct it and that he, in fact, failed to do so. The indi vidual defendants argue that this allegation should be in the complaint. 

I disagree, and I have found no cases to sustain their position. "Indeed, the Government must prove that the defendants were in 

44 September 1981 FDA Consumer

a position to prevent or correct violations of the provisions of Title 21 U.S.C. §301 et seq., but it is not necessary to allege their positions in the Information itself so long as the provisions of the act and the violations thereof are included in the Information. "The argument by a defendant that the corporate structure is one avenue of responsibility does not diminish the charges against an individual defendant, and he need not necessarily be an officer to be in a position of responsibility and authority. See U.S. v. Dotterweich, 320 U.S. 277 (1943); and U.S. v. Park, supra. "The theory upon which responsible corporate agents are held criminally accountable for causing violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (Title 21) permits the claim that the agent was powerless to prevent or correct violations to be raised defensively at trial on the merits. United States v. Park, supra. “United States v. Park, supra, in effect stands for the proposition that the head of a corporation can be charged because of his position as a corporate chief. Park held, citing Dotterweich, supra, at page 

668: ...the Act is of "now familiar type" which "dispenses with the conventional requirements for criminal conduct—awareness of some wrongdoing. In the interest of the larger good it puts the burden of acting at hazard upon a person otherwise innocent but standing in responsible relation to a public danger." "The defendants argue that there is a special prejudice inasmuch as each individual has a different responsibility and authority, yet all the defendants cannot have a position of responsibility in the company so as to warrant a violation of Title 21, U.S.C. §331(k), Park v. 

U.S., supra, and King v. U.S. 355 F.2d 700 (1st Cir. 1966). I do not agree. 

Conclusion 

"On the basis of the foregoing, therefore, this motion is denied.

Motion [#2] "When this motion was originally filed, it applied to all defendants. 

Each requested a separate trial. "Curtin, [one of the three defense counsels] at this hearing, stated on behalf of her client, Schultz, that she waived this motion and assented that Schultz be tried together with the other defendants. 

Curtin also spoke on behalf of Cullen and Skerry (Skerry was in the courtroom), stating that the defendants represented by Cullen and Skerry, namely, Julian, Joel, and New England, also waived this motion. "Goodwin, on behalf of Cain and Kaminski, pressed the motion and indicated that there was a possible Bruton problem; therefore, severance is necessary. In addition, he argued that Motions [#3] and [#4] were in line with Motion [#2] in that the information he received with respect to Motion [#2] will substantiate his position with respect to the need for severance. "The only question, then, with respect to Motion [#2], is whether Kaminski and Cain should be tried separately. 

Defendants' (Kaminski and Cain) Contentions 

"The defendants, Kaminski and Cain, contend: "1. That there should be severance because they would be prejudiced as the result of a joint trial which would constitute a violation of their Sixth Amendment rights. "2. That there is a Bruton problem in this Action [Bruton v. U.S., 391 U.S. 123 (1968)], inasmuch as there is a question of limiting instructions by the court which may prejudice these two defendants. "3. That the statement by the defendant, Leavitt, that Kaminski, Cain, and Schultz were responsible for supervising the sanitation program in the warehouse is prejudicial and, therefore, causes the problem which calls for severance of their case. They cite Varela Cartagena v. U.S., 397 F.2d 278 (1st Cir. 1968), in support of this contention. "4. That there should be severance in order that they may obtain exculpatory testimony from the codefendants. 

Pertinent Rules and Law 

"In Bruton v. United States, 88 S.Ct. 1620, 391 U.S. 123 (1968), the decision was principally based on the fact that certain kinds of hearsay are at once so damaging, so suspect, and yet so difficult to discount, that jurists cannot be trusted to give such evidence the minimum weight it logically deserves, whatever the instructions the trial judge might give. However, in Bruton, the court also said that the defendant is entitled to a fair trial, but not a perfect trial. "The circumstances in the instant matter do not satisfy this Court that the severance requested is justified and, in fact, the Court has already examined the various documents with respect to this action in camera, has granted discovery in certain aspects, and is satisfied, in the overall examination of these documents, briefs and arguments of the parties, that severance is not justified. "While the joinder requirements of the federal rules are satisfied, relief in the reviewing court is available only upon the showing of abuse of discretion by the trial court in refusing severance. Rules 8(b) 

and 14 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure. 

"In Varela Cartagena v. U.S., supra, there were no statements contained in the admissions attributable to the defendants. There is nothing that has indicated to this Court that there are any such statements which would warrant a severance. "Rule 8(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure provides that two or more defendants may be charged in the same information if they are alleged to have participated in the same act or transaction or in the same series of acts or transactions constituting an offense or offenses. They may also be charged in one or more counts together or separately. "In this information, the defendants, Kaminski and Cain, are charged with having participated actively and jointly with the other defendants in a series of criminal acts; therefore, joinder of these defendants is permissible. Rule 8(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure and 

United States v. Martinez, 479 F.2d 824 (1st Cir. 1973). "Generally, persons indicted jointly should be tried together, particularly in cases that are complex and would require lengthy trials. 

The rules with respect to joinder and severance are designed to promote economy and efficiency and to avoid a multiplicity of trials, where these objectives can be achieved without substantial prejudice to the right of a defendant to a fair trial. Bruton v. United States, supra. Persons jointly indicted for substantive offenses should be tried together except for most compelling reasons. United States v. Melville, 312 F.Supp. 234 (D.C. N.U. 1970). 

"Rule 14 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure provides for severance in the event the Court determines that in an indictment, joinder may be prejudicial to one of the defendants. In ruling on a motion by a defendant for severance, the court may order the attorney for the Government to deliver to the court for inspection in camera any statements or confessions made by the codefendants which the Government intends to introduce in evidence at the trial. No such statements apparently exist in this action and the in camera inspection has already been made by me with respect to Jencks Act material. 

"The Court has examined this information, and it is clear that the charges are interrelated with each defendant and a separate trial is unwarranted, for the evidence would be effective against each of the defendants. "There is no allegation here that there is a possibility of a confession or other possible violation of the Bruton rule which would warrant severance; Bruton v. United States, supra; nor is there an allegation that other individual defendants desire to call a codefendant to testify which would be thwarted if the defendants were tried together. United 

States v. Sweig, 316 F.Supp. 1148 (D.C. N.Y. 1970). "Although the defendants' argument may have some merit, the federal court has held that this danger, with respect to the prejudice 

FDA Consumer / September 1981 | 45

that may be caused, can be remedied simply by suitable instructions to the jury by the court to avoid any prejudice and to guide the jury through the complex proof in long and complicated cases. United States v. Boswell, 372 U.S. 780 (1966). Here, there is no jury; therefore, any such risk is minimal or non-existent. "First, this Court concludes that the possibility of the other defendants testifying is purely conjectural and secondly, that this is not a sufficient reason to warrant severance of trials. "Generally, persons jointly indicted should be tried together, and the granting of separate trials is a matter of discretion. Sagansky v. 

United States, 358 F.2d 195 (1st Cir. 1966), cert. denied 385 U.S. 816; 

United States v. Clayton, 450 F.2d 16 (1st Cir. 1971). "On the basis of the foregoing, therefore, this motion is denied. 

"With respect to these motions to produce any statements of codefendants, clearly there is no requirement that this be done. This 

Court has held consistently that the defendant is not entitled to a list of the Government's witnesses except pursuant to Title 18, U.S.C. $3500. Campbell v. U.S., 373 U.S. 487 (1963); U.S. v. Murphy, 480 

F.2d 256 (1st Cir. 1973), cert. denied 414 U.S. 912. "In addition, this material has been examined in camera (Motion [#6]). Certain discovery has been ordered, and this Court is satisfied that no further discovery is necessary or warranted. The codefendants' statements, if there are any, are not discoverable under the established cases. See U.S. v. Withers, 303 F.Supp. 641 (N.D. Ill. 1969). "On the basis of the foregoing, therefore, these motions are denied. Motion [#5] "Curtin argued that a view of the premises would produce a better understanding of the case as it could affect the findings of fact. Curtin is depending, in part, on the case of U.S. v. Park, supra, which, she contends, holds that people cannot be expected to do the impossible, notwithstanding the objective of the FDA regulations. "I have considered this motion, and I think it wise to view the premises prior to trial. "Therefore, the premises shall be inspected on the 10th day of

After an 8-day trial before the United States magistrate, James J. 

Kaminski was found not guilty; and the corporation and remaining individuals were found guilty. In making such findings, the magistrate said: 

Findings of Fact 

"The court finds beyond a reasonable doubt: "1. That the articles of food mentioned in Counts I and II of the 

Information were contaminated with rodents and rodent filth and that the articles of food referred to in Counts I-VII were adulterated in that they were held in conditions whereby they may have become contaminated. "2. That flour, sugar, potatoes, potato chips, tomato puree, and salt are foods within the meaning of 21 USCA §321(f). "3. That the food referred to in the indictment was held for sale and traveled in interstate commerce. "4. That the individual defendants, Joel and Schultz are liable for the adulteration as well as the corporation. "5. That the individual defendants Joel and Schultz were in a position of authority to prevent or correct the violations of the Act, within the meaning of Title 21 USCA § 331(k). 

“6. That the person primarily responsible for the operation of the warehouse was Schultz who was knowledgeable concerning the firm's daily operation particularly including sanitation. "7. That Julian who was President, although active in the operation of the company, had no direct involvement in sanitation problems, except as senior officer with ultimate authority and responsibility for preventing any violations of the Act. "8. That both Joel and Schultz were directly responsible and in control of the warehouse and its sanitation.. . . 

Conclusions 

"1. That both Julian and Joel had been consulted with respect to the condition at the warehouse and were in direct contact with Schultz who was in complete control, in charge and had the power to act and expend funds. "2. That Kaminski who worked under Schultz and Cain could not in the opinion of this court be said to share in the 'responsibility in the business process resulting in a violation.' "3. That Julian had no direct contact except as Chief Supervisory

Officer and in the overall charge of the corporation. His only contact was one session with respect to the correction of the sanitation problem. “4. That Julian, by virtue of office, as one in complete control is guilty within the meaning of the Act as interpreted by Park, supra, in that he possessed the final authority to institute whatever effective programs that were required. "5. That Joel was Executive Vice President and he too visited the warehouse often and attended sanitation meetings. "6. That Schultz was Executive Vice President and General Manager of the company at the time of the offenses charged. His office was located at the warehouse and he was there on a day to day basis and the person most responsible for sanitation at the warehouse. He toured the warehouse almost daily and received copies of sanitation reports from Kaminski. When he received the sanitation reports, he was shocked by the findings and admitted to having been lax in the past and admitted also that there was room for improvement. "7. That Kaminski, who was sanitation officer and supervisor of the company, was at the time of the alleged violations responsible for the day to day sanitation operation and maintaining sanitation. He reported to his superior Cain and to Schultz and he had the power to destroy food which was found to be adulterated. "8. That the warehouse had been inspected in January and the defendants were informed of sanitation problems; in June, the same problems existed. "9. That with respect to the union upheaval, defendants (except
