That Kaminski did what he was required to do but his power and authority were limited. "12. That the defendant, Julian acknowledged that their sanitation program was inadequate at the time of the January and June 1975 

General Discussion 

"It appears that the Government has seen fit to indulge in wholesale prosecution of every individual that had contact with this warehouse and who was in a position of authority pursuant to the Act. The finding made by this court with respect to Julian was made only on the basis that in Park, the court stated that the position of the President made him liable, responsible and subject to prosecution. "With respect to Kaminski, the court concludes that his power was limited and although he was responsible for the warehouse as a supervisor and sanitation officer, he reported to Cain and Schultz. "Clearly, both Joel and Schultz were familiar with the operation and the court is satisfied that they knew the warehouse conditions and failed to correct them. The court is further satisfied that it was not 'objectively impossible' to maintain the warehouse in a sanitary condition."

The corporation was sentenced to be fined $7,000, Joel Leavitt and Julian Schultz to be fined $3,500, and Julian Leavitt to be fined $3,750. 

Upon appeal to the district court, the case was remanded to the magistrate for further proceedings not inconsistant with the district court's opinion. In that opinion, the court said: "The scope of review by a district court on appeal from a conviction before a magistrate is 'the same as on an appeal from a judgment of a district court to a court of appeals.' 18 U.S.C. §3402; Rule 8(d), Rules of Procedure for the Trial of Minor Offenses Before United States 

Magistrates. The defendants challenge the conviction below on several grounds.

"The first ground of appeal relates solely to the defendant Julian 

Leavitt, president of NEGSC [New England Grocers Supply Co.]. 

FDA Consumer | September 1981 | 47

He contends that he was found guilty by the magistrate solely because he was company president at the time the violations occurred. This was error, defendant argues, because the Supreme Court's decision in United States v. Park, 421 U.S. 658 (1975), requires a finding of negligence or other blameworthiness in order to sustain a conviction for violation of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. "In Park, the Supreme Court reconsidered and reaffirmed the standard of liability set forth in United States v. Dotterweich, 320 U.S. 

277 (1943), for conviction of a corporate officer under the Act. Dotterweich established two propositions. First, the Act 'dispenses with the conventional requirement for criminal conduct-awareness of some wrongdoing.' Id. at 281. Second, the scope of liability includes all those who have 'a responsible share in the furtherance of the transaction which the statute outlaws. . . Id. at 284. In Park, the Court reaffirmed the first proposition and elaborated somewhat on how the Government establishes a 'responsible relationship' under Dotterweich. "The Park Court stated that Dotterweich and the cases following it establish that 'the Act imposes [on responsible corporate agents] not only a positive duty to seek out and remedy violations when they occur but also, and primarily, a duty to implement measures that will insure that violations will not occur.' 425 U.S. at 672. The Government establishes a prima facie case against corporate officer 'when it introduces evidence sufficient to warrant a finding by the trier of the facts that the defendant had, by reasons of his position in the corporation, responsibility and authority either to prevent in the first instance, or promptly to correct, the violation complained of, and that he failed to do so.' Id. at 673-74. The Court made it clear, however, that a finding of guilty cannot be predicated solely on the defendant's corporate position. Id. at 674-75. "The defendant in Park was the president and chief executive officer of a national retail food chain. He was charged with the same crime as is the defendant in the instant case, viz., causing foodstuffs being held for sale following shipment in interstate commerce to become adulterated in violation of 21 U.S.C. §331(k). Park contended, as does the defendant here, that the jury instructions allowed the jury to convict him solely on the basis of his corporate position. The Supreme Court did not agree. Viewing the charge in its entirety, the 

Court was convinced that 'the charge did not permit the jury to find guilt solely on the basis of respondent's position in the corporation; rather it fairly advised the jury that to find guilt it must find respondent "had a responsible relation[ship] to the situation, "and" by virtue of his position. . .had. . .authority and responsibility" to deal with the situation.' Id. at 674. The Court was also satisfied from its reading of the trial record that 'the jury could not have failed to be aware that the main issue for determination was not respondent's position in the corporate heirarchy, but rather his accountability, because of the responsibility and authority of his position, for the conditions which gave rise to the charges against him.' Id. at 675. "The defendant in the instant case contends that the magistrate found him guilty solely because of his corporate position as chief executive officer and that this was error since Park requires a finding of negligence or other blameworthiness. Although the defendant makes only one argument with two conjunctive parts, he asserts two separate and distinct grounds for reversal and I will treat them as such. The first ground is that the magistrate erred by convicting him solely on the basis of his corporate position; the second ground is that the magistrate erred by not making a finding of negligence or other blameworthiness. "Reviewing the magistrate's memorandum and findings, I conclude that the magistrate misconstrued the Park decision with regard to defendant Julian Leavitt. Although it appears that the magistrate understood and correctly applied Park's requirement of a 'responsible relationship' in finding two other individual defendants guilty, several statements in his opinion convince me that he did not do so in convicting Julian Leavitt. Early in his opinion, the magistrate made the following observation about the Park decision: 'Park (President of the corporation 'Acme') was individually convicted for violation of the Act by virtue of his position as president.' (Opinion at 3) (emphasis added). Later on, the magistrate again noted that Park 'stands for the proposition that the head of a corporation can be charged because of his position as a corporate chief.' (Opinion at 7) (emphasis added). 

These two statements demonstrate a basic misinterpretation of Park, since the Supreme Court made it clear that a corporate officer cannot be convicted solely on the basis of his position in the corporate heirarchy. This misunderstanding of Park is reflected in the magistrate's finding that defendant Julian Leavitt was guilty of violating the Act. 

In his 'general discussion' section, the magistrate stated explicitly that the 'finding made by this court with respect to Julian was made only on the basis that in Park, the court stated that the position of the 

President made him liable, responsible and subject to prosecution. (Opinion at 10) (emphasis added). This comment clearly indicates that the magistrate applied the wrong legal standard in convicting Julian Leavitt, finding him guilty solely by reason of his position as president. "To be sure, as the Government points out, there are some contrary indications. In his findings of fact, the magistrate found that, beyond a reasonable doubt, 'Julian who was President, although active in the operation of the company, had no direct involvement in sanitation problems, except as senior officer with ultimate authority and re sponsibility for preventing any violations of the Act.' (Opinion at 8). 

This finding could be interpreted as indicating that the magistrate based the defendant's conviction on his 'responsible relationship' to the violation rather than on his position as president; this interpre tation is, however, negated by the explanation which the magistrate gave for his finding in his 'general discussion' section. The Goverment also points to statements made by the magistrate in a section entitled 'conclusions.' The Government appears to rely primarily on the following 'conclusion' by the magistrate: 'That Julian, by virtue of office, as one in complete control is guilty within the meaning of the Act as interpreted by Park, supra, in that he possessed the final authority to institute whatever effective programs that were required. (Opinion at 9). Although the last part of this 'conclusion' does comment on the defendant's 'authority' to prevent violations of the Act. the 'conclusion' as a whole is tainted by the same misinterpretation of the Park decision. And, even if the 'conclusion' could be read as a finding on the defendant's responsible relationship with the violations, it would not support a conviction because the magistrate did not make the finding ‘beyond a reasonable doubt.' The Government also points to other 'conclusions' by the magistrate: that Julian Leavitt 'had been consulted with respect to the condition at the warehouse and [was] in direct contact with' defendant Julian Schultz who was general manager and 'in complete control'; that Julian Leavitt and other individual defendants could have prevented the violations had they used 'higher standards of foresight and vigilance'; and that the defendant Julian Leavitt acknowledged that the 'sanitation program was inadequate' at the time of the inspections. Whatever effect these 'conclusions' would have in establishing a responsible relationship on the part of Julian Leavitt had the magistrate employed the proper legal standard, I choose not to credit them because of the magistrate's misinterpretation of Park. 

"Admittedly, looking for guidance in the Park decision is a difficult experience. The line drawn by the Court between a conviction based on corporate position alone and one based on a 'responsible relationship' to the violation is a fine one, and arguably no wider than a corporate bylaw. Nevertheless, the Court clearly stated that a conviction under the Act could not be based on corporate position alon and required a finding as to the defendant's responsibility and a 

48 September 1981/ FDA Consumer

thority to correct violations of the Act. The magistrate made such a finding with regard to the other individual defendants, but not as to Julian Leavitt. Therefore, his conviction must be reversed. "As noted earlier, defendant's contention that he was convicted solely on the basis of his corporate position was made conjunctively with the contention that the magistrate erred by convicting him without making a finding of negligence or other blameworthiness. Because this second half of the argument speaks to the same issue raised by the second ground of appeal, I will not consider it separately here. "Thus, the conviction of defendant Julian Leavitt is reversed and his case is remanded to the magistrate for an express finding as to whether the Government sustained its burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant bore a responsible relationship to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act violations alleged in the information. If the magistrate determines that defendant did not bear a responsible relationship to the violation, he should enter a judgment of acquittal. If, however, the magistrate finds that the evidence did establish a responsible relationship, he may reinstate the defendant's conviction, but only if reinstatement is warranted after the magistrate makes the findings required by this Court's ruling on defendants' second ground of appeal. In either event, the magistrate is to state the evidentiary basis for his ruling on the responsible relationship issue.

II 

"The defendants' second ground of appeal is that the convictions of Julian Leavitt, Joel Jeavitt, and Julian Schultz must be reversed because the magistrate did not find, beyond a reasonable doubt, that these defendants were not powerless to prevent or correct the violations of the Act. Instead, the defendants argue, the magistrate used a less rigorous, and therefore infirm standard of guilt. To support this contention, the defendants point to the magistrate's comment in his 'general discussion' section that the 'court is further satisfied that it was not 'objectively impossible' to maintain the warehouse in a sanitary condition.' (Opinion at 10). This finding is invalid, the defendants posit, because the magistrate did not mention that he was satisfied 'beyond a reasonable doubt', a finding they contend is required by Park. It is important to note that the defendants do not challenge the sufficiency of the evidence to make such a finding, just that the magistrate employed an improper legal standard. "The defendants' contentions relate to what is generally referred to as the 'impossibility' defense. . "One interpretation of the impossibility defense is that it relates only to the power of the corporate officer, by virtue of his position in the corporation, to correct or prevent violations of the Act. Under this interpretation, the evidence introduced by the defendant at trial to sustain his impossibility defense would serve only to rebut the evidence introduced by the Government in establishing its prima facie case. Both sides would direct their proof to the responsible relationship vel non which the defendant bore to the violations of the Act. . . . "Under this interpretation, then, the impossibility defense would not serve as an affirmative defense, but would merely provide corporate officers a defense open to all who are criminally accused, that is, rebuttal of the Government's proof. “An alternative interpretation of the impossibility defense is that it is satisfied by evidence that the corporate officer exercised 'extraordinary care' and was still unable to prevent the violations. Under this interpretation, the impossibility defense would serve as an affirmative defense, incorporating an objective mental element-use of extraordinary care-into a strict liability offense. That this interpretation is what the Park Court intended is suggested by the Court's insistence that 'the Act, in its criminal aspect, does not require that which is objectively impossible.' This interpretation is also suggested by the 

Court's repeated emphasis that corporate officers must exercise the 'highest standard of foresight and vigilance,' id. at 672, 673, and the 'highest standard of care,' id. at 676. These references to a standard of care indicate that the Court intended to temper the strict liability crime with a defense based on a mental element, albeit an objective one imposing the highest level of care. The Park Court's citation to 

United States v. Wiesenfeld Warehouse Co., 376 U.S. 86 (1964), is also illuminating. In Wiesenfeld, the Court first suggested the existence of the impossibility defense, stating that 'one "who is, by the very nature of his business powerless" to protect against this kind of contamination, however high the standard of care exercised' may raise such defense at trial. Id. at 91. Wiesenfeld clearly suggests that a corporate officer who exercises extraordinary care and still is unable to prevent violations of the Act will not be held criminally culpable. Finally, further support for this second interpretation of the impossibility defense can also be found in the Court's suggestion that a corporate officer who introduces sufficient evidence of impossibility is entitled, upon request, to a jury instruction that the Government is required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was not without the power or capacity to affect the conditions which founded the charges in the information. 421 U.S. at 676-77. This suggests a separate and distinct burden on the Government to disprove an affirmative defense of impossibility, at least once sufficient evidence has been introduced by the defendant to raise that defense. "On balance, although support can also be found for the first interpretation of the impossibility defense in the language of Park, it appears that the second interpretation is the proper one. Moreover, this interpretation appears to be in accord with the two cases which have considered the impossibility defense since Park, United States v. Y. 

Hata & Co., 535 F.2d 508, 510–12 (9th Cir.), cert. denied, 429 U.S. 

828 (1976); United States v. Starr, 535 F.2d 512, 515-16 (9th Cir. 

1976). . "In light of the severe penalties which may be imposed for a second conviction under the Act, 21 U.S.C.A. §333, I am inclined to adopt this more lenient interpretation of the impossibility defense. . . . "In sum, the impossibility defense allows the corporate officer to introduce evidence to establish an affirmative defense that he exercised extraordinary care and still could not prevent violations of the Act. The defense is raised when the defendant introduces a sufficient quantum of evidence as to his exercise of 'extraordinary care' so as to justify placing an additional burden on the Government. At this point, the Government must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant, by the use of extraordinary care, was not without the power or capacity to correct or prevent the violations of the Act. "Turning to the record of the instant case, I rule that it is impossible to determine whether the magistrate applied the proper legal standard. 

His comment that the 'court is further satisfied that it was not "objectively impossible” to maintain the warehouse in a sanitary condition' can be read either as a finding that the defendant did not introduce sufficient evidence to raise the impossibility defense, or as a finding that, although the defendant introduced sufficient evidence to raise the defense, the Government sustained its additional burden to disprove the defense. If the latter, the magistrate's finding is legally deficient because he does not state that the Government sustained its burden beyond a reasonable doubt. Because of this uncertainty in the magistrate's finding on the impossibility defense, the convictions of Joel Leavitt and Julian Schultz are also reversed. On remand, the magistrate is to make a finding as to these two defendants whether they introduced sufficient evidence to raise the impossibility defense, and, if so, whether the Government sustained its burden of disproving the defense beyond a reasonable doubt. And, if the magistrate determines on remand that defendant Julian Leavitt bore a responsible relationship with the violations charged in the information, he should also determine whether Julian Leavitt succeeded on his impossibility defense. The magistrate is to make clear the evidentiary basis for his findings.

FDA Consumer / September 1981 | 49

III 

"The defendants' remaining arguments on appeal relate to the denial of their motion to suppress evidence gained during two warrantless administrative inspections of their warehouse. These warrantless inspections, conducted pursuant to the authority granted by 21 U.S.C. $374, took place in January and June of 1975; the FDA investigators discovered evidence of rodent infestation and took various product samples for testing. "The defendants first contend that the warrantless inspections violated their Fourth Amendment rights. The defendants raised this argument in their motion to suppress prior to trial. On September 1, 1977, the magistrate ruled that, under the rationale of United States v. Biswell, 406 U.S. 311 (1972), which sanctioned warrantless searches in certain 'pervasively regulated' industries, warrants are not required for inspections conducted pursuant to §374. . . . "The defendants now ask this Court to reconsider its previous ruling as to the applicability of Biswell to $374 inspections, based primarily on the Supreme Court's recent decision in Marshall v. Barlow's, Inc., 436 U.S. 307 (1978). "In Barlow's, the Court held that the warrantless searches author ized by §8(a) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, 29 U.S.C. 

§657(a), violated the Fourth Amendment. In so doing, however, the Court expressly left intact the exception to the warrant requirement recognized in Biswell and Colonnade Catering Corp. v. United 

States, 397 U.S. 72 (1970), for closely regulated industries. 436 U.S. at 313. In those cases, the Barlow's Court explained, warrantless searches were upheld because a businessman voluntarily entering a closely regulated industry can have 'no reasonable expectation of privacy,' and 'in effect consents to the restrictions placed upon him.'. . . 'After the Court's decision in Biswell and prior to its decision in Barlow's, the weight of authority upheld the constitutionality of the warrantless inspections authorized by $374. . . . 66 "Contrary to the only other post-Barlow's decision thus far considering the constitutionality of $374, United States v. Roux Laboratories, Inc., 456 F.Supp. 973, 977 n.2 (M.D. Fla. 1978), I do not read

Barlow's as requiring a knee-jerk invalidation of the warrantless in spections authorized by §374. . . . 

"Rather, given the pervasive nature and long history of federal regulation of the food and drug industry, considering that, in contrast to the situation in Barlow's, these regulations apply to a particular industry and not a wide range of business establishments, and mindful of the urgent public health interests that are served by the inspections, I rule that warrantless inspections pursuant to $374 are fully consistent with the Fourth Amendment. Therefore, neither a warrant or consent was required to conduct the inspections of defendants' warehouse. "Defendants make several other contentions with regard to the denial of their motion to suppress. First, the defendants argue that the warrantless inspections were invalid because the FDA agents did not secure the defendants' consent. Because of my ruling that the

Biswell rationale applies to warrantless inspections conducted pursuant to $374, I need not consider whether the defendants, in fact. consented to the inspections. The defendants next contend that, even if no warrant or consent was required initially, the warrantless inspections became unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment once the FDA agents had probable cause to suspect violations of the Act. 

As to this contention, I rule that the FDA agents were not required to suspend the valid warrantless inspections and secure a warrant once they had reason to suspect violations of the Act, so long as the searches were otherwise reasonable in time, manner, and scope as required by $374. "Defendants' final contention is that the inspections did not comply with $374, both because the FDA agents did not initiate the inspections by presenting a written notice to the 'owner, operator, or agent in charge' and because the inspections were unreasonable' in time, manner, and scope. As to the first part of this argument, it is relevant that the FDA agent commenced each inspection by asking to see the person most responsible or the person in charge. In January. the agent was directed to David Ginsberg, vice-president of purchasing, whereupon he presented his credentials and issued a notice of inspection to both Mr. Ginsberg and James Kaminsky, the warehouse sanitation officer. In June, the agent presented his credentials and issued a notice of inspection to Peter DeGannaro, the assistant treasurer. I rule that Ginsberg, Kaminsky, and DeGannaro were all ‘agents' within the meaning of $374 since they were 'responsible representatives of management.' See S.Rep. No. 712, 83d Cong., 1st Sess.. 

reprinted in 2 U.S. Code Cong. & Ad. News 2203 (1953). The second part of defendants' argument with regard to $374 is that the inspections were unreasonable in time, manner, and scope and were nothing more than 'fishing expeditions. Although both the January and June inspections extended over a period of approximately five days, that period was not unreasonable in light of the very large size of defendants' warehouse. Moreover, in assessing reasonableness it is relevant that the inspections occurred during normal business and apparently did not interfere with the normal course of business. Durovic v. Palmer, 342 F.2d 634, 636 (7th Cir. 1965). Based on these considerations, I rule that the inspections were not unreasonable. In all material respects, the inspections complied with the dictates of $374. "In sum, the Court rules that the evidence obtained from the January and June inspections was properly admitted at the trial of defendants, and may be considered by the magistrate on remand." 

Upon remand, the magistrate considered each of the individual defendants separately, saying:

Defendant Julian J. Leavitt, President of NEGSC 

"The finding on page 2 of Chief Judge Caffrey's Remand, hereinafter referred to as 'Remand,' states that it was error for me to find this defendant guilty solely because he was company president at the time the violations occurred. Indeed, that was the only reason I found this defendant guilty and I again state that I did not find him negligent or blameworthy in this matter. “I found, on page 9 of my Memorandum and Order of February 21, 1979, 'That Julian, by virtue of office, as one in complete control is guilty within the meaning of the Act as interpreted by Park, supra. in that he possessed the final authority to institute whatever effective programs that were required.' Page 5 of this Remand determined that 

I had misconstrued the Park decision with respect to Julian Leavitt The findings made by me against Julian Leavitt were made only on the basis that, in Park, the court stated that the position of president made him 'liable, responsible and subject to prosecution. I interpreted Park to establish absolute liability. "In light of that finding, and the Remand at page 2, this court finds the defendant, Julian J. Leavitt, NOT GUILTY.

Defendants Julian Schultz and Joel A. Leavitt 

"With respect to each of these defendants, the Remand states at page 13 with reference to my findings that: His comment that the 'court is further satisfied that it was not "objectively impossible" to maintain the warehouse in a sanitary condition' can be read either as a finding that the defendant did not introduce sufficient evidence to raise the impossibility defense, or as a finding that, although the defendant introduced sufficient evidence to raise the defense. the 

Government sustained its additional burden to disprove the defense If the latter, the magistrate's finding is legally deficient because he does not state that the Government sustained its burden beyond a reasonable doubt. Because of this uncertainty in the magistrate's finding on the impossibility defense, the convictions of Joel Leavitt and Julian Schultz are also reversed. On remand, the magistrate is to mak a finding as to these two defendants whether they introduced sufficier 

50 September 1981 FDA Consumer

evidence to raise the impossibility defense, and, if so, whether the Government sustained its burden of disproving the defense beyond a reasonable doubt. . . The magistrate is to make clear the evidentiary basis for his findings.' "With respect to each of these defendants, the court is satisfied that the defendants did introduce a sufficient quantum of evidence to raise the impossibility defense. However, the Government did not disprove this defense 'beyond a reasonable doubt.' "That NEGSC's warehouse facility at Northboro, as a result of a personal inspection by me, as well as testimony, was a very large warehouse consisting of approximately 415,000 square feet and the warehouse proper approximately 352,000 square feet. "Prior to December 31, 1974, NEGSC had a formal sanitation program with a full-time sanitation officer in charge of the program...and on October 21, 1974, the Massachusetts public health inspector inspected the warehouse and found it clean and commented that the sanitation program was well set up (exhibit p) and that this program was an effective program and met all FDA published guidelines.. "Immediately after the FDA inspection, the Commonwealth of Massachusetts on February 3, 1975, inspected the premises and found no violations or fault with the sanitation program. . "The testimony of witness Hillhouse was convincing and credible that it was extremely difficult to keep a warehouse of this size free of rodent infestation. "Although my original findings indicated that it was not impossible to make the plant free from infestation, I interpreted the cases strictly rather than giving them the more favorable interpretation as indicated by the Remand. Based on this more favorable interpretation I find that both Julian Schultz and Joel A. Leavitt have introduced a sufficient quantum of evidence to establish an affirmative defense that they exercised extraordinary care and could not prevent violations of the Act. Therefore, applying the more liberal view and applying further the principal that the Government must then present evidence to prove 'beyond a reasonable doubt' that the defendants could by the use of extraordinary care correct or prevent the violations of this Act, I cannot say that the Government did so prove beyond a reasonable doubt. "I conclude further that there was introduced a sufficient quantum of evidence as to both defendants' exercise of extraordinary care so as to place an additional burden on the Government. "The Government in its brief and memorandum in support of the Government's proposed findings of fact, refers to my findings numbered 9 and 12. However, pursuant to the Remand, I am required to indicate whether ‘extraordinary steps' were taken to prevent or mitigate the problem of sanitation at the plant. Throughout the entire trial, the principal argument made by these defendants was that they had done everything within their power and they could do no more. 

If my opinion in any way indicated that they did not make such defense, then the opinion is misconstrued, or at least I did not so intend. True, under 9 and 12, there is a statement that they could have done more but the point of fact is that they did take extraordinary measures and the testimony so indicated. "Considering the size of the plant, the fact that they worked constantly to prevent this contamination, I conclude that the Government has not complied with the requirements presented to me by the Remand. "The evidentiary basis for my findings are as follows: "1. The inspection by the State indicating that everything was in order. "2. The fact that numerous checks were made by the defendants through their subordinates in setting up their own program. "3. Both Schultz and Leavitt did have control of the warehouse and they did hold a responsible relationship with respect to the violations charged in the Information. "4. That although they did use extraordinary measures in an attempt to rid themselves of infestation, they did not succeed. "Defendants' memorandum of law with respect to this Remand which was filed on May 8, 1980, is a substantial document which outlines the issues in this matter. They need not be repeated here. "Following, therefore, the instructions on Remand, this court on the basis of the foregoing finds each of these defendants NOT GUILTY." 

Accordingly, the individual defendants were found Not Guilty.

However, the guilty verdict as to the corporation continued to stand, and ultimately the corporation satisfied the fine. (F.D.C. No. 60661; 

S. No. 110-434 et al.; N.J. No. 35)

The defendants admitted that, in 1973, FDA had been notified of two violations which had been corrected but it was denied that the violations had anything to do with the installations of the x-ray systems; that the basic problem was with the collimator which was the product of another firm, that the certification of conformance did not include the previously owned collimator of the user and the Government regulations permitted the installation of, or assembly of, one existing uncertified component with certified components, which is what the defendants did in the installation assembly complained of; that the certification was not misleading, was accurate in its factual statement, and the purchaser knew that the collimator was a predated or uncertified one and that, when the collimator was attached to the new certified x-ray system, positive beam limitation would not be provided, and this had been discussed with the purchaser prior to sale and installation, so that the purchaser could not possibly have been misled by the certification; that the defendants denied the Government's allegations, denied the alleged violation, and affirmed compliance with the law in the past and in the future. Ultimately, the defendant entered into a consent decree of permanent injunction enjoining the complained of violation and stating: that the defendants had sold an uncertified collimator on August 10, 1977, to a Great Neck, N.Y., medical facility, at which time the facility was utilizing a completely uncertified x-ray system and that the assembly of such collimator into the uncertified system would not have been a violation of the law; that the defendants concede that they subsequently, during 

August 1977, sold the facility additional certified x-ray system components which were assembled into an x-ray system together with the uncertified collimator (i.e., assembled an x-ray system containing certified and uncertified components); and that such assembly and certification of that x-ray system was a mistake which would not occur again. Update 

Vitamin Proposal Withdrawn

Vitamins and minerals sold as non-prescription drugs should be taken only when their need has been determined by a physician. So said a panel of experts reviewing over-the-counter drugs. The panel's report was the subject of Vitamins Over the 

Counter: Take Only When Needed, in the April 

1979 FDA CONSUMER. Confusion over the report has led to an unusual move by FDA, as is seen in this update: 

FDA is withdrawing an advisory panel's proposal to regulate some vitamins and minerals marketed as OTC drugs. A task force of FDA personnel recommended the action to end public confusion about the difference between vitamins and minerals sold as dietary supplements, the major way these products are sold in the United 

States, and those sold as drugs for specific medical conditions, the subject of the panel's report. 

Commissioner , concurred in the task force recommendation. 

The expert panel's report was part of FDA's massive review of the safety and effectiveness of all non-prescription drugs. The panel identified nine vitamins and three minerals that are safe and effective as single ingredient, non-prescription drugs for prevention of vitamin and mineral deficiencies.

FDA was barred from regulating the composition of vitamins and minerals for dietary supplementation, except when safety is an issue, by the

Proxmire Amendment of 1976. 

Notification of the withdrawal of the expert panel's report will appear in an upcoming

FEDERAL REGISTER.

Pregnancy and Alcohol Warning 

The more a pregnant woman drinks, the greater the risk of giving birth to an abnormal baby. That was the message in the article, Alcohol and Birth 

Defects in the May 1978 FDA CONSUMER. That warning bears repeating, as is evident from this update: 

Women who are pregnant, or considering pregnancy, should not drink alcoholic beverages and should be aware of the alcoholic content of certain foods and drugs, according to the Surgeon General of the U.S. Public Health Service. 

A recent report to the president and Congress, summarizing current scientific knowledge about health hazards associated with alcohol consumption, revealed that: • Babies of some women who drank as little as one ounce of absolute alcohol (two standard drinks) per day during pregnancy weighed significantly less at birth than the norm. • Sizeable and significant increases in spontaneous abortions have been reported for women who drank as little as one ounce of absolute alcohol twice a week during pregnancy. • A woman who drinks enough to fit the ordinary diagnosis of being alcoholic risks bearing a child with severe physical and mental defects known as the fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS). These defects include mental retardation, central nervous system disorders, growth deficiencies, facial abnormalities and other malformations. • Even if she does not bear a child with full 

FAS, a woman who drinks heavily is more likely than the non-drinker to bear a child with one or more of the birth defects included in the syndrome.

The reported effects of alcohol on pregnancy appear to be independent of other variables, including nutrition and smoking. It also has been demonstrated that alcohol readily enters breast milk when the mother drinks and thus is transmitted to the nursing infant. Heavy alcohol consumption is known to reduce the production of mothers' milk.

FDA, through its July 1981 DRUG BULLETIN, urged health professionals to inquire routinely about alcohol consumption by patients who are pregnant or considering pregnancy, and to warn patients about the risks of alcohol consumed dur ing pregnancy. The DRUG BULLETIN is sent to doctors and other health professionals throughout the country. 

2 October 1981/ FDA Consumer

Warning Label Stayed 

Four years ago FDA proposed that bubble bath labels carry a warning statement that would alert consumers to adverse reactions that could occur in using these products. The reasons were discussed in a news highlight item, Label Warning Proposed for 

Bubble Bath, in the March 1977 FDA CONSUMER. 

Here's an update:

The Food and Drug Administration has stayed, temporarily, the effective date of a rule requiring that bubble bath labels include in their labeling that prolonged use may cause skin or urinary tract irritation.

The rule, which was scheduled to take effect in August, is being reviewed to see whether it is the most effective and appropriate way to inform the public of this problem, particularly in children. 

The problem, recognized for more than a decade, is that the foaming agents in bubble baths can remove the skin's natural oil and cause drying, fissuring, irritation, and inflammation.

During the mid-1970 s, the manufacturer of the largest selling children's bubble bath reformulated the product and also voluntarily put a cautionary label statement on it. In the past 3 years, few adverse reactions to this product have been reported to FDA or the company.

The label rule was published in the FEDERAL 

REGISTER on August 19, 1980, and was to apply to all bubble baths introduced into interstate commerce after August 19, 1981. 

In regard to the label, Dr. Arthur Hull Hayes 

Jr., the Commissioner of FDA, said: "It is clear that people, especially parents, need to know that remaining in bubble baths for prolonged periods of time, or using bubble baths excessively, can cause health problems. "But we need to examine carefully whether a caution statement on the label is the most effective and appropriate way to bring this problem to parents' attention. We also need to reconsider whether the cautionary statement is needed on bubble baths intended only for use by adults."

Dr. Hayes said a FEDERAL REGISTER notice urges the manufacturers of bubble baths to develop and submit to FDA alternative approaches to deal with the problem. 

The label statement would have said: "Caution-Use only as directed. Excessive use or prolonged exposure may cause irritation to skin and urinary tract. Discontinue use if rash, redness or itching occur. Consult your physician if irritation persists. Keep out of the reach of children."

Lab Work Brings Indictments 

Testing new drugs to meet FDA requirements for safety and effectiveness is often done by independent laboratories. How FDA keeps an eye on these investigations was told in the article Kelsey's Kops: 

They Investigate the Investigators, in the March 

1981 issue of FDA CONSUMER. Here's the result of a recent investigation:

A federal grand jury in Chicago has indicted four individuals formerly employed by Industrial Bio-Test Laboratories, Inc. (IBT), a research laboratory that conducted animal studies for the manufacturers of various drugs, pesticides and chemicals. The indictment, announced by the Department of Justice, alleges that the defendants entered into a scheme to defraud the sponsors of the studies, the Food and Drug

Administration, and the Environmental Protection 

Agency by producing study reports that contained false descriptions of the studies, fabricated data and fraudulent conclusions.

Included was a 2-year toxicology study on Trichlorocarbanilide (TCC) for Monsanto Corp. TCC is an antibacterial agent used in many deodorant soaps. A 22-month toxicity study for Syntex Corp. on Naprosyn, a drug used in the treatment of arthritis, was also involved, as were two 18-month carcinogenic studies for Chemagro Corp. (now a division of Mobay Chemical Corp.) on Sencor, a herbicide, and Nemacur, a pesticide.

The four individuals indicted were the former 

President of IBT, Dr. Joseph C. Calandra, Boyn ton Beach, Fla.; the former manager of toxicology, Dr. Moreno J. Keplinger, Northbrook, Ill.; the former section head for rat toxicology at IBT and manager of toxicology at Monsanto Corp., Dr. 

Paul L. Wright, Kirkwood, Mo.; and the former assistant manager of toxicology, James B. Plank, Buffalo, N.Y.

Each is charged with three counts of mail fraud, one count of wire fraud and four counts of submitting false documents to the government. Each mail and wire fraud count carries a maximum penalty of 

5 years in prison and a $1,000 fine. The false statement count carries a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

The TCC and Naprosyn study reports were submitted by the manufacturers to FDA to evaluate the safety of the test substances. The agency said both substances have been further tested and found safe, and both are currently on the market.

Artificial Valves A Heart-Rending Story 

The development of artificial heart valves has come a long way in the 29 years since Dr. Charles M. Hufnagel designed and implanted the first model. 

Today, the cow and pig are used to construct new valves and, as a result, thousands of people are breathing a lot easier. by Marti Asner ry to imagine standing with your blood draining away. 

First the precious life fluid empties from your brain, your heart. Slowly by gravity it glides downward through the body's narrow network of veins and arteries, joining more of the thick liquid from the upper limbs, kidneys, liver and spleen. Finally this great pool of life-5 quarts in all-settles toward the lower part of your body, where it stops.

Not a pleasant picture, but that's what would happen if there were no valves in the body to regulate blood flow. 

Small valves are located throughout the circulatory system in the arms, legs and head. Their purpose is to keep blood flowing in one direction. Any of these valves can develop a mechanical problem and fail to open or shut on cue. But the most harm can come, even death, if the four larger valves inside the heart become defective and fail to operate properly. If that happens, an artificial heart valve may be called for.

The artificial heart valve is a typical medical success story of the 20th century, involving as it does both technology and technique. At least 400,000 men, women and children have been helped by these devices in their battles against cardiac valve disease. But the modern advances that have made heart valve technology possible are only the climax of medical and scientific discoveries that began deep in the past. 

It was the Greeks who first learned that the heart had valves. Later, in the 17th century, William Harvey, an

English physician, studied the mechanics of blood flow both in his native country and with Galileo at the University of Padua in Italy. In 1628, after 20 years of research and experimentation on 15 different species of animals, Harvey published "ON THE MOVEMENT OF THE HEART 

AND BLOOD." This classic work set down the principles of blood flow through the heart and blood vessels and became a medical bulwark for the next 350 years.

The heart itself is about as big as a good-sized fist. It is located in the mid-section of the chest and weighs less than a pound. Within its thick walls are four hollow chambers: a left and right atrium and below them a left and right ventricle. A solid wall of membrane and muscle called the septum separates the two sides. Blood flows not from left to right as one might think, but from top to bottom. One valve is located between each atrium and ventricle. A third valve separates the left ventricle from the aorta, a major blood vessel. Between the pulmonary artery (connected to the lungs) and the right ventricle lies the fourth valve. To get from the left to the right side of the heart, blood must take the long way around by first circulating within the body.

It is difficult to say exactly where the circulation process begins because blood flows continuously. But between beats when the heart is relaxed, fresh, oxygen-rich blood enters the left atrium and left ventricle. The left atrium fills up and expands like a balloon. The heart then beats. the left ventricle tightens, and the aortic valve opens. The simultaneous closing of the mitral valve between the atrium and ventricle prevents the backflow of blood. The aorta then transports the blood to smaller blood vessels scattered throughout the body. The head, arms, legs and organs receive the oxygen and nutrients in the blood that are needed for life. In exchange, body tissues give up waste products such as carbon dioxide and urea. 

As it travels through the body, the blood color changes from a bright to a dull shade of red. It returns to the right atrium, then through an opened valve called the tri-

cuspid and into the right ventricle. The tricuspid valve closes to prevent backflow. Blood then passes out of the right ventricle through another valve and moves to the lungs to pick up a fresh supply of oxygen. The entire process-which takes about 20 seconds begins anew at the left atrium.

Blood flow through the heart remains constant and smooth only if the valves are working properly. Problems occur if a valve fails to open easily, or fails to shut securely, or if a hole develops in it. If the valve fails to shut or has a leak, the blood flows backwards, or regurgitates, and the heart is forced to pump harder and faster.

Such valve defects are usually congenital or are caused by advancing age. Complications from rheumatic fever and syphilis have resulted in many valve defects, but these diseases and their side effects have been on the wane since antibiotics have been used on them.

About 15,000 people each year in the United States undergo cardiac valve surgery. Called a "valve job," this delicate operation involves replacing a defective or wornout valve with an artificial one. 

The first such operation was performed in 1952 in a 4hour operation at Georgetown University Hospital in 

Washington, D.C., by Dr. Charles M. Hufnagel. A few years earlier, Hufnagel had also performed the first human kidney transplant operation. In the pioneering valve job, Hufnagel placed a plexiglass ball-type valve in the chest of a 30-year-old hospital technician. The patient lived 8 years before dying of complications from rheumatic fever. The original "Hufnagel valve" has since been displayed at the National Museum of American History (formerly the National Museum of History and 

Technology). About 25 types of heart valves are in use today. 

All valves fall into one of two categories—mechanical and tissue. Although the perfect artificial valve has yet to be designed, the best ones sold today should be durable and provide the least resistance to blood flow. 

Of the mechanical types, the caged-ball design has been on the market longest. Metal bars or struts enclose a free-floating hollow ball. The pressure of the blood rushing into the base of the cage forces the ball upward; the blood then exits out between the struts. One-third of a second later, when the heart is between beats, the ball drops down and blocks blood from flowing backwards.

The caged-ball valve appears to be durable and its blood flow characteristics are fairly good. The design has changed little since 1965. However, thanks to improvenents in surgical techniques, valve-related deaths using his type of device have dropped 50 percent, the overall i-year survival rate has climbed to 76 percent, and failure of the valve itself has been running less than 1 percent. 

There are some drawbacks, however, to the caged-ball ype. The ball often gives out a perceptible clicking sound is it taps against the bars. This slight noise can be heard p to a foot away from the wearer. In addition, all mechanical valves require lifelong use of anticoagulant drugs to prevent blood clots from forming. 

In the mid 1960's, another type of mechanical valve came into relative popularity. It is known as the tilting disc mechanical valve. As blood flows in, the disc opens and then shuts again to prevent backflow. Manufacturers of this device claim that it causes little resistance to the flow of blood. 

A third, more recent mechanical valve is the bi-leaflet type. This device is currently being reviewed by the Food and Drug Administration's Bureau of Medical Devices and is not yet available to the public. Its manufacturer claims better blood flow characteristics for it than other mechanical valves. The bi-leaflet valve is made of Pyrolyte, a new material. Two flaps, resembling French doors, swing open allowing blood to enter, and then close to prevent backflow. 

All three mechanical valves are enclosed by a ring of metal (or Pyrolyte) which, in turn, is surrounded by a ring of woven Dacron. The fabric constitutes the "sewing ring," which is used by the surgeon to stitch the valve to the heart.

Tissue valves, the other basic kind of heart valve, work more like human valves. Most are made of either pig (porcine) heart valves or cow (bovine) pericardium (the tissue covering the heart). After selection, the tissue is subjected to a tanning process to toughen it. It is then stretched over a curved metal support called stent.

As the heart chambers constrict, forcing blood out, the pressure of the blood forces the tissue to expand and the sections to separate. The tissue then opens to its maximum, blood passes through, and the sections close. 

People with tissue valves usually do not require any follow-up medication. The incidence of clotting has been less than 1 percent, and the valves are soundless. However, there are problems associated with tissue valves. 

They do not wear as well as mechanical valves, and the stents may weaken with time. But both problems can usually be detected and remedied before any serious harm is done. 

Artificial heart valves are Class III devices under the definitions of law. According to the Medical Device 

Amendments of 1976, all devices that are implanted into the body (i.e., Class III devices) must be tested for safety and effectiveness before they can be sold. The manufacturers do their own testing; however, FDA scientists and an independent panel of cardiovascular experts evaluate the heart valve test data for the agency. The panel then makes recommendations on the device.

The progress of artificial heart valve development has soared in the 29 years since Dr. Hufnagel first dared to try. If the pig and cow are used today to save lives, what other treasures are still out to pasture? 

Marti Asner is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

We don't fully understand even today what occurs in the wall of the artery. But we know that what happens is that a leak occurs in the artery and a hemorrhage develops into the brain. The basic cause of most heart attacks is another disease called atherosclerosis in which there is a blockage inside the artery from cholesterol deposits on the wall of the artery. When an individual has atherosclerosis, with the resulting narrowing of the coronary artery, high blood pressure makes the possibility of having a heart attack even greater. So the two diseases are synergistic in terms of producing adverse effects, particularly relative to the heart. The same is true of kidney disease. When hypertensive disease gets very bad, a lot of troubles arise in the kidneys.

Over time, the untreated patient will suffer a decline in kidney functionthe ability of the kidneys to clean blood and to excrete products into urine that the body wants to get rid of. So when we're talking about hypertension, we're talking about the possibility of serious brain disease, serious heart disease and serious kidney disease. Hypertension is directly or indirectly contributory to the top four or five causes of death in the 

United States.

So my belief is that there is a high probability that if there was a reasonable moderation of sodium content in our food supply gradually and over time, that the American public will adapt to that quite readily.

Alert Cook 

+ 1 Bad Can Of Mushrooms = A Total Recall 

"When I opened the first can, the water came out... sorta pushed itself out. . . The odor was hard to describe. . . . It was highly fermented. It wasn't 5 seconds before the smell permeated the kitchen . . and it stayed there for 6 or 8 hours.... When I opened the second can, the same thing happened." 

There aren't many occasions in which the FDA undertakes a Class I, or total, recall of a product. Such a case occurred earlier this year after an Illinois fireman opened a can of mushrooms and became suspicious. When he opened that can he opened up the way for mobilization of a system to prevent a possible outbreak of food poisoning.

By Roger W. Miller fireman's life can be full of

A fire drama. But that usually doesn't occur in the kitchen of the firehouse when preparing food for fellow smoke-eaters. Nevertheless, that's what happened to fireman Ron Hill of Rockford, Ill. 

But let him describe it: "When I opened the first can, the water came out . . . sorta pushed itself out. The odor was hard to describe. It was highly fermented. It wasn't 5 seconds before the smell permeated the kitchen ... and it stayed there for 6 or 8 hours. . . . When I opened the second can, the same thing happened."

Hill suspected that he had a couple of badly tainted cans of mushroom stems and pieces and he realized right then that he ought to be telling someone about it. So he called the store where he had purchased the mushrooms. Neither the manager nor assistant manager was in, and the clerk he talked to didn't seem to sense the possible gravity of the situation. She told Hill to return the cans to the store and she'd give him his money back.

In retrospect, Hill says he probably never would have called the Winne bago County Health Department if the clerk hadn't shown such disinterest. And, if Hill hadn't called the health department, a major food poisoning epidemic might have been the tragic outcome. There were hundreds and possibly thousands of contaminated cans similar to those that Hill had reported. Each of these cans

might have contained harmful microorganisms with the potential to produce a dangerous poison. 

Hill's call to the county health department set the stage for the rest of the drama. Thousands of FDA, state and local officials visited tens of thousands of wholesale and retail food outlets nationwide searching for the suspect 4-ounce cans of mushroom stems and pieces.

Hill's presence of mind and his tenacity subsequently led to what is called a Class I recall. The object of this full-fledged recall was to recover similar cans produced by the firm that processed the mushrooms that stunk up the firehouse kitchen. With assistance from state and local authorities, the recall was carried out and the resulting statistics were significant: • More than 132,000 "audit checks" were made at retail stores that received or might have received the suspect mushrooms. • A total of $1,868,752 spent by

FDA and the states, including such expenses as $5,059 for telephone calls, $15,070 for lab costs, and $110,108 for travel expenses. • 139,560 employee hours expended through July 15 by FDA and state personnel. That figure includes 

14,858 hours of overtime for FDA employees and is equivalent to 67 employees working full time for a year. 

But let the drama unfold itself.

Hill's information about the badmelling, strange acting cans of mushrooms was relayed to Arlyn 

Baumgarten, supervisory investigator t FDA's resident inspection post in 

Waukegan, Ill., late on a Friday ight. Baumgarten directed Charlie 

Peterson and Bill Nelson of the 

Rockford FDA office to obtain the amples of the potentially dangerous roduct. The Winnebago County 

Health Department had already emargoed all similar cans of mushpoms in the store chain where Hill ad made his purchase.

By midnight, Baumgarten had also erted FDA's emergency and epideiologic branch, as well as the gency's Cincinnati laboratory, that a otentially dangerous product was on e way. 

Baumgarten also got the name of the buyer for the store chain and determined that the chain's warehouse was located at Milan, Ill., near Peoria. Leroy Kipp, investigator from 

FDA's Peoria office, visited the warehouse on Saturday morning and found a number of cans described as "hard swells," "soft swells" and "leakers."* Any of these are indicators of a problem.

Samples of the products were flown from Chicago's O'Hare Field 

Saturday, headed for the FDA laboratory at Cincinnati, which has the facilities needed for detecting the suspected poison. 

By Monday morning, the Cincinnati lab had evidence of what everyone suspected-the cans contained botulinum toxin, which is fatal in about one-fourth of all its poisoning cases. Even a tiny taste of this poison can be fatal, and scientists are unsure about the consequences of inhaling the stuff. 

That same morning, investigators from FDA's Philadelphia district office arrived at the manufacturer, Oxford Royal Products, Inc., of Kelton,

Pa., to investigate possible causes for the swollen, putrid cans of mushrooms found by fireman Hill. After tests confirmed the identification of the toxin, the manufacturer voluntarily initiated a Class I recall of that lot. Further investigation by FDA found more swollen cans of mushrooms in a Denver warehouse. After 

FDA's Dallas lab confirmed the same toxin in the Denver lot, the firm extended the recall to all 4-ounce cans of mushroom stems and pieces. The five FDA district offices checking on the recall of the first lot were joined by FDA employees from all 151 locations around the country as well as employees from all 50 states and a number of local jurisdictions looking for Oxford's products.

The firm's computer records told where the suspect cans were sent, but not all wholesalers had records of *"Swells" are cans that are swollen on both ends; "soft swells" yield to hand pressure; "hard swells" do not. "Leakers," as the name implies, are cans that leak. their distribution. Consequently, it was necessary to visit every retail outlet in given area to search for the suspect mushrooms.

It soon became clear that FDA did not have enough investigators to quickly visit all possible locations. 

Chemists, microbiologists, consumer affairs officers and others from virtually all walks of FDA life were sent out to look for the mushrooms.

Nationwide publicity was generated to alert the public about the recall and to warn them to look for the suspect mushrooms in their own cupboards and pantries. FDA headquarters issued press releases on May 14, 22 and 29, and district FDA offices turned out their own releases and answered questions from scores of reporters and the public. Several trade associations pitched in to help by notifying their member firms.

In all, the number of cans involved ran into the millions. Thousands were returned to the manufacturer for reprocessing and thousands more were destroyed by state and local authorities. 

What went wrong? The answer to that, according to Paula Oliver, director of investigations for FDA's 

Philadelphia District, was a combination of factors, including plant equipment failure and inexperienced personnel. 

Was the recall successful? Well, there were no cases of poisoning reported anywhere in the country, even though the spores were found in hundreds of cans among the limited number of lots that were analyzed. 

And, says Philadelphia's Oliver, "Look how fast we got it done-most of it in two weeks."

The recall workings impressed 

WASHINGTON POST reporter T. R. 

Reid. Writing about the incident in the newspaper, Reid concluded that the system worked "swiftly and smoothly.' 

And the syndicated "Wagman 

File" by Robert J. Wagman for the 

Newspaper Enterprise Association commented that the "quick action may have saved your life or the life of someone you know."

NCTR 

Among The Questions There: 

How Secure Is The Womb? 

This is the last of a three-part series on the National Center for Toxicological Research (NCTR). Although much of the research there is long-term and deals with improving the methodology of scientific examination of toxic substances, the center also is involved in projects that are of future regulatory concern to FDA.

By Chris Lecos 

On the ground floor of Building 53-A at the National Center for Toxicological Research in central Arkansas, a colony of rhesus monkeys flourishes in a protected but caged environment. Each primate is nameless, identified only by four digits tattooed on its lower chest or abdomen. The humidity, temperature and air exchange are controlled automatically and even the light in the three rooms where the cages are located is left on for 10 to 12 hours a day. Twice daily they are fed high protein biscuits, a specially prepared monkey chow, and several times a week their diet is supplemented with fruit. Their bedding is changed daily and there is always enough water to drink. There is a folder for each of the 63 monkeys in the colony that details its weight progress and medical history. The "good proven breeders" among the 

43 females produce more than 20 palm-sized babies year, fathered by seven males that range up to 10 years of age.

Nearby, on the same floor, is an operating room where some of the pregnant primates are wheeled so that rubber tubing or catheters can be inserted surgically into the blood vessels that are linked to the mother's placenta. 

The anesthetized mother and her fetus are unaffected by this surgical intrusion that is a vital part of the experimental efforts of scientists there who are trying to determine how much of a toxic substance has crossed the placenta to the unborn progeny and what effect this transfer has on the developing fetus. The human implications of the research are obvious when one considers the amount of human exposure to chemicals and the problems of birth defects, gene damage and cancer that many chemicals can cause.

Dr. William Slikker, chief of the Pharmacodynamics Branch of NCTR's Division of Teratogenesis Research, says primates are ideal animal models for this kind of research because their reproductive physiology and metabolism is so similar to that of humans. Like the human female, the rhesus mother has single births; the anatomy of the placenta is much the same; and the ratio of mater- 

Simultaneous blood samples are drawn from the maternal artery and a fetal artery at the National Center for Toxicological Research in Arkansas. Monkeys are used to see what possible effects certain chemicals might have on them and might be passed along to their offspring. The information can give a clue as to effect on humans.

The data obtained during animal surgery are entered into a computer terminal at the time of the operation, as shown at left. The terminal is linked to a computer system located in another NCTR building. 

18 October 1981 FDA Consumer

FDA Consumer / October 1981 / 19

nal to fetal weight during pregnancy is similar. However, most rhesus females also have distinct feature two placental discs or lobes-that enhances their usefulness as experimental animals.

Like the human female, the rhesus has a placenta that links the mother to the fetus via the umbilical cord, which serves as a conduit for the transfer of nutrients as well as for the exchange of toxic materials that normally develop in the fetal blood and which must be cleared out through the mother. The distinct anatomical feature of the rhesus female, however, is that its placental unit is separated into two almost equally sized parts which are linked or bridged by several sets of interplacental blood vessels. None of the vessels attach directly to the fetus. 

The vessels, however, contain fetal blood and are accessible through surgery. NCTR scientists, using lights to illuminate and locate the vessels connecting the two placental discs, surgically place the catheters without affecting the fetus or the delicate umbilical cord. "It allows access to fetal circulation without passing through the amniotic sac that encloses and protects the fetus," Slikker explained. 

From these blood samples the scientists can measure how much of an agent given to the mother is transferred to the fetus and how it is metabolized. The scientists also monitor blood pressure and other critical physiological data. In a paper published last year, NCTR was able to report that its research there clearly established that the placenta does not always serve as a protective barrier to outside intrusion by toxic substances. Through various ongoing experiments, the scientists now are trying to find out how this chemical transfer from mother to fetus takes place, how it affects the fetus, how both naturally occurring and synthetic chemicals are transferred from mother to fetus, how the body metabolizes both kinds, and whether this transfer eventually can lead to cancer, birth defects and damage to genes. 

NCTR scientists believe their work can play an important role in developing the kind of methodology that will provide government agencies like the Food and Drug Administration (which funds much of NCTR's operations) and private commercial interests as well with testing guidelines for future research. Slikker said there is a major need for more extensive research into drugs that may be prescribed to pregnant women because the number of drugs approved and available to pregnant women is comparatively limited today. "Some of the more effective agents available to nonpregnant individuals are not available to pregnant women," he said. "Research on drugs that can be made available to pregnant women is probably 20 years behind the times compared to that for drugs prescribed to nonpregnant persons. There just have not been that many medicines that have been completely tested or approved as safe and effective for use during pregnancy. One reason is that there are not that many good ways to test for the harmfulness of these agents. We at NCTR are trying to develop some basic techniques that may be usedmethods that can be used to study a number of agents and to help describe their safety.'

Much of the ongoing research at NCTR today with rhesus monkeys focuses on three major classes of estrogens (female sex hormones) with particular emphasis on experiments that compare the effects of endogenous or naturally occurring substances with their synthetically developed counterparts. The compounds are diethylstilbestrol, or DES, a once widely used synthetic estrogenic drug prescribed to prevent miscarriages; ethynylestradiol, a major synthetic estrogen in oral contraceptives; and estradiol, a major naturally occurring sex hormone. In addition, other research is being done on substances like corticosteroids, anti-inflammatory agents applied topically for skin rashes and hives, and on ethanol or alcohol, a major cause of birth defects. "DES has been of strong interest to FDA for some time," Slikker noted, "and it became apparent that DES could serve as a compound that resembles a great variety of compounds. DES has been the subject of scientific scrutiny for a long time. We know it has adverse effects, but we don't know how they occur." Developed in 1938 from coal tar derivatives, DES was widely prescribed to prevent miscarriages from the early 1940's to 1971 when FDA withdrew its approval after various studies of humans showed a disturbing rise in vaginal cancer among the daughters of women who had been taking the drug during their pregnancies.

DES's ability to cause malignant tumors was reported in laboratory animals in 1938 and in later studies as well. but natural estrogens also were known to cause tumors and many scientists felt those traced to DES were a result of its estrogenic characteristics rather than a specific cancer-causing property. An estimated 4 to 6 million women and their children were exposed to the drug. The exposure was even more widespread, but at considerably lower amounts, because of DES use to promote rapid growth in beef cattle and other animals. FDA banned the use of DES as a growth promoter in cattle and sheep in 1979. The agency had attempted to prohibit its use in animal feed and as an implant in 1972 and 1973 but these efforts were overturned by the courts. DES use with poultry was banned by FDA in 1959.

At present, all estrogens including DES are approved by FDA for estrogen replacement therapy in younger women, for the symptoms of menopause in older women and for selected cases of advanced cancer of the breast in women and prostatic carcinoma in men. It also is ap- 

20 October 1981 FDA Consumer

proved for the treatment of atrophic vaginitis, kraurosis vulvae, female hypogonadism, female castration, and primary ovarian failure. FDA forbids its use during pregnancy and requires that the drug label warn of the drug's ability to cause uterine cancer.

Although by no means complete, the research there already has indicated differences in the way the primate system handles naturally occurring and synthetic estrogens. "I find this intriguing," Slikker said. "This interests us because there seems to be some differences in their toxicity and perhaps some of that is a result in differences in the way an endogenous (naturally occurring) estrogen and a synthetic estrogen are delivered from the mother to the fetus. "For example, in the case of estradiol, when a pregnant animal is exposed to it, it is modified to estrone, a metabolite of estradiol, and it is further modified to estrone sulfate," Slikker explained. "In other words, it undergoes two metabolic conversions and the effect is to reduce the potency of these endogenous estrogens," he added. 

Is that good or bad? He replied: "It depends on what camp you're in, but one hypothesis is that some of the adverse effects of estrogens are due to their estrogenic potency and that overexposure to estrogens at certain stages of development will cause abnormal development. If endogenous estrogens are converted to less potent agents by the fetal placental system, then it might be one of the ways that normally developing systems detoxify these otherwise very potent estrogenic compounds, thus indicating that the body has a normal controlling mechanism. "However, we also know that DES, because of its structure, cannot undergo these same metabolic conversions (like estradiol does). Therefore, it is not detoxified or not changed as rapidly to an inactive compound like estradiol is. In effect, we are trying to understand the processes by which agents like DES may subvert the normal protection type mechanism that seems to exist. This is theory right now but the idea here-and we have some evidence to support this-is that the conversion rate to an inactive metabolite is slower for DES than for estradiol and this may be one contributing factor among many that makes DES seemingly more toxic to the organism." 

Still other scientists take the position that DES produces its toxicity much like other known chemical carcinogens, through the binding of critical cellular materials, thereby causing the compound to behave inappropriately in the human system. Acknowledging this division of scientific opinion, Slikker said it was his view that neither side had enough evidence to back its theories. "Right now, there is not enough information," he added. "As most groups have been doing, we've been working on 23 1 4 0000
