FDA Consumer / October 1981 / 21

This piece of equipment into which a sample is being inserted is a spectrometer. It enables scientists to tell about the structure of a molecule by seeing how much light is absorbed by atoms of the molecule. both possibilities." Some of the answers may come from various research efforts at NCTR on estrogen metabolism and toxicity.

Another important area of research at NCTR is the work being done with saccharin. FDA proposed banning the artificial sweetener's use in foods in 1977 after laboratory studies showed it caused bladder tumors in rats. The substance is still in widespread use because of a continuing moratorium placed by Congress on any action until further evaluations and studies were made. 

During the 1970's, three experiments with rats played major roles in triggering FDA's attempted ban. The key one was that of Canada's Health Protection Branch, which reported that saccharin, and not any other factor, caused the bladder tumors in the animals. In late 1978, in a report to Congress, the National Academy of Sciences described the sweetener as a carcinogen but one of low potency-in effect, a weak cancer-causing agent. 

For more than a year now, NCTR has been testing saccharin on large populations of mice and rats. However, the emphasis is not on confirming whether saccharin by itself is able to cause bladder cancer but whether the sweetener is a potential health hazard when it is ingested along with other small amounts of carcinogens. In other words, the question the scientists there are trying to answer is whether saccharin is able to promote tumor development in animals that have had prior low level exposure to other carcinogens.

There are certain parallels that can be drawn to humans. Most people during their lifetimes are exposed to low amounts of potentially cancer-causing substances. 

Hopefully, the body copes with this exposure and no tumors develop. But what happens when people also ingest consistently and over a long period of time a chemical substance that may be capable of amplifying the effects of other carcinogens in the body? Is this exposure more likely to promote tumor development? Can it reduce the latency period it takes for cancer to develop? These are some of the questions the NCTR experiments hope to answer, says Dr. Clay B. Frederick, a research scientist in

NCTR's Division of Carcinogenesis and a principal investigator in the saccharin research. 

Outlining the general thrust of the experiment now underway with more than 1,600 mice, Frederick said: "If you take a small group of mice-perhaps 50 of themand give them a small amount of a known carcinogen and you don't feed them anything else, chances are there will either be no tumors or a very small number of them. 

However, if you take a second group of mice and you give them a low level dose of a known carcinogen followed by a possible promoter (saccharin in this experiment), you may see a higher yield of tumors." 

22 October 1981 FDA Consumer

Frederick pointed out that much of the past research with saccharin involved feeding high doses of saccharin to rats-doses in which the sweetener comprised at least 5 percent of the animals' diets. NCTR's present experiments involve dosages that range as low as one-tenth of 1 percent of the animals' diets to no more than 5 percent. "The problem for us as scientists," Frederick said, "is that Canada's study did not tell us a lot mechanistically how saccharin does what it does. We know that almost all carcinogens conform to certain molds in terms of their chemical reactivity. We can say that most of them are electrophillic, which means they react with certain body tissue components, specifically DNA (or deoxyribonucleic acid, the agent that transmits the information of heredity in genes). 99 In the case of many carcinogens, he continued, if they are not electrophillic or mutagenic by themselves, the body can change them to a form that is. "However," he added, "none of these things appears to be true about saccharin. The consensus of most people is that it is not mutagenic, or if it is, it is very weak. We also know that it does not appear to be metabolized into anything that is electrophillic or mutagenic. That is, there is no evidence that it is changed within the body into anything that would act like a cancer-like molecule. So, if saccharin is a carcinogen, how does it work in the body if it does not act like other carcinogens that, typically, are electrophillic and mutagenic?" 

The 1,600 mice in Frederick's experiment are divided into 10 treatment groups. The known carcinogen selected for the experiment was 2-AAF, or 2-acetylaminofluorene, cancer-causing agent NCTR had tested on more than 24,000 mice several years ago. In that earlier experiment, tumors did not start appearing in the mice until after they had been feeding on 2-AAF for at least 12 months. In the present experiment, the mice were fed a small amount of 2-AAF for a much shorter period of time to be sure the animals were not overexposed. 

After receiving 2-AAF, one group of mice was then placed on a normal cereal chow diet. Hopefully, these will show few or no tumors. Four other treatment groups-key ones in this experiment—were given an iniial dose of 2-AAF and then were placed on saccharin diets ranging from 5 percent to one-tenth of 1 percent. 

Four other treatment groups are receiving only saccharin at those diet ranges, and no 2-AAF. The control group is on a normal cereal diet that contains neither 2-AAF nor accharin. 

If a high tumor yield results, Frederick said, it may nly be among those mice that receive a combination of -AAF first and then saccharin. Their research, he dded, also calls for projections on the potential risks to the public-what is commonly referred to as risk assessment.

There is some scientific evidence that some chemicals do act as promoters of tumors and there are several studies from outside NCTR which already have implicated saccharin as a promoter of bladder cancer, Frederick said. For example, he said, one study in 1977 involved the treatment of rats with saccharin after they received an initiating dose of a strong bladder carcinogen known as MNU, or N-methyl-N-nitroscurea. The rats that received a single dose of MNU developed no tumors. However, 47 to 57 percent of the animals on both MNU and saccharin (which comprised 4 and 8 percent of their diets) developed tumors. Another study in 1979 resulted in bladder tumors of 80 percent of the rats that received a dose of FANFT followed by a 5 percent diet of saccharin. 

FANFT is a known bladder carcinogen that belongs to a class of compounds known as nitrofurans which in turn are related to antibacterial compounds that are used to treat chronic or recurrent urinary tract infections. 

Robert W. West, a co-worker of Frederick, also is using saccharin and MNU in an experiment on nearly 1,600 rats to determine the sweetener's effects on the urinary tracts of the animals and its ability to cause lesions in the epithelium of the rat bladder. The epithelium is composed of three layers of cells that line and protect the bladder. 

There are 18 treatment groups in this study that began more than a year ago. After an initial feeding of MNU, five groups of rats were placed on a sodium saccharin diet ranging from 5 percent to one-tenth of 1 percent. 

Five other groups received no MNU but are getting saccharin only at those diet levels. Still another group of rats received an initial feeding of MNU followed by a 4 percent diet of saccharin in their drinking water instead of their chow. A comparison group of rats also is getting saccharin in the water but was given no MNU. Still another treatment group was given MNU followed by a 5 percent diet of acid-saccharin (which has no sodium) and these findings will be matched with rats on just acid-saccharin. Still another group of rats will receive four doses of MNU to produce a "complete carcinogenic response to see what kind of tumors we would get." In all instances, MNU was injected into the anesthetized bladders of the rats before the saccharin feeding was started soon afterwards.

West's experiment will include close examination of the animals' urinary tracts, including kidney, ureter, bladder and urethra, all of which will be removed for analysis. 

Chris Lecos is a member of FDA's public affairs staff.

Exposing foods to radiation can give longer shelf and storage life. To much of the food industry, it is an acceptable preservation technique. But not all consumers are convinced that such foods are safe. Now the lines are being drawn on this long-dormant issue, as FDA takes another look at regulating irradiated foods. 

by Richard Thompson 

The time has come to legitima- "Trize food preservation by irradiation. Food safety concerns for this process appear to be nil." S. W., Lincoln, Neb. "A large body of knowledge gathered over 20 years demonstrates that foods treated by irradiation are safe, wholesome, and palatable." J.L.B.,

U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, Japan. 

99 "I don't care how low level the radiation is, it contributes to cancer.' 

R.B., Van Nuys, Calif. "Here in the Islands, pesticide residues are everywhere, even in our drinking water. We consider it vital hat irradiation [of bulk foods to conrol insects] be approved, to elimiiate further buildup of pesticides in ›roducts we consume." S. C.C., Kaeohe, Hawaii. "I am against irradiation of food at ny level for any purpose." L.E.R., Honolulu. 

What prompted these strong statenents was an announcement last

March in the FEDERAL REGISTER 

hat the Food and Drug Administraon (FDA) was ready to re-think its osition on irradiating food to help reserve it, and wanted to hear coments on the subject. 

And comments it got, nearly 100 tters from scientists, food manufacrers, government officials, health id medical professionals, and pri- Purifying

Food Via 

Irradiation vate citizens. Some sent lengthy documentation in their comments that food irradiation is long overdue. 

Others sent a simple message: the "I am against . . ." from Hawaii was handwritten on a postcard. 

What many of the latter may not know or won't accept-is that a great deal has been learned about food irradiation (treating food to preserve it) over the past three decades.

Much knowledge has come from a study begun by the U.S. Army in 

1953 at its research facility at Natick, Mass., where food, clothing, and similar supplies are tested for military use. There a variety of foods of all types (but especially meats) were treated with various degrees of radiation, and the effects on those foods were carefully examined. 

Questions the study asked-and the answers it provided—included: • Did irradiation change the chemistry of the food? Natick found no harmful chemical effects produced by irradiation of beef, ham, pork and chicken, the high-protein foods of most concern to the Army. • Did it affect food packaging or containers? Natick found that packaging materials are not absorbed by the irradiated meats, and that the wholesomeness (quality) of the foods irradiated through their packages is not adversely affected. • Did irradiation provide preservation for these foods? Natick found that irradiation does destroy harmful spoilage bacteria in these meats, giving them a longer shelf and storage life. • How did the irradiated foods taste? In acceptance studies, Natick reported that both military and civilian test panels judged irradiated foods (the meats listed above, plus fish, bread and potatoes) to be only slightly less tasty than fresh or frozen foods. 

Irradiation is a straightforward process. The materials to be treated in this case, food-are exposed momentarily to a controlled amount of radiation from cobalt 60, cesium 137, or some other radiation source, much as an individual is briefly exposed to diagnostic x-rays.

The food can be treated in cartons as it moves along a packing line, or it can be treated in bulk. 

The amount of radiation the food receives is measured in "rads," a rad meaning units of radiant energy absorbed. A kilorad is one thousand rads, a megarad is 1 million.

Below 100 kilorads is considered a low dose. From 100 kilorads to 1 million rads is considered medium dose, and above 1 million is high dose.

Foods can be irradiated at low and medium doses for limited effects, such as inhibiting the growth of bacteria that cause foods to spoil, thus permitting longer storage without spoiling. FDA has approved low doses for killing insects in grain and for inhibiting the growth of sprouts (eyes) on potatoes, but the process has not been adopted commercially in the United States. 

High-dose irradiation (more than one million rads) will render a food product completely sterile, because it destroys all living organisms (mold, bacteria, spores, etc.) in or on the food. It was high-dose irradiation that Natick used in most of its studies during the 1950's and 1960's, but the data supplied to FDA did not demonstrate to FDA's satisfaction that the process was completely safe. 

One reason that irradiation hasn't been adopted by food manufacturers in this country is that the process would be regulated under the 1958 

Food Additives Amendment to the 

FDA Consumer / October 1981 / 25

Food, Drug, and Cosmetic (FDC) 

Act. That amendment prohibits use of a new additive (for taste, preservation or other effect) until the sponsor of the additive has shown by testing that it is safe. Only then may FDA approve it, by issuing a regulation that specifies the food and the conditions of use for the additive. 

When Congress was writing that amendment, it was especially concerned with what was, in 1958, promising new method of preserving food by irradiating it, then under study by the Army at Natick. Because of its concern, Congress classified the radiation source itself-the cobalt 60 or whatever-as a food additive, because that source can affect the characteristics of a food as conventional additives do. The law further said that a food is considered adulterated if it has been intentionally subjected to radiation, unless 

FDA has approved the use of such radiation. 

What Congress wanted was assurance that the food would not become radioactive when treated and that there would be no harmful chemical changes (no toxic substances created) in the food itself. Those who were advocates of irradiation could not devise tests that would meet this requirement, and irradiation never took hold.

In this complicated situation-and hampered by testing technology of the late 1950's and 1960's-irradiation as a method of preserving food could not live up to promise. Food manufacturers who wanted to use irradiation did not seem able to conduct tests that could demonstrate to FDA (under the food additive amendment) that the process was as safe as the law required.

In 1963 FDA did approve an Army 

26 October 1981 FDA Consumer

petition to irradiate canned bacon, based on a summary of data from the Natick studies. But closer examination of that data and of the study itself revealed discrepancies in the findings, and that approval was revoked without its ever having actually been used.

The Army had this early interest in food irradiation because it needed foods that could be stored for long periods of time in unfavorable conditions, and still provide nutritious meals for troops in the field. For those reasons, it set up the massive program at Natick. The Army was also encouraged by the Eisenhower Atoms for Peace doctrine of the 1950's that encouraged other-thanmilitary uses for atomic energy.

Much that is known about food irradiation and its technology in this country came out of the Natick studies, which the Army operated experimentally for more than 25 years, at a total cost of $50 million. The project has now shut down, and its records and some of its staff transferred to the Department of Agriculture, where work will be continued at an installation near Philadelphia. 

If food irradiation as a preservation process is to move forward, it must be supported by the food industry, which has to overcome consumer wariness about the safety of irradiated foods. In its March notice in the 

FEDERAL REGISTER, FDA asked for comment on a number of points regarding food irradiation. Among these are whether special good manufacturing practice regulations are needed for this technique, and what might be the economic impact (cost or savings to industry and consumers) f the process were approved. But one point that seems to demonstrate he gap between the food industry and the consuming public is the question of labeling irradiated foods. 

FDA's present rules would require that "treated with radiation" appear on the labels of the foods. Those in the food industry who object to this requirement believe it would be the "kiss of death" for products with these labels. "I believe it is discriminatory and not in the public interest to require that irradiated foods be labeled as such," said a food technologist. "The public equates 'irradiation' with 'radioactive,' and therefore the labeling would be misinformation." The same point was expressed by an industry consultant in Michigan. "Canned foods carry no information as to their processing. Why should irradiated foods?" But a woman writing from 

Van Nuys, Calif., echoes what most others commenting as ordinary consumers told FDA: "To irradiate foods without the public's knowledge is to betray the public trust."

The food industry, judging from its comments to FDA, is convinced that the technology is available to irradiate foods that are safe and wholesome for consumption. It sees public acceptance as the real obstacle, and thinks public fears are unfounded. "The problem we face," said a seafood processor who has worked with irradiation, "is the word itself. Consumers do not know how to handle 'radiation.' Finding the word on retail shelves would cause great alarm in the marketplace."

These are some of the issues that 

FDA must resolve before making a decision about food irradiation. After all comments have been reviewed, the agency must sort out the pros and cons on what everyone agrees is a lively subject before it prepares its proposed final regulations.

Some proponents of food irradiation claim that changing the definition of irradiation in the lawmaking it a process rather than an additive-would simplify getting the technology adopted. But they miss. the point, say FDA officials. It does not matter what irradiation is called, it would still be regulated in terms of food safety.

Even though activity in food irradiation declined in the 1970's, FDA's interest did not. FDA scientists believe enough is now known about radiation chemistry to warrant re-opening the question of food irradiation. They believe that criteria can be set for measuring the safety of irradiated foods.

The food industry is not unanimous in its endorsement of irradiation. Some seem willing to stay with the present commercial methods of preserving foods. Both the Florida and California citrus growers associations have asked in their petitions that citrus products be excluded from the list of foods approved for irradiation. Their experience shows that the process damages the peel and allows the fruit to bruise easily in packing and transport. Conventional refrigeration is still the best way. 

And a nutritionist writing from, of all places, Citrus Springs, Fla., told 

FDA that food safety, not quality, has been the only question raised in the proceedings. "Radiation destroys vitamins and enzymes," he said. "Don't let this process be used."

Persons close to this issue in industry, consumer organizations, and 

FDA sense that lines are being drawn for a controversy that could take years to resolve.

Richard Thompson is a member of 

FDA's public affairs staff.

Newport Pharmaceutical Company's New Drug 

Application (NDA) for isoprinosine is not approvable, FDA told the company in July. The NDA was not approved because of problems with Newport's analyses of results of tests in patients with the drug, which is intended for treatment of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. This encephalitis is a rare and usually fatal disease of the central nervous system occurring in about 200 persons each year, primarily children. 

FDA is concerned about the wide variation of lead levels found in nine samples of commercial bonemeal recently analyzed by the agency. While the average lead level was about 8 parts per million (ppm), some analyses revealed lead levels as high as 12 and 15 ppm, while others revealed 5 ppm or less. 

As a result, the agency plans to conduct another more extensive sample survey for lead in bonemeal.

Bonemeal is finely crushed bone, usually from a cow or horse, that is used as a calcium supplement, primarily by women over 50 and by some pregnant women and nursing mothers. It is also used by some infants and young children who are allergic to milk. 

FDA is permanently listing caramel as a color additive for general use in cosmetics, effective August 

28. Caramel is already permanently listed for use in drugs and foods. The agency also postponed until 

September 29 the closing date for the provisional listing of D&C Green No. 6 used as a color additive in drugs and cosmetics to provide time for the completion of the agency's review and evaluation of research data. (FR July 28).

The Doctor Is In-Jail 

If Cyrus Maxfield wants to play doctor again, he'll have to do it from his cell in the Idaho penitentiary. In 

April of this year, Maxfield, 67, was sentenced to 15 years in prison on 21 counts, including manslaughter and practicing medicine without a license. 

For approximately 10 years Maxfield treated patients in his home in Boise, Idaho, where he lived with his wife and two children. Frequently he called himself a "naturopath," explaining that he used homeopathic preparations and "natural" methods to cure illness. Sometimes he called himself "Doctor," although he was not a licensed M.D. or Ph.D., and his car sported a personalized license plate reading "DOCTOR." Possibly some of his patients didn't worry about his lack of official credentials. 

But they might have been more concerned had they known Maxfield had spent time in a Washington State prison for performing an illegal abortion and had been convicted of manslaughter after one of his patients died.

Idaho state officials started investigating Maxfield on October 30, 1980, when the Idaho Office of the Attorney 

General learned that one of

Maxfield's patients-Lloyd Hill of 

Burns, Ore.-had died and that his death might have been caused by the treatment he received at Maxfield's hands. The attorney general's office had already discovered that the "naturopath" had been peddling sugar pills labeled inaccurately as vaccines in his guise as a doctor, and criminal investigator Judy Burton of that office had been gathering evidence to support a charge of practicing medicine without a license. The death of Hill made immediate action imperative. 

Burton traveled to Hill's home in

Oregon to talk to his widow and physician and retrieve drugs-including digitalis, a potent heart drug-that 

Maxfield had given the deceased. In the last week of November, Burton and a second investigator teamed with the Dr is in the Boise City Police to obtain a warrant for searching Maxfield's office on two separate days. They were assisted by members of the State Board of Pharmacy, who identified a number of drugs found as prescription and controlled products. A large variety of drugs were seized (including the fake vaccines), along with treatment devices and patient files. Maxfield himself was arrested and charged with practicing medicine without a license. 

When released on bail, investigator

Burton later testified, he continued to treat patients in his home. 

The trial date was set for March; and Dennis L. Johnson, deputy prosecuting attorney for Ada County, named as prosecutor. The attorney general's office consulted with the state boards of medicine, nursing and pharmacy to verify that Maxfield was not licensed with any of them. Investi gators tracked down former patients who had been displeased with Maxfield's doctoring and were willing to testify to that effect. The office sought help from FDA, asking the agency to assist with the analysis of the seized drugs and to testify as to the findings. 

The drugs were shipped to several agency facilities: Seattle District laboratory, laboratories at the Bureau of 

Biologics and Bureau of Drugs in 

30 October 1981 / FDA Consumer

Washington, D. C., and the National Center for Drug Analysis in St. 

Louis. FDA arranged for six FDA 

employees to serve as scientific witnesses for the prosecution. 

In February 1980, the attorney general's office added 20 charges, both felonies and misdemeanors, to the original one of practicing medicine without a license. These included = manslaughter, illegally selling or dispensing prescription drugs, obtaining money under false pretenses, unlawful assumption of a title, and possessing a controlled substance with intent to sell. 

Many of the charges depended on identification of the nature and legal status of the drugs found in 

Maxfield's possession. Over a 3-day = period, the FDA employees who analyzed the seized samples testified that they included prescription medications such as penicillin, rauwolfia, propoxyphene hydrochloride, digitalis, Librium, and sodium phenobarbital. 

These drugs can be prescribed legally only by a licensed physician. 

One witness testified that Maxfield had sold her pills he claimed would immunize her child against measles, smallpox, polio, whooping cough and flu. She had paid $25 for these "vaccines." A Bureau of Biologics biochemist reported that his analysis of the 

Investigators' Reports presents infor mation on inspections, product seizures, court proceedings and other administrative and regulatory actions by federal, state, and local food and drug agencies across the country to provide health and economic protection to consumers of foods, drugs, cosmetics and medical devices.

Aflatoxins, highly toxic and carcinogenic chemicals, are by products of a type of mold (Aspergillus flavus) that grows under certain conditions on particular crops, such as corn and peanuts. Because aflatoxins are impossible to eliminate completely-the mold can grow on crops both during storage and before harvest-FDA has set a tolerance of 20 ppb (parts per billion) for products shipped in interstate commerce. This level is also enforced by the North Carolina

Department of Agriculture. 

Aflatoxin levels in the dog food, which had been manufactured by 

Bladen Farmer's Exchange in Bladen 

County, were as high as 1,920 ppb. | drug that should be prescribed only by a physician.

He did not explain why he was using powerful drugs to treat his patients when traditional naturopaths, by definition, avoid drugs and try to treat patients "naturally" with air, water and sunshine. 

Maxfield was convicted on all 21 charges and is now in jail. In conjunction with the trial, he was convicted of being a "persistent violator" because of the previous felony convictions in Washington State. He was sentenced to 15 years in the Idaho

County (Idaho) Jail on most of the misdemeanor convictions, which he will have to serve when and if he is released from the penitentiary. Deadly Tonic The Goyescas Corporation of 

Miami manufactures and markets a variety of drugs and dietary supplements, mostly for the Spanish-speaking populations of south Florida and for export to Central America.

Its products include a popular vitamin-mineral tonic sold as "Nervo 

Forza," which translates freely as "vigorous strength." It is shipped in 

5-gallon containers and in 8-ounce bottles, and is available in food stores and pharmacies. 

An FDA inspection of the firm found a number of things wrong with the operation, such as mislabeled products, violations of good manufacturing (quality control) practices, and products that were over and under strength. But most alarming was the discovery that "Nervo Forza" contained strychnine sulfate-a toxic chemical compound-in amounts that could be dangerous to a small child who might drink an entire bottle. Labels on the bottles were an attractive yellow, red and black, and the tonic itself was flavored and was not protected by a child-resistant (hard-toopen) bottle cap. 

FDA's Orlando District office issued a bi lingual news release warning consumers in that part of Florida not to drink any "Nervo Forza" tonic they might have, but instead to return it to the place of purchase or destroy it. The strychnine sulfate could be "life threatening" to small children, the news release said. An adult drinking the entire 8-ounce bottle, the release went on, might experience an unpleasant tightening of jaw and neck muscles and spasms in various body muscles. 

Goyescas recalled its "Nervo 

Forza" from all domestic wholesale and retail outlets. Its export firm- 

Pharmacal Products-recalled ship ments to Central America. No deaths or injuries were traced to the tonic. 

Goyescas also recalled and destroyed other drug, dietary supplement, and vitamin-mineral products that FDA inspectors found in violation of the law, including 14 drug and vitamin products (36 batches) that were over or under strength.

No Breath For Life When Green Cross Solid State 

Oxygen Company of Dania, Fla., went bankrupt, its assets were purchased by Green Cross of Canada.

Those assets included 860 oxygen kits that the Florida firm had manufactured that were intended for emergency medical use, such as treating heart attack victims. 

But before the bankruptcy, FDA's

Orlando District had inspected the Florida firm and found the kits they made were "dangerously defective."

The units would not, as the labels claimed, deliver an effective flow rate of 6 liters of oxygen per minute for 

15 minutes. Also, the flow rate, already bad, could be expected to decrease as the units became older.

Because of these findings (and because the company was bankrupt), FDA had quickly sent notification letters to 482 retailers, distributors and other individuals that company records showed had been shipped the defective kits. The letters warned against using or selling those kits.

Meanwhile, Green Cross of Can ada stored the 860 kits it had purchased from the bankrupt Florida firm with Green Cross Oxygen of 

Cambridge, Mass. 

Alerted by the Orlando office, the

Boston District inspected the stored kits at nearby Cambridge and found them to be identical with the defective units checked in Florida. The entire stock-valued at $14,000-was seized by a U.S. marshal and destroyed by order of a federal court. 

FDA learned that Green Cross of

Canada, which had bought up the defective units, was actually a subsidi ary of Green Cross of Cambridge 

(where the units had been stored) and was also an outlet for the Florida manufacturer. FDA found that the 

Cambridge firm intended to export the units, until the agency told them that a "violative article" offered for sale in domestic commerce cannotunder the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic

Act-be offered for export later. 

During the investigation, FDA also learned that several of the Green

Cross kits had failed to operate in emergency situations, but that other sources of oxygen had been available and no deaths or injuries resulted.

Some Like It Cold 

Most people think consommé madrilene is best when well chilled.

But the canned consommé being processed by one manufacturer in 

Ontario, N. Y., would have had to be boiling hot to be assuredly safe. The reason: laxity in the company's manufacturing practices that could have resulted in underprocessing of the soup and thus possible contamination by the deadly Clostridium botulinum toxin.

Several inspections by FDA's Buf falo District showed that American 

Kitchen Products Co. was violating low-acid good manufacturing practice regulations (GMP's) for heat processing of hermetically sealed low-acid foods. These were adopted by FDA specifically to ensure adequate processing to prevent contamination by the microorganism Clostridium botulinum. In an anaerobic environment. viable C. botulinum spores can produce the toxin that causes botulism, a type of food poisoning that is frequently fatal.

The first inspection was routine and turned up some recordkeeping problems-specifically, the omission of required information-which the firm quickly corrected. But then other, more serious problems were uncovered, including improper retort venting times that could result in underprocessing, improper calibration of thermometers, inadequate written procedures, and incomplete shipping records. 

The firm's parent company- 

S. Gumpert Co., Jersey City, N.J.was notified and was looking at the problems. Only the consommé madrilene appeared to have been underprocessed and the firm is recalling all questionable lots. (Although boiling of contaminated soup for 20 minutes may destroy the toxins, this is not recommended. Any canned food suspected of containing botulinal toxin should be thrown away uneaten and should not even be tasted.) FDA's Buffalo and Newark 

Districts were monitoring the recall 

32 October 1981 FDA Consumer

and the firm's progress in correcting the violations.

Water Makes Its Mark The inspector at FDA's resident post in Mobile, Ala., knows about high marks and how to use them-especially those made by flood water. 

The inspector's expertise was put to use recently during the salvage operations at two area hospitals where a total of $260,000 worth of drugs, pharmacy items, and central supplies were damaged when flood water got into the lower floors of their buildings.

Both the University of South Alabama Medical Center and Doctors 

Hospital of Mobile had flooding up to 4 feet deep in their storage rooms after a deluge of over 7 inches of rain fell on the city within 6 hours. 

While taking photographs of the flooded rooms in both the hospitals, the inspector noticed that the photos of each room clearly showed water marks on the walls and stored items. 

He decided to hold up salvage operaions until the water receded, and use he highest water marks as a guide in separating the good from the damaged items.

When the water had subsided, peronnel in both hospitals began sepaating the merchandise. All items tored above the water marks were onsidered safe; all below were conidered damaged and were segreated in an area where they could be eld under guard until they could be estroyed. 

Once the salvage operations were omplete, the damaged items were aken to a landfill where they were rushed and buried.

Insects Up To Here 

An anonymous caller phoned 

DA's Buffalo District office recently complain that his employer was kerally bugging him. The call ultiately led to the recall of over 5,000 cases of insect-contaminated araschino cherries. 

The caller, who identified himself an employee of Lansmith Inc., a ew York processor of maraschino erries and other food products, was upset with the unsanitary conditions at the plant that he called FDA to make a complaint. 

Acting on the lead, FDA investigators inspected the plant and took samples of finished cherries for labo ratory analysis. The analysis con firmed the caller's complaint: the samples were laden with insect filth. 

Investigators discussed their findings with company officials who promised to correct the problem and recall all maraschino cherries processed from

November 1980 to March 1981. 

A follow-up inspection, however, showed the firm had neither corrected the problem nor started a recall, so the district filed requests for seizure in Alabama and New Jersey, where cherries had been shipped.

The company then requested a meeting with the district and agreed to cease production until an FDA inspection confirmed the plant had been properly cleaned. Additional seizure actions were pending until the company agreed to recall all maraschino cherries previously processed.

Mexican Mollusks 

Oysters from Mexico have not been shipped into the United States because FDA, which regulates food imports, could not be certain that they were taken from non-polluted waters or that they were being properly packed and transported. 

But that changed this summer when two firms in Mexico that had been "certified" by the Mexican

Secretariat of Health began sending shipments of oysters across the border into the U.S. "Certification" means that the growing waters where these firms obtain their oysters have been inspected and found free of pollution. It also means that the entire process of washing, packing, and refrigerated transport is done according to the same standards that U.S. firms must meet. 

Oysters and other mollusk shellfish (clams and mussels) can be a public health problem. They feed by pumping the water in which they lie in and out of their digestive systems, and retaining the nourishing substances. 

But along with the nutrients, the shellfish absorb whatever else is in the water, including microorganisms that produce typhoid, cholera and other diseases in humans. If the shellfish are in clean water, they will be clean. If in polluted waters, they will be polluted and dangerous to eat. 

The problem with mollusks is further complicated by the fact that they are often eaten raw, or if cooked, are not heated to the point where harmful organisms are destroyed. 

For these reasons, FDA and state health departments are careful that mollusk shellfish are not taken from waters polluted by sewage, industrial chemicals or other contaminants, and that they are properly cleaned, packed and shipped. 

FDA and the states monitor the mollusks through a National Shellfish

Sanitation Program that samples shellfish and the waters they grow in, and closes those waters to shellfish harvest when pollution is found. Now the Mexican government has set up a similar program, certifying that firms offering shellfish for import into the

United States will meet the sanitation standards of the U.S. program. 

This was done under an agreement between FDA and the Mexican health secretariat that took several years to negotiate before it was signed in 1979. Another 2 years has been needed for Mexico to train inspectors and get the system in place, with the first shipment (oysters) coming into the United States in June. 

Clams are expected to be added later to the certified imports. 

FDA has similar shellfish certification agreements, some started as many as 20 years ago, with Canada,

FDA Consumer / October 1981 / 33

Japan, Korea, England, Iceland and New Zealand. 

Easing Labor Pains 

The use of what are called "birthing rooms" is a fairly new development in maternity hospital care. Only a few hospitals around the country have them, although they are becoming increasingly popular. 

They are home-like rooms, where the expectant mother is domiciled throughout her hospital stay. She is not taken into labor, delivery or recovery rooms. Instead, unless there are complications, she goes through the entire sequence in the birthing room. 

The rooms are fitted with equipment, such as oxygen, suction lines, and anesthesia, to assist in labor and delivery. They also have "birthing beds" that, with special finish and trim, do not look like the usual hospital bed, although they can be raised, lowered and tilted as necessary. 

One such line of beds, model 66, made by Borg-Warner of Maryland 

Heights, Mo., has brought problems in recent months. As reported to a hospital information exchange, the electrically operated move-and-tilt operation mechanism has been shorting out, subjecting the nurse at bedside in one case to a mild electric shock. In another, the patient complained of sharp "pins and needles" feelings in her legs. At the same time the head of the bed began to rise of its own accord. 

Hospital staff members quickly unplugged the electric cord from the wall outlet and the movement stopped. When they examined the control box at the foot of the bed, they found the wiring connections corroded and the box interior wet with amniotic (placental) fluid.

Hospital beds are regulated by 

FDA as medical devices. Working from reports of these incidents, the 

Bureau of Medical Devices asked 

FDA's St. Louis Station to check with Borg-Warner, the manufacturer. 

The firm could not duplicate the shock conditions at its assembly plant, but surmised that a protective mattress flap might not have been pulled into position by the hospital staff, allowing the fluid to spill into the control box where it shorted out the wiring. 

Borg-Warner instructed its sales representatives to visit each location. where the birthing beds were in use (166 beds in all, throughout the 

United States) and install a splash guard over the control box. The firm has also added the guard to the beds' design. 

Gerovital Again 

Gerovital will not stop trying. 

For almost 20 years promoters of this drug, who claim that it will retard or even reverse the aging process in people, have attempted to expand their European market into the United States. Each time they run into the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, enforced by FDA. (See "Time Marches On Despite Gerovi tal," FDA CONSUMER, March 1980). 

The act says in effect that a drug must be shown by its manufacturer to be safe and effective for the conditions it is supposed to treat before it can be sold in the United States. The makers of Gerovital have offered no scientific evidence that their product can affect the aging process or diseases associated with age. Therefore, FDA holds that the product is unsafe and ineffective under the law. 

Gerovital (also known as H-3 and GH-3) is actually the chemical compound procaine hydrochloride, the numbing agent used by dentists. The compound is approved by FDA for that and similar anesthetic purposes. 

But it is not approved when it is called Gerovital and advertised as an anti-aging drug. 

Procaine hydrochloride-as Gerovital-became a fad drug in Europe in the 1950's after a woman scientist at a Rumanian health spa claimed that it restored youthful health and vigor to elderly persons. It is still widely used in Europe and has become popular enough in the United

States to cause a continuous trickle of illegal imports, which FDA and the U.S. Customs Service detain as they find them.

Recently the trickle seemed to be building, as has happened from time to time, and FDA has issued an "import alert" to all its field offices and installations, calling for increased activity to intercept Gerovital imports. 

Two mail shipments from England of what was suspected to be Gerovital were detained by FDA this past spring: one in Lorane, Ore., by the 

Seattle District, the other in Long 

Beach, Calif., by the San Francisco 

District. Both shipments contained orange-coated tablets in unlabeled packages, and analysis by FDA's 

New York Regional Laboratory showed procaine in the tablets. The shipments were unclaimed and were destroyed. 

Gerovital also struck out in the

U.S. District Court for the Southern 

District of California. There Judge 

Edward Schwartz ruled May 4 that a shipment of Zell H-3 (a German manufacturer's version of Gerovital) that had arrived at the Los Angeles international airport could not be trucked across the U.S. border to Tijuana, Mexico.

The shipper claimed that the drug was "bonded" and therefore immune from U.S. laws on its way to Mexico. 

The judge ruled otherwise, saying that goods that are subject to condemnation (as Gerovital would be) could not travel freely around the

United States without being subject to its laws. 

U.S. marshals seized and later destroyed the shipment of 750,000 tablets, which had a declared value of $35,000. Sold at retail, the tablets were worth more than $300,000.

Charged 6-6-80 by grand jury against Best Brands, Inc., Weivoda and Eisenschenck: with intent to defraud and mislead, non-fat mil was caused to be shipped alleged above (as in the information filed on 5-14-80). These defendants pleaded not guilty. The corporation moved for relief from a prejudicial joinder of the defendants and moved to dismiss the indictment. These individual defendants moved to suppress their oral statements to FDA agents. The motions to suppress were denied. As to the motion to dismiss, the U.S. Magistrate said: "The motion, in part, is based upon defendants' contention that the government promised not to prosecute them if they did not claim any interest in a quantity of dried milk seized for forfeiture in the state of North Dakota. Defendants did not file a claim for the dried milk and lost, they claim, Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000) which they had invested in the product. Gary Annear, an assistant United 

States Attorney for the District of North Dakota, who was in charge of the forfeiture case, testified that shortly before a hearing on the forfeiture was scheduled in the United States District Court, Grand Forks, North Dakota, he said during a discussion at which defendants were present that if someone filed a claim in the forfeiture proceeding there was a possibility they would be prosecuted. No other testimon or documentary evidence was submitted. The Court finds that the was no agreement between the United States and defendants that the would not be prosecuted if they did not file a claim to the dried m 

40 October 1981/ FDA Consumer

See U.S. v. Minn. Min. & Mfg. Co., 55 F.2d 1106 (8th Cir. 1977). "The defendants next contend the indictment should be dismissed because the Food and Drug Administration did not give defendants an opportunity to present their views before referring the matter to the United States Attorney as required by 21 U.S.C. § 335. Contrary to defendants' contention, such a hearing is not a prerequisite to prosecution. U.S. v. Dotterweich, 320 U.S. 277, 279 (1943). "Defendants also seek to dismiss the indictment on the ground the court lacks jurisdiction. They do not set forth specifically the bases for their contention but appear, in their moving papers, to argue that the District of Minnesota is not the proper venue. Rule 18 of Fed. 

R. Crim. P. implements the constitutional mandate that trial be held in the state and district where the crime was allegedly committed. 

Accordingly, the nature of the crime must be examined. Travis v. 

"The defendants are charged with violating 21 U.S.C. § 331(a). 

The key verbs in that statute are ‘introduce' or 'deliver for introduction' into interstate commerce. Counts II and III of the indictment allege that the defendants introduced, delivered for introduction, and caused to be introduced into interstate commerce at Alcester, South Dakota, for delivery to Iowa City, Iowa, nonfat dry milk. These allegations and the statutory language suggest acts which took place in South Dakota and not in Minnesota; therefore, this Court lacks jurisdiction. Newton v. U.S., 162 F.2d 795, 796 (4th Cir. 1947); U.S. v. Waldon, 464 F.2d 1015 (4th Cir. 1972) cert. den. 409 U.S. 867.

Accordingly, it is recommended that Counts II and III be dismissed unless the government supplies a bill of particulars with its appeal from this recommendation setting forth acts which would establish that Counts II and III were properly venued in the state of Minnesota. 

See U.S. v. Sweig, 316 F. Supp. 1148, 1159 (S.D. N. Y. 1970). It should be noted that Count IV may also be improperly venued. "In summary, it is recommended that Counts II and III of the indictment be dismissed and that all other motions to dismiss the indictment be denied. . . .

The government secured the dismissal of the indictment of 6-6-80 and sought a re-indictment to cure the venue defects present in two counts of the original indictment. 

Charged 10-10-80 against Weivoda, Eisenschenk, and Best Brands, Inc., by grand jury: (Count 1)—that the defendants willfully, unlawfully, knowingly and feloniously conspired to commit offenses against U.S. laws (i.e., 1. with intent to defraud and mislead to ship non-fat dry milk which had been held under insanitary conditions from Duluth, Minn., to various other states; and 2. with intent to defraud and mislead to alter the labeling of the non-fat dry milk while it was held for sale in South Dakota so that its labeling would be false and misleading—18 U.S.C. 371, 402(a)(3), 403(a)(1); (Count 2)—with intent to defraud and mislead, when shipped from Duluth, Minn., to Sioux 

Falls, S. D., non-fat dry milk had been held under insanitary conditions-402(a)(4); (Counts 3 & 4)—with intent to defraud and mislead while in transit from Alcester, S. D., to Iowa City, Iowa, non-fat dry milk had a Best Brands' customer invoice prepared which falsely and misleadingly represented the food to be "Pure Milk Powder" and failed to reveal the material facts that the food had been held under insanitary conditions, had been rejected as human food, and had been classified as suitable for animal use only-403(a)(1); and with intent to defraud and mislead, when shipped from Alcester, S. D., to St. 

Paul, Minn., non-fat dry milk contained rodent filth and had been held under insanitary conditions-402(a)(3) and (4).

The corporation moved for discovery, for suppression of confessions or statements in the nature of confessions, for inspection of the grand jury minutes, for the compelling of the disclosure of evidence favorable to the defendant, for disclosure and suppression of any electronic surveillance evidence, and for discovery and inspection. Weivoda moved for the indictment be made more certain, for the venue be changed to any non-dairy producing district, for suppression of evidence, for dismissal of the indictment, and for four other orders. Eisenschenck moved for the striking of the words "feloniously" and "rodent gnawed and contained rodent excretion pellets," for dismissal of the indictment on grounds of improper venue and failure to state an offense, for dismissal of the indictment because its purposes and basis was discriminatory, and for other orders.

The court denied Weivoda's motions for a bill of particulars, for a change of venue, and to suppress evidence; and denied Best Brands 

Inc.'s motions to dismiss on double jeopardy and collateral estoppel grounds and for suppression of statements. Eisenschenk's motions to dismiss for selective prosecution, to suppress statements and evidence, and to dismiss on the ground of compromise and settlement were denied; however, Eisenschenk's motion to strike as surplus the words "feloniously" and "rodent gnawed and contained rodent excreta pellets" was granted because, as the court said: "These words are unnecessarily prejudicial to the defendant, and are not vital to charge the offenses alleged. See United States v. Hubbard, 474 F. Supp. 64, 82-83 (D.D.C. 1979)." 

Ultimately, Best Brands, Inc. pleaded guilty to counts 2 and 3 of the second indictment and was fined $10,000. Boston Farm Center, Inc., and James R. Gordon, Jr., president, Boston, M. Dist. Ga. 

Charged 11-22-77 in a complaint for injunction: that the defendants were engaged in their Boston, Ga., facility in receiving, storing, and shipping outside the state shelled corn; that samples of the corn collected and examined by FDA established that recently shipped corn contained aflatoxin in excess of 20 ppb; that FDA had determined that more than 20 ppb of aflatoxin in food or feed may be injurious to health and had therefore amended its previous action level by lowering it to 20 ppb in 1969; that the defendants' shelled corn bor and contained the added poisonous and deleterious substance aflatoxin which might render the food injurious to health; that the de fendants were aware that the corn they were shipping in interstat commerce contained aflatoxin in excess of 400 ppb; and that plainti was informed and believed that unless restrained by the court, th defendants would continue to violate the law; 402(a)(1).

The government's motion for a temporary restraining order was denied. However, the court subsequently granted a preliminary in junction, saying: .. Boston Farm Center, Inc. operates a grain distribution bus ness with storage facilities at Boston, Thomas County, Georgia, which is approximately 15 miles north of the Florida line, and also has storag facilities for the distribution of grain at Miccosukee, Leon County 

Florida. Boston Farm Center distributes grain to consumers in Geor gia and Florida from the aforementioned facilities, its distribution from its Florida facility consisting of grain purchased from farmers Florida, and its entire distribution from that facility is in the state 

Florida. The grain distribution from the Boston, Georgia, facility primarily Georgia grain, and the distribution from this facility is both Georgia and Florida consumers. So, it is the Georgia facility with which we are here primarily concerned. The distribution of grai by the Defendants is to customers who utilize the grain, primarily corn, for the feeding of livestock and poultry and the distribution is made on a daily basis during the workweek. "Aflatoxin is a metabolic by-product of the mold Aspergillus flav and it is generally known, and in fact conceded by the defendants this case, that aflatoxin is present in some amount in all corn produce in south Georgia and north Florida during the crop year 1977. "It is also known, and the Court finds it to be a fact, that aflatou in sufficient amount is an ingredient which renders corn injurious t the health of men and animals, and 21 U.S.C. $342(a)(1) provides that a food is deemed to be adulterated if it bears or contains any added poisonous or deleterious substance which may render the foo injurious to health. The term 'food' is defined in the Act as meaning articles which are used for food for man and other animals and $ of the Act prohibits the introduction or delivery for introduction in interstate commerce of any food that is adulterated. "Since we have already noted that a food is deemed to be adulte ated if it contains any added poisonous or deleterious substance whe may render the food injurious to health, it becomes necessary determine whether the aflatoxin is an added substance within th meaning of the Act. Since aflatoxin is not a naturally occurring com stituent ingredient of corn, it must be regarded as an 'added' substand within the meaning of the Act because the Act distinguishes substance which are natural constituents of food and substances which are n While it is recognized that aflatoxin is a naturally occurring to substance (created by the forces of nature), it is not a naturally curring ingredient of corn, and must, therefore, be regarded as substance added to the corn. It is not necessary that the eviden show that the defendants themselves added the substance to the com It is sufficient if the evidence shows that the substance was added some way, or, stated otherwise, that it is not a natural ingredient of food. "The evidence clearly shows that aflatoxin has the capacity to cause injury to both man and to other animals and if present in suffic quantity may cause cancer and produce other toxic effects suc liver damage. Although some animals are more resistant to afla than others, the evidence shows that aflatoxin is transmitted to 

42 October 1981 FDA Consumer

edible tissues of animals through the consumption of aflatoxin-contaminated feed. The evidence also shows possible injurious effects to health in humans as a result of consumption of foods containing aflatoxin such as milk from cows which have been fed aflatoxin-contaminated corn. "Samples collected and examined by representatives of the Food and Drug Administration established that corn recently shipped in interstate commerce by the defendants contains aflatoxin in varying amounts. "The Food and Drug Administration has not issued a regulation for public or industry guidance specifying the level beyond which the substance would be injurious to health, but the department has made an administrative 'in house' determination that if a food or feed contains more than 20 parts per billion (ppb) of aflatoxin it may be injurious to health. There is controversy concerning the validity of this determination, it being contended by some that injury to health is not likely unless the content exceeds approximately 400 parts per billion (ppb). In any event, the samples taken of shipments recently made by the defendants as above referred to and samples taken at the storage facility of the defendants indicate in most instances the presence of aflatoxin in excess of 20 ppb and in a number of instances in excess of 400 ppb. "From the evidence presented the Court determines that corn containing an aflatoxin level of more than 100 ppb should be regarded as containing a deleterious substance to a degree which renders it injurious to health and unacceptable for interstate shipment, and that corn containing an aflatoxin level of less than 100 ppb does not contain a deleterious substance to the degree which would render it injurious to health and, therefore, generally acceptable for interstate shipment. "The defendants have indicated that it is their intention to continue to distribute in interstate commerce shelled corn derived from the same sources and therefore containing amounts of aflatoxin which in some instances would be greater than 100 ppb. "The district courts of the United States have jurisdiction to restrain violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and having determined that distribution of corn containing an aflatoxin level of more than 100 ppb would be distribution of an adulterated food and, therefore, prohibited by the Act, it is the duty of this Court to enjoin such distribution. 66 Accordingly, the Court will issue a preliminary injunction in terms deemed by the Court to be appropriate in the circumstances." 

The plaintiff moved for modification of the preliminary injunction, requesting that the court provide for sampling and testing methods, procedures and controls which would insure that the defendants were in compliance with the court's order. Subsequently, the parties entered into a consent decree for modification of the preliminary injunction which incorporated a number of specified methods, procedures and controls concerning sampling, testing and notice of the results of the testing. 

Upon appeal, the government contended that the district court erred in finding that amounts of aflatoxin between 20 and 100 ppb did not render corn adulterated. The court of appeals found for the government and remanded the case to the district court for an injunction prohibiting the interstate shipment of corn from the 1977 season containing more than 20 ppb aflatoxin, saying: 66 ". . . Not often does this Court deal with disputes in which the judgment is easier to pronounce than the name of the matter in controversy, but this is such a case. Our problem involves aflatoxin, a metabolic by-product of the polysyllabic mold Aspergillus flavus, but our solution is a by-product of monosyllabic words and logic. "Boston Farm Center, appellee, is a grain distributor in Boston, Georgia. On November 22, 1977, the United States, appellant, applied for an injunction under section 302 of the Federal Food, Drug, and

Cosmetic Act, 21 U.S.C. § 332(a), (the ‘Act'), seeking to halt the 

Center's interstate shipment of corn containing more than 20 parts per billion (ppb) of the substance aflatoxin. "Section 301(a) prohibits the interstate shipment of 'adulterated' food. Adulterated food is defined as, among other things, food containing ‘any poisonous or deleterious substance which may render it injurious to health,' 21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(1). The lower court issued a preliminary injunction against the Center, but enjoined only the Center's interstate shipment of corn containing more than 100 ppb of aflatoxin. The United States appealed the judgment of the lower court arguing that the injunction threshold should be set at the 20 ppb level it requested. "The 20 ppb level proposed by the government is the Food and Drug Administration's 'action level' for aflatoxin in corn. An action level, to be defined properly, must be explained in the broader context of the FDA's general regulatory scheme. In implementing the Act, the FDA either may adopt formal regulations, 21 U.S.C. § 346, or may litigate alleged violations on a case-by-case basis. Although the 

Act makes illegal any amount of substance which ‘may render (food) injurious to health,' 21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(1), the FDA is not required to seek to enjoin, prosecute or otherwise litigate "minor violations" 

of the Act, 21 U.S.C. § 336. To guide its prosecutorial discretion in the bringing of non-rule enforcements of the Act, the FDA may establish certain in-house guidelines called action levels. Since 1969 the action level for aflatoxin in corn has been 20 ppb. This means that since 1969 the FDA's internal policy has been to try to prevent the shipment of corn containing more than 20 ppb of aflatoxin, but not of corn containing 20 ppb or less. "The FDA argues that the court should defer to this action level because it represents the expert, technical judgment of the agency. 

The government argues in its brief that, '[a]lthough not a regulation, an action level represents the agency's considered judgment as to the level of a contaminant that can be permitted in food without significant risk to public health or to the fitness of food for consumption.' In essence, the government implies with such terms as 'the agency's considered judgment' that a court should defer to an action level much as it defers to an agency regulation. Indeed, some cases approach this position. . . . We accept this argument for deference to the agency but only up to a point. The deference principle is less compelling when the agency threshold is a matter of prosecutorial discretion instead of rulemaking. Congress requires considerably more fact-finding due process, most especially full notice and comment, in agency rulemaking than in agency prosecutorial discretion. The fuller rulemaking due process serves the purposes of accuracy and fairness. When an agency proceeds in non-rule, case-by-case adjudication, much of the factfinding process is shifted to the courts. The purposes of accuracy and fairness require that the courts not slavishly defer to the agency's in house prosecutorial guidelines arrived at without benefit of even minimal due process protections. At the extreme, the deference argument in this context sets up the blocking for an end run by the agency of the procedural checks in the statute for formal rulemaking. "Nevertheless, in this circuit we have evolved a policy of considerable deference to agency action levels. "We need not decide in this case 'the power of the Court to allow a greater departure from purity than the administrative tolerance,' 

FDA Consumer / October 1981 / 43

because we find that the facts in this case are so one-sided that any finding of non-adulteration for amounts of aflatoxin between 20 ppb and 100 ppb would be clearly erroneous. Thus, even if the court were to afford no deference whatsoever to the action level set by the agencythat is, even if the court were to make a wholly independent decision as to whether the Boston Farm corn was adulterated-it would still be clearly erroneous on this record to find that amounts of aflatoxin between 20 and 100 ppb do not adulterate corn. Only one expert testified before the lower court on the potential hazardousness of aflatoxin. That expert, Dr. Rodricks, testified that 'there is no known level of exposure which can be considered safe, without risk to people.' 

Dr. Rodricks cited numerous studies to support this expert opinion, including one showing the adverse effects of aflatoxin in doses as low as 15 ppb. . . . In addition, Dr. Rodricks testified that aflatoxin accumulates in body tissue. Thus, without statistics showing the amount of long-term consumption of corn by livestock and by humans, it makes little sense to draw any bright line between doses of aflatoxin which 'may' render food injurious to health and doses which are not possibly dangerous. "Aside from Dr. Rodricks' expert testimony, there was no other evidence in this record on the question of the potential harmfulness of aflatoxin. Appellees presented no evidence on the question and did not elicit from Dr. Rodricks during cross-examination any contradictory evidence on this question. Certainly there is no evidence in the Record to support the Court's assertion that 'there is controversy concerning the validity of this determination, it being contended by some that injury to health is not likely unless the content exceeds approximately 400 parts per billion (ppb).' "As a result, we find the lower court was clearly erroneous in finding that amounts of aflatoxin between 20 and 100 ppb do not render corn adulterated. "We want to emphasize the limited nature of our ruling today. To an extent the statutory scheme permits the FDA to adopt a relatively ad hoc case-by-case approach to regulating the poisons in our food. 

The statute does not demand rigid and permanent fixity in the numbers game, mainly because our social policies and scientific knowledge about dangerous food are not themselves steady and static. As scientific research and measurement progress, the digits and integers of thresholds, action levels, and tolerances will necessarily change with them. But, in this case the expert evidence is uncontradicted that 20 ppb of aflatoxin may render corn harmful. Other days and other records may yield other figures, but in this case, with this evidence, only one result is possible. The court must enjoin the corn containing more than 20 ppb of aflatoxin. "We remand to the lower court for it to enter an injunction prohibiting Boston Farms from shipping interstate any corn from the 1977 season containing more than 20 ppb aflatoxin." 

The government moved for entry of a permanent injunction restraining the interstate distribution of corn from the 1977 corn crop containing more than 20 ppb of aflatoxin and setting forth sampling and testing procedures as in the modified consent decree. The court entered a permanent injunction incorporating the above terms. (Inj.

Update 

Charges Challenged

Two recent articles in READER'S DIGEST have resulted in a number of inquiries to FDA about the safety of indoor lighting and outdoor tanning products. However, neither the Food and Drug Administration nor the companies making the products in question have been able to substantiate the factual basis of any of the health hazard charges made in the articles. Both articles were written by Lowell 

Ponte. FDA's concern with the articles was expressed in the following letter, addressed to the magazine's editor in chief:

Twice in the past six months, READER'S DIGEST has published articles by Mr. Lowell Ponte: How Artificial Light Affects Your Health (February) and Sunbathing In A New Light (July). Both stories were reported in other media nationally and resulted in considerable consumer and professional inquiries to the Food and Drug Administration. 

Both pieces made sensationalistic statements about the cancer-causing potential of commonly used consumer products. In both cases, these statements and their implications contradict the state of science, especially about human exposure. 

In particular, the sunbathing article totally ignored the comprehensive findings of a 1978 committee report whose members are the foremost authorities about sunscreens in the country. None of these experts has any knowledge of the unnamed scientists and unidentified research reports Mr. Ponte claims. FDA has written Mr. Ponte requesting documentation for his statements. 

The readership of your publication is so large and its impact so great that the credibility of what is printed is of special concern. In the future, should Mr. Ponte provide manuscripts to 

READER'S DIGEST, we believe that they should receive better scrutiny and unsubstantiated statements should be verified with knowledgeable government or private sector officials.

PPI Study Completed 

Last year FDA was about to embark on a threeyear program to test the feasibility of providing patients with information leaflets on drugs, called patient package inserts (PPIs). How the program would work was outlined in Rx With a Dose of 

Info in the November 1980 FDA CONSUMER. 

FDA's program is "on hold" while the agency reviews its regulations, but another test of PPIs has been completed. Here are the results of that study: 

About 70 percent of patients interviewed said they read a patient package insert (PPI) that was included with their prescription in a survey completed for FDA by the Rand Corp. of Santa Monica, Calif.

There were more readers among first-time users of the drug but reading was not limited to the younger or more educated, according to the survey. Patient package inserts are leaflets for consumers describing a prescription drug's purpose, directions, precautions and side effects. 

The Rand study was a three-year, $525,000 project in which a sample of 1,821 people who had prescriptions filled at 69 Los Angeles pharmacies were interviewed. Subjects were given one of several PPIs, or they served in a no-PPI control group. They were interviewed by telephone two to three weeks after receiving their prescriptions and also were asked to respond to a mail questionnaire.

The drugs chosen for the study were erythromycin, an antibiotic; flurazepam, a sleeping pill; and estrogens, for menopausal symptoms. (Estrogen drugs are currently distributed with an FDA-required PPI. For the other two drugs, special PPIs were developed for the study.)

The study was reported by Rand scientists at an 

August 1981 meeting of the American Psychological Association in Los Angeles. Other principal findings: 

2 November 1981 FDA Consumer

About half of the subjects said they kept the PPI, and 20 to 30 percent said they read it more than once. 

People who received PPIs could answer more questions correctly about how to use a drug, its interactions and contraindications, than those who did not get PPIs.

Few respondents changed their minds about whether to take a drug after reading the PPI. 

Only 3 of over 2,000 prescriptions dispensed with PPIs were returned for a refund. • PPIs did not generally increase side-effect reporting. People generally did not "imagine every side effect" listed in the leaflet, as critics of PPIs have predicted would happen. However, certain. styles of presentation, in which the PPIs include many specific instructions, increased the reporting of side effects.

People getting PPIs did not contact their physicians more often but were more likely to discuss drug safety and side effects with physicians during these contacts. • Patients reported that PPIs helped them to understand their drugs, to follow their doctors' advice and to know when to take their drug. The less educated respondents reported the most favorable reaction.

In a related matter, Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals of Cincinnati, Ohio, has agreed to issue a PPI on Bendectin, as recommended by an FDA advisory committee. Bendectin is a prescription drug often prescribed for nausea and vomiting during pregnancy. 

In a September 1981 press release announcing its decision, the firm said that it "feels patients need to have accurate information about the drugs they are taking. This is particularly important in pregnancy, where special care is always required.'

The press release said the company felt that the physician is the primary source of such information. but that further study is needed. 

Bendectin was one of the 10 drugs slated for the pilot PPI program. 

Probe of Contraceptive 

A number of contraceptive methods were described in Contraception: Comparing the Options in the July-August 1977 FDA CONSUMER. One not mentioned was Depo-Provera; FDA has not approved the additional use of this drug, now used in cancer treatment, as an injectable, long-lasting con traceptive. The situation regarding Depo-Provera could change, however, as the result of this recent 

FDA action: 

FDA Commissioner , has named a public board of inquiry to weigh the risks vs. benefits of Depo-Provera, a controversial contraceptive. This is only the second time such a board has been convened. 

Dr. Judith Weisz, professor and head of the di 

FDA Consumer / November 1981 / 3

vision of reproductive biology in the department of obstetrics and gynecology at the Milton S. Hershey 

Medical Center, Pennsylvania State University in

Hershey, will be chairman of the board. Other members are Dr. Griff T. Ross, associate dean of clinical affairs at the University of Texas in Houston; and Dr. Paul D. Stolley, professor, departments of medicine and research medicine, University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine in Philadelphia. 

Depo-Provera has been manufactured and marketed by the Upjohn Co. of Kalamazoo, Mich., for the treatment of cancer of the endometrium (lining of the uterus) and kidney cancer. In 1967 the firm began tests to learn if the drug was also effective as an injectable, long-lasting contraceptive.

In 1974, shortly before FDA had planned to approve this new use for the drug, an additional review of the safety data raised a question about the incidence of cancer of the cervix among the women who participated in the Upjohn studies. 

For that reason, FDA stayed the approval. 

An advisory committee set up to study Depo Provera found no valid evidence that the drug is associated with cervical cancer, but indicated the possibility can't be ruled out. Therefore, in 1978, FDA told the firm the agency did not have sufficient information to determine whether Depo- 

Provera is safe for general marketing in the United

States. The firm then requested a public board of inquiry. 

Depo-Provera is approved for contraception in some other countries and is manufactured in several. 

The board will consider: . Whether, in comparison with other drugs approved for contraception, the benefits of Depo- 

Provera in the United States outweigh its risks under conditions of general marketing. . Whether data from beagle dog and monkey studies submitted by Upjohn indicate a potential risk of breast or endometrial cancer in humans from Depo-Provera.

Whether the human data submitted by Upjohn can, as Upjohn claims, successfully refute the risk of human cancer suggested by the animal data. • Whether an approval of Depo-Provera for contraception under general marketing conditions is likely to increase use of the drug as a contraceptive under conditions not stipulated in the approved labeling or is likely to increase its use for unrelated indications for which safety and effectiveness have not been established (for example, for hygienic purposes in mental retardees). 

Whether, in the event of contraceptive failure. use of Depo-Provera may increase the risk of teratogenic effects to a greater extent than would other systemic contraceptives. 

Whether, in view of Depo-Provera's adverse side effects or pharmacologic effect, estrogen therapy is likely to be prescribed in addition to Depo- Provera in a significant number of patients. 

Whether there are conditions of labeling and distribution controls that would permit marketing of Depo-Provera as a safe and effective drug on a limited basis. (There may be certain patients in the 

United States for whom benefits of Depo-Provera for contraception outweigh potential risks. This population, if it exists, may be very small and may not warrant general marketing of Depo-Provera for contraception.) 

Fat Won't Melt "Getting the fat off"' appears to be a major obsession in the United States and consumers would appear to be willing to believe any theory or try any device to realize this objective (see Cellulite: Hard to Budge Pudge, FDA CONSUMER. May 1980). 

Here's a report on yet another product that promises miracles: 

4/ November 1981/ FDA Consumer

A nationwide promotion is under way in behalf of La Creme "body contour cream," aimed at women and being marketed by La Creme Inc., New York, N. Y., and Morristown, N.J. Advertisements claim that the product will "help melt away. inches of unwanted bulge in just 60 minutes." The ads say, "Its gentle warmth penetrates deep into your skin and helps melt fatty deposits." Promotional literature distributed to retail stores and franchises (though not necessarily to consumers) also claims that FDA has approved or classified La Creme as a skin toner, tightener and smoother. In some locations, La Creme is demonstrated or sold with a form of body wrap. Customers are told that 

La Creme may be used under pantyhose while at work for the same effect as and in lieu of wrapping. 

Consumers should be aware that:

No known product can penetrate the skin and melt away fat. • La Creme, the product, has not been reviewed, analyzed or approved by FDA. 

FDA has received neither safety and efficacy data nor adverse reaction reports about La Creme. (Promoters claim La Creme's formulation was invented in California 12 years ago during arthritis research. FDA's Bureaus of Drugs and Medical

Devices and its Division of Cosmetics Technology have no record of any related correspondence.) • FDA is looking into La Creme's marketing status under the law. The firm claims La Creme is a cosmetic.

Any loss of inches that ensues after combining a cream product with a body wrap probably is due to a transitory "wristwatch band" pressure effect that will disappear soon after the wrap is removed. 

Any loss of weight from induced moisture loss will be regained as soon as the user eats or drinks.
